Chapter 0: 1. Introduction

p9-p20

ISPE Good Practice Guide: HVAC | p9 - p20

Learning Objectives for This Chapter

  • Understand the critical role of HVAC (heating, ventilation and air conditioning) systems in pharmaceutical facilities: they control not just comfort but also directly affect product quality and sterility assurance
  • Grasp the scope and structure of this Guide, and how it supplements the ISPE Baseline Guides and covers every stage of the facility life cycle
  • Become familiar with the 26 key concepts in Section 1.6, including air change rate, differential pressure control, particle monitoring, airlock types, and AHU zoning
  • Understand how the cleanroom classification systems (EU Grade vs FDA ISO Class vs ISPE Grade) correspond to and differ from one another
  • Build the overall mindset that "air quality = filtration + dilution + differential pressure + airflow direction"
1.1 Background

Original Text

Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) can be a critical system that affects the ability of a pharmaceutical facility to meet its objective of providing safe and effective product to the patient. Environmental control systems that are appropriately designed, built, commissioned, operated, and maintained can help ensure the quality of product manufactured in a facility, improve reliability, and reduce both initial costs and ongoing operating costs for a facility.

The design of HVAC systems for the pharmaceutical industry requires additional considerations, particularly with regard to providing a clean and safe space environment. HVAC can consume a major portion of the energy used by a facility, and requires a blend of Good Engineering Practice (GEP) and Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: The Role of HVAC in Pharmaceuticals

HVAC (heating, ventilation and air conditioning) in a pharmaceutical plant is not just equipment that "keeps people comfortable"; it is a critical system that directly affects product quality. The original text states plainly that HVAC is a "critical system", which means it is subject to qualification.

GEP (Good Engineering Practice): the fundamentals of engineering design, ensuring systems are reliable, economical and maintainable.

GMP (Good Manufacturing Practice): the regulatory quality baseline, ensuring products are safe and effective.

The core philosophy of this Guide: HVAC design must satisfy both GEP and GMP. The aim is not to blindly pursue the highest specification, but to find the best balance between regulatory compliance and engineering economics.

Analogy

Imagine running an operating-theatre-grade restaurant, with HVAC as its air management system. An ordinary restaurant only needs heating and cooling to keep guests comfortable (GEP), but an operating-theatre-grade restaurant must also control airborne particles and microorganisms (GMP). You cannot rely on opening windows, and you do not need to turn the whole restaurant into a cleanroom; the key is to apply the right grade in the right place.

Key Notes

Note that the original text says HVAC consumes a "major portion of energy" in a facility. In practice, HVAC typically accounts for 40-60% of a pharmaceutical plant's total energy use. Over-design therefore wastes capital and also keeps adding to operating costs. Section 1.4 discusses in more depth how to avoid unnecessary cost.

Practice Questions

  1. In your plant, roughly what percentage of total energy consumption does the HVAC system account for? Which areas may be over-designed?
  2. How do GEP and GMP complement each other in HVAC design? Can you give an example of how to make a trade-off when the two conflict?
1.2 Purpose

Original Text

This Guide is intended to supplement published ISPE Baseline Guides for facilities (Reference 13, Appendix 12), providing detailed information and to recommend practices for implementation of HVAC systems in pharmaceutical facilities.

This Guide emphasizes the importance of understanding the role of HVAC system performance in protecting product, personnel, and the environment. Air filtration, Differential Pressure (DP), and airflow/air change rates are covered in detail to assist comprehension of airborne particulate control.

The information provided in this Guide reflects the cumulative knowledge and experience of the authors and reviewers with input from members of the ISPE HVAC Community of Practice (ISPE HVAC COP).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: The Three Protection Goals of HVAC

The design purpose of this Guide revolves around three things to be protected:

  • Product: control particles, temperature and humidity to avoid contamination or degradation
  • Personnel: protect operators from exposure to hazardous substances
  • Environment: prevent hazardous substances from escaping outside the plant

The original text identifies three means by which HVAC controls air quality: filtration, differential pressure (DP) and air change rate. Together they form a "tripod" of air quality control; none can be omitted.

Analogy

Think of the three HVAC means as three lines of defense in hospital infection control:

  • Filtration = scrubbing and disinfecting before surgery (keeping dirt out)
  • Differential pressure = the positive-pressure design of an operating theatre (clean air flows only outward, and dirty corridor air cannot come in)
  • Air change rate = continuous air exchange for dilution (even if someone brings in a few bacteria, they are quickly diluted and removed)

Key Notes

This Guide is a "supplement" to the ISPE Baseline Guides, not a "replacement". In practice, when designing an HVAC system you should first consult the relevant Baseline Guide (such as Sterile or Oral Solid Dosage), and then use this Guide as an in-depth reference on HVAC technology.

Practice Questions

  1. In your sterile filling area, how are the three HVAC means (filtration, differential pressure, air change rate) each set? Which one is the most critical?
  2. The HVAC needs for "protecting the product" and "protecting personnel" sometimes conflict (for example, highly potent drugs need negative pressure, but sterile products need positive pressure). How would you handle this situation?
1.3 Scope

Original Text

The ISPE Good Practice Guide: HVAC provides:

  • supporting information and HVAC practices for facility types covered by ISPE Baseline Guides
  • an overview of the basic principles of HVAC to facilitate a common understanding and consistent nomenclature

This Guide addresses HVAC requirements in areas of the facility life cycle, including:

  • establishing user requirements
  • design, including the requirements of outdoor conditions
  • construction, including good practices for equipment specification and installation
  • commissioning/qualification
  • operation/maintenance

Requirements of regulatory agencies other than the FDA may differ significantly and may not be covered in the facility ISPE Baseline Guides (Reference 13, Appendix 12), and therefore, they may not be considered by this Guide.

This Guide references ISPE Baseline Guides (Reference 13, Appendix 12) and provides associated examples. The relevant Baseline Guide should be consulted for regulatory expectations in a specific topic area.

GEP should be applied in assessing which of the recommended practices is most applicable to a situation.

This Guide refers to recommendations, standards, and guidelines published by:

  • World Health Organization (WHO)
  • International Conference on Harmonisation (ICH)
  • International Standards Organisation (ISO)
  • Institute of Environmental Sciences and Technology (IEST)
  • European Medicines Agency (EMEA)
  • US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
  • Pharmaceutical Inspection Convention and Pharmaceutical Inspection Co-operation Scheme (PIC/S)
  • American Society of Heating, Refrigeration and Air Conditioning Engineers (ASHRAE)
  • International Society for Pharmaceutical Engineering (ISPE)
  • American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM) International
  • Chartered Institute of Building Service Engineers (CIBSE, UK)
  • American Council of Government Industrial Hygienists
  • Instrumentation, Systems, and Automation Society (ISA)
  • Sheet Metal and Air Conditioning Contractors National Association (SMACNA, North America)
  • National Environmental Balancing Bureau (NEBB, US)
  • Heating and Ventilating Contractors Association (HVCA, UK)

The Guide is not intended to be a complete handbook for HVAC design and does not address every HVAC situation.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: The Facility Life Cycle

This Guide covers the whole life cycle of an HVAC system, "from cradle to grave":

  • User Requirements: defining "what I need"
  • Design: turning requirements into engineering specifications
  • Construction: building and installing to specification
  • Commissioning/Qualification: verifying that the system meets requirements
  • Operation/Maintenance: day-to-day operation and continued compliance

This is fully consistent with the life cycle concept in the ISPE Baseline Guide Vol. 5, Commissioning & Qualification.

Analogy

This Guide is positioned like a "specialist medical textbook on HVAC". The ISPE Baseline Guides are the textbooks of the general disciplines, such as internal medicine or surgery (covering the design of the whole facility), while this HVAC Guide is like "respiratory therapy", focused on in-depth knowledge of the air system as one "organ". You read the internal medicine overview first, and turn to the specialist book when a respiratory problem arises.

Key Notes

Note the disclaimer in the original text: this Guide focuses mainly on FDA and EMEA regulations. If your plant is governed by other regulators (such as PMDA, ANVISA or TGA), you need to confirm the local regulatory requirements separately. In addition, this Guide is "not a complete HVAC design manual"; it provides principles and best practices, but specific engineering calculations still require a professional HVAC engineer.

Practical Application

In a CDMO environment, you may manufacture both OSD (oral solid dosage) products and sterile injectables for different clients. This means one facility may need to refer to several Baseline Guides (Oral Solid Dosage + Sterile), with this HVAC Guide serving as the unified reference for air system design. The 16 standards organizations listed are also authoritative sources you will need to cite when writing a URS (User Requirements Specification).

Practice Questions

  1. At which stage of the life cycle is your facility currently? At that stage, what are the main HVAC concerns?
  2. Of the 16 standards organizations listed, which do you refer to most often in your daily work? Are there any you are unfamiliar with but should know?
1.4 Benefits

Original Text

This Guide introduces the fundamentals of HVAC systems that control the GMP workplace environment and provides:

  • the life science engineering community with common language and understanding of critical HVAC issues
  • guidance on accepted industry practices to address these issues
  • a common resource for HVAC information currently included in appendices of the various ISPE Baseline Guides
  • help to less experienced personnel in understanding the options available to HVAC designers
  • assistance with prevention of airborne product contamination to assure product quality
  • quality professionals with an understanding of which HVAC parameters are important to product quality and patient safety
  • information on how to avoid increasing facility costs without providing benefit (e.g., over-designing of room classifications for aseptic processing)
  • highlights on the differences between HVAC parameters that address product requirements and "discretionary" HVAC specifications that tend to be more business driven, such as custom air handlers, redundant systems, all stainless air duct, and DP controls

1 The WHO TRS 937 reference document (Reference 2, Appendix 12) aims to promote discussion regarding quality in preparation of Oral Dosage Pharmaceuticals and provide practical guidance for inspectors in countries without a robust history of GMP regulations (particularly in support of WHO HIV/AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria programs). Per the WHO purpose statement: "These guidelines are intended as a basic guide for use by GMP inspectors. They are not intended to be prescriptive in specifying requirements and design parameters. There are many parameters affecting a clean area condition and it is, therefore, difficult to lay down the specific requirements for one particular parameter in isolation. Design parameters should, therefore, be set realistically for each project, with a view to creating a cost-effective design, yet still complying with all regulatory standards and ensuring that product quality and safety are not compromised." WHO TRS 937 (Reference 2, Appendix 12) has been adopted as the GMP standard in some countries where prior regulation was inadequate or did not exist. (In regions with existing regulation (e.g., the US, Japan, Australia, and the EU) this document normally does not carry the force of law.) HVAC engineers should understand the applicability of WHO TRS 937 before discussing user requirements for new OSD facilities.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: "Necessary" vs "Optional" HVAC Specifications

The most important message in this section is in the last two bullet points, which distinguish two types of HVAC specification:

  • Product-driven: parameters that directly affect product quality, such as cleanroom classification, HEPA filtration and differential pressure. These are GMP requirements and "must be met".
  • Business-driven / Discretionary: specifications that improve reliability or convenience but are not regulatory requirements, such as all-stainless-steel ductwork, redundant systems and automatic differential pressure control. These are "optional".

Understanding this distinction is the key to avoiding over-design.

Analogy

It is like buying a car: airbags and ABS are required by regulation (product-driven), while leather seats and a panoramic sunroof are personal choices (business-driven). Both have value, but confusing them makes you spend the "safety" budget on "comfort". HVAC design is the same: secure GMP compliance first, then consider business needs.

Key Notes

The original text specifically calls out "over-designing of room classifications for aseptic processing", a common problem in industry. For example, some plants design all support areas as ISO 7/Grade B when ISO 8/Grade C, or even CNC (Controlled Not Classified), would be sufficient. Over-classification directly leads to higher air change rate requirements, more HEPA filters and larger AHU capacity, and ultimately sharply increases construction and energy costs.

Practical Application

In competitive CDMO quoting, the economics of HVAC design directly affect product cost. If sound classification design lets you cut air volume by 20%, you may save millions in energy costs every year. This is why the Guide stresses that both QA and engineers need to understand HVAC: QA needs to know what is "sufficient", and engineers need to know what is "necessary".

Practice Questions

  1. In your facility, which HVAC specifications may be "business-driven" rather than "product-driven"? Can you quantify their cost?
  2. In which situations does WHO TRS 937 apply? Why do HVAC engineers need to understand it when designing OSD facilities?
1.5 Objectives

Original Text

The Guide:

  • aims to clarify HVAC issues critical to product quality for the production of drug substances and drug products, and biopharmaceuticals
  • considers the requirements for HVAC control and monitoring systems
  • addresses how to implement the recommendations provided in relevant ISPE Baseline Guides to meet FDA and EMEA regulatory expectations for HVAC system design

This Guide is intended for a global audience with particular focus on US (FDA) and European (EMEA) regulated facilities, including:

  • HVAC personnel, including those less experienced with HVAC systems
  • quality professionals

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Target Readers and Applicability

The Guide explicitly targets two groups of readers:

  • HVAC engineering personnel (including less experienced staff): learning the special requirements of pharmaceutical HVAC
  • Quality professionals: understanding which HVAC parameters affect product quality

This reflects an important reality: in the pharmaceutical industry, communication barriers often exist between HVAC engineers and QA. Engineers understand the technology but not the regulatory logic, while QA understands the regulations but not the engineering constraints. The aim of this Guide is to establish a common language.

Analogy

This is like a "multidisciplinary consultation" in a hospital: the surgeon (engineer) and the infectious disease specialist (QA) need to use the same language to discuss an air management plan for the operating theatre. This Guide is the "consultation handbook" that both sides can understand.

Key Notes

The original text covers three major product types: drug substances, drug products and biopharmaceuticals. Each has different HVAC needs: OSD focuses on cross-contamination control, sterile products focus on particle and microbial control, and biopharmaceuticals may also require consideration of containment of active materials.

Practice Questions

  1. Is your role closer to "HVAC engineering personnel" or "quality professional"? As you read this Guide, which area of knowledge do you most need to strengthen?
  2. What are the core HVAC needs of drug substances, drug products and biopharmaceuticals, respectively?
1.6 Key Concepts

Original Text

This section is intended to introduce Key Concepts, which are essential to understanding this Guide. Further detailed information on these concepts is provided in Appendices 1 to 3, in addition to a primer for readers unfamiliar with HVAC equipment and theory. Readers with limited experience in either HVAC or design for pharmaceuticals, biologics, and medical devices are encouraged to examine Appendices 1 to 3 before reading and interpreting this Guide.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Notes

Sections 1.6.1 to 1.6.26 that follow are the most important foundation chapters of the whole book. If you are unfamiliar with pharmaceutical HVAC, it is recommended to read Appendices 1-3 (HVAC fundamentals) first and then return to these key concepts. Treat this section as the "glossary + concept map" of the whole Guide.

1.6.1 Ventilation

Original Text

Ventilation is the movement and replacement of air for the purpose of maintaining a desired environmental quality within a space. The term "Ventilation" has two common uses:

  • It may refer to the movement or exchange of air through a space, which is responsible for the transport of airborne particles, the mixing, or displacement of masses of hot or cold air, and the removal of airborne contaminants (e.g., vapors and fumes).
  • It may refer to the supply of "fresh" oxygen-rich air.

This Guide uses the definition only for movement or exchange of air through a space (see Appendix 1).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Two Meanings of Ventilation

Ventilation in pharmaceutical HVAC refers specifically to "air movement and replacement", whose purposes are to:

  • Carry away airborne particles and contaminants
  • Mix or replace hot and cold air
  • Remove vapors and fumes

This Guide deliberately does not use the definition "providing fresh air", because in a pharmaceutical cleanroom what we care about more is "air cleanliness and direction of flow", not "oxygen content".

Analogy

In an ordinary home, opening a window for "ventilation" is for breathing fresh air (the second definition). But cleanroom "ventilation" is more like the circulation and filtration system of a swimming pool: the aim is not to bring in "new water" but to keep filtering and diluting the impurities in the water to keep it clean.

Practice Questions

  1. Why does this Guide choose to use only the definition "air movement and replacement"? What practical impact does this have on cleanroom design?
1.6.2 Product and Process Considerations

Original Text

HVAC aims to make personnel comfortable and to protect both workers inside a facility and the environment outside a facility from airborne materials that could be hazardous. In pharmaceutical manufacturing facilities, there also is a specific requirement to control the impact of the environment on the finished product (to assure product quality).

Products may be sensitive to temperature, humidity, and airborne contamination from outside sources or cross-contamination between products. Process operators may need protection from exposure to airborne hazardous materials.

Understanding the product and process is the key to good HVAC design (see Appendix 1).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: HVAC Design Starts with the Product

HVAC design for ordinary commercial buildings starts from "human comfort". Pharmaceutical HVAC design, however, must start from "product requirements":

  • Temperature sensitivity: protein drugs may degrade at high temperatures
  • Humidity sensitivity: hygroscopic powders cake in high humidity
  • Cross-contamination: in a multi-product facility, particles from product A must not reach the production area of product B

"Understanding the product and process is key to good HVAC design": this sentence is the soul of the whole Guide.

Key Notes

In a CDMO environment, "understanding the product" is even more challenging: you may manufacture a different product every month, and each has different sensitivity to temperature, humidity and cross-contamination. CDMO HVAC design therefore needs greater flexibility, able to meet the needs of the most sensitive product without wasting resources through over-design.

Practice Questions

  1. Among the products you currently manufacture, which are the most temperature-sensitive? Which are the most humidity-sensitive? Do the HVAC settings reflect these differences?
  2. When manufacturing multiple products in the same facility, how can HVAC design be used to prevent cross-contamination?
1.6.3 Contamination Control

Original Text

Pharmaceutical HVAC should control airborne contamination and needs to help to ensure the "...purity, identity and quality..." of the product (21 CFR Part 211) (Reference 8, Appendix 12). Room contamination control generally is achieved by filtering the incoming air to ensure that it does not carry unwanted particles, then introducing the air to the work space to mix with ambient air and dilute any contaminants (see Appendix 1).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Basic Principles of Contamination Control

HVAC contamination control follows a dual strategy of "filtration + dilution":

  • Filtration: HEPA (high-efficiency particulate air) filters capture 99.97% of 0.3 micron particles
  • Dilution: clean air enters the room and mixes with the room air, lowering the concentration of contaminants

The original text cites 21 CFR Part 211, the FDA's CGMP regulation, which explicitly requires assurance of the product's "identity, strength, quality, and purity". This is the regulatory basis for the existence of HVAC systems.

Analogy

Imagine a glass full of ink (contaminated room air). You keep pouring in clean water from a water filter (HEPA-filtered air) while letting the dirty water overflow (exhaust). The faster you pour (the higher the air change rate), the faster the water in the glass becomes clean. This is the principle of "filtration + dilution".

Practice Questions

  1. What specific HVAC requirements does 21 CFR Part 211 set? Besides particle control, which other environmental parameters does it involve?
1.6.4 Impact of Temperature and Humidity on Contamination Control

Original Text

Comfortable personnel produce fewer environmental contaminants: a typical worker will discharge 100,000 particles (sized 0.3 μm and larger) a minute doing relatively sedentary work. A worker who is hot and uncomfortable may shed several million particles per minute in the size range, including a greater number of bacteria. Additionally, environmental conditions inside a building, such as high humidity, can influence the product by increasing microbial and mold growth rates on surfaces (see Appendix 1).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: People = the Biggest Source of Contamination

This passage provides very specific data:

  • A worker in a comfortable state sheds 100,000 particles of ≥0.3 μm per minute
  • An uncomfortable (overheated) worker sheds millions of particles per minute, with a higher bioburden

This means temperature control is not just about "keeping people comfortable" but also about "reducing the contamination source". A poorly designed HVAC system that cannot maintain a comfortable temperature turns operators into even bigger particle generators.

Analogy

A person is like a "particle generator": at rest it runs in "low-speed mode" (100,000 per minute), and when overheated or agitated it switches to "high-speed mode" (millions per minute). HVAC temperature control makes sure this "generator" always stays in "low-speed mode".

Key Notes

High humidity also promotes the growth of microorganisms and mold on surfaces. In tropical and subtropical regions (such as Taiwan), humidity control is especially important. Typical cleanroom settings are a temperature of 18-25°C and a relative humidity of 30-65% RH. Going outside this range not only affects personnel comfort but directly increases contamination risk.

Key Data

Comparison of particle shedding rates for personnel:
  Comfortable (sedentary work):  ~100,000 particles/min (≥0.3 μm)
  Uncomfortable (hot/uncomfortable): ~several million particles/min (≥0.3 μm)

Difference factor: 10-50x

Conclusion: temperature control = contamination source control

Practice Questions

  1. If the cleanroom temperature rises from 22°C to 28°C, by how many times might personnel particle shedding increase? What does this mean for an ISO 7 room?
  2. In Taiwan's summer, outdoor air humidity often exceeds 80% RH. How does your HVAC system handle such high-humidity air?
1.6.5 Total and Viable Particulate

Original Text

The majority of airborne particles are non-viable. A fraction (< 1%) of airborne particles are viable, e.g., bacteria and viruses; however, these can multiply. Viable particles travel with non-viable particles; therefore, controlling the total number of airborne particles also controls the number of viable particles (see Appendix 1).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Two Types of Particles

Non-viable particles: dust, fibers, metal fragments and so on; they do not multiply but do contaminate the product.

Viable particles: bacteria, viruses, mold; they make up less than 1% of total particles, but they multiply and pose the greatest threat to sterile products.

The key logic: viable particles "hitch a ride" by attaching to non-viable particles as they move. Controlling total particle counts therefore also controls viable particle counts. This is why cleanroom classification standards are based on "total particle counts".

Analogy

Imagine fish (viable particles) and silt (non-viable particles) in a river. There are very few fish (<1%), but they move along with the current and the silt. If you can filter the river water until it has almost no silt, the fish are naturally blocked as well. This is the reasoning behind "controlling total particles = controlling viable particles".

Practice Questions

  1. Why do both EU GMP Annex 1 and the FDA set limits for both total particles and viable particles? Why is neither one enough on its own?
1.6.6 Classified Space

Original Text

The concentration of total airborne particles and microbial contamination within the space is a key measurement of room environmental conditions for pharmaceutical operations, particularly for sterile products and some biopharmaceutical API. The target maximum reading for these measurements is referred to as the "classification" of the space.

Several similar systems exist for the classification of space; however, there is no consensus on a single terminology for classification. This Guide uses the term "Grade" (from the EMEA standard) followed by an ISO level number. Therefore, "Grade 7" meets ISO 7 (10,000 0.5 micron particles per cubic foot or 352,000 per cubic meter) in use only with bioburden limits of 10 per cubic meter. By comparison, a Grade 7 space looks much like a European Grade B space, but the European Grade (A, B, C, D) also has at-rest limits. This terminology was developed within ISPE to help bridge the gap between the various standards (see Appendix 1).

Table 1.1: Comparison of Classified Spaces

Notes:

  • There are small differences in numerical values between the US and European air classes.
  • The US particle levels are for the 'in operation' state only, but it is considered GEP to measure periodic at rest particle levels to monitor the overall health of a facility.
  • The US has no equivalent to EU Grade D although the term Controlled Not Classified (CNC) has been used in the pharmaceutical industry and is discussed in the ISPE Baseline Guides for Sterile and Biopharmaceuticals. A CNC space may meet ISO 8 at rest without the use of HEPA filters if the airborne challenge is low.
  • Air quality for facilities that do not require classified spaces (e.g., oral dosage, packaging, warehousing, closed biopharmaceutical, most APIs (except aseptic processing), and API intermediates) is described in the relevant ISPE Baseline Guide.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: The Cleanroom Classification Systems

The pharmaceutical industry has three main cleanroom classification systems, which are easily confused:

  • EU/EMEA: Grades A, B, C and D (with limits for both at-rest and in-operation states)
  • FDA: ISO 5, 7 and 8 (in-operation state only)
  • ISPE: Grades 5, 7 and 8 (a unified naming that bridges the EU and FDA systems)

The ISPE Grade system is one of the core contributions of this Guide: it pairs ISO numbers with Grade names so that readers worldwide can communicate in the same language.

Analogy

It is like clothing sizes: Europe uses 36/38/40 (EU Grade), the US uses S/M/L (FDA ISO), and ISPE provides a conversion chart so everyone knows "European 38 ≈ US M". The "Grade 7" used in this Guide is like an "international standard size".

Key Notes

Table 1.1 is one of the most important reference tables in the book, and you should memorize a few key numbers:

  • ISO 5 / Grade A: ≤3,520 particles ≥0.5 μm/m3, viable count <1 cfu/m3
  • ISO 7 / Grade B (in-operation): ≤352,000 particles ≥0.5 μm/m3
  • ISO 8 / Grade C (in-operation): ≤3,520,000 particles ≥0.5 μm/m3

The biggest difference between the EU and the FDA: the EU requires limits for both at-rest and in-operation states, while the FDA requires only in-operation (although GEP recommends testing at-rest as well). In addition, the US has no equivalent of Grade D and uses CNC (Controlled Not Classified) to describe similar areas.

Practical Application

If your CDMO serves both European and US clients, you need to meet the stricter of the two sets of standards. For example, EU Grade B at-rest requires ≤3,520 particles ≥0.5 μm/m3, while FDA ISO 7 at-rest has no explicit requirement. If you serve both the European and US markets, you must meet the EU at-rest standard.

Practice Questions

  1. Which classification system does your facility use? If clients use different systems, how do you map between them and communicate?
  2. How are CNC (Controlled Not Classified) areas defined and monitored in your facility? What is the main difference between CNC and EU Grade D?
1.6.7 Maintaining Classification

Original Text

Designers may default to "rules of thumb" for ventilation rate by the class of a space. Knowledgeable designers use rules of thumb for only conceptual design with the intent of later reducing air changes, based on further knowledge of the process.

The relationship between air change rate, ventilation rate, air particle concentration in the space, and recovery rates from in-use to at-rest conditions should be considered. Although "air change rates" are important parameters in pharmaceutical HVAC system design, air change rates are more related to a room's ability to recover from an upset, rather than the room classification. Arbitrary air change rates associated with area classifications may be either excessive or insufficient. Arbitrarily set air change rates often drive decisions regarding room size and airflows. This can have significant cost implications, but does not relate directly to the particle count in a room (see Appendix 9).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Air Change Rate ≠ Cleanliness Class

This is one of the most important conceptual breakthroughs in this Guide:

Traditional myth: "ISO 7 = 20 air changes per hour" and "ISO 8 = 10 air changes per hour"

Correct understanding: the air change rate mainly determines how quickly a room recovers from a "disturbed" state to its "at-rest" state (recovery rate), rather than directly determining particle counts. An arbitrarily set air change rate may be too high (wasting energy) or too low (not achieving the effect).

Analogy

It is like water circulation in a swimming pool: the circulation rate (air change rate) determines "how long it takes to become clear again if someone pours a cup of ink into the pool" (recovery rate). But the basic cleanliness of the pool water depends on filtration quality and the initial water quality, not on speeding up circulation. Blindly increasing the circulation rate only wastes electricity.

Key Notes

The original text clearly states that arbitrarily set air change rates carry "significant cost implications", including:

  • Larger AHUs (air handling units) = higher equipment cost
  • Larger duct sizes = higher construction cost
  • More supply air = higher energy cost (continuous, 24/7/365)
  • Larger room area requirements = higher construction cost

A smart designer first uses "rules of thumb" for the conceptual design, then optimizes the air change rate based on actual process data.

Practice Questions

  1. What air change rate is currently set for your ISO 7 rooms? Is that number based on calculation or a "rule of thumb"? Is there room for optimization?
  2. If the air change rate of an ISO 7 room is reduced from 25 per hour to 15 per hour, how much energy cost would be saved? How would the recovery time be affected?
1.6.8 Particle Generation Rate

Original Text

The Particle Generation Rate (PGR) for an existing process may be calculated if the steady-state room particle count, the room supply airflow, and the supply airflow particle level are known (see Appendix 9). The calculated value of PGR can then be used for the same process in a new facility.

When using empirical data for airborne particulate monitoring, it should be taken into consideration that particulate of the product being processed is not a contaminant. This is of particular interest in aseptic powder filling operations, where high particle counts may be associated with the filling process, but do not indicate failure of a cleanroom design.

Although equipment in operation can generate many times more particles per minute, personnel are a primary source of viable contamination. Increased control of total particles released from personnel leads to an increased control of viable particles in a room (see Appendix 1).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: PGR and Data-Driven Design

Particle generation rate (PGR) is a quantifiable value: if you know the steady-state particle count of the room, the supply air volume and the particle level of the supply air, you can calculate the PGR of the process. This value can be "transplanted" into the design of a new facility, enabling data-driven HVAC design rather than guesswork based on experience.

Key Notes

Two key reminders:

  • Product particles ≠ contamination: during sterile powder filling, the product's own particles cause high particle counts, but this does not mean the cleanroom design has failed. Interpretation of monitoring data must take the characteristics of the process into account.
  • People = the biggest source of viable organisms: although equipment generates many particles, they are mainly non-viable. People are the main source of viable particles (bacteria). This is why gowning procedures in aseptic areas are so strict.

Practical Application

In a CDMO, if you are transferring an existing process to a new facility, you can first measure the PGR in the old facility and then use that data to design the HVAC system of the new facility. This is more precise than directly applying "rules of thumb" and may also reveal opportunities to reduce the air change rate.

Practice Questions

  1. Has your facility calculated the PGR? If so, how has the data been used in HVAC design or optimization?
  2. In sterile powder filling operations, how do you distinguish "product particles" from "environmental contamination particles"?
1.6.9 Effective Ventilation Rate

Original Text

The relationship between air change rate, supply and extract locations, filtration, terminal devices, contaminations sources, etc., is expressed in the "effective ventilation rate." This measure expresses the efficiency of the dilution air supply at removing contaminants expressed as a percentage of the theoretical performance with perfect (complete) dilution. For further information and calculations, see Appendix 9.

A comparison of the effective ventilation rates of various designs indicates that good air supply layout, good return/exhaust layout, and effective supply filtration may produce desired airborne particulate levels and recovery rates with less air change rates than used traditionally (see Appendix 1).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: "Effective" vs "Nominal" Ventilation Rate

The effective ventilation rate measures actual dilution efficiency as a percentage of theoretically perfect dilution. In other words, not all the air supplied to a room dilutes contaminants effectively: if the supply and return locations are poor, the air may "short-circuit" and never pass through the contamination source area at all.

The good news: by optimizing the layout of supply and return air, the same particle control can be achieved with a lower air change rate.

Analogy

Imagine two fans in a smoke-filled room. If the fans' inlet and outlet are on the same side (short circuit), the smoke only circulates on that side, and the other half of the room stays dirty. But if the supply is in the ceiling and the exhaust is diagonally opposite at floor level, the air can sweep effectively through the entire space. With the same airflow, a different layout can make the effect several times better.

Practice Questions

  1. How are the supply and return air locations in your cleanrooms designed? Is there a risk of "short-circuiting"?
  2. If the effective ventilation rate could be raised from 60% to 85%, by how much could the air change rate theoretically be reduced?
1.6.10 Impact of Unidirectional Flow Hoods (UFHs) on Air Change Rates

Original Text

Air leaving the processing space inside a hood is often significantly cleaner than the air of the room into which it moves. The relatively clean air from the hood may help, along with the supply air from the HVAC system to dilute airborne particles in the room.

In addition to reducing airborne particles, air flow from a hood may accelerate the recovery time of a room from in-use to at-rest conditions. The entire air flow from a hood may not be available to include in air change calculations because the added dilution will affect only areas near the airflow path. Short circuiting of filtered air back to the air intake may create only localized "super-clean" areas, as with UFHs.

Similar increases in room air cleanliness and recovery can be accomplished with HEPA-equipped Fan-Filter Units (FFU) operating inside a room (see Appendix 1).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: The Room-Cleaning Effect of UFHs and FFUs

Unidirectional flow hoods (UFHs) and fan-filter units (FFUs) not only protect a local work area; the clean air they discharge also helps dilute particles in the room and speeds up room recovery.

But there is an important limitation: this additional dilution effect is mainly effective near the airflow path and cannot be added directly into the air change rate calculation for the whole room. The "short-circuit" effect may create only a local "ultra-clean" zone.

Key Notes

In a sterile filling area, the space under a UFH/LAF is usually ISO 5 (Grade A), while the background environment is ISO 7 (Grade B). The clean air discharged by the UFH does help lower background particles, but you cannot therefore reduce the HVAC supply air to the background environment, because short-circuiting may leave some dead-corner areas without sufficient airflow coverage.

Practice Questions

  1. How many UFHs or FFUs are in your facility? Is their airflow included in the room air change rate calculation?
  2. How can CFD (computational fluid dynamics) simulation be used to evaluate the contribution of a UFH to the overall air quality of the room?
1.6.11 Room Airflow Patterns

Original Text

The locations of air inlets and outlets relative to the location of sources of contamination/heat and to expected airflow obstructions are crucial to controlling contamination. The orientation of airflows can be aligned to protect product or personnel by sweeping across one or the other (or both) between the supply terminal and the extract point. Local (usually high level) supply or extraction, or complete enclosure of the process also can create a local environment that excludes or removes particulates. Air velocity that is too high can create eddies and vortices near operators and increase the risk of exposure to hazardous material. Local supply or extraction is considered most effective when located near the point of contaminant generation.

Contaminants may be removed more rapidly using displacement airflow of adequate velocity and direction (e.g., in a unidirectional flow hood, local extraction vent, or via non-aspirating diffusers) than with dilution ventilation. Numerous air outlets equally spaced with equal flow rates, can create a "plug flow," which is a situation where air generally moves downward from ceiling to floor, but not at constant velocity. This can lead to faster recovery (often less than 10 minutes for 20 ac/hr) and also prevent "hot spots" of high particle count in a room. The number and intensity of contamination sources in a room should be considered; if low, a displacement airstream may be more useful in controlling airborne contaminants than dilution (see Appendix 1).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Two Airflow Strategies

Dilution ventilation: using large volumes of clean air to mix with room air and dilute contaminants. Suitable when contamination sources are dispersed and of low intensity.

Displacement airflow: using directional airflow to "push" contaminants toward the exhaust. Suitable when contamination sources are concentrated, and more efficient.

Plug flow: approximately unidirectional downward airflow produced by multiple evenly distributed supply outlets. Air moves from the ceiling to the floor and pushes contaminants downward like a piston. Recovery within 10 minutes can be achieved at 20 air changes per hour.

Key Notes

Two key warnings:

  • The risk of excessive air velocity: excessive air velocity creates eddies and vortices near operators, which can instead increase personnel exposure to hazardous substances. This is especially important in areas handling highly potent drugs (HPAPI).
  • The most effective position for local exhaust: as close as possible to the point where contamination is generated. The farther away it is, the more widely contaminants spread and the less effective the local exhaust becomes.

Analogy

Dilution ventilation is like spraying air freshener in a room, hoping to "dilute" the odor. Displacement airflow is like installing an extractor fan next to a chimney to "pull" the smoke directly away. If you know where the smoke comes from (the contamination source location is known), the extractor fan (displacement airflow) is far more effective than spraying freshener everywhere (dilution ventilation).

Practice Questions

  1. Do your cleanrooms mainly use dilution ventilation or displacement airflow? Why was this approach chosen?
  2. If a room's recovery time exceeds 20 minutes, what improvement measures would you consider?
1.6.12 HVAC Relationship to General Construction

Original Text

Pharmaceutical HVAC can help control contaminants within a space, but facilities should be designed with physical architectural features, such as airlocks, which limit the migration of contaminants (see Appendix 1).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: HVAC Is Not a Cure-All

This passage is short but important: HVAC is only one part of contamination control. The physical building design (such as airlocks, wall sealing and treatment of pipe penetrations) is equally critical. If the building structure has gaps, even the best HVAC system cannot maintain the designed differential pressure and air quality.

Key Notes

This echoes the Contamination Control Strategy (CCS) concept in EU GMP Annex 1: contamination control is not the responsibility of a single system but an integration of multiple lines of defense, including the building, HVAC, personnel behavior and cleaning procedures. HVAC is the most active line of defense, but the building structure is the most fundamental one.

1.6.13 Airflow Direction and Pressurization

Original Text

A continuous flow of air in the desired direction through the cracks in building construction (door gaps, wall penetrations, conduits, etc.) can reduce unwanted passage of airborne particulates. A velocity of 100 to 200 FPM (0.5 to 1.0 m/sec) usually will capture and transport light powders and bioburden, assuming there are no strong drafts.

One method to control the direction of airflow is to control the relative pressurization of adjacent spaces. GMPs for classified spaces, such as EMEA Grade B or FDA ISO7/Grade 7, require a measurable Differential Pressure (DP) between cleanrooms and adjacent less clean spaces, suggesting 10 to 15 Pa (0.04 to 0.06 inch wg) DP between air classes.

Products in rooms that are not classified may be protected by measurable DP or by airflow velocity and direction that cannot be measured with traditional DP instrumentation.

A simplified method (neglecting the orifice coefficient for the opening) to calculate the expected velocity of airflow through a "crack" (e.g., around a closed door) resulting from a given pressure differential is given in Chapter 7 of this Guide.

Other "cracks" in the fabric separating a pressure controlled room from other spaces may not be accounted for using this calculation. A common method to account for this additional airflow is to allocate 0.05 to 0.5 CFM per square foot of room surface, depending on construction and (DP) (see Appendix 1).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Differential Pressure (DP) Control

Differential pressure (DP) is the key means of maintaining cleanroom air quality. The basic principle: a space at higher pressure "pushes" air out through gaps to a space at lower pressure, preventing dirty air from entering.

Key numbers:

  • Standard differential pressure: 10-15 Pa (0.04-0.06 inch wg) between different grades
  • Capture velocity: 100-200 FPM (0.5-1.0 m/s) is sufficient to carry away powder and microorganisms
  • Leakage compensation: allocate 0.05-0.5 CFM per square foot of room surface area to compensate for building gaps

Analogy

Differential pressure is like blowing up a balloon: the air pressure inside the balloon is higher than outside, so air can only flow from the inside out and never from the outside in. A cleanroom is an "inflated balloon": clean air continuously leaks outward through door gaps and pipe penetrations, preventing dirty corridor air from entering.

Key Notes

10-15 Pa sounds very small (atmospheric pressure is 101,325 Pa), but it is enough to create a clear airflow direction at a door gap. Too large a differential pressure causes problems instead: doors become hard to open, and opening a door creates violent airflow disturbance. When designing the differential pressure, you need to balance "enough to prevent contamination" against "not hindering operations".

Key Data

Recommended differential pressure range:
  Between different grades: 10-15 Pa (0.04-0.06 inch wg)

Leakage air compensation:
  Per ft² of room surface area: 0.05-0.5 CFM
  (depending on building quality and differential pressure)

Capture velocity:
  100-200 FPM (0.5-1.0 m/s)
  Sufficient to carry away powder and microorganisms

Practice Questions

  1. What differential pressures are set between the cleanroom grades in your facility? Do they meet the recommended 10-15 Pa?
  2. If the differential pressure between a cleanroom and the corridor drops from 15 Pa to 5 Pa, can the airflow direction still be maintained correctly? What are the risks?
1.6.14 Automated Differential Pressure Control

Original Text

There is no GMP requirement that DP or airflow direction be automatically controlled (such as by using actuated dampers or CV devices). Satisfactory designs using "static" air balance to achieve desired DP values are common in the pharmaceutical industry (see Appendix 2).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Automated Control vs Static Balance

A common misconception is that "differential pressure must be automatically controlled". In fact:

  • Static air balance: maintaining differential pressure through fixed damper positions and airflow settings; simple, reliable and low-cost. This is very common and accepted in the pharmaceutical industry.
  • Automated control: dynamic adjustment using motorized dampers or constant air volume devices; more precise, but more complex and more costly.

GMP does not require automated control; it is a "business-driven" specification as mentioned in Section 1.4, determined by facility needs.

Key Notes

This is a classic "necessary vs optional" case. Automated differential pressure control can indeed provide more stable differential pressure management (especially in facilities with many rooms and complex airflow paths), but it is not a regulatory requirement. When deciding whether to use automated control, you should do a cost-benefit analysis rather than blindly pursuing the "most advanced" technology.

Practice Questions

  1. Does your facility use static balance or automated differential pressure control? What was the basis for the choice?
  2. Under what circumstances would the return on investment (ROI) of automated differential pressure control clearly exceed that of static balance?
1.6.15 Airlocks or "Ante Rooms"

Original Text

The primary role of airlocks is to provide an effective obstacle to airborne contamination. These rooms control traffic into and out of a space through a series of doors and also provide a location for gowning/de-gowning, sanitizing/decontamination, etc. Airlocks can prevent DP between air classes from dropping to zero when doors are opened between the classes (see Appendix 2). Three primary types of airlock pressure arrangements are common:

  1. Cascade – air flows from area at highest pressure, through the airlock to the area of lowest pressure.
  2. Bubble – airlock is at highest pressure, air flows from the lock to the cleanroom and corridor.
  3. Sink – airlock is at lowest pressure, air flows from the cleanroom and corridor.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Three Airlock Pressure Configurations

The core function of an airlock: to maintain the direction of airflow between different grades even when the door is open. There are three types:

  • Cascade: pressure decreases step by step from high to low. The most commonly used for personnel entering and leaving cleanroom areas. Airflow direction: cleanroom → airlock → corridor.
  • Bubble: the airlock has the highest pressure, and air flows out to both sides. Suitable where both sides need protecting at the same time (such as between the production areas of two different products).
  • Sink: the airlock has the lowest pressure, and air flows in from both sides. Suitable where hazardous substances must be prevented from escaping (such as highly potent drug areas).

Analogy

An airport security zone is an example of the airlock concept:

  • Cascade: an ordinary airport passage, where air from the clean area only flows outward (from the restricted area → security passage → hall)
  • Bubble: a standalone VIP lounge, where air flows from the lounge to both sides, ensuring the air inside is the cleanest
  • Sink: the anteroom of an isolation ward, where air flows into the anteroom from both sides and is then exhausted, preventing pathogens from escaping

Key Notes

Decision logic for choosing an airlock type:

  • Protecting the product (sterile filling) → cascade or bubble
  • Protecting personnel (high potency/high toxicity) → sink
  • Protecting both sides at once (cross-contamination between different products) → bubble

In a sterile products CDMO, the most common is the cascade airlock, because the primary goal is to protect the product from contamination by external particles.

Practice Questions

  1. Which airlock configuration is used at the entrance to your aseptic area? Why?
  2. If you need to manufacture antibiotic and non-antibiotic products in the same building, how should the airlocks be designed?
1.6.16 Differential Pressure Measurement

Original Text

Two methods of measurement are commonly used to monitor room pressure relationships:

  • room-to-room
  • room-to-common reference point

Small or simple facilities with just a few DP sensors may prefer to read pressures from area class to area class (or from room to room if there are no airlocks). Larger facilities needing to record numerous pressure differentials usually use the common reference point method to minimize the number of pressure sensors and to minimize compounded error. The size of the pressure reference piping can be small, because the flows are very small; the only effect of pipe sizing is to slow the progress of pressure waves. The ideal pressure reference location has a large volume, few openings, and an unvarying or slowly changing pressure relationship to the outdoors (see Appendix 2).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Two Methods of Measuring Differential Pressure

  • Room-to-room: directly measuring the differential pressure between two adjacent rooms. Simple and intuitive, but in a large facility it needs many sensors and produces cumulative error.
  • Room-to-common reference: measuring the pressure of every room relative to the same reference point and then calculating the differential pressure between rooms. It needs fewer sensors and avoids cumulative error.

An ideal reference point should have a large volume, few openings and a stable pressure relationship with the outside, for example a well-sealed large corridor or a technical interstitial space.

Key Notes

Large CDMO facilities usually choose the common reference method. Imagine you have 50 rooms: with the room-to-room method you might need over a hundred sensors, while with the common reference method you need only 50 sensors plus one reference line. More importantly, the common reference method avoids the cumulative error problem where the "A-to-B differential pressure" plus the "B-to-C differential pressure" may not equal the "A-to-C differential pressure".

Practice Questions

  1. Which differential pressure measurement method does your facility use? If you were to expand into a new production area, which method would you choose?
1.6.17 HVAC Controls and Monitoring

Original Text

It is common practice to qualify monitoring systems (sensors, transmitters, indicators, recorders, alarms, etc.) for those parameters defined as critical and to use GEP to ensure the development and maintenance of a robust control system.

HVAC control systems or multi-use systems, such as Building Management System/Building Automation System (BMS/BAS) also can act as the quality 'system of record' to provide electronic data records, as well as direct environmental monitoring data that may be used to support product release or other GMP processes.

A common alternative approach is to employ an independent system for alarming and managing critical data. The HVAC control system is limited to control and maintenance information. A BMS/BAS could be used as a data source interface to equipment and instruments, transmitting information to the monitoring system, which is responsible for all other data management and backup/archiving functionality. In smaller facilities needing to monitor just a few HVAC parameters, the data management and the control of all HVAC points can be included in the process control system (Distributed Control System (DCS), Direct Digital Control (DDC), PLC, etc.). The critical parameter data may originate from a common device and be relayed to the BMS/BAS or the output may go to both systems (see Appendix 2).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Monitoring System Architecture

There are two common HVAC monitoring architectures:

  • Integrated: the BMS/BAS handles both control and GMP data recording. Simple, but the entire system needs to be qualified.
  • Separated: HVAC control and GMP monitoring use independent systems. The HVAC control system only handles "control", while the independent monitoring system handles "recording, alarms and data management". More flexible but more complex.

Key principle: the monitoring system for "critical parameters" needs to be qualified; the control system for "non-critical parameters" only needs GEP.

Key Notes

When a BMS/BAS serves as the GMP "system of record", it must meet the requirements of 21 CFR Part 11 (electronic records/electronic signatures) and EU GMP Annex 11 (computerised systems). This includes audit trails, data integrity and access control. The BMS in many older facilities lacks these functions and needs to be upgraded or combined with an independent monitoring system.

Practical Application

In a CDMO environment, client audits often ask: "Which system do your environmental monitoring data come from? Has that system been qualified? Is the audit trail complete?" If the BMS is also the GMP record system, it needs to go through CSV (computer system validation). When choosing an architecture, consider the validation cost and the ongoing system maintenance burden.

Practice Questions

  1. Does your facility use an integrated or a separated monitoring architecture? What are the advantages and disadvantages of each?
  2. If the BMS/BAS is a GMP record system, what data integrity requirements does it need to meet?
1.6.18 Alarm Time Delays

Original Text

Rapidly changing parameters, such as room pressure, have the potential to create frequent (nuisance) alarms, such as when a door is opened. Differential Pressure alarms often have time delays, the duration of the time delay should be sufficient to permit normal passage through a door (see Appendix 2).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Avoiding Nuisance Alarms

Every time a door is opened, the differential pressure temporarily drops to zero. Without an alarm delay, the system would generate hundreds of "false alarms" every day. The alarm delay setting must balance two needs:

  • Long enough: to allow normal door openings and passage (usually 15-30 seconds)
  • Not too long: otherwise genuine differential pressure excursions will also be ignored

Key Notes

The alarm delay setting should be defined in the URS and design stage and verified during qualification. EU GMP Annex 1 requires that differential pressure excursions be recorded and investigated. If the delay is set improperly, it may lead to large numbers of deviation records or, worse, miss a genuine differential pressure failure.

Practice Questions

  1. What is the differential pressure alarm delay set to in your facility, in seconds? What is the basis for this setting?
1.6.19 Time Weighted Averaging

Original Text

Measurements with "noisy" (rapidly changing) signals, such as airflow measurements, may require filtering to avoid nuisance alarms. A commonly used filter is to use a rolling time weighted average signal, rather than an instantaneous signal for recording and alarming. A rolling average of readings from 4 to 10 seconds typically is capable of smoothing out signal noise without missing significant failure events (see Appendix 2).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Signal Filtering

Time weighted averaging is the standard method for handling "noisy" signals. Airflow measurement signals usually fluctuate rapidly, and alarming on instantaneous values would produce large numbers of false alarms.

Recommended rolling average window: 4-10 seconds, enough to filter out noise without missing a genuine failure event.

Key Notes

The rolling average window setting also needs to be documented and verified. Too short (<4 seconds) and it cannot filter effectively; too long (>30 seconds) and it may mask genuine abnormalities. During qualification, you should test whether the rolling average triggers an alarm in simulated failure scenarios.

Practice Questions

  1. What signal filtering method does your HVAC control system use? What is the rolling average window setting?
1.6.20 Airborne Particle Monitoring

Original Text

The 2004 FDA Guidance for Industry, "Sterile Products Produced by Aseptic Processing – Current Good Manufacturing Practice" (Reference 9, Appendix 12) states "Regular monitoring should be performed during each production shift."

More recent guidance also is available from the EMEA (EU GMP Annex 1) and ISO (14644-1).

Based on this guidance, there is a trend toward the installation of continuous monitoring systems since they provide a better understanding of the process, and the data can be used to support a reduced frequency of testing, while assuring continued levels of control (see Appendix 2).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: From Periodic to Continuous Monitoring

The evolution trend in particle monitoring:

  • Traditional practice: periodic sampling in each production shift (for example, once every 4 hours)
  • Modern trend: installing continuous monitoring systems that provide real-time data

Advantages of continuous monitoring: better understanding of the process, support for reducing the frequency of other tests, and assurance of a sustained level of control. But the investment cost is higher.

Key Notes

The revision of EU GMP Annex 1 (revised draft in 2017, effective in 2023) is more explicit about continuous particle monitoring, especially for Grade A/B areas. If your facility serves the European market, continuous monitoring is close to "necessary" rather than "optional". ISO 14644-3 also provides detailed guidance on monitoring methods.

Practice Questions

  1. Does your facility currently use periodic or continuous monitoring? If you were to upgrade to continuous monitoring, how much investment would be needed?
  2. How can continuous monitoring data help you detect potential problems in the HVAC system?
1.6.21 Air Handling Unit Zoning

Original Text

A manufacturing area often is divided into zones with a separate AHU used for each zone. In the pharmaceutical industry, a zone is usually considered to be an area with one type of manufacturing process or area cleanliness classification, e.g., a tablet compression suite in an oral solid dosage facility or all classified areas for aseptic product. The decisions for zoning should be based on risk to product and to operators; taking into account the preferred air filtration and monitoring technology (see Appendix 2).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: AHU Zoning Strategy

Principles for zoning an air handling unit (AHU):

  • Areas with the same process type share one AHU (for example, all tableting rooms share one)
  • Areas of the same cleanliness grade share one AHU (for example, all ISO 7 areas)
  • Zoning decisions are based on risk assessment of the product and the operators

Production areas for different products should not share the same AHU (unless return air is HEPA-filtered), to prevent cross-contamination.

Analogy

AHU zoning is like a restaurant's kitchen ventilation: the Chinese stir-fry area and the Western baking area should each have an independent exhaust hood system, otherwise the stir-fry fumes will affect the quality of the cakes. Likewise, a high-dust tableting area and a sterile filling area must never share an AHU.

Practice Questions

  1. How many AHUs does your facility have? Which areas does each serve? Is the zoning logic sound?
  2. If you need to add a new production line in an existing facility, how would the AHU zoning need to be adjusted?
1.6.22 Use of Air Handling Units in Parallel or Series

Original Text

Air Handling Units (AHUs) may be placed in series, e.g., if a higher air pressure is required to offset the pressure drop through HEPA filters in ductwork to just one area served by the primary HVAC system. A common series configuration uses an AHU to precondition outdoor air as makeup air to one or more 'local' AHUs downstream. The use of parallel AHUs is common practice where large areas are being conditioned, e.g., warehouses and large research laboratories. This approach increases reliability allowing acceptable conditions in the area to be maintained if one unit fails or when the load on the system is light (see Appendix 2).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Series vs Parallel AHUs

  • Series: one AHU pre-conditions outside air (a MAU, makeup air unit) and then supplies downstream local AHUs for fine adjustment. Common in systems that need extra pressure to overcome the pressure drop of HEPA filters.
  • Parallel: multiple AHUs serve the same large area at the same time. This provides redundancy: when one fails, the others can still maintain basic conditions. Commonly used in warehouses and large laboratories.

Key Notes

Redundant design with parallel AHUs is a "business-driven" decision in the pharmaceutical industry: it is not a GMP requirement, but for critical production areas that cannot be shut down (such as cell culture areas), a redundant AHU can avoid batch loss caused by HVAC failure. A batch of biologics may be worth tens of millions or even hundreds of millions, so the cost of a standby AHU is negligible by comparison.

Practice Questions

  1. Does your facility use series or parallel AHU configurations? If an AHU fails, what is the backup plan?
1.6.23 Psychrometrics

Original Text

Sensible (dry) heat causes a change in the temperature of a substance. Addition or removal of sensible heat will cause the measured air temperature to rise or fall.

Latent heat is the heat of vaporization carried by the moisture in the air/water mixture. The addition of water vapor to air may increase the humidity of the air without changing the temperature of the air.

Relative Humidity is the amount of moisture in the air versus the air's capacity to hold moisture.

The Dew Point temperature is the temperature at which water vapor leaves the air and collects on cool objects in the form of fine droplets or bands together and becomes fog.

See Appendix 3 for further information on Psychrometrics.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Four Core Psychrometric Concepts

  • Sensible heat: temperature change you can feel; heating makes the air hotter and cooling makes it colder.
  • Latent heat: energy consumed or released during humidification or dehumidification; the temperature stays the same but the humidity changes.
  • Relative humidity (RH): actual moisture content of the air / maximum moisture the air can hold × 100%
  • Dew point: the temperature at which water vapor in the air begins to condense. If the surface temperature of ductwork or equipment is below the dew point, it will "sweat" (condense).

Analogy

Sensible heat is like heating water: as the water goes from 20°C to 80°C, you can measure the temperature change. Latent heat is like water turning into steam: at 100°C the water keeps absorbing large amounts of heat but the temperature no longer rises, because the energy is used to change the state of the water (liquid → gas). Likewise, in an HVAC system the cooling coil must handle both sensible heat (cooling) and latent heat (dehumidification), so the energy consumption is greater than you might think.

Key Notes

In high-humidity regions such as Taiwan, dehumidification (latent heat treatment) may account for more than 40% of total HVAC energy consumption. Dew point control is especially important: if the surface temperature of chilled water pipes or ducts is below the dew point, condensate can drip into the cleanroom and create a risk of microbial contamination.

Practice Questions

  1. What is the relative humidity set point of your cleanrooms? If the outdoor air humidity is 85% RH, how does the HVAC system bring it down to the set point?
  2. What GMP problems can improper dew point control cause? How can they be prevented?
1.6.24 Life Cycle Cost Approach

Original Text

In addition to protecting the product and patient, HVAC designs need to consider economics. Overall cost is a major factor in deciding which options to implement for an HVAC system. Life cycle cost is usually much greater than the initial (capital) cost of an HVAC system.

The impact of an HVAC system failure could be financially significant in the pharmaceutical industry, possibly causing loss of a batch of product or the loss of control of the conditions in a research laboratory and potentially invalidating the results of a long term test (see Appendix 9).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: TCO (Total Cost of Ownership) Thinking

The life cycle cost of an HVAC system is usually far greater than the initial construction cost. In general:

  • Initial capital expenditure (CAPEX): about 30-40%
  • Operating expenditure (OPEX, including energy, maintenance and spare parts): about 60-70%

The cheapest HVAC system is not necessarily the one with the lowest initial cost, but the one with the lowest total spend over the whole life cycle (usually 15-25 years).

Analogy

This is like the total cost of ownership (TCO) of a car: buying a cheap but fuel-hungry car may cost more over 10 years than buying an expensive but fuel-efficient one. HVAC systems are the same: for a more expensive high-efficiency AHU, the long-term energy savings may far exceed the extra money paid up front.

Key Notes

The indirect costs of HVAC failure can be astronomical:

  • A sterile product batch scrapped because of loss of environmental control = losses of millions to tens of millions
  • A stability chamber losing temperature control and invalidating data = possible delay of months in product launch
  • Production downtime = delayed client deliveries and damage to the CDMO's reputation

This is why investment in redundant AHUs and spare components, although it may look "excessive", can be entirely reasonable from a risk perspective.

Practice Questions

  1. Has your facility ever lost a batch because of an HVAC failure? Roughly how much was the loss?
  2. If the HVAC system needs to be renewed, how would you present a TCO analysis to management to secure the budget?
1.6.25 Sustainability

Original Text

For a facility that is aiming to be considered as "green" or sustainable, HVAC systems are an important component. Compliance with sustainability guidelines has been optional and considered progressive, and provided market differentiation for the building owners. Compliance with sustainability guidelines and standards is becoming required in some regions (see Appendix 9).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: HVAC and ESG

HVAC systems account for the largest share of energy consumption in pharmaceutical facilities, making them a core focus of sustainability and ESG (Environmental, Social, Governance) strategy. As global carbon emission regulations tighten, "green HVAC" is moving from a "nice-to-have" to a "must-have".

Key Notes

For a CDMO, green building certification (such as LEED or BREEAM) can be a market differentiation tool: more and more multinational pharmaceutical companies include sustainability performance in their criteria when choosing a CDMO partner. Investing in energy-efficient HVAC systems not only lowers operating costs but also improves market competitiveness.

Practice Questions

  1. Does your facility have sustainability or energy-saving targets? What role does the HVAC system play in them?
  2. Which HVAC energy-saving measures can be implemented without reducing GMP compliance?
1.6.26 Key Terms

Original Text

This Guide uses the term 'controlled space' to refer to an enclosed volume that is provided with HVAC for control of one or more environmental parameters. (See Glossary for possible alternative terms.)

Air Flow: the volume per unit time of air moving through a duct or space.

Air Change: the volume per unit time (in this case hours) of air entering a space, divided by the total volume of that space. As an example: 1000 cfm (cubic feet of air per minute) delivered into a room measuring 10 ft × 10 ft × 10 ft would have an air change rate of 60/hr (1000/min * 60min/hr = 60000 ft3/hr / 1000 ft3 = 60 ac/hr).

Psychrometrics: the measured properties of air/water gaseous mixtures. The science of psychrometrics tells us the energy states, density, and makeup of ambient air at various temperature and humidity levels.

Static Pressure: similar to atmospheric pressure, that component of total pressure which is exerted equally in all directions (as described by Pascal). This pressure represents potential energy in a fluid system and can be converted to velocity across any opening to a lower pressure space.

Velocity Pressure (VP): the component of total pressure that is exerted only in a single direction (or vector) because of the velocity of a fluid. This pressure represents the kinetic energy in a fluid system and can convert back to static pressure (potential energy) when flow is stopped.

Total Pressure: a measurement taken by a tube or probe facing upstream, it has both the components of velocity and static pressure.

Differential Pressure (DP): the difference in static pressure between two spaces. DP between spaces results in airflow through any openings between spaces to help control contamination.

Dalton's Law of Partial Pressures: states that the pressure of any gas in a space is independent of the pressure of every other gas in that space. This is important in HVAC because, while air pressure within a low humidity space may be higher than ambient, the pressure of the water vapor may be lower, and therefore, moisture will flow into the higher pressure space.

Classified Space: a space in which several parameters (e.g., temperature, relative humidity (RH), total particulate, and viable particulate) are maintained within specified limits. In classified spaces, total particulate is defined and controlled. In the pharmaceutical industry, viable particulate is controlled, and temperature, RH, DP, or direction of airflow usually are controlled.

OR

The concentration of total airborne particles and microbial contamination within the space is a key measurement of room environmental conditions for pharmaceutical operations, particularly for sterile products and some biopharmaceuticals. The target maximum reading for these measurements is referred to as the "classification" of the space.

This Guide uses terms as defined in the online ISPE Glossary of Pharmaceutical Engineering Terminology (Reference 17, Appendix 12). New terms or terms specific to the content of this Guide are defined in the Glossary.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Essential HVAC Glossary

Below are the key terms defined in this section, which you must understand:

  • Air flow: the volume of air passing through a duct or space per unit time (such as CFM or m3/h)
  • Air change rate: the volume of air entering the room per hour / the total volume of the room. For example, 1000 CFM supplied to a 1000 ft3 room = 60 per hr
  • Static pressure: pressure exerted equally in all directions, representing the potential energy of a fluid system
  • Velocity pressure: unidirectional pressure produced by flow velocity, representing kinetic energy
  • Total pressure: static pressure + velocity pressure
  • Differential pressure (DP): the static pressure difference between two spaces, which drives the direction of airflow at gaps

Formula

Air change rate calculation example:
  Supply airflow: 1000 CFM
  Room volume: 10 ft × 10 ft × 10 ft = 1000 ft³

  ACR = (1000 CFM × 60 min/hr) / 1000 ft³
      = 60,000 ft³/hr / 1000 ft³
      = 60 per hr (ac/hr)

Pressure relationship:
  Total pressure (TP) = static pressure (SP) + velocity pressure (VP)

Key Notes

The HVAC application of Dalton's Law of partial pressures is especially interesting: even if a room's air pressure is higher than the outside (positive pressure), the partial pressure of water vapor may be lower than outside (because the room has been dehumidified). The result is that water vapor can seep from the outside into the higher-pressure room! This explains why cleanrooms in high-humidity regions can still have humidity control problems even with positive-pressure protection.

Practice Questions

  1. Calculate the air change rate of your main cleanroom: given the supply airflow and room dimensions, what is the ACR?
  2. How does Dalton's Law explain "why a positive-pressure room can still be affected by high outdoor humidity"?
  3. What is the practical significance of the difference between static pressure and velocity pressure in HVAC design? (Hint: duct sizing)
1.7 Structure

Original Text

This Guide is divided into three main topic areas:

  • introduction, principles, and recommended practices for HVAC systems
  • appendices on fundamentals of HVAC, and HVAC applications and equipment
  • appendices containing additional topics, detailed information on specific topics and examples, such as controls, science- and risk-based specification and verification approach, HVAC economics and sustainability, HVAC equations, and psychrometrics

Figure 1.1: Chapter Structure

This Guide is written in inch-pound (I/P) units with reference to metric units (the International System of Units (SI)), where practical.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: A Three-Tier Structure

The structure of this Guide is divided into three main parts:

  • Main text (Chapters 1-9): introduction, principles and recommended practices; this is the core content for daily reference
  • Appendices 1-3: HVAC fundamentals, to strengthen the technical background of less experienced readers
  • Appendices 4-10: advanced topics, with in-depth content on control systems, risk assessment, economic analysis, equations and so on

Suggested reading order: if you are new to HVAC, read Appendices 1-3 first and then the main text. If you are experienced, go directly to the main text and consult the appendices when a concept is unclear.

Key Notes

This Guide uses inch-pound units primarily and SI units secondarily. Readers working in the Asia-Pacific region need to get used to converting between them, as follows:

  • 1 CFM = 1.699 m3/hr
  • 1 inch wg = 249 Pa
  • 1 FPM = 0.00508 m/s

Practice Questions

  1. Based on your needs, which part would you start with when reading this Guide? Why?
