  2. The appendices of this Guide contain many equations and calculation examples. Which calculations do you think are used most often in daily work?

Section Summary

  • HVAC is a critical system in pharmaceutical facilities, directly affecting product quality, personnel safety and environmental protection. The design needs to satisfy both GEP and GMP.
  • The three means of air quality control: filtration, differential pressure (DP) and air change rate; none can be omitted.
  • Air change rate ≠ cleanliness class: the air change rate mainly determines the recovery rate rather than directly determining particle counts. An arbitrarily set air change rate may lead to over-design.
  • Cleanroom classification systems: EU Grade (A/B/C/D) vs FDA ISO (5/7/8) vs ISPE Grade (5/7/8); ISPE provides bridging terminology. The EU requires both at-rest and in-operation limits.
  • People are the biggest source of viable particles: a comfortable operator sheds 100,000 particles per minute, and up to millions when uncomfortable. Temperature control = contamination source control.
  • Distinguish "necessary" from "optional" HVAC specifications: product-driven (GMP requirement) vs business-driven (discretionary). Avoid over-design.
  • Three airlock types: cascade, bubble and sink; the choice depends on what is being protected (product vs personnel vs both).
  • Recommended differential pressure: 10-15 Pa between different grades; automated control is not a GMP requirement but is good practice.
  • Life cycle cost (TCO) is usually far greater than the initial capital cost; the indirect costs of HVAC failure (batch loss, delivery delays) can be astronomical.
  • Sustainability trend: green HVAC is moving from a "nice-to-have" to a "must-have" and is a market differentiation tool for CDMOs.
1

Chapter 1: 2. Design Process

p21-p46

ISPE Good Practice Guide: HVAC | p21 - p36

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the four-step HVAC design process: user requirements → functional design → detailed design → construction documents, and the deliverables of each step
  • Understand the content of the URS (User Requirement Specification) and how it drives the entire HVAC design strategy
  • Understand how the key HVAC parameters (temperature, humidity, differential pressure, air change rate, particle control) affect different facility types differently
  • Learn to distinguish Critical HVAC Parameters from Non-Critical Parameters, and the corresponding Direct Impact / Indirect Impact system concepts
  • Understand the focus of DQ (Design Qualification) in the HVAC design process
  • Master the alarm and monitoring strategy: the hierarchy of Design Point, Design Tolerance, Alert Limit and Action Alarm Limit
2.1 Introduction

Original Text

The objectives of HVAC design are to provide GMP compliant systems that meet product and process needs, along with GEP and business requirements (such as reliability, maintainability, sustainability, flexibility, and safety). In addition, the design needs to comply with local codes and standards.

Therefore, the HVAC design team should understand both advanced HVAC system design and the current requirements of regulatory authorities that govern a facility's operations. This includes the GMPs of the regions where a facility's product will be sold, as well as where a facility is located. The team also should consider how HVAC systems integrate with, and are affected by, other aspects of the facility design and expected operation. Issues that are typically associated with HVAC design are:

  • personnel, equipment, and material flow patterns
  • open or closed manufacturing
  • manufacturing activities envisioned in each room
  • architectural layout
  • finishes and tightness of room construction
  • door selection and location
  • air lock strategy
  • gowning and cleaning strategy
  • spatial requirements for HVAC equipment and ductwork
  • intake locations and exhaust locations

The requirements of pharmaceutical regulatory bodies, such as the FDA and the EU regulators, will affect the project design at the HVAC system design level, particularly relating to establishment of critical parameters. For further information, see the relevant ISPE Baseline Guides (Reference 13, Appendix 12).

The design team should deal with conflicts between GMP requirements and local building codes/standards that apply to the design of facilities and HVAC systems. These include applicable local building, mechanical, electrical, fire, energy, and seismic codes circulated by organizations, such as the International Code Council (ICC), National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) (US), and local building authorities. Other compliance related requirements from organizations such as Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) (US), Health and Safety Executive (HSE) (UK), and European Union – Occupational Safety and Health Administration (EU-OSHA)/European Agency for Safety and Health at Work (EASHW) deal with employee health and safety and process safety. The owner's insurance representative also may have requirements beyond those of the local codes authority.

HVAC design engineers should work closely with other disciplines to maximize the success of a project. This chapter provides suggestions to help determine the user requirements (the 'what') and the functional design (the schematic 'how to') that define a facility's objectives. It also provides options to be considered in creating a design that has low life cycle cost and is sustainable.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Dual Goals of HVAC Design

HVAC design in a pharmaceutical plant carries two core missions:

  • GMP compliance: protecting product quality. Environmental parameters such as temperature, humidity, particles and differential pressure directly affect the sterility and stability of the drug product
  • GEP (Good Engineering Practice): ensuring the system is reliable, maintainable, sustainable and economical. This is the basic duty of engineering design

This section makes it clear from the outset that HVAC design is not finished once it meets "regulatory requirements"; it must also meet business needs (reliability, maintainability, sustainability, flexibility, safety). This is the spirit of GEP.

Analogy: HVAC Design Is Like City Planning

Imagine a pharmaceutical plant as a small city:

  • Personnel flow = citizens' commuting routes. People from the "dirty zone" must not cross the "clean zone"
  • Airlock strategy = the city's security checkpoints. Just as you pass security to enter an airport restricted area, you must pass through an airlock to enter a cleanroom
  • Differential pressure control = the direction of water flow. Water always flows from high ground to low ground, and air must likewise flow from the "clean area" to the "dirtier area"

The HVAC engineer is the city planner of this "pharmaceutical city" and must satisfy both "resident safety" (GMP) and "municipal efficiency" (GEP).

Key Point: Conflicts Between GMP and Local Codes

This section specifically reminds the design team to deal with potential conflicts between GMP requirements and local building codes. For example:

  • Fire codes may require corridors to be positively pressurized for smoke extraction, whereas GMP requires corridors to be negative relative to the cleanrooms
  • Energy-saving codes may limit air change rates, whereas GMP requires high air change rates
  • Seismic codes may affect ductwork routing

In practice, GMP requirements usually take precedence, but the trade-off logic must be formally documented through a risk assessment.

Practice Questions

  1. Your plant is in Taiwan and must meet both PIC/S GMP and Taiwan building codes. If the fire code requires positive-pressure ventilation of the corridor but GMP requires the corridor to be negative relative to the production area, how would you resolve the conflict?
  2. Why does ISPE specifically stress that HVAC design requires "cross-disciplinary collaboration"? List at least three professional roles that need to work closely with the HVAC engineer.
HVAC Design Process

Original Text

The design process may be considered as several steps; each step provides a deliverable:

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Four-Step Design Process

HVAC design follows a four-stage process of progressive refinement, and each stage has clear deliverables. This ensures the design converges step by step from the "big picture" to "construction details":

  • Step 1 - URS/CDR: defines "what I want" (What), the user requirements
  • Step 2 - FDS/BOD: defines "how to do it" (How), the functional design solution
  • Step 3 - Detailed Design: turns the "how" into technical details that can be built
  • Step 4 - CDs: drawings, bidding and site support

Analogy: The Four Stages of Building a House

It is like building a house:

  • Step 1 = telling the architect "I want three bedrooms and two living rooms, facing south, with a garage" (requirements)
  • Step 2 = the architect draws the floor plan and circulation layout (conceptual design)
  • Step 3 = the structural engineer calculates beam and column sizes and the routing of plumbing and electrical lines (detailed design)
  • Step 4 = awarding the work to a contractor, with site supervision (construction)

The logic of pharmaceutical HVAC is exactly the same, with the added dimension of "GMP compliance".

Key Point: The Earlier You Decide, the More You Save

Note the importance of Step 1 (user requirements). The document states explicitly that the requirements definition stage "has the greatest effect on the size and complexity of the facility, and ultimately, the cost". A small increase in cleanliness requirements at Step 1 can multiply the cost later. This is why the URS stage must be extremely rigorous.

2.1.1 User Requirements

Original Text

The first step in the design process is the definition and documenting of the key requirements of the user (process and quality criteria, maintainability, etc.) by the HVAC design engineer. This requires collaboration with both the user and the Quality Unit to determine critical HVAC performance parameters, and therefore, the environmental requirements for the facility design. Some parameters are directly controllable (such as room temperature), while other parameters (such as airborne particles) cannot be controlled directly, but are the result of controllable parameters (room DP, airflow, filters, etc.).

Performance parameters may have been established through a user's internal standards. The definition of user requirements is a critical step in the design process and has the greatest effect on the size and complexity of the facility, and ultimately, the cost to construct, commission, qualify, operate, and maintain that facility. Small incremental increases in the level of cleanliness or in the area of classified space can result in relatively large increases in the initial cost and ongoing operating costs of a facility. The required levels of cleanliness for airborne particles, biological or chemical contamination for processes, equipment, and personnel in a facility should be carefully considered, via risk assessment and established explicitly.

HVAC engineers should play a key role throughout the design process in helping project teams to understand the implications of requirements on product quality and life cycle cost of a facility or process. Time should be allowed to establish user requirements thoroughly and to ensure that they are understood by all parties involved. This should provide benefit in the long term with fewer changes (and costly changes/delays) in the detailed design.

User requirements for HVAC typically include:

  • A room schedule with environmental parameters:
    • Temperature
    • RH
    • Classification (if any)
    • Recovery time (if any)
    • Air change rate requirements
    • Particulate control or filtration expectations (if not classified)
    • DP or direction of airflow requirements
    • Ancillary ventilation or extraction requirements (e.g., dust collection)
  • Preliminary AHU count or list with zoning assumptions:
    • Areas served
    • AHU basic configuration (e.g., recirculated or 100% fresh air)
  • Ancillary HVAC systems list:
    • Dust collection
    • Chilled water
    • Cooling Towers
    • Scrubbers/Carbon Adsorption
  • System Qualification Philosophy (e.g., system boundaries at room or AHU level)

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Directly Controllable vs. Indirectly Controllable Parameters

This section introduces an important distinction:

  • Directly controllable parameters: such as temperature. You can set the HVAC temperature controller directly
  • Indirectly controllable parameters: such as particle counts. You cannot "set" a particle count; it must be achieved indirectly by controlling differential pressure (DP), air change rate and filtration efficiency

This distinction is critical for HVAC design. Achieving an indirectly controllable parameter requires several systems working together, so design complexity and validation effort are much higher.

Key Point: Higher Cleanliness = Exponentially Rising Cost

The source text gives an explicit warning: "Small incremental increases in the level of cleanliness... can result in relatively large increases in the initial cost and ongoing operating costs."

This is the most common trap in HVAC design: raising the cleanliness grade excessively "just to be safe". For example:

  • Raising a room from Grade D to Grade C may increase the air change rate from 6-20 AC/hr to 20-40 AC/hr
  • This means a larger AHU (air handling unit), bigger ducts and double the energy consumption
  • The extra annual operating cost can reach several million NT dollars

Cost Impact Model

Cost impact of raising the cleanliness grade (rough estimate):

Grade D → Grade C: initial cost +30~50%, operating cost +40~60%
Grade C → Grade B: initial cost +50~80%, operating cost +60~100%
Grade B → Grade A: initial cost +100~200%, operating cost +150~300%

Key variables:
  - AHU capacity ∝ air change rate × room volume
  - Energy consumption ∝ airflow × pressure drop × operating time
  - Maintenance cost ∝ number of HEPA filters × replacement frequency

Analogy: Investing in a Restaurant's Hygiene Grade

It is like deciding what hygiene level to build into a restaurant:

  • An ordinary restaurant (Grade D): basic ventilation and regular cleaning are enough
  • A high-end sushi bar (Grade C): needs temperature-controlled air conditioning and a dedicated refrigerated area
  • Operating-theatre level (Grade A/B): HEPA filtration, positive pressure control and full cleanroom gowning, so costs soar

You would not build an operating-theatre kitchen just to make fried rice. Likewise, HVAC design must set the cleanliness grade according to actual product needs, not "default to the highest standard".

Practical Application

As the operations head of a CDMO (contract development and manufacturing organization) planning a new line, your client demands "Grade B for all production areas". Based on the principles in this section, you should:

  1. Perform a risk assessment to confirm which areas truly need Grade B
  2. Communicate with the client's quality team and explain the cost impact of Grade B
  3. Propose alternatives, for example Grade B for critical operation areas plus Grade C/D for support areas
  4. Support your recommendation with a TCO (total cost of ownership) analysis

Practice Questions

  1. Why are particle counts an "indirectly controllable parameter" rather than a "directly controllable parameter"? List at least three means of controlling particle counts.
  2. If you are the HVAC engineer and the client asks for "Grade D in all warehouse areas", but you find that some of these areas only store finished product in sealed containers, what would you recommend?
2.1.2 Functional Design

Original Text

Once user requirements are established, HVAC engineers should work with other disciplines to develop a functional (or schematic) design. The functional design should include:

  • flow patterns of people, product, equipment, and other materials; a basic layout
  • further clarification of the requirements established in the user requirements
  • a basic AFD and critical elements of an AF&ID for each system
  • AHU zoning map
  • room classification map
  • pressure or direction of airflow map
  • airlocking schemes
  • potential contamination sources, paths, risks and their control
  • a risk assessment of alternative engineering solutions that can meet the user requirements
  • preliminary sections or service zoning
  • preliminary specifications

The risk assessment can be combined with an economic analysis to assist in design choices that yield a facility and HVAC system that will meet requirements effectively with best total cost of ownership.

The project teams should consider the following issues during development of the functional design:

  • relationship between room cleanliness and contamination risks to product
  • procedures to control deposited contamination (i.e., cleaning or sanitization)
  • reliability and redundancy of equipment and systems
  • flexibility of the facility and systems
  • ease of construction and of startup/commissioning
  • ease of maintenance, servicing, and operation
  • qualification strategy
  • commissioning and qualification plan
  • economics and facility life cycle cost

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Key Deliverables of Functional Design

The functional design stage translates the URS "requirements language" into "engineering language". Several key deliverables deserve particular attention:

  • AFD (Air Flow Diagram): shows how air moves through the facility
  • AF&ID (Air Flow & Instrumentation Diagram): similar to a P&ID but specific to HVAC systems, showing the layout of ducts, dampers and sensors
  • AHU Zoning Map: shows which rooms are served by which air handling unit (AHU)
  • Pressure Map: shows the differential pressure distribution, i.e. the pressure cascade design for the whole facility

Key Point: Risk Assessment + Economic Analysis = Best TCO

ISPE explicitly recommends combining risk assessment with economic analysis. This is a very practical engineering decision method:

  • Option A may carry the lowest risk but the highest cost
  • Option B may have the lowest cost but require more monitoring
  • Option C may be the best balance: reasonable risk plus acceptable cost

In a CDMO environment this analysis is especially critical for investment decisions, because you need data to persuade management and clients.

Analogy: Choosing Among Renovation Proposals

Functional design is like the "concept proposal" stage of a home renovation. The designer does not give you just one option but 2-3 different layouts, each marked with its budget and pros and cons, so you can choose the best one for your needs and budget. HVAC functional design works the same way: propose several alternatives and use risk assessment and economic analysis to support the decision.

Practice Questions

  1. Why does the "qualification strategy" need to be considered already at the functional design stage? What problems could occur if it is only considered at detailed design?
  2. What is the relationship between the AFD and the AF&ID? Why does the functional design stage need only a "basic AFD" and the "critical elements of the AF&ID" rather than complete drawings?
2.1.3 Detailed Design

Original Text

Once the BOD is approved the project moves into Detailed Design. During this phase, the technical details of how the systems will work should be established. The Detailed Design for HVAC systems should include:

  • updates and further detail for all documents produced previously
  • draft ductwork plans
  • detailed AHU layouts with performance specifications
  • draft sections, elevations, and coordination drawings
  • final AF&ID for each system
  • control system sequences of operation
  • final equipment selections
  • final specifications
  • system commissioning and qualification draft protocols

Commissioning and qualification requirements should be considered during the design phase to avoid a negative impact on the project in scope, cost, and schedule. HVAC engineers should include planning for commissioning and qualification activities during the design phase, before detail design is complete, because flaws in HVAC system design often initially become apparent during commissioning.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Detailed Design Starts Only After BOD Approval

The BOD (Basis of Design) is the final deliverable of functional design and serves as the design's "locked document". Detailed design should begin only after the BOD has been approved by all stakeholders. This gate exists to prevent requirements from still changing during detailed design, which is when changes are most expensive.

Key Point: Design Flaws Often Surface Only During Commissioning

One sentence in the source text is very important: "flaws in HVAC system design often initially become apparent during commissioning".

This means:

  • If design problems are discovered only at commissioning, the cost of correction can be 10-50 times that at the design stage
  • ISPE therefore strongly recommends preparing a draft C&Q (Commissioning & Qualification) plan already during design
  • "Design for Qualification" is the best practice

Analogy: Look at the Exam Scope Before the Exam

Preparing the C&Q plan during detailed design is like checking the scope of an exam before sitting it. Once you know what will ultimately be tested, you can leave test points, measurement ports and sensor locations in the design. If you only discover "on exam day" that you need to drill holes in the wall to install sensors, the cost is far too high.

Practice Questions

  1. Why must the "control system sequences of operation" be completed during detailed design? What risks arise if the control logic is defined only at the construction stage?
  2. What are the typical commissioning activities for an HVAC system? Why is it often the most challenging part of bringing a whole facility into operation?
2.1.4 Design Review and Qualification

Original Text

At specific points in the design process (e.g., at the end of functional design and at the end of detailed design) a formal design review/design qualification should be performed to verify that the project design to date is fit for use. This review should focus two main areas:

  • GEP
    • Is the design technically robust?
    • Does the design satisfy user preferences as expressed in the user requirements?
    • Can the design be constructed, commissioned, operated, and maintained?
  • GMP
    • Does the design meet the product requirements as expressed in the user requirements?
    • Is the design aligned with the risk assessment?
    • Does the design meet regulatory expectations?

For HVAC systems, typical areas to check during design qualification include:

  • compliance to temperature, humidity, and classification requirements
  • use of classified space, where required
  • AHU system map coordination with manufacturing activities
  • dust or contaminant generation coordination with mitigation (e.g., LEV)
  • cross-contamination controls
  • airlock plan coordination with pressure regime
  • air change rates used
  • compliance with fire and smoke codes, compliance with emissions permits
  • maintenance, testing, and commissioning access and clearances
  • redundancy and reliability
  • integration of process systems with facility

For further information on Design Review, see Chapter 4 of this Guide.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Two Review Dimensions of DQ

DQ (Design Qualification) is not just "checking whether the drawings are right". It is a systematic review from two completely different perspectives:

  • GEP dimension (engineering quality): can the system be built? Is it easy to maintain? Have user preferences been met?
  • GMP dimension (regulatory compliance): can product quality be protected? Is the risk assessment aligned? Have regulatory expectations been met?

A design that passes the GMP review but is not feasible from an engineering standpoint is useless; a design that passes the GEP review but does not comply with GMP is a violation. Both are indispensable.

Key Point: The 11-Item HVAC DQ Checklist

The 11 DQ review points listed in the source text make a very useful checklist in practice. In a CDMO environment, we recommend turning these 11 items into a formal DQ checklist form and requiring the design engineer to sign off each item. Pay particular attention to:

  • Cross-contamination controls: in a multi-product CDMO facility, this is a focus for both clients and regulatory inspectors
  • Maintenance access and clearances: forgetting to provide maintenance access during design is one of the most common design defects

Analogy: Dual Acceptance by the Architect and the Fire Department

The dual review of DQ is like the acceptance of a new building:

  • Architect's acceptance (GEP): Is the structure safe? Is the circulation reasonable? Is the construction quality good?
  • Fire department's acceptance (GMP): Do the escape routes comply with fire codes? Does the sprinkler system work? Are the fire doors in place?

Only when both acceptances are passed can the building obtain its occupancy permit. The DQ of a pharmaceutical plant follows the same logic.

Practice Questions

  1. Why is "AHU system map coordination with manufacturing activities" a DQ checkpoint? What potential problems arise if one AHU serves both the sterile filling area and the packaging area?
  2. In a multi-product CDMO facility, which HVAC design elements should the DQ review of cross-contamination controls pay particular attention to?
2.1.5 Construction Documents and Construction Support

Original Text

After detailed design is completed the HVAC design team should complete bid documentation, resolve construction questions, and perform on-site construction reviews. HVAC engineers also may be involved in activities related to the receipt and installation of equipment and systems, to verify that they were delivered and installed in a manner consistent with the design.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Bridging Design and Construction

Although this stage is short on paper, it is extremely important in practice. The HVAC engineer's roles during construction include:

  • Bid documentation: converting the design into tender documents the contractor can understand
  • Responding to requests for information (RFIs): giving technical guidance when site conditions differ from the design drawings
  • Site inspection: confirming that equipment delivery and installation quality match the design intent

In Taiwanese CDMO practice, problems often arise at this stage because the design team "leaves the project too early". The contractor then interprets the design intent on their own, leading to deviations.

Key Point: Conveying the Design Intent

The construction quality of an HVAC system directly determines the success of the later C&Q. Duct weld quality, insulation thickness, damper orientation and sensor locations: any single construction deviation can cause commissioning to fail. The design team's continued involvement during construction (Construction Support) is therefore not an "extra service" but a necessary step to ensure the design intent is faithfully executed.

2.2 Developing User Requirements
2.2.1 Introduction

Original Text

Users should define the quality critical environmental requirements (the HVAC critical parameters and their acceptance criteria), typically in a User Requirements document. This may include the following:

  • temperature for product, process, or worker comfort
  • humidity for product, process, worker comfort, or microbial control
  • air flow directions/DPs for contamination control, properties of expected airborne contaminants
  • area classification – airborne particles – viable and non-viable (classified spaces)
  • clean up (recovery) times from in-use to at-rest (classified spaces)
  • process containment and exposure sites (high contamination risk areas)

User requirements provide information that defines the processes, activities, and environments for an operating facility. Assembling programming data for a facility early in the design process is critical to a successful project, both in terms of production output and efficiency, and in delivering the asset at the right time to maximize Return on Investment (ROI) and provide the lowest Total Cost of Ownership (TCO).

HVAC costs, both operating and initial capital costs, usually account for a significant portion of a facility's cost. Decisions and commitments made in the early phase of project planning often are too costly to change as the project advances to the final design and then to the execution phase. User requirements should be understood, agreed to by all parties, and properly applied early in the design process. Establishing, early in the project planning, fixed user requirements that drive HVAC design criteria is critical to the overall HVAC strategy for a facility.

For HVAC systems, user requirements are developed as a result of gathering relevant data with regard to:

  • process: critical environmental parameters that must be achieved and maintained
  • quality: regulatory guidance and quality principles to guide decision making on HVAC parameters that can have product impact
  • operations: correct environment for working conditions that affect the HVAC system design
  • maintenance: provide input on critical aspects of the HVAC system design that would ensure a low TCO

Critical HVAC parameters often associated with qualification (e.g., temperature, humidity, DP, air quality, etc.) are treated differently from non-critical HVAC parameters. Critical HVAC parameters are part of direct impact systems, while systems providing only non-critical HVAC parameters are either indirect or no impact systems as defined in the ISPE Baseline Guide for Commissioning and Qualification.

HVAC systems are commissioned following GEP, while those that provide critical HVAC parameters (direct impact systems) are further qualified.

User requirements can either be in the form of performance-based information that describes an operation and sets expectations, or may be strict criteria where critical HVAC parameters are defined by the product or regulations, e.g., air classifications (operational, or possibly at-rest or as-built).

For performance based information, relevant information should be obtained and the necessary criteria to meet the user requirements should be proposed. It is accepted practice to copy (similar) HVAC criteria from one facility to another facility, as long as the rationale for the original criteria is properly understood. For example, temperature and RH design criteria in an aseptic environment depend on:

  • the type of process (closed or open)
  • powder or liquid
  • local regulatory expectations
  • gowning procedures
  • environmental monitoring procedures
  • the level and type of activity in the area
  • required alert and alarm limits

Each of these variables should be considered when proposing criteria. Using "industry norms" or "accepted industry practices" without understanding the variables involved should be avoided.

Once user requirements are established, design strategies and their effects should be considered. It may be desirable to segregate HVAC systems, such that only one system deals with critical parameters, and therefore, has direct impact (e.g., processing areas on one HVAC system, support areas on another HVAC system). This may help simplify the scope of qualification.

The flow diagrams shown in Figure 2.1 are a simple model segregating critical HVAC parameters with separate HVAC systems versus combining critical and non-critical areas in a single HVAC system. Both design approaches would meet user requirements, but illustrate the potential complexity when using a single HVAC system to serve areas with both critical HVAC parameters and non-critical HVAC parameters. It should be noted that not every room parameter affected by a direct impact system will be critical (e.g., humidity may not be critical in a storage area inside a production facility where humidity is critical elsewhere although both areas are on the same AHU).

The impact assessment methodology evaluates the HVAC system at the component level to identify critical (with potential impact on product) and non-critical components; therefore, making it possible to have a single HVAC system that can serve all areas. Well-defined and accepted procedures should be established, or agreed upon, when defining user requirements, allowing a single HVAC system with perhaps a lower total cost of ownership. If these concepts are not well understood, or if established procedures or practices do not recognize this methodology, the HVAC design may increase the total cost of ownership.

Figure 2.1: User Requirements that Drive HVAC Critical Parameters

Figure 2.1 reflects a traditional approach, as described in the ISPE Baseline Guide on Commissioning and Qualification, where two systems, one direct impact and one indirect or no impact, can serve a facility. The second approach is a single system that is qualified to serve both process and support areas in the facility with a focus on critical components where the system has direct impact on the process/product.

An alternative approach is to define systems by function, rather than by AHU. For example, monitoring systems for critical HVAC parameters are direct impact. If all the room DP monitors were grouped as the DP monitoring system they could be qualified as a single system, the air handlers themselves being indirect impact systems. Should any AHU fail to deliver the correct quantity of air, the direct impact system (the DP monitoring system) would detect it. Other grouped systems can be temperature monitoring, HEPA filtration (periodic testing), airflow monitoring (to verify air changes and recovery), RH monitoring, etc.

An enhanced science- and risk-based approach to verifying that HVAC systems are fit for intended use are currently being developed based on recent regulatory and industry trends and guidance. For further information, see Appendix 6.

References for User Requirements

ISPE Baseline Guides (Reference 13, Appendix 12) provide a framework to understand the different products and processes within pharmaceutical and biopharmaceutical manufacturing facility. Section 2.2.2 describes HVAC parameters as covered in the ISPE Baseline Guides and the importance of each parameter to each type of facility.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Direct Impact vs. Indirect Impact System Concept

This is a core classification in the ISPE qualification framework:

  • Direct Impact System: a system that provides critical HVAC parameters; it must undergo GEP commissioning + qualification
  • Indirect Impact System: does not directly affect product quality but supports the operation of Direct Impact systems; it needs only GEP commissioning
  • No Impact System: unrelated to product quality; managed under GEP only

This classification directly determines the scope and depth of C&Q. Only Direct Impact systems require full qualification.

Key Point: Do Not Blindly Copy "Industry Norms"

The source text specifically warns: "Using 'industry norms' or 'accepted industry practices' without understanding the variables involved should be avoided."

This is a very common mistake in practice: transplanting Plant A's temperature and humidity standards directly into Plant B while ignoring that the two plants differ completely in products, processes, climate and gowning rules. The setting of every HVAC parameter must have a traceable technical rationale.

Core Concept: System Zoning Strategy - Two Approaches

This section presents two very different approaches to HVAC system design:

  • Approach 1 (traditional): zoning by physical AHU. Direct Impact AHUs serve process areas and Indirect Impact AHUs serve support areas. Clear, but possibly more costly.
  • Approach 2 (functional zoning): grouping by function. For example, all differential pressure monitors form one Direct Impact System, while the AHUs themselves are Indirect Impact. More flexible but more complex to manage.

The core logic of Approach 2: if the DP monitoring system can detect an AHU failure (because the differential pressure will drift), then the AHU itself can be treated as Indirect Impact. The true Direct Impact item is the "monitoring system" itself.

Analogy: Security System vs. Door Locks

Imagine the security system of a building:

  • Approach 1: install the best lock on every door (fully qualify every AHU). Safe but expensive
  • Approach 2: ordinary door locks are fine, but install a surveillance camera system (qualify the DP monitoring system, and only commission the AHUs). If someone breaks in, the cameras detect it immediately

The premise of Approach 2 is that your "camera system" (the monitoring system) must be 100% reliable.

Practical Application

In your CDMO facility, one AHU serves both a Grade B filling room and the Grade D gowning anteroom. Based on the concepts in this section:

  • This AHU as a whole is a Direct Impact System (because it serves a Grade B area)
  • However, the dampers and sensors on the duct branch serving the Grade D area may be Non-critical Components
  • The Impact Assessment can identify at component level which are Critical and which are Non-critical
  • This avoids unnecessary qualification testing of non-critical components

Practice Questions

  1. Suppose your plant has 10 AHUs, of which 3 serve Grade B/C process areas and 7 serve non-classified areas. Using the functional zoning approach (Approach 2), how would you define the Direct Impact systems?
  2. Why does ISPE say "not every room parameter affected by a direct impact system will be critical"? Give a specific example.
2.2.2 HVAC Parameters

Original Text

HVAC parameters that may have an effect on product generally include:

  • temperature
  • RH (dry products, some liquids)
  • airborne contamination (viable and non-viable particles) which is affected by:
    • room relative pressure
    • airflow patterns (especially Unidirectional Flow Hoods (UFHs))
    • air flow volume and air changes
    • air filtration

Within the context of the ISPE Baseline Guides some parameters are common to all facility types, while other parameters apply only to specific facilities. Table 2.1 depicts an overview of typical HVAC parameters that would generally apply to each facility type.

Table 2.1: Typical HVAC Critical Parameters by Facility Type

Notes:

  • Shaded areas represent HVAC parameters that commonly have a product impact or are required for operator comfort to keep airborne contamination low. Some products may not have temperature, humidity, or particulate limits, but USP temperature and humidity limits may apply.
  • Non-shaded areas are HVAC parameters that normally do not have product impact. However, there may be other requirements, such as local codes or regulations that may require specific parameters be considered in the design. For example, room relative pressure may not have product impact in an API facility where processes operate closed, but because of governing codes, the design may include room negative pressurization in order to meet fire safety requirements because of the presence of flammable liquids or vapors.

Individual HVAC parameters are discussed with an emphasis on minimum requirements to achieve "compliance," the importance of the parameter, the impact on design, and the challenges faced in determining these requirements.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: HVAC Parameter Needs Differ by Facility Type

Table 2.1 is one of the most important reference tables in this chapter. It clearly shows a key fact: not every type of pharmaceutical plant needs to control every HVAC parameter.

  • Sterile manufacturing facilities: all parameters are critical, the most stringent case
  • Oral solid dosage (OSD): the main concerns are temperature, humidity and airflow direction (to prevent cross-contamination), while particles and air change rates are not necessarily critical parameters
  • Active pharmaceutical ingredients (API): temperature is critical; other parameters matter only under specific conditions
  • Warehousing/packaging: only temperature (and humidity where product is exposed) needs to be controlled

Table Analysis

Two points to note when reading Table 2.1:

  1. "X" does not mean "mandated by regulation": it only indicates that the parameter will "commonly have a product impact". Whether it is a Critical Parameter still has to be determined by risk assessment.
  2. Non-critical does not mean not needed: even if a parameter does not affect product quality, local codes may still require it to be controlled (for example, fire codes requiring negative pressure for explosion protection in API facilities).

Analogy: Different Restaurants Focus on Different Hygiene Controls

Different types of pharmaceutical plants are like different types of restaurants:

  • Sterile manufacturing = an operating-theatre-grade clean kitchen. Temperature, humidity, particles, differential pressure and ventilation are all tightly controlled
  • Oral solid dosage = a bakery. Temperature and dust control matter, but a dust-free environment is not needed
  • Warehousing = a food cold store. As long as the temperature is right, it is fine

You would not manage a cold store to operating-theatre standards, and likewise you should not design a warehouse with the HVAC standards of a sterile plant.

Practice Questions

  1. Your CDMO plant has both a sterile filling line and an oral solid dosage production area. According to Table 2.1, what are the core differences in HVAC design needs between the two areas?
  2. Why is Room Relative Pressure marked "Low" rather than "X" for API facilities? What does this mean for HVAC design?
2.2.2.1 Temperature and Humidity

Original Text

General Requirements

Room temperature and RH requirements depend on the application (process design), product requirements, and operator comfort.

When operator comfort is the only requirement, the ranges, e.g., 65-74°F (18-23°C)/30-60% RH, are well understood and usually are based on historical operating practices that include gowning requirements, type of work being performed, and local climate (e.g., tropic or temperate zone).

EU Guide Annex 12 reinforces that the temperature and humidity within a sterile facility be kept at a comfortable condition, presumably to avoid shedding of particles and bioburden from excessive perspiration.

Specific Requirements

Room temperature and RH requirements at which product quality is adversely affected should be based on stability studies or process parameters that demonstrate the acceptable operating ranges for the product or process. In the case of sterile facilities, where air is in direct contact with the product (Grade A/Grade 5 open processing areas) temperature may have an effect on product quality, and therefore, the temperature range may be limited to plus/minus a few degrees.

Room temperature and RH for bulk biological processing areas generally are maintained just for operator comfort. Most product processing occurs in Grade C or D (Grade 8 or CNC) areas with closed operations. In areas with unjacketed processing, when it can be demonstrated that room temperature and RH may affect product quality or processing, these HVAC parameters are considered critical.

For solid dosage facilities, although air is in direct contact with product, temperature generally is not as critical to product quality. Set points often are based on operator comfort for the level of gowning. Many powder products are hygroscopic and require lower humidity than usually provided for operator comfort. Products or processes may require strict environmental room conditions for production or to maintain product quality (e.g., where the hygroscopic nature of an ingredient causes a weight gain when exposed to ambient humidity, which may affect weight upon formulation).

Storage of finished goods or raw materials, as stated by regulatory requirements, requires environmental control and monitoring of storage conditions. Generally, space temperature and humidity are monitored and controlled because of labeling requirements of the finished product or raw material. For closed and sealed containers, humidity requirements usually are not as stringent.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Three Drivers of Temperature and Humidity Control

Temperature and humidity control is not as simple as applying "one uniform standard". There are three drivers:

  1. Product requirements: stability study data determine the acceptable temperature and humidity range for the product
  2. Process requirements: for example, hygroscopic powders need a low-humidity environment, otherwise they gain weight and compromise formulation accuracy
  3. Operator comfort: people working in cleanroom garments sweat more if the environment is too hot and stuffy, which increases particle shedding and affects cleanliness

The first two are usually the "regulation-driven" critical parameters. The third looks "non-critical" but in a sterile environment can also affect product quality.

Key Point: The "Comfort" Requirement in EU Annex 1

EU GMP Annex 1 (the source text cites the old Annex 12; the new version has been consolidated into Annex 1) requires sterile facilities to maintain "comfortable" temperature and humidity. This may sound vague, but there is rigorous science behind it:

  • People in uncomfortable environments sweat heavily
  • Evaporating sweat releases particles and microorganisms
  • In a Grade A/B environment this directly threatens sterility assurance

Therefore, "operator comfort" in a sterile facility is not merely a human-factors issue but part of the sterility assurance strategy.

Analogy: Temperature Control in a Chocolate Factory

Hygroscopic powder drugs are like the chocolate in a chocolate factory. If the ambient humidity is too high, the chocolate surface "sweats" (sugar bloom) and the quality is completely ruined. The hygroscopicity problem is even more serious for drugs, because water uptake and weight gain directly affect dose accuracy (formulation weight) and can cause potency shifts.

Practice Questions

  1. The temperature control accuracy for a Grade A area is "plus/minus a few degrees" (e.g. 20±2°C), while a typical Grade D area may be 18-25°C. Explain why the temperature range for Grade A must be narrower.
  2. Taiwan lies in the subtropics, with hot and humid summers. What special challenges does this pose for pharmaceutical HVAC design? How would you reflect these challenges in the URS?
2.2.2.2 Airborne Particles

Original Text

Airborne particles should be controlled in classified facilities; i.e., Grade A, B, C (Grade 5, 7, 8), etc. Other types of facilities, e.g., oral solid dosage, bulk chemical, warehouse/storage, and packaging/labeling, generally have no specific criteria for airborne particulate, except that filtration is provided to reduce particulates below ambient levels. Local requirements may stipulate a minimum level of particulate control in specific types of facilities or product manufacture. These should be reviewed with the local quality unit for application and impact. In general, user requirements should not specify space classification for applications that do not require them. See the appropriate facility ISPE Baseline Guide.

Airflow patterns can influence local airborne particle levels significantly. For aseptic and classified areas, a protective isolator or UFH can isolate the product area from the room substantially. Although airflow patterns are not monitored, the performance of the protective device (isolator, UFH) can be monitored (e.g., pressure monitoring for an isolator or air flow monitoring for a UFH).

Elevators present a particular challenge in the control of airborne particulates. The piston action of the cab in the elevator shaft causes DPs change as the elevator cab moves. This makes elevators and elevator shafts difficult to construct as classified space. If elevators are needed for transport of material, closed transfer procedures are recommended.

For further information on the requirements for routine particle monitoring see Appendix 2. Continuous particle monitoring systems may provide a financial benefit by allowing the period between formal re-qualification and a quality benefit by providing a continuous set of environmental data.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: A Tiered Strategy for Particle Control

Particle control is not as simple as "install HEPA (high-efficiency particulate air) filters everywhere". The strategy hierarchy ISPE proposes is:

  1. Areas that do not need classification: only basic filtration is needed, reducing particles to below the level of the external environment
  2. Classified space: set particle limits by grade, achieved through HEPA + air change rate + differential pressure
  3. Product exposure points: use an isolator or UFH (unidirectional flow hood) to provide local Grade A protection

Key principle: user requirements should not specify space classification for applications that do not require them. Do not over-classify.

Key Point: The Elevator "Piston Effect"

This is a problem rarely discussed in textbooks but extremely important in practice. As an elevator car moves in its shaft it acts like a giant piston: moving down, it compresses the air below and lowers the pressure above, causing severe differential pressure fluctuations in the adjacent corridors.

Solutions:

  • Do not make the elevator shaft a classified space
  • When materials must be transferred between floors, use a closed transfer method
  • Provide an airlock in the elevator vestibule to buffer pressure fluctuations

Analogy: An Isolator Is Like a Space Station

The concept of an isolator is like a space station. In the "particle-filled" environment of space (the background room), it creates a completely sealed clean space (Grade A) whose internal pressure is higher than the outside, so any leakage goes "from inside to outside" rather than "from outside to inside".

A UFH (Unidirectional Flow Hood) is like a "clean-air umbrella": it blows a steady layer of clean air from above, pushing particles away and protecting the product under the umbrella.

Practice Questions

  1. Your CDMO client demands "Grade C for all corridors". Based on the principles in this section, how would you evaluate whether this requirement is reasonable?
  2. What are the regulatory and economic advantages of continuous particle monitoring compared with periodic re-qualification?
2.2.2.3 Room Relative Pressure/Direction of Airflow

Original Text

General Requirements

Room relative pressurization (direction of airflow control) is critical to protecting most manufacturing operations and often becomes the most challenging part of commissioning and qualification. A pressurization or airflow direction scheme should be established early in the design process to integrate the HVAC design with the architectural features of the facility, for example:

  • door swings
  • airlock strategy
  • wall and floor openings
  • pass-throughs

HVAC engineers should assist in the selection of the building and room fabric (i.e., walls, ceilings, etc.) during building design. Control of room pressurization can range from simple (manual balancing) to complex (fully automated dynamic control).

Manual systems are less complex, less expensive, and require less effort to commission and qualify, but are not flexible and may need to be checked and adjusted periodically.

Fully automated systems are more complex and expensive, can take considerably more effort to commission and qualify, have a greater tendency to tuning upsets, but are very flexible, provide consistency in measurement, and a have a high degree of reliability (as long as the correct hardware has been specified). Door closure devices that can work against the anticipated pressure differential should be specified by the architect.

Specific Requirements

Sterile Facilities

Room pressurization for sterile facilities normally is designed to cascade from areas of highest cleanliness to areas of lower cleanliness. The design DP measured between different grade rooms, inclusive of airlocks, should be held between 10 Pa to 15 Pa with the doors in their normal closed positions. For complex facility designs, where there are many different levels of pressurization, consideration should be given to avoiding an absolute pressure above 37 Pa, which could lead to excessive air leakage, building fabric failures, and difficulty in opening/closing doors. Special consideration should be given to product conveying lines that pass from a higher-pressure area to a lower pressure area. Such high differential room pressures also create significant air velocity through the "mouse hole" that can lead to toppling of vials or product. This DP is critical, and generally, will tend to be the highest DP across one wall in a facility.

Where rooms are of the same cleanliness class, a more critical room may be the same pressure, but is usually slightly higher. General industry practices have shown that, while DPs as low as 1.2 Pa are achievable, DPs of approximately 5 Pa between rooms are easily measurable and controllable.

Bulk Biological Facilities

Bulk biological facilities generally will operate under the same principles for pressurization as sterile facilities, where open operations are performed. Closed processes may be in a CNC space. In both types of facilities, where there are live viruses, organisms, or open powder handling, rooms may be designed as containment areas. In these cases, there should be a negative pressure "sink" or pressure "bubble" airlock to interrupt the path of fugitive airborne particles.

Oral Solid Dosage Facilities

In oral solid dosage facilities where airflow direction is considered critical to maintaining room cleanliness, the direction of airflow at room interfaces (doors, pass-through(s) or other openings) can be controlled by an offset between supply and return/exhaust with periodic verification. DP also can be used to ensure the direction of airflow and can be a critical parameter. Although there are no regulatory guidelines that state DP values for these facilities, internal company guidelines or policy may stipulate criteria. Generally, any measurable DP will work. Room DP strategy is influenced by the following:

  • facility usage (dedicated, multi-product, or flexible/campaigned)
  • product mix
  • process characteristics (open or closed)
  • unit operations
  • air filter capture and location
  • material and people flow

Solid dosage facility pressurization strategies focus on airflow direction that minimizes contamination from extraneous matter and cross-contamination from one product to another.

In general, measurement of DP is performed directly (room-to-room) or indirectly (room-to-reference) and may employ both strategies. Alert and alarm levels that a facility will be observing should be considered when choosing a measurement strategy.

Action alarms (unusual events for the most critical rooms) may be measured directly (across the airlock) to ensure end-to-end data accuracy, rather than indirectly where DP is calculated in a control system (computer based).

Alerts (maintenance/operations notification of potential problems) can be measured indirectly.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Key Values for Differential Pressure (DP) Control

This section gives three extremely important differential pressure values that must be remembered:

  • 10-15 Pa: the standard design differential pressure between rooms of different grades (including airlocks)
  • 5 Pa: the minimum controllable differential pressure between rooms of the same grade but different criticality
  • 37 Pa: the upper limit of cumulative absolute pressure. Beyond this, doors become hard to open, the building structure can be damaged and leakage increases

These values are the basis for designing the HVAC pressure cascade.

Pressure Cascade Calculation Example

Typical sterile facility pressure cascade (from outside to inside):

Corridor (non-classified) → Airlock → Grade D → Airlock → Grade C → Airlock → Grade B → Grade A
   0 Pa         +10Pa    +10Pa       +10Pa    +10Pa      +10Pa    +10Pa

Cumulative pressure: 0 → 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50 → 60 Pa ← exceeds the 37 Pa limit!

Solutions:
- Reduce the pressure step (e.g. use 7.5 Pa instead of 10 Pa)
- Provide a "pressure break"
- Re-plan the number of classifications to reduce the number of steps

Key Point: The "Mouse Hole" Problem

The source text mentions a very practical problem: when a product conveyor (such as a vial conveyor) passes through a wall with a high differential pressure, the high-velocity airflow at the pass-through opening (mouse hole) can knock over the vials. This is not only a quality issue but also a production efficiency issue, because fallen vials require the line to be stopped.

Practical solutions include:

  • Install adjustable air curtains at the pass-through opening
  • Design a larger opening to reduce the air velocity
  • Use a pressure buffer zone

Analogy: Differential Pressure Control Is Like a Dam System

Room differential pressures are like a series of dams:

  • Each dam (wall) maintains a certain water-level difference (differential pressure)
  • Water always flows from high to low (air flows from high pressure to low pressure)
  • If the cumulative water-level difference is too large (over 37 Pa), the dam may burst (building structure damaged)
  • The sluice gates in the dam (doors) must withstand the water pressure difference (door closers must overcome the differential pressure)

Practical Application

Your CDMO plant is planning a new oral solid dosage line that will manufacture 5 different products (campaigned) in the same facility. Based on this section, the pressure strategy should consider:

  1. Setting the airflow direction with "preventing cross-contamination" as the primary goal
  2. Because it is a multi-product facility, dynamic differential pressure control is recommended so that the pressure direction can be adjusted at product changeover
  3. Using direct measurement (room-to-room) for the Action Alarm and indirect measurement (room-to-reference) for the Alert
  4. Clearly defining the differential pressure target and the Alert/Action limits for each room in the URS

Practice Questions

  1. In a biologics facility handling live viruses, why is a "negative pressure sink" or "pressure bubble airlock" needed? Explain using contamination control logic.
  2. What are the advantages and disadvantages of direct measurement (room-to-room) and indirect measurement (room-to-reference)? Why is direct measurement recommended for the Action Alarm?

Core Concept: Manual Balancing vs. Fully Automatic Control

There are two extreme approaches to differential pressure control:

In a multi-product CDMO environment, a fully automatic system is usually more suitable, because frequent product changeovers require the pressure strategy to be adjusted flexibly.

2.2.2.4 Air Changes

Original Text

There is a common understanding in the Pharmaceutical Industry of a regulatory requirement for a minimum air change rate for an area – typically a rate of 20 per hour for classified areas. There is no minimum air change rate for non-classified areas, except as defined in local Building Codes (often 4 or 6 per hour), although the WHO guidance for OSD HVAC suggests that a room class, air change rate, and recovery period be established by the facility owner. The European GMP regulations have a requirement for a "clean up" time of 15 to 20 minutes in a sterile product processing facility. The 2004 FDA "Guidance for Industry for Sterile Drug Products Produced by Aseptic Processing – Current Good Manufacturing Practice" gives the following guidance:

"For Class 100,000 (ISO 8) supporting rooms, airflow sufficient to achieve at least 20 air changes per hour is typically acceptable. Significantly higher air change rates are normally needed for Class 10,000 and Class 100 areas."

There is no minimum air change rate for non-sterile product facilities, except as defined in local Building Codes (often 4 or 6 per hour due to chemical storage) although the WHO guidance for OSD HVAC suggests that a room class, air change rate, and recovery period be established by the facility owner.

The resultant particulate level achieved in the various operating states (at-rest and dynamic) that are affected by the supply airflow volume, which can then be translated to air changes for a particular room is more important than the number of air changes. For further information, see Appendix 1.

However, the recovery of a room from in-use to at-rest is directly related to its air change rate; the higher the air change rate, the quicker the recovery. As shown in the ISPE Baseline Guide on Sterile Manufacturing Facilities, calculating recovery based on 20 AC/hr of clean air supplied to a Grade B (Grade 7) room with completely uniform mixing, the recovery time from ISO 7 in use to ISO 5 at rest is 14 minutes, which meets the EU requirement.

Designers may default to "rules of thumb" for ventilation rate by the class of a space, rather than calculating the actual airflow required by the process. Knowledgeable designers use rules of thumb for only conceptual design with the intent of later reducing air changes (and thus overall capital and energy costs) in detail design, based on further knowledge of the processes to be protected. Typical values of rules of thumb are:

  • 6 to 20 AC/hr for CNC, EU Grade D spaces
  • 20 to 40 AC/hr for Grade 8 (EU Grade C) spaces
  • 40 to 60 AC/hr for Grade 7 (EU Grade B) spaces
  • Grade 5 (EU Grade A) spaces: For unidirectional flow, air changes do not matter; air flow velocity and pattern are important.

The number of air changes can have a significant influence on system cost and should be considered carefully and defined. Organizations may require air change rates that are not based on operating data. Airflow (volume/time) determines steady state particle levels, and should be used where historical process data are known. Utilizing arbitrary air change rates throughout a design should be avoided; the designer and owner should take responsibility for defining the required airflow based on a number of factors as discussed in this Guide.

In order to define the actual volumetric flow rate required (CFM or cu.M/hr), the following interrelated factors should be considered:

  • heat gain to the conditioned space due to external influences, e.g., solar gain, wall gain
  • heat gain to the space because of internal influences, e.g., equipment and people
  • moisture gain to the conditioned space because of external influences, e.g., external humidity
  • moisture gain to the space because of internal influences, e.g., occupants, processes, such as washing activities
  • the number and location of the occupants in the space
  • the tasks the occupants are doing
  • the clothing (gowning level) of the occupants
  • the process and its particle generation rate (PGR) (generally, the driver requiring the most airflow)
  • the cleanliness of the supply air
  • the means and efficiency of coverage of distributing the supply air
  • the means and location of extracting the air from the conditioned space
  • the locations where the specified conditions are critical, e.g., in a tablet compression room, the process will add a considerable amount of heat to the product; the critical area is likely to be where the raw material is exposed
  • airflow required to achieve required DPs (usually small compared to other factors)

Heat and humidity gain typically are more easily offset, and therefore, less critical for establishing airflow for classified space than particulate load. The cost of installing a system to deliver higher than required air change rates is significant both in terms of the capital and system operating costs. A process that generates low volumes of particles in a large room may need fewer air changes to maintain desirable particle levels. For classified spaces (Grade C/Grade 8 or cleaner), however, 20 AC/hr is a common minimum design target, as it is cited in the FDA Sterile Guidance and meets EU Annex 1 recovery requirements. Acceptable recovery tests and particle measurement during HVAC and process qualification may justify setting lower air change rates after startup of process equipment. (Air changes should not be reduced to the point that HVAC equipment is significantly oversized and difficult to control.)

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Rules of Thumb for Air Change Rates

The air change rate (AC/hr) is the parameter most prone to "over-design" in HVAC. The rules of thumb given in this section are:

  • Grade D / CNC：6~20 AC/hr
  • Grade C (ISO 8)：20~40 AC/hr
  • Grade B (ISO 7)：40~60 AC/hr
  • Grade A (ISO 5): regardless of AC/hr, what matters is the unidirectional airflow velocity and flow pattern

However, ISPE specifically stresses that these are reference values for conceptual design only; during detailed design they should be calculated from actual process requirements.

Recovery Time Calculation

Relationship between recovery time and air change rate:

Assumption: perfect uniform mixing (ideal mixing)
Formula: C(t) = C₀ × e^(-n×t)

Where:
  C₀ = initial particle concentration (in-use state)
  C(t) = particle concentration after time t
  n = air change rate (AC/hr)
  t = time (hr)

Example (Grade B, 20 AC/hr):
  ISO 7 (in-use) → ISO 5 (at-rest)
  Requires a reduction of about 100 times
  t = ln(100) / 20 = 4.6 / 20 = 0.23 hr ≈ 14 min

  ✓ Meets the EU recovery time requirement of 15-20 minutes

If AC/hr drops to 15:
  t = 4.6 / 15 = 0.31 hr ≈ 18.4 min (still acceptable)

If AC/hr drops to 10:
  t = 4.6 / 10 = 0.46 hr ≈ 27.6 min (exceeds the EU requirement)

Key Point: Avoid "Arbitrary" Air Change Rates

The most important warning in the source text: "Utilizing arbitrary air change rates throughout a design should be avoided".

Why? Because every additional 10 AC/hr means:

  • Higher AHU airflow, so larger AHU size and cost
  • Larger ducts, so more ceiling space required
  • Higher energy consumption, so a significant rise in annual operating cost
  • More noise, possibly requiring additional attenuation measures

The right approach is to start from the conceptual design rules of thumb and, in detailed design, optimize based on actual PGR (Particle Generation Rate) and heat load data.

Analogy: Air Change Rate Is Like Pump Flow

Imagine someone in a swimming pool continuously throwing in rubbish (particle generation). Air change is the pump's job: drawing out the dirty water (air containing particles) and pouring in clean water (filtered air).

  • AC/hr too low: rubbish accumulates faster than it is removed, and the pool gets dirty
  • AC/hr just right: rubbish is removed as fast as it is generated, keeping the pool clean
  • AC/hr too high: the pool is certainly clean, but the electricity bill will hurt, and a current that is too strong may even disturb the swimmers (airflow too strong interferes with the process)

Practical Application

You are evaluating the HVAC design of a Grade C room. The engineering consultant proposes 40 AC/hr, but the room contains only one automated closed filling machine (low particle generation rate). Based on the principles in this section:

  1. First confirm whether 20 AC/hr can meet the EU Annex 1 recovery requirement
  2. If the process particle generation rate is low, 20-25 AC/hr may be sufficient
  3. Use recovery test data to justify the reduced AC/hr
  4. Calculate the energy cost saving: going from 40 to 25 AC/hr may save several hundred thousand NT dollars per year

Practice Questions

  1. Why do Grade A (ISO 5) areas discuss "airflow velocity and pattern" rather than "air change rate"? How is this related to unidirectional flow?
  2. A Grade B room has a recovery test result of 18 minutes (from in-use back to at-rest). Does this meet the EU requirement? If not, by how much would you recommend increasing AC/hr?
2.2.3 Managing Critical HVAC Criteria and Non-Critical HVAC Criteria
2.2.3.1 Alarming of Parameters

Original Text

Temperature, RH, and room pressurization may be critical to product quality or patient safety; organizations may decide which through policy, internal guidelines, or operating experience. Critical parameters should be defined during the creation of the User Requirements document with the involvement of the HVAC design, development, production, and Quality Assurance groups.

Specific terms should be understood in context (for definitions see Appendix 13):

  • Action (or Alarm) Limit
  • Alert Limit
  • Design Point
  • Design Tolerance
  • Normal Operating Range

The illustrations provided are intended to assist in establishing ranges of critical HVAC parameters within a facility and describe critical HVAC parameters that are normally monitored. They are intended to help to illustrate the difference between design criteria and operating values; to provide a sample framework to show how critical HVAC parameters are controlled, monitored, and communicated.

Figure 2.2 shows a room pressure plot. The design point is the target value for the control system to achieve. The design tolerance is the expected variance of the measured pressure around the design point, given instrumentation accuracy, drift, and normal activity in the room. Alert and Action Alarm limits are the points that lie beyond the design point and tolerance, and also should lie beyond the Normal Operating Range.

Figure 2.2: Example 1: Pressurization – Monitoring and Control Diagram

Figure 2.3 shows a similar profile for room temperature. Unlike the pressurization profile, most HVAC parameters will have different set-points for alert and action alarm limits. Usually temperature has a wider range in which to operate and changes slowly, allowing different alert and alarm limits. For example, if a chiller fails, a high room temperature alert would signal that something is happening and provide time to react to a potential action alarm. If product requirements have tight environmental limits, however, it may not be practical to have alert and alarm levels at widely different set-points. Therefore, alarms would revert to the same alert/alarm strategy as for pressurization, setting time delays around the same set point. This is usually not necessary with temperature or humidity.

Figure 2.3: Example 2: Temperature – Monitoring and Control Diagram

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: A Five-Layer Parameter Control Architecture

ISPE defines a five-layer parameter control architecture running from design to operation, listed from the inside out:

  1. Design Point: the target value of the control system, e.g. a differential pressure target of 12.5 Pa
  2. Design Tolerance: the expected range allowing for instrument accuracy and normal fluctuation, e.g. ±2.5 Pa
  3. Normal Operating Range: the range of normal fluctuation actually observed in operation
  4. Alert Limit: an early warning of departure from the normal range, notifying maintenance/operating personnel to pay attention
  5. Action (Alarm) Limit: near or beyond the acceptable range, requiring immediate action

Key principle: the Alert and Action Limits must lie outside the Normal Operating Range, otherwise large numbers of false alarms will result.

Key Point: Different Alarm Strategies for Differential Pressure vs. Temperature

Why do the alarm strategies for differential pressure and temperature differ?

  • Differential pressure: changes fast (opening a door shifts it within seconds) → Alert and Action are usually set at the same value and distinguished by a time delay
  • Temperature: changes slowly (after a chiller failure it may take 30 minutes or more for the temperature to rise noticeably) → Alert and Action can be set at different values, providing an "early warning window" that gives maintenance staff time to respond

This difference directly affects control system programming and SOP writing.

Analogy: Warning Lights on a Car Dashboard

This five-layer architecture is like a car's temperature warning system:

  • Design Point = normal engine operating temperature of 90°C
  • Design Tolerance = normal fluctuation of 85-95°C
  • Normal Operating Range = 82-98°C actually observed while driving
  • Alert = the gauge enters the yellow zone at 100°C: "Attention, there may be a problem"
  • Action Alarm = the gauge enters the red zone at 110°C: "Stop immediately and check!"

If you set the Alert at 90°C, it would sound constantly during normal driving. This is why the Alert/Action limits must lie outside the Normal Operating Range.

Practice Questions

  1. You are setting differential pressure alarms for a Grade B room. The Design Point is 15 Pa and the Design Tolerance is ±3 Pa. How would you set the Alert Limit and Action Limit? Explain your reasoning.
  2. Why does the source text say "if the product has strict environmental limits, the temperature Alert and Action may need to revert to the differential pressure strategy (same value + time delay)"? Under what circumstances would this happen?
2.2.3.2 Managing HVAC Parameters - Monitoring

Original Text

Considerations for a monitoring system for the critical parameters (see Appendix 2) include:

  • Accountability for alerts and alarms:
    • Who deals with them?
    • Written procedures should be established.
    • The location of alarm indicators affects design of monitoring systems.
  • Methodology in determining appropriate alarm delays:
    • Will they be based on actual operating data or upon predetermined values?
  • How to monitor – in the DCS:
    • Process control system, in the BAS, by procedural means, or by manual monitoring?
  • What should be monitored:
    • Every room or select representative rooms?

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Four Considerations in Monitoring System Design

A monitoring system is more than just "installing sensors". It must answer four key questions:

  1. Accountability (Who): who responds when an alarm sounds? There must be a written SOP. Where is the alarm displayed: the control room, the production area, or the QA office?
  2. Alarm delays: set from historical data or from default values? Historical data is more precise but requires a period of operating data collection.
  3. Monitoring platform (How): a DCS (distributed control system), a BAS (building automation system), manual rounds, or a combination?
  4. Monitoring scope (What): monitor every room, or select representative rooms?

Key Point: Choosing Between DCS and BAS

In practice, HVAC monitoring often faces a system integration problem:

  • DCS (Distributed Control System): usually manages process equipment and has strict GMP validation requirements
  • BAS (Building Automation System): usually manages utilities such as HVAC, with a lower validation level

If critical HVAC parameters are monitored in the BAS, the BAS may need to be raised to the validation level of a Direct Impact system. This decision must be made at the very start of design because it affects the system architecture and overall cost.

Analogy: A Factory Security Control Room

A monitoring system is like a factory security control room, where you need to decide:

  • Which camera feeds appear on the screens (which rooms are monitored)?
  • Who is responsible when someone breaks in (who handles the alarm)?
  • Central monitoring or independent alarms at each door (DCS vs. BAS vs. manual)?
  • Sensors on every door or only on the main entrances (monitor every room or a representative selection)?

Practice Questions

  1. Your plant has 50 production rooms. If differential pressure is not monitored in every room, which "representative rooms" would you choose? What is the logic behind your selection?
  2. What problems result from setting the alarm delay too short and too long, respectively? How do you find a suitable delay time?

Section Summary

  • The four-step HVAC design process: URS → Functional Design (FDS/BOD) → Detailed Design → Construction Documents. Each step has clear deliverables, and the earlier the decision, the greater its impact.
  • The URS is the cornerstone of HVAC design: a small increase in the cleanliness grade can cause a large cost increase. User requirements must be based on risk assessment, not blind application of "industry norms".
  • Critical vs. Non-Critical parameters: only Critical HVAC Parameters need full qualification; Non-Critical ones need only GEP commissioning. The system zoning strategy (by AHU or by function) directly affects the qualification scope and cost.
  • Differential pressure control is the most challenging HVAC parameter: the standard 10-15 Pa step, the 37 Pa cumulative limit, and the trade-off between manual and automatic control. In a multi-product CDMO environment, dynamic control is usually more suitable.
  • Air change rates should not be set arbitrarily: 20 AC/hr is the minimum design target for Grade C/ISO 8 (as cited by the FDA), but actual needs should be calculated from PGR, heat load and recovery requirements.
  • The five-layer alarm architecture: Design Point → Design Tolerance → Normal Operating Range → Alert → Action Alarm. For differential pressure, Alert and Action are distinguished by time delay; for temperature, different values can be used.
  • The dual review of DQ: GEP (engineering feasibility) + GMP (regulatory compliance), and both are indispensable. The 11-item HVAC DQ checklist is an important practical tool.
ISPE Good Practice Guide: HVAC | p35 - p44

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the HVAC System Risk Assessment process: how to break the system down into components and assess each component's impact on CPPs/CQAs
  • Master the Impact Assessment method: use the Parameter Risk Assessment Table to distinguish Critical from Non-Critical HVAC parameters
  • Learn the four-step risk assessment approach: define the CPPs, define the system boundary, define how they are monitored, and define how they are achieved and how failures are detected
  • Understand Programming for Detail Design: facility layout, maintenance strategy and process considerations
  • Master the differences, content and applications of the AFD (Air Flow Diagram) and the AF&ID (Air Flow & Instrumentation Diagram)
  • Understand the limitations and points of attention that Modular Construction places on HVAC design
2.3 HVAC System Risk Assessment

2.3.1 Introduction

Risk assessment is used as a process to evaluate the impact of systems or components on product quality. The risk assessment is performed by dividing the systems into components and evaluating the impact of those systems/components on the Critical Process Parameters (CPPs) (derived from the relevant Critical Quality Attributes (CQAs)). As the components included within a system can significantly affect the ability to maintain CPPs within their acceptable limits, the definition of system boundaries is a critical step in a successful risk assessment.

The risk and potential impact of system failure should be reviewed by HVAC engineers with consideration given to the potential modes of failure, for example:

  • airflow failure
