  • filter failure (loss of control of airborne particles or cross-contamination)
  • failure of temperature control
  • failure of humidity control
  • failure of one AHU, upsetting DP created by other AHUs

The potential impact of system failure can influence significantly the HVAC system design and maintenance, as well as the design of the supporting utilities. The scope of the analysis may include business as well as quality aspects. (If a system fails and the qualified (verified) monitoring system advises the Quality Unit that the area is not within specifications, there is no risk to patient, but the cost to the business could be considerable.)

The risk assessment process may be used to determine:

  • the testing (commissioning, qualification) requirements for the system and its controls
  • the level of documentation that is appropriate
  • the individual components that should be verified (commissioned/qualified)
  • the necessary level of change control to apply to system components

Teaching Notes

Core Concept: The Logic of HVAC Risk Assessment

HVAC risk assessment is essentially a "break down, assess, classify" process:

  • Break down: split the whole HVAC system into individual components (fans, filters, cooling coils, sensors, etc.)
  • Assess: if each component fails, will it affect the Critical Process Parameters (CPPs)?
  • Classify: components with major impact go under GMP Change Control (quality change control); those with minor impact go under GEP Change Control (engineering change control)

Key terms: CQA (Critical Quality Attribute) is a quality standard the final product must meet; a CPP is a process parameter that must be controlled to achieve the CQA. The job of the HVAC system is to keep CPPs within acceptable ranges.

Analogy: A Car Safety Inspection

HVAC risk assessment is like a safety inspection of a car:

  • Braking system (Critical) → a failure directly endangers life → it must be inspected regularly and rigorously
  • Air conditioning (Non-Critical) → a failure does not affect driving safety → just repair it when it breaks
  • System Boundary → when checking the brakes, you must include the brake lines, brake pads and ABS sensors; none can be left out

Likewise, an HVAC risk assessment does not look only at the AHU itself; it must cover the complete chain "from the AHU to the room terminal".

Important Concept: Quality Risk vs. Business Risk

The source text draws an important distinction:

  • Quality/patient risk: if the monitoring system detects an abnormality immediately, QA intervenes at once and the product is not released → no risk to patients
  • Business risk: but all product made during the system failure may have to be scrapped, and the downtime losses can be considerable

In a CDMO environment this distinction is especially important, because liability for a client's scrapped product is a major business risk.

Typical HVAC Performance Parameters Affecting CPPs

Typical HVAC performance parameters that may affect CPPs include the following:

  • temperature
  • RH
  • particle count at rest
  • total particle count in use (area classification)
  • clean up and room recovery time from in-use to at-rest
  • supply air HEPA filter performance (capture of contaminants)
  • air change rates/airflow volumes (affecting particle counts and recovery)
  • area DPs (room protection)
  • airflow patterns at critical site
  • microbial viable particulate test results – in air (related to total airborne particles)
  • microbial viable particulate test results – swab tests (indirectly affected by HVAC)

The list of critical parameters should be reviewed to ensure it minimizes risk to product quality and patient safety. The impact of the failure of a component should be assessed.

Teaching Notes: HVAC Parameters That Affect CPPs

Classifying the Key Parameters

The list can be grouped by "control purpose" into three categories:

  • Particulate/microbial control: particle counts (at rest/in operation), recovery time, HEPA filter performance, air change rate, airflow pattern
  • Environmental condition control: temperature, relative humidity (RH)
  • Cross-contamination protection: differential pressure (DP), airflow direction

CDMO Practical Application

In a sterile filling CDMO, the most critical HVAC parameters are usually:

  1. Differential pressure (DP) — prevents lower-grade air from entering higher-grade areas; it is the first line of defense against cross-contamination
  2. HEPA filter integrity — if a HEPA filter in a Grade A/B area leaks, the cleanliness classification of the whole area fails
  3. Recovery time — after personnel activity, can the room return to the at-rest standard within the specified time (typically 15-20 minutes)?
  4. Airflow pattern — especially the unidirectional airflow of Grade A laminar flow areas, which directly protects exposed product

Note: The Indirect Relationship Between Microbial Swabs and HVAC

The source text describes surface microbiology (swab tests) as "indirectly affected by HVAC". This means that surface microorganisms come mainly from personnel and material contact, but the airflow design of the HVAC system influences where and how many particles settle, so it is an indirect influencing factor. Do not ignore it just because it is "indirect": in regulatory inspections, surface microbial excursions are often traced back to poor HVAC design.

2.3.2 Impact Assessment

2.3.2 Impact Assessment

A recommended practice is to begin the impact assessment process with a table of HVAC monitoring points and evaluate them for impact on product quality or patient safety. Table 2.2 is intended to encourage discussions between the Quality Unit, process, and engineering to identify and segregate critical and non-critical HVAC points using appropriate risk analysis when no formal guidance or written procedures exist.

Table 2.2: Parameter Risk Assessment Table

Notes:

  • Although one room for various facilities is included, the intent is to develop a room-by-room analysis for each facility, segregating critical HVAC parameters from non-critical HVAC parameters.
  • Parameters inside the AHU (except possibly supply airflow) usually are not considered critical, as they are the value needed to satisfy room parameters. Excessive constraints on parameters inside the AHU or ductwork should be avoided.

Typical critical HVAC parameters under a given process or classification should be identified, i.e.:

  • Product Driven
  • Flammability or Hazard Issues
  • Environmental Air Classification
  • Open/Closed processes
  • Terminally Sterilized
  • Oral Solid Dosage Forms

Assumptions or clarifications should be discussed and documented.

Teaching Notes: Impact Assessment in Practice

Core Concept: How to Use the Parameter Risk Assessment Table

Table 2.2 is a very practical template. How to use it:

  1. List all monitoring points: every HVAC monitoring parameter for each AHU and each room
  2. Decide Critical Y/N one by one: does loss of control of this parameter directly affect product quality?
  3. Set Alert/Alarm: for parameters with Critical = Y, alarm limits and delay times must be set

The point of this table is not to "get it filled in" but to get Quality, Process and Engineering talking and reach consensus.

Key Reminder: AHU Internal Parameters Are Usually Not Critical

The source text states clearly that AHU internal parameters (such as return air temperature, return air humidity and static pressure) are usually not considered Critical, because they are a "means" rather than an "end"; the real objective is the temperature, humidity and cleanliness at the room.

Common mistake: marking every AHU internal parameter as Critical → this leads to over-monitoring, excessive alarms and an inflated validation scope.

Correct approach: only the AHU supply airflow may be Critical, because it directly determines the room's air change rate.

Analogy: Quality Management in a Restaurant

Imagine you are the quality manager of a restaurant:

  • The dishes the customer eats (room parameters) = Critical; taste, temperature and hygiene must be tightly controlled
  • The flame level on the kitchen stove (AHU internal parameters) = Non-Critical; as long as the final dish is acceptable, that is enough
  • If you try to control even how many times the chef flips the pan (over-controlling AHU internals), the chef will break down and efficiency will drop sharply

CDMO Practice: Critical Parameters Differ by Product Type

The six categories listed in the source text apply in a CDMO as follows:

  • Product Driven: lyophilized products are very sensitive to temperature and humidity → both temperature and RH are Critical
  • Open/Closed processes: closed processes using RABS or isolators → room environmental requirements can be lower
  • Terminally Sterilized: because there is a terminal sterilization step → requirements for environmental particulate/microbial control are lower
  • Flammability: use of solvents such as ethanol → explosion-proof ventilation and exhaust design need additional consideration

Practice Questions

  1. In your sterile filling facility, should "Room Humidity" in a Grade B area be marked Critical or Non-Critical? What is your rationale?
  2. If one AHU serves both Grade B and Grade C areas, how should the system boundary be handled in the risk assessment?
2.3.3 Risk and Components

2.3.3 Risk and Components

The risk assessment process is used to determine which HVAC system components are critical to the product quality. These components then require additional attention through qualification and may require installed redundancy to avoid business impact. This could be extended to determine which components should be under GMP change control with the remainder of the direct impact system under GEP change control.

One method to address this is a matrix in which the individual components of the HVAC system (e.g., preheat coil, fan, temperature sensor, HEPA filters) are listed on one axis, and a series of challenge questions to aid in determining the GMP-critical nature of that component are listed on the other axis. Generally, failure does not make a component critical if its failure can be detected quickly (through monitoring, see Appendix 2).

There are several approaches to performing a risk assessment, for example:

STEP 1.0 Define the CPPs for the area served by the HVAC system, together with the supporting rationale. Some examples may be:

  • Humidity is not a critical factor for the product as it is an aqueous liquid.
  • Temperature is not a critical factor as the product is contained in temperature-controlled vessels.
  • Air quality is considered a critical factor – the room supplied is classified as Grade 8 (EU Grade C) because product-contact equipment is exposed.
  • Room pressure differentials are considered critical to maintain the room environment, minimizing the risk of contamination/cross contamination, because the room is classified Grade 8.

STEP 2.0 Define system boundaries for HVAC systems:

  • Systems can be organized by components of like type (i.e., system that is all one type of components, such as only HEPA filters).
  • Systems can be organized geographically (i.e., at room level).
  • Systems can be organized by connected components (i.e., an AHU system).
  • Control and monitoring system can be either a separate system, or may be included as part of another system.

STEP 3.0 Define how the CPPs are monitored. Some examples may be:

  • Humidity is monitored by an independent SCADA based environmental monitoring system.
  • Temperature is monitored by an independent SCADA based environmental monitoring system.
  • Air quality is monitored by a routine test using a particle counter per ISO CEN 14644-2 for particles, and also via microbial testing.
  • Microbial monitoring for viable particles is tested per local SOP.
  • Room pressure differentials are monitored by an independent SCADA based environmental monitoring system.

STEP 4.0 Define how the CPPs are achieved, and any associated equipment risks of failure and the probability of detection of those failures. Some examples may be:

  • Humidity control is achieved by either dehumidifying (through cooling or desiccant) or by adding moisture with a steam humidifier. As humidity is continuously monitored by a verified system, it is considered adequate to commission the humidifier/dehumidifier system, and maintain it under engineering change control.
  • Temperature control is obtained through the use of the heating or cooling coils. As temperature is continuously monitored by a verified system, it is considered adequate to commission the heat system, and maintain it under engineering change control.
  • Air quality in Grade 8 is obtained through the final HEPA grade filter, which is leak tested annually with a particle count conducted periodically. As the HEPA filter integrity is not continuously monitored and is directly responsible for this aspect of the system performance, it will be verified and maintained under quality change control.
  • Room pressure differentials are the result of resistance to leakage from and to the conditioned space from adjacent areas. As pressure is continuously monitored by a verified system, it is considered adequate to commission the duct/damper system and maintain it under engineering change control.

Based on the above examples, the equipment to be verified and maintained under formal Change Control is shown as shaded boxes in Figure 2.4.

Figure 2.4: A Typical Schematic of Critical Devices

Examples of other methods for performing an HVAC risk assessment, including some typical risk assessments of HVAC components are included in the appendices.

Teaching Notes: The Four-Step Risk Assessment Approach

Core Concept: The Logic Chain of the Four Steps

These four steps form a complete risk assessment logic:

  1. Step 1 — Define the CPPs: first be clear about "what matters", and provide the rationale
  2. Step 2 — Define the system boundary: decide the scope of the assessment: by component type, by geographic location, or by connected systems?
  3. Step 3 — Define how they are monitored: how is the CPP detected? Continuous monitoring or periodic testing?
  4. Step 4 — Define how they are achieved and how failures are detected: what equipment achieves the CPP? If the equipment fails, how quickly can the failure be found?

The final key judgment: if a failure can be detected immediately by continuous monitoring → Engineering Change Control is sufficient; if it cannot be detected immediately → Quality Change Control plus periodic verification is required.

Key Insight: Why HEPA Filters Are the Highest-Risk Component

The Step 4 example shows that, of the four CPPs, only the HEPA filter requires Quality Change Control, because:

  • Temperature, humidity and differential pressure all have continuous monitoring (SCADA), so failures are detected immediately
  • HEPA filter integrity has no continuous monitoring and can only be verified through annual leak testing and periodic particle counts

This is why the HEPA filter is marked as a Critical Device (shown with a shaded box) in Figure 2.4.

Analogy: Detection Capability Determines the Level of Control

Imagine two burst-pipe scenarios:

  • Bathroom pipe: a leak sensor is installed and gives an alarm the moment the pipe bursts → you only need to make sure the sensor works (Engineering Control)
  • Hidden pipe inside the wall: no sensor, so it may leak for months before anyone notices → it must be inspected regularly and recorded rigorously (Quality Control)

A HEPA filter is like the "hidden pipe inside the wall": its failure is not noticed immediately, so it needs the strictest control.

CDMO Practice: Strategies for Defining the System Boundary

Step 2 offers three ways to define the system boundary; recommendations for a CDMO:

  • Define by AHU system (most common): one AHU plus all the ducts and terminal equipment it serves = one system. Suitable for most situations.
  • Define by room: when a room is served by several AHUs (for example, Grade A laminar flow plus Grade B background), the boundary needs to be defined by room.
  • Define by component type: for example, manage all HEPA filters as one "system", which suits scheduling leak tests together.

Practical recommendation: use both the AHU system boundary (for validation) and the component-type boundary (for maintenance scheduling); the two complement each other.

Practice Questions

  1. If your CDMO adds a PAT (Process Analytical Technology) real-time particle monitoring system that continuously measures particle counts downstream of the HEPA filters, would this change the risk classification of the HEPA filters? Why?
  2. In the Step 1 example, "temperature is not Critical because the product is in a temperature-controlled container". Would this conclusion change for a lyophilized product filling line?
2.4 Programming for Detail Design

2.4.1 Programming and Layout Considerations (Schematic Design)

Issues with HVAC systems may affect the programming and layout of a facility design to avoid future problems in the construction, commissioning and qualification, operation, and maintenance of the facility. The impact of HVAC varies by type of facility, generally increasing as the complexity of the facility increases from general administrative office areas to more complex facilities for aseptic or potent compound processing.

In general, the larger the classified area and the more stringent the environmental cleanliness class, the more complex and costly the HVAC system, both in first cost and ongoing operating costs. Once the user requirements document is formally approved, design can begin. Changes in scope that affect the user requirements should be formally approved before design can be changed.

Special requirements should be determined for temperature or RH for specific rooms (freezers, chill rooms, stability storage chambers, R&D suites, etc.).

HVAC engineers should understand the flow of materials, equipment, and personnel (unidirectional flow; gravity flow, etc.) in determining area classifications, pressurization strategies, and airlock strategies (the use of airlocks to separate areas of different requirements for cleanliness, pressure, temperature, and RH), their classification, HVAC system zoning, etc., and location of changing rooms and their classification. Note: Elevators serving classified spaces should be located outside those classified spaces.

Area functionalities and adjacencies (both horizontal and vertical) should be determined.

Functional/relational adjacencies should be determined (e.g., avoid placing large AHUs next to a laboratory with vibration-sensitive precision analytical equipment).

There may be special considerations in the layout and adjacencies for projects employing prefabricated modular construction.

HVAC and utilities equipment, duct/pipe routing and supply/exhaust/return, and diffusers/grilles locations and issues should be considered. Outside air intakes and exhaust stacks should be located to avoid entrainment/re-entrainment of unwanted fumes and odors, such as laboratory fume hood exhausts, process vents, and fumes from idling trucks near docks and other loading/unloading facilities. Major equipment may be located, e.g., in a basement, penthouse, or roof, accordingly. Building configuration (H × W × L) may affect the location of central services and how they are distributed.

Teaching Notes: Facility Planning and HVAC Layout

Core Concept: The Pyramid of HVAC Complexity and Cost

From simple to complex facility types, HVAC cost grows exponentially:

  • General office → basic air conditioning (lowest cost)
  • OSD (oral solid dosage) → temperature and humidity control plus dust control (medium cost)
  • Sterile filling → multiple cleanroom grades, HEPA filtration and differential pressure control (high cost)
  • Highly potent/highly active drugs → all of the above plus negative-pressure containment and dedicated exhaust (highest cost)

Key principle: the larger the cleanroom area and the higher its grade, the higher both the HVAC construction cost and the operating cost. This is why requirements must be defined precisely at the URS stage, to avoid over-design.

Important Reminder: Layout Determines Everything

Several key layout considerations raised in the source text:

  • No elevators inside the cleanroom area: the piston effect of an elevator seriously disturbs differential pressure control
  • Keep AHUs away from precision instrument laboratories: vibration from large fans affects precision equipment such as analytical balances
  • Location of the outside air intake: it must avoid exhaust outlets, truck loading docks (diesel exhaust) and laboratory exhaust

These must be decided early in design (Schematic Design); changes later are extremely costly.

Analogy: The Order of Building a House

HVAC facility planning is like building a house:

  • Layout is decided first → the positions and sizes of the living room, bedroom and kitchen
  • Flow is decided next → the routes for clean and dirty laundry must not cross
  • Utilities (HVAC routing) follow the layout → you do not run the pipes first and then decide the layout

In a pharmaceutical plant, the "layout" is the arrangement of the cleanroom grades, the "flow" is the movement of personnel and materials, and the "utilities" are the HVAC ducts. The order of these three decisions must not be reversed.

Maintenance & Process Considerations

Maintenance

The requirements for maintenance, testing, repair, and replacement should be considered, including the locations for access doors/panels for HVAC system inspection, testing, maintenance, and HEPA filter scan testing and replacement.

Access to field instruments for calibration, testing, and repair also should be considered.

For AHU maintenance, removal or replacement of large motors and fans, dehumidifier wheels, coils, and filters should be considered. Access to AHUs should allow the removal and replacement of large equipment (clear pathways, hoists/elevators, etc.).

Locations and access requirements for BMS/EMS data and control should be identified. Requirements for local indications and control features for BMS/EMS should be determined.

Facility maintenance philosophies (i.e., maintain from inside or outside of room) should be defined.

Process

Materials to be used in a process (i.e., potent, solvents, cytotoxic, sterile) and the approaches and technologies for product containment and clean/sterile processing should be determined.

The use of micro-environments (barrier isolators, Restricted Access Barrier System (RABS), biosafety cabinets, etc.) may reduce both the required amount and grade of classified space, compared to traditional dedicated classified rooms for open pharmaceutical processing. This may result in a smaller facility footprint, fewer airlocks, and lower overall HVAC system life cycle cost.

The location and associated maintenance of hazardous equipment and ductwork may affect facility layout.

Process issues related to codes and standards, include:

  • codes and standards applicable to the region (e.g., Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), Fire, OSHA, Energy, IMC)
  • ease of egress and other safety considerations
  • risks associated with various layout and programming issues (i.e., area electrical classification, explosion-relief panels, product risks)
  • special considerations associated with hydrogen or nitrogen operations
  • Where facility modules are prefabricated in a jurisdiction different to that of the facility location, special attention should be given to requirements of local codes and standards. Applicable requirements should be identified early in the design process.

Process issues within a room which should be considered include:

  • locations of personnel, processes, and product with respect to HVAC supplies and exhaust/returns
  • equipment heat loads (where is heat generated and how is it cooled or extracted?)
  • Locations of utilities connections in regard to the operations to be performed. Room HVAC system should be designed as an integrated system in rooms with fume hoods, biosafety cabinets, LEV systems, and process equipment HVAC systems. Using a manifold exhaust system rather than one fan per hood may affect facility layout.

Teaching Notes: Maintenance and Process Considerations

Two Philosophies of Maintenance Strategy

The source text mentions "maintain from inside or outside of room", which is a fundamental decision in cleanroom design:

  • Maintenance from inside the room (inside-out): maintenance personnel enter the cleanroom to work → gowning procedures and cleanroom discipline demands are high, but the equipment layout is simpler
  • Maintenance from outside the room (outside-in): maintainable components (filters, motors, valves) are placed in a service corridor → cleanroom operations are not affected, but building cost is higher

In a sterile CDMO, Grade A/B areas almost always use the "maintain from outside" strategy.

Key CDMO Application: The Impact of Microenvironment Technology

RABS (Restricted Access Barrier System) and isolators, mentioned in the source text, have a major impact on HVAC design:

  • Traditional open process: the whole room needs Grade A → the HVAC must provide laminar flow over the whole room
  • RABS: Grade A inside the barrier, Grade B background → the room HVAC only needs to maintain Grade B
  • Isolator: Grade A inside the isolator, background can drop to Grade C/D → HVAC complexity and cost are greatly reduced

Conclusion: microenvironment technology is not only an upgrade in sterility assurance but also an important strategy for optimizing HVAC cost.

Note: Regulatory Risks of Modular Construction

The source text specifically warns that if modules are prefabricated in different countries/regions, differences in local regulations must be taken into account. For example:

  • A module prefabricated in China and installed in Taiwan → must comply with the fire, electrical and building codes of both places
  • European ATEX explosion-protection standards vs. the US NEC Class/Division classification → the two systems do not correspond exactly

These must be confirmed early in design; otherwise, if non-compliance is found after the modules arrive on site, the cost of retrofitting is extremely high.

2.4.2 Architectural Considerations

2.4.2 Architectural Considerations

HVAC engineers and the project architects should coordinate HVAC on issues and considerations which affect both the architectural aspects of a project and HVAC systems. Problems in the construction, commissioning and qualification, operation, and maintenance of a facility may be avoided.

The materials of construction of a facility include:

  • Room Finishes: these should be cleanable, resistant to cleaning and sanitization chemicals, suitable for the environment, and be wear/bump resistant.
  • Flooring: appropriate flooring materials should be selected for an application. The technique and skills of flooring installers should be verified. Installing test patches of the materials and the techniques being considered may be used to evaluate their performance in a specific application. Poor flooring can add to airborne particle levels.

For further information, see relevant ISPE Baseline® Guides.

Construction methodologies for both architecture and HVAC designs should be coordinated:

  • Room tightness: where pressure differential is significant, floor to ceiling walls should be used. Hard (gypsum or gasketed, interlocking, steel or FRP panels) ceiling construction may be used for pressure-controlled spaces. In addition, air migration above a ceiling should be minimized between controlled and uncontrolled spaces. If RH is significant, reducing moisture migration through unsealed penetrations, drains, door seals, and porous wall materials should be addressed. Door specifications should address seals, windows, interlocks, construction of the door, actuation, direction of swing, and hardware.
  • To minimize air leakage, the gap between finished floor and the bottom of door should be uniform (typically approximately .125 to .5 inch (3 to 14 mm)) when closed. Door sweeps are typically not recommended for swinging doors in manufacturing spaces, because of their accumulation of dirt, scratching of the floor, and increased maintenance.
  • A commissioning test to verify room tightness (i.e., room leakage test or room integrity test per ISO 14644-3) should be considered.
  • The use of prefabricated modular facility construction techniques may impose additional restrictions on a HVAC design (e.g., design may be limited to equipment suppliers with which the module contractor has an established relationship; the size of AHUs may be limited to the size of a standard module). Owners should understand the limitations and preferences associated with each module supplier, for example:
    • duct and piping joints at each module interface, misalignment, and leakage potential
    • limited height
    • constraints on duct routing
    • tight access to mechanical spaces for service and removal/replacement
  • Where possible, service distribution and pipe work should be located outside a cleanroom in an adjacent utility space to promote better airflow patterns and to produce fewer pockets for dirt to accumulate. In addition, this location is helpful for the maintainability of equipment.
  • The effect of HVAC systems on programming and layout will vary depending on the type of facility. See Chapter 3.

Teaching Notes: Coordination Between Architecture and HVAC

Core Concept: Room Tightness

Room tightness is the physical basis of differential pressure control. If the room "leaks", no amount of supply air can maintain the pressure differential. Key points:

  • Walls: must be fully sealed from floor to ceiling, and the space above the ceiling must also be isolated
  • Door gaps: the gap at the bottom should be 3-14 mm and uniform
  • Door sweeps are not recommended: they collect dust, scrape the floor and add to the maintenance burden
  • All penetrations: places where ducts and cables pass through walls must be sealed

Analogy: Inflating a Tire

Maintaining room differential pressure is like inflating a tire:

  • If the tire has a hole (the room leaks), no matter how much air you pump in (how much supply air you provide), you cannot maintain the pressure
  • Fix the hole first (make sure the room is airtight), then add the right amount of air (design a suitable supply airflow)
  • The ISO 14644-3 room leakage test is "checking the tire for holes"

Important Reminder: Floor Quality Affects Air Quality

The source text raises an easily overlooked point: Poor flooring can add to airborne particle levels.

Reason: if an epoxy floor is poorly applied (bubbles, cracks, peeling), it continues to generate particles in use. It is advisable to do a "test patch" to verify workmanship before full installation. In a CDMO, floor problems often only emerge after operation begins, and repairing them requires stopping production, which is very costly.

CDMO Practice: HVAC Limitations of Modular Construction

Modular construction has become increasingly common in recent years as CDMOs expand rapidly, but HVAC design must take note of the following:

  • AHU size limits: constrained by the transport dimensions of standard modules, the AHU may need to be split into several smaller units
  • Module interfaces: duct connections where two modules join are the biggest leakage risk points
  • Maintenance space: mechanical spaces within modules are usually cramped, making it difficult to replace large components
  • Duct routing: modular design offers far less flexibility in duct routing than conventional construction
2.4.3 AFD and AF&ID

2.4.3 AFD and AF&ID

Once functional relationships between areas are established along with their HVAC requirements, and product contamination and operator risks are identified, a simple AFD can be created. Critical components of filtration or parameter monitoring systems also may have been identified, and provide the initial elements of an AF&ID. (On completion, an AF&ID should show all instrumentation.)

An AF&ID may be considered the HVAC version of a P&ID. For a definition of P&ID, see Appendix 12.

An AF&ID usually will include:

  • instrumentation with tag numbers
  • equipment with tag numbers
  • control and manual valves/dampers with tag numbers
  • duct and piping, sizes, and identification references
  • vents, drains, fittings (e.g., reducers, increasers), sample points
  • flow directions
  • control inputs and outputs, interlocks
  • safety and regulatory requirements, including seismic category
  • annunciation inputs
  • supplier and contractor interfaces
  • identification of components and subsystems delivered by others, i.e., system boundaries

This should be supplemented by documentation of intended physical sequence of the equipment, startup, and operational information.

An AF&ID typically does not include:

  • instrument root valves
  • control relays
  • manual switches
  • equipment capacity
  • pressure temperature and flow data

An AFD will usually include:

  • ductwork
  • major HVAC equipment with tag numbers
  • valves and dampers that affect operation of the system, including balancing dampers
  • interconnections with other systems
  • system ratings and operational values as a minimum, normal and maximum flow, temperature, and pressure

An AFD typically does not include:

  • duct classification and material
  • line numbers
  • minor bypass duct
  • isolation and shutoff dampers
  • access points
  • safety and regulatory requirements, including seismic category

As there is no standardized in its approach, organizations may have "standard practices" that fall between AFDs and AF&IDs.

An AFD/AF&ID may be used as a master "record" that is maintained on an ongoing basis for regulatory purposes. The master record AFD/AF&ID should include:

  • the volumetric airflows to the rooms and acceptable tolerances
  • the design and operating limits for room temperature and humidity
  • area classifications
  • airflow directions/pressure differentials and infiltration/exfiltration
  • the process flow
  • critical instruments

Note: References pipe and ductwork routing (dimensional) drawings may be included in the list of requirements for an 'as built' record drawing, but these are not considered to be critical for an HVAC application.

Other drawings, such as installation drawings which are kept for engineering record purposes, may be updated on an 'as needed' basis.

A nomenclature for "tag numbers" shown on AF&IDs should be established to help improve understanding between designers, contractors, and operators. Industry systems, such as the tagging nomenclature established by ISA, commonly are used. For example, in ISA TE-209 is a Temperature Sensing Element (TE) on control loop 209 or room 209.

As the AF&ID develops, a description of how a HVAC system satisfies User Requirements can be developed (i.e., the 'functional design'). Programmers of the HVAC control and monitoring systems, commissioning personnel, and regulators who need to understand the role of the HVAC system in protecting product should find this helpful.

Teaching Notes: Differences and Applications of AFD and AF&ID

Analogy: Different Views in Google Maps

The relationship between AFD and AF&ID is like different zoom levels in Google Maps:

  • AFD = zoomed-out view: you can see the main roads (ducts), interchanges (AHUs) and cities (rooms), but not the traffic lights and road signs
  • AF&ID = zoomed-in view: every traffic light (sensor), road sign (label) and lane marking (valve/damper) is clearly shown

For a long-distance drive the zoomed-out view (AFD) is enough, but city navigation needs the zoomed-in view (AF&ID).

Important: The AF&ID as the Regulatory Master Record

The source text emphasizes that the AF&ID can serve as the regulatory master record for ongoing maintenance. This means:

  • Any change to the HVAC system must be reflected in an update to the AF&ID
  • During a regulatory inspection, inspectors will ask to see the AF&ID to understand the system design
  • The Master Record AF&ID must include: airflows, temperature and humidity limits, area classification, differential pressure directions and critical instruments

Note: routing drawings for ducts are not considered critical documents for HVAC applications and can be updated when needed.

ISA Tag Nomenclature

The source text gives an example from the ISA tagging system: TE-209 = Temperature Sensing Element, located in loop 209 or room 209.

Common ISA tag prefixes for HVAC:

  • TE = Temperature Element
  • TT = Temperature Transmitter
  • PT = Pressure Transmitter
  • PDT = Pressure Differential Transmitter
  • FT = Flow Transmitter
  • ME = Moisture Element

A uniform naming convention lets designers, contractors and operators "speak the same language".

Practice Questions

  1. Your plant is about to be inspected by the FDA. The inspector asks to see the "HVAC system control strategy document". Would you provide the AFD or the AF&ID? Why?
  2. If you need to add a differential pressure sensor to an existing Grade B corridor, which documents need to be updated? Should the change control follow the GMP or the GEP route?
  3. The source text states that the AF&ID does not include "equipment capacity" and "pressure temperature and flow data". In which documents should this information be recorded?

Core Concept: AFD vs. AF&ID

A simple way to tell the two drawings apart:

The AF&ID is the HVAC version of the P&ID and is one of the most important engineering documents of the whole system.

Section Summary

  • The essence of HVAC risk assessment: break the system down into components and assess each one's impact on CPPs/CQAs. The key criterion is "whether a failure can be detected immediately": failures that can be detected immediately fall under Engineering Change Control, and those that cannot (such as HEPA filters) fall under Quality Change Control.
  • The four-step risk assessment approach: define the CPPs → define the system boundary → define how they are monitored → define how they are achieved and how failures are detected. Each step needs input from Quality, Process and Engineering together.
  • Application of the impact assessment table (Table 2.2): fill in Critical Y/N room by room and parameter by parameter; its core value is promoting cross-functional dialogue. AHU internal parameters are usually Non-Critical (except supply airflow).
  • Three principles of facility planning: keep the cleanroom area as small as possible (cost-effectiveness), do not let flows cross (separate personnel and material flows), and maintain from outside the room (avoid contaminating the cleanroom). Microenvironment technology (RABS/isolator) can greatly reduce HVAC complexity and cost.
  • Coordination of architecture and HVAC: room tightness is the basis of differential pressure control. Floor quality affects air quality. Modular construction places several limitations on HVAC design, which must be confirmed early in design.
  • AFD vs. AF&ID: the AFD is the overview air flow diagram (similar to a PFD) and the AF&ID is the detailed air flow and instrumentation diagram (similar to a P&ID). The AF&ID can serve as the regulatory Master Record, and any system change must be reflected in it. The ISA tag nomenclature ensures consistent communication among all parties.
2

Chapter 2: 3. Design Considerations

p47-p80

ISPE Good Practice Guide: HVAC | p45 - p53

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the core principles of HVAC design - how physical segregation, the pressure cascade and dedicated AHUs prevent cross-contamination
  • Master the design considerations for heating, cooling and humidity control, and why solvent areas must use 100% outside air (once-through) systems
  • Understand exhaust and containment strategies for hazardous materials (solvents, highly potent compounds), including LEV, bag-in/bag-out filters and explosion-protection requirements
  • Distinguish the HVAC design differences between the API wet end and dry end, and understand when a cleanroom classification is needed
  • Recognize the different HVAC needs of upstream and downstream biologics processes
  • Understand the advantages, disadvantages and suitable applications of outside air pretreatment
3.1 Introduction

Original Text

This chapter is intended to assist HVAC system design and commissioning personnel; providing suggestions and a selection of typical schematics.

Specific regulatory requirements are covered in the relevant ISPE Baseline Guides (Reference 13, Appendix 12). As there is no Baseline Guide for medical devices, a brief overview is provided in Appendix 3.

Air handling systems should provide physical separation to prevent airborne cross contamination between products. Cross contamination control can be achieved with stringent air filtration, by using only once-through air, or by the use of separate (dedicated) air handling units. Separate air handling units may be used for different product areas to prevent cross contamination via ductwork, and are often used to segregate different building functions, such as:

  • production
  • production support
  • warehouse
  • administration
  • mechanical areas

Within production areas for a given product, the cost of further segregation may be justified for various unit operations, e.g., upstream cell culture versus downstream purification, pre- versus post-viral processing, or aseptic filling. See the appropriate facility Baseline Guide for considerations (Reference 13, Appendix 12).

Manufacturing areas supporting key unit operations usually require maximum on-stream reliability. The air-handling units supporting these areas may be configured for partial operation during routine maintenance operations to support areas still in production. Shutdowns for routine maintenance are permissible for specific product forms, while not in production.

"It should be noted that simplicity of design often assures greater uptime and compliance with fewer maintenance procedures."

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Three HVAC Segregation Strategies

Cross-contamination is one of the most serious risks in GMP manufacturing. HVAC systems use three main strategies to prevent it:

  • Rigorous air filtration: use HEPA filters in the recirculation system to remove particles and active ingredients
  • Once-through air (100% outside air system): air is used once and then exhausted, never recirculated; suitable for solvent or highly potent compound areas
  • Dedicated AHU: provide independent air-handling systems for different product areas, eliminating cross-contamination at the ductwork level

In practice, these three strategies are often combined to give layered protection.

Analogy

Think of a hospital: the operating theater has its own air-handling system (dedicated AHU) and does not share it with general wards; infectious disease wards use once-through air exhaust to keep pathogens from spreading through the ductwork to other floors. A pharmaceutical plant follows exactly the same HVAC logic - areas of different "risk levels" need different levels of air segregation.

Key Notes

Simple design = high reliability: the guide specifically stresses that "simplicity of design often assures greater uptime". This is very practical advice - an over-complicated HVAC system may look perfect but needs frequent maintenance and has many failure points, which actually reduces production stability. In a CDMO, AHU downtime directly affects customer batch schedules, and the loss can far exceed the cost of the equipment itself.

Practical Application

When a CDMO evaluates a new project, its HVAC segregation capability directly determines whether it can run several customers' products at the same time. With only one shared AHU, two different APIs cannot be produced in adjacent rooms at the same time. Investing first in dedicated AHUs when expanding a facility can therefore greatly improve capacity utilization and scheduling flexibility.

Practice Questions

  1. Why do biologics plants often use different AHUs for the upstream cell culture area and the downstream purification area?
  2. How is "partial operation during routine maintenance" achieved in practice? How should an AHU be configured so that part of it can keep running during maintenance?
3.2 General Design Considerations

3.2.1 Heating and Cooling

Original Text

  • Heating coils may be required for air handler systems in cold climates with higher percentages of outside air.
  • Energy recovery may be justifiable. Enthalpy wheels may be justifiable for non-production areas.
  • Unidirectional flow hoods that have recirculation may be supplied with a small percentage of fresh (or cooled) air to offset fan heat. This is usually not a problem in smaller UFHs.
  • Use of energy conserving enclosures such as glove boxes is encouraged.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Balancing Energy Efficiency and GMP

Enthalpy wheel: an energy recovery device that recovers both temperature and humidity energy from the exhaust air. Because a small amount of cross-leakage between exhaust and supply air is possible, it carries a cross-contamination risk in production areas and is therefore recommended only for non-production areas.

Glove box: a more energy-efficient alternative to containing the whole room. Only a small volume needs temperature and humidity control and air exchange, rather than the entire room.

Analogy

An enthalpy wheel is like a hotel's hot-water recovery system - the outgoing hot water first passes through a heat exchanger to preheat the cold water, saving energy. But if the drain water might contain contaminants, you would never let it touch the drinking water line. Likewise, exhaust air from a production area may contain product particles or solvents and is not suitable for recovery with an enthalpy wheel.

Key Notes

The fan of a UFH (unidirectional flow hood) generates heat, which raises the temperature inside the hood after long operation. The effect is minor for a small UFH, but a large UFH (for example, at a freeze dryer loading area) needs a small amount of supplementary cooling air, otherwise the quality of temperature-sensitive products may be affected.

3.2.2 Humidity

Original Text

  • Humidification should be considered for cold or arid climates where static control is a concern.
  • Desiccant dehumidification and post cooling coils should be considered for low humidity room control (i.e., powder handling). Desiccant dehumidifiers should be used sparingly, usually when a dew point below 40°F (5°C) is needed, because of high capital and energy cost. If humid outdoor air can leak directly into a processing room, however, cooling/condensing coils alone may be incapable of meeting room humidity requirements and a chemical dehumidifier may be needed. Room pressurization may be considered to improve this situation.
  • Exposed powder products may require RH below 40% to prevent absorption of moisture. If RH is too low (below 20 to 30%), workers may experience irritation of throat and eyes.
  • Where low RH is required, special attention may be given to sealing the return duct systems to prevent inward air leakage from uncontrolled spaces and resultant high humidity.
  • Humidifier locations can vary with the most common being AFTER final filters in the AHU, and before cooling coils in climates where cooling and humidification are unlikely to occur simultaneously. Designs with humidifiers before fans should be sure that water droplets do not impinge on the fan inlet, possibly leading to corrosion. Humidifiers are covered in more detail in Chapter 5 of this Guide.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Upper and Lower Humidity Limits

RH (relative humidity) control is critical in powder handling:

  • RH > 40%: powder absorbs moisture and cakes, affecting flowability and dose uniformity
  • RH < 20-30%: operators suffer throat and eye discomfort, and static electricity problems worsen
  • The sweet spot: 30-40% RH is usually the ideal range for powder handling

Desiccant dehumidifier: consider one only when a dew point below 5°C is required, because both capital and energy costs are high.

Key Notes

Return duct sealing is the hidden killer: the guide specifically mentions sealing of the return duct system - if the return ductwork has gaps, humid air from uncontrolled areas leaks in and the room humidity goes out of control. This is especially important in Taiwan's humid environment; be sure to verify the airtightness of return ducts during C&Q.

Humidifier location: the most common position is after the final filter of the AHU. If it is placed before the fan, water droplets may hit the fan blades and cause corrosion - a mistake new designers often make.

Formula and Calculation

Ideal humidity range for powder handling:
  Product protection limit: RH ≤ 40% (prevents moisture uptake)
  Personnel comfort limit: RH ≥ 20-30% (prevents mucous membrane irritation)
  Practical target: 30% ≤ RH ≤ 40%

Dew point conversion reference:
  40°F = 4.4°C (threshold for using a desiccant dehumidifier)

Practice Questions

  1. In a climate where cooling and humidification are unlikely to occur at the same time, why can the humidifier be placed before the cooling coil?
  2. Summer outdoor RH in Taiwan often reaches 80-90%. If a powder handling room needs RH < 35%, which dehumidification strategy would you recommend, and why?

3.2.3 Hazardous Materials and their Removal

Original Text

  • Where solvents are handled, 100% exhaust (once-through) systems are recommended. Oxygen depletion and LEL monitors may be employed, as appropriate, to assure that dangerous conditions do not occur, especially when using recirculated systems. Such systems should also comply with fire and building codes.
  • Once-through air systems are common where potent compounds are handled in the open.
  • Recirculation of room air is not allowed by most codes and insurers when solvents may be present above 25% of LEL. Where solvent use is occasional and small in volume, return air ducts should be equipped with control device sensors to switch the system to 100% outdoor air in the event of a spill.
  • There may be specific requirements for storage and handling of hazardous materials, e.g., once-through ventilation and high extract rate capability in the event of smoke detection (see applicable Fire/Safety Codes).
  • The storage of incompatible materials may dictate specific HVAC design requirements (see applicable Fire/Safety Codes).
  • Exhaust should be hard connected wherever possible. Movable arms (trunks) should be provided for point exhaust sources that do not support hard duct connections or fixed exhaust hoods. These supplemental point exhausts should be served by an independent exhaust box (where possible) or connected directly to the main (with a volume damper or blast gate).
  • Exhaust ductwork does not normally require insulation except if part of a heat recovery system or where internal condensation is possible (high concentration of corrosive vapor).
  • The use of emergency power for exhaust systems should be considered on a case-by-case basis. In multi-fan manifolded systems (such as in laboratories or API chemical facilities), the use of emergency power for at least one fan should be considered.
  • Where emergency power is not provided for exhaust fan(s) alarms should be connected to emergency power or furnished with UPS to signal exhaust failure. (Recommended for fume hoods in laboratories without room pressure monitoring.)
  • Provide LEV (Local Exhaust Ventilation) for control of fugitive active dusts or aerosols in the room; LEV should be provided at emission points and equipment break points. Containment devices with leak free equipment connections are recommended.
  • Provide LEV for containment devices, such as glove boxes, isolators, and powder transfer equipment.
  • A testing and preventive maintenance program should ensure the integrity of exhaust cleaning system and LEV performance.
  • Dust collection systems designed to allow removal of contaminated media without contact or exposure with harmful compounds (e.g., bag in/bag out filters) should be considered where handling potent compounds.
  • Spark-proof exhaust equipment should be provided when serving process areas where flammables are handled. As a minimum, exhaust fans should be AMCA Type B spark resistant construction.
  • Explosion proof or intrinsically safe electrical components should be provided in potentially flammable exhaust air stream. Non-explosion proof fan motors may be used if outside the air stream.
  • Wherever exhaust to atmosphere is shown, the contents of the exhaust stream should be evaluated, e.g., material, form (solid, vapor, etc.), expected quantity, and times when exhausted. Scrubbers, dust collection, thermal oxidation, carbon adsorption, and "polishing" filters may be required to protect the outdoor environment and prevent re-entrainment into HVAC systems. If used, energy from exhaust streams should be recovered before scrubbers in order to capture as much of the wasted energy as possible. The recovery unit's construction should deal with the contents of the exhaust stream.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Hierarchy of Hazardous Material Exhaust

This section covers two types of risk - solvents (flammability/explosion risk) and highly potent compounds (personnel exposure risk). The HVAC responses differ but are complementary:

  • LEL (Lower Explosive Limit): recirculation is prohibited once solvent vapor concentration reaches 25% or more of the LEL
  • LEV (Local Exhaust Ventilation): extract directly at the point where dust or aerosol is released, preventing it from spreading through the whole room
  • OEL (Occupational Exposure Limit): highly potent compounds require closed handling + LEV + HEPA treatment of the exhaust
  • Bag-in/bag-out filter: the filter can be changed without opening the housing, protecting maintenance staff from hazardous dust

Analogy

Think of a kitchen range hood:

  • LEV = the hood directly above the stove - removes the fumes right at the source
  • Once-through system = all the air in the whole kitchen goes out and none is recirculated - what you do when frying (solvent vapor present)
  • Hard connect = fixed duct connection vs. movable arm duct - a fixed connection seals better; a movable arm is the fallback when a fixed connection is not feasible
  • Bag-in/bag-out = like replacing the sealed bag for hospital infectious waste - handlers never come into contact with the contents

Key Notes

Emergency power is a life-or-death decision: whether exhaust systems need emergency power must be evaluated case by case. But the guide is clear: even if the exhaust fan itself is not on emergency power, the alarm system must be on a UPS. The reason is simple - if a power failure stops the exhaust and nobody knows, solvent vapor can build up to explosive concentrations.

Exhaust treatment is not optional: every airstream discharged to atmosphere must be evaluated for its contents, and scrubbers, HEPA filters, activated carbon or other treatment installed as needed. Energy recovery should be arranged before the scrubber to maximize recovery efficiency.

Practical Application

When a CDMO evaluates whether to take on an API synthesis project involving solvent reactions, the HVAC retrofit cost is often the deciding factor. If the existing facility uses recirculated air, switching to once-through means: (1) a much larger exhaust volume, requiring a larger AHU and more chilling capacity; (2) additional explosion-proof electrical equipment; (3) investment in exhaust treatment equipment (such as scrubbers or activated carbon towers). These costs must be reflected in the quotation to the customer.

Practice Questions

  1. Why does exhaust ductwork usually not need insulation, except when it carries corrosive vapors?
  2. The guide requires fans to be at least AMCA Type B spark-resistant - explain why an ordinary fan is unsafe in a flammable environment.
  3. What does "re-entrainment into HVAC systems" mean? How can it be prevented?

3.2.4 Product Contamination Control

Original Text

  • If near a production area, schemes using return air from a general area to a common plenum (such as to the plant room) may create pressure control problems in the production area.
  • Manufacturing rooms should be protected from migration of contaminants or solvent vapors via the use of room pressure or differential airflows. Where multiple products are handled concurrently, HEPA air filtration is recommended; once-through air or dedicated air handling systems for each product area also are options.
  • Monitoring and alarm of direction of airflow or DP (Differential Pressure) (for classified areas) is suggested where airborne cross-contamination is an issue.
  • A remotely operated or automatic damper may be provided in the return air duct from each room as a means of setting the desired pressure differentials. Duct pressure control also may be needed. Simple facilities may be balanced successfully using only manual dampers, especially if terminal HEPA filters do not load quickly or differentially, and therefore, change supply airflow (i.e., are preceded by high efficiency filters in the AHU).
  • If manual/remotely operated dampers are used, the damper controls should be tamper-proof or concealed in a lockable cabinet accessible only to authorized personnel. A DP gauge should be provided for each room adjacent to the damper controls to facilitate balancing.
  • Packed silencers are not recommended where they can harbor contaminants and viable organisms.
  • Low returns in CNC (Controlled Not Classified) processing areas (with local monitoring, equivalent to EU Grade D) are recommended and should be located behind process equipment where applicable and where clearance is sufficient to allow proper air extraction from the space. CNC areas (airflow filtration on supply air with personnel access control) do not require low level returns, but can be used if deemed necessary by the design team.
  • Grade 5 (Grade A) rooms and large UFHs may be unavoidable (such as for manual multiple lyophilizer loading) but are not recommended because:
    • They place the operator in the clean space with the product. Special procedures are needed and should be verified with airflow visualization (smoke tests).
    • Airflow pattern tests may reveal a "dead zone" near the area of the room farthest from low wall air returns, often in the center of the room where critical activities are located. This problem is solved in the electronics industry with perforated floors and a return air plenum below the floor. However, this solution creates a cleaning issue and is a potential harbor for bacteria so it is not recommended for pharmaceutical cleanrooms. A low wall return below a lyophilizer door can improve patterns in front of the door.
    • If the supply air filters are too high, airflow patterns can greatly deteriorate before the air reaches the critical site. Open Grade 5 areas should be kept small with HEPA filters as near as possible to critical sites.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Differential Pressure and Air Flow Direction Control

Pressure cascade is the core design principle of pharmaceutical HVAC - air always flows from "clean" to "less clean". It is achieved through:

  • DP (differential pressure): the clean area is usually 10-15 Pa higher than the corridor, ensuring that air flows outward when a door is opened rather than leaking inward
  • Return duct damper control: differential pressure is set by adjusting the return air volume of each room. Automatic dampers are precise but complex; manual dampers are simple but must be tamper-proof
  • Air flow direction monitoring and alarms: classified areas must be continuously monitored for pressure differential direction, with an immediate alarm if it reverses

Analogy

The pressure cascade works like water flowing downhill - except here "air flows toward lower pressure". Imagine a three-storey building: the top floor (cleanest area) has the highest water pressure, the second floor medium, the ground floor the lowest. Valves (dampers) sit between floors, so when a door opens, water only flows from top to bottom. If someone tampers with the valve on one floor, the flow direction could reverse - which is why dampers must be locked.

Key Notes

A Grade A whole room is a choice of last resort: the guide states clearly that Grade 5 (Grade A) for an entire room is "not recommended", and gives three main reasons:

  1. People next to the product: operators are the biggest source of particles, and smoke tests must verify that the air flow effectively separates people from the product
  2. Dead zones: air flow dead spots often occur in the middle of the room, which is exactly where the critical operation takes place. The electronics industry solves this with perforated floors, but this is not feasible in a pharmaceutical plant (cleaning difficulties + bacterial growth)
  3. HEPA height: the higher the ceiling, the more turbulent the unidirectional flow when it reaches the working surface. HEPA filters should be as close to the critical working surface as possible

This is why the modern trend is to replace Grade A whole rooms with RABS or isolators.

Terminology: CNC vs Classified

CNC (Controlled Not Classified): the supply air is filtered and personnel are controlled, roughly equivalent to EU Grade D, but particle classification certification is not required. The difference from a Classified area is lower monitoring and verification requirements, while the level of environmental control is similar. This is a pragmatic choice for API handling areas (non-sterile).

Practice Questions

  1. Why is a packed silencer unsuitable for pharmaceutical environments? What is the problem with its material and construction?
  2. Why does the guide recommend placing low-level return air grilles behind the equipment? What would be the effect of placing them directly opposite the operator?
  3. When freeze dryer loading requires a Grade A environment, why should the low-level return be placed beneath the freeze dryer door?

3.2.5 General AHU and Control Considerations

Original Text

  • Air systems may recirculate with the minimum outdoor air necessary to maintain pressure relationships, in support areas, and where no solvents or potent compounds are handled.
  • HEPA filtration should be considered to prevent cross-contamination and limit operator exposure in manufacturing area recirculation systems.
  • Once-through systems do not require HEPA filtration for cross-contamination control.
  • Recirculation of return air from production areas as supply to non-production areas is not recommended.
  • The most common air handling system for pharmaceutical production is the Constant Volume (CV) terminal reheat type.
  • The supply fan should be equipped with variable dampers, vanes, or speed controls that can be reset in order to maintain design airflow for the life of the air filters (whose pressure drop increases with time).
  • Risk assessment should be performed to determine the need for fan redundancy (parallel fans or multiple plug fans in the AHU). Use of standby electric power systems to maintain fans and design pressure differentials in the event of local power failures should be considered.
  • 100% outside air handling units are prone to freezing in preheat coils; variable temperature constant internal flow volume pumped preheat coils or Internal Face and Bypass (IFB) steam coils help to reduce this risk. Propylene glycol solution for preheating also may prevent freeze-ups.
  • Backup power for monitoring systems to determine if critical parameters are compromised during a power outage should be considered.
  • Successful HVAC systems may not have DP controllers, constant air volume boxes, or HEPA prefilters, etc. The need for complexity and its added cost should be justified.
  • Access doors are suggested wherever maintenance or testing is required. Minimum locations include access to key air handler components and in-duct sensors. Access doors provide a route for leakage and contamination, so keep their use to a minimum.

For further information on additional equipment considerations, see Chapter 5 of this Guide.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Key AHU Design Choices

CV terminal reheat (constant volume with terminal reheat) is the most common HVAC type in pharmaceutical plants:

  • Constant volume: ensures a stable air change rate in every room
  • Terminal reheat: the AHU first cools and dehumidifies all air to the lowest required temperature, then heats it to the target temperature at the terminal of each room
  • Advantages: stable differential pressure, simple control, high reliability
  • Disadvantages: higher energy consumption (cool first, then reheat)

Fan redundancy: whether dual or multiple fans are needed depends on risk assessment - if AHU downtime would lead to batch rejection, redundancy is economically justified.

Analogy

CV terminal reheat is like a central air conditioner that first cools the whole building to 16°C, and then each room heats itself to 22°C. It looks like a waste of energy, but the benefit is that the temperature and humidity of each room do not affect one another, giving precise control. It is like freezing all the ingredients first and then thawing them individually for cooking - an extra step, but consistent quality.

Key Notes

"Justify the complexity" - this phrase deserves to be engraved on the heart of every HVAC engineer. The guide says directly that a successful HVAC system may not need pressure controllers, constant volume boxes or HEPA prefilters at all. Every added component adds a failure point and a maintenance requirement. When choosing a solution, always ask first: "What problem would occur if we did not add this?" If the answer is "none", do not add it.

Filter pressure drop increases over time: this is a problem novices often overlook. A new filter has a low pressure drop and high air flow; an old filter has a high pressure drop and low air flow. If the fan has no variable speed drive or variable damper, room air flow gradually falls as the filter loads, and the differential pressure changes with it.

Practical Application

In the annual maintenance plan of a CDMO facility, judging when to change AHU filters is critical. Changing too early wastes cost; changing too late gives insufficient air flow that affects differential pressure. We recommend building a "filter pressure drop trend chart" - record the pressure drop regularly and schedule replacement when it approaches 80% of the design margin. This data is also an important indicator for energy management.

Practice Questions

  1. Why should "production area return air not be used as supply air for non-production areas"? What risks might arise if a warehouse used return air from a production area?
  2. Why is a 100% outside air AHU prone to coil freezing in cold climates? How does the IFB steam coil solve this problem?
  3. Access doors are both necessary and a leakage risk - how can the design balance "maintainability" and "tightness"?

3.2.6 Application of Outside Air Pretreatment

Original Text

It may be more energy efficient to pre-treat incoming outside air and supply it to one or more recirculation units, rather than overcooling or desiccant dehumidification of an entire recirculated air stream.

Applicability:

  • The desired mixed air condition should be established; there will be a limit to the achievable humidity levels.
  • The moisture load in the return air should be less than the desired mixed air condition (low internal latent load).
  • Outside air volume requirements should be sufficiently understood to size the pre-conditioning equipment.
  • Excursions above humidity setpoint, because of intermittent activities that create additional latent load (e.g., cleaning), should be tolerable.

Configuration Options:

  • Where internal sensible heat gains are low or where outside air is a large percentage of the total airflow, the pre-treated air may provide all cooling for a space. This configuration has a low first cost and low energy cost, but may lead to temperature variations within a controlled space. It should be employed only when the processes, systems, and environment are sufficiently understood.
  • Where multiple recirculation units are employed, a central pre-treatment system may provide outside air to all AHUs.
  • Coils in the recirculation airstream may be configured for sensible cooling only with fewer rows, lower air pressure drop, and no drainage pans. Alternatively, larger coils and drainage pans may be installed in the recirculation unit for flexibility and faster recovery from excursions.
  • The use of a small dehumidifier to provide pre-treated air at low moisture levels may eliminate the need for moisture reduction (via over-cooling and reheat) in the recirculation air stream.
  • It is recommended that air from the pretreatment system is introduced into the inlet of the recirculation system to ensure acceptable blending and temperature control, ease of balancing, and duct pressure control; however, it is possible to blend the air downstream of the recirculation unit.

Advantages:

  • eliminates wasted energy from overcooling and reheating or dehumidifying the entire recirculated airstream
  • lower first cost, because of elimination of drain pans, smaller (fewer rows) cooling coils, smaller dehumidifier (if applicable)
  • lower energy cost, because of lower air pressure drop over smaller cooling coils
  • effective where most humidity is from external sources

Disadvantages:

  • may not be able to achieve low humidity, where required, because of internal latent heat gain or leakage into return air ducts from unconditioned spaces
  • has limited flexibility for later changes to conditions
  • may not be applicable if return humidity is too high (high internal latent load)
  • additional maintenance (for pretreatment equipment)
  • additional space required for pretreatment equipment and associated ductwork
  • if a desiccant dehumidifier is added to the pretreatment system, in place of over-cooling and preheat in recirculation, it increases complexity and may add a new type of equipment

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Outside Air Pretreatment vs Full-flow Dehumidification

The core logic of outside air pretreatment:

  • Traditional approach: mix all the return air and outside air, then cool and dehumidify it together → overcooling → reheating = high energy consumption
  • Pretreatment approach: deeply dehumidify only the outside air, which makes up 10-30% of the total air volume, then mix it with return air that is "already relatively dry" → the return air coil only needs to do sensible cooling → energy saved

The prerequisite is a low internal latent load - that is, the room itself does not generate a lot of moisture (for example, no open washing operations).

Analogy

Imagine you have a pot of soup whose saltiness you need to control:

  • Traditional approach: every time you add water, you re-season the whole pot (equivalent to dehumidifying all the air together and then reheating it)
  • Pretreatment approach: the newly added water (outside air) is first filtered and diluted separately before being poured into the soup, and the soup itself needs only slight adjustment (the return air only gets temperature control)

The latter is more efficient, but only if "the soup itself does not get saltier as it cooks" (the room does not continuously generate latent load).

Key Notes

Taiwan's climate is particularly suited to outside air pretreatment: summer outside air in Taiwan has a very high moisture content (20+ g/kg), whereas the moisture content of indoor return air is usually lower. Deeply dehumidifying only the outside air can save a great deal of energy. Note, however:

  • Washing operations (rinsing equipment with WFI) suddenly increase the room latent load, and the pretreatment system may not respond in time
  • If the return ductwork draws in humid air from uncontrolled areas, the whole strategy fails
  • It is advisable to retain the drain pan of the return air coil as backup capacity for "abnormal recovery"

Energy Comparison

Traditional full-flow dehumidification (assuming 20% outside air, 80% return air):
  Cooling load = 100% air volume × (mixed enthalpy - target enthalpy)
  Reheat load = 100% air volume × (target temperature - cooled temperature)

Outside air pretreatment:
  Pretreatment cooling = 20% air volume × (outside air enthalpy - target enthalpy)  ← treats outside air only
  Return air sensible cooling = 80% air volume × (return air temperature - target temperature)  ← no dehumidification needed
  Reheat ≈ 0 (because there is no overcooling)

Energy saving potential: typically 30-50% saving in cooling energy

Practice Questions

  1. Why does the guide recommend introducing pretreated air at the inlet of the recirculation unit rather than downstream of it? Think from the perspective of air mixing and control.
  2. If an API powder handling room needs RH < 30% but also has regular WFI washing operations (high latent load), is an outside air pretreatment solution feasible? Why?
3.3 Air Flow Diagrams by Facility Type

Original Text

The typical basic AFDs included in this section were developed as examples and may not be appropriate for all products or facilities. Some instrumentation (as found on an AF&ID) is shown. The detail of design and the extent of control are meant for example only and do not constitute recommended practice.

Note that RHC stands for Reheat Coil, and Constant Volume Damper (CVD) is an airflow control device to hold air flow constant.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: AFD and AF&ID

AFD (Air Flow Diagram): a simplified HVAC system diagram showing only air flow direction, filter locations and major components, used at the conceptual design stage.

AF&ID (Air Flow & Instrumentation Diagram): the detailed version, including all sensors, control valves, damper positions, alarm points and so on. It plays the same role as the P&ID does for piping systems.

RHC (reheat coil): the heating element at the terminal of each room.

CVD (constant volume damper): a device that automatically adjusts its opening to maintain a constant air volume.

Key Notes

The guide specifically states that these diagrams "do not constitute recommended practice" - they are teaching examples only and cannot be copied directly into an actual design. Every project needs a customized design based on product characteristics, regulatory requirements, local climate and facility conditions.

3.4 Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs) - Wet End

Original Text

Figure 3.1: Chemical APIs (AFD schematic — not available for embedding)

3.4.1 System Design Considerations

  • Product-specific requirements are covered in the ISPE Baseline Guide on APIs (Reference 13, Appendix 12).
  • Air systems should be once-through where solvents or potent compounds are handled in the open. Additional emergency ventilation may be required by local code or by insurers, activated by manual "help/evacuate" alarm or by sensors.
  • Where processes are proven closed, air recirculation may be considered with LEL monitoring in return air to detect a flammable spill. If processes are in closed temperature controlled vessels, room HVAC should satisfy operator comfort requirements.
  • Use of adequate dilution ventilation and exhaust on emergency power may be used to minimize electrical classification requirements in some jurisdictions. AHU should have MERV 7 followed by MERV 13 filters for good housekeeping.
  • Manufacturing rooms should be fitted with low or combination high/low returns.
  • Provide LEV for dry product addition sites, drum handling, manways, and spills in wet areas. The use of charging isolators or booths to minimize the flammable and potent/hazardous material exposure in the room should be considered.
  • Aqueous chemistry usually does not require once-through air; the AF&ID for OSD may be applied in these areas.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: HVAC Design Logic for the API Wet End

The API wet end is the chemical synthesis stage, typically involving solvent use, chemical reactions and intermediate handling. The core HVAC considerations are safety (solvent explosion risk) and personnel protection (exposure to highly potent compounds):

  • Open operation + solvents → must be once-through (100% exhaust)
  • Closed process → recirculation is possible, but LEL monitoring is needed as a safety net
  • Aqueous chemistry → no solvent risk; general OSD-level HVAC can be used

MERV 7 + MERV 13 is a "good housekeeping" level filtration configuration - HEPA is not required because the API wet end is usually not a cleanroom.

Analogy

The HVAC of an API wet end is like the ventilation design of a gas station:

  • Open fueling area (open operation): full ventilation with no recirculation, because gasoline vapor poses an explosion risk
  • Sealed tank area (closed process): partial recirculation can be allowed, but gas detectors are needed
  • Car wash area (aqueous chemistry): only water, no flammability risk, ordinary ventilation is enough

Key Notes

Charging isolator/booth is a key concept in this section. In the API wet end, one of the most hazardous operations is charging - opening the reactor manway to add solid raw materials. At this point large amounts of solvent vapor escape and dust may also spread. Using a charging isolator or booth confines this high-risk operation to an enclosed space and greatly reduces the room-level HVAC burden.

Low-level return grilles are standard in API areas: because solvent vapors are heavier than air (most organic solvents have a vapor density > 1), they settle near the floor, and low-level returns remove them effectively.

Practical Application

When a CDMO evaluates an API synthesis project, it must confirm the types and quantities of solvents used in the process. If the main reaction is aqueous chemistry (such as a biocatalytic reaction), the HVAC retrofit cost is very low. But if large quantities of organic solvents (such as THF, DCM or methanol) are involved, a once-through system, LEL monitoring, explosion-proof electrical equipment and emergency exhaust are needed - all major capital investments. Be sure to include the HVAC retrofit cost at the quotation stage.

Practice Questions

  1. Why does the API wet end need only MERV 7 + MERV 13 filtration rather than HEPA? Think from the perspective of product risk.
  2. What does the statement "Dilution ventilation on emergency power may minimize electrical classification requirements" mean? Why can adequate dilution ventilation lower the explosion-protection classification requirements?
3.5 Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs) - Dry End

Original Text

Figure 3.2: Final API Dry-End Schematic (Once-Through for Solvents or Potency) (AFD schematic — not available for embedding)

3.5.1 System Design Considerations
