  • Pressure bubble airlock: pressure bubble airlocks are recommended for areas using solvents, to prevent flammable vapors spreading to other parts of the building

Practice Questions

  1. What grade of HVAC should an assembly line for an implantable orthopedic device (such as an artificial joint) use? What if the device will undergo downstream gamma sterilization?
  2. Why must LEV exhaust in medical device manufacturing not be recirculated to the AHU? How is this similar to the rule for OSD facilities?

Section Summary

  • OSD non-potent: CNC environment, MERV 7+13/14 filtration, airlock isolation, LEV dust control. Concurrent multi-product needs double HEPA and pressure airlocks
  • OSD potent: closed containment is the first choice, 100% once-through air or double HEPA, BIBO filters, audible/visual alarms. Operator protection is as important as product protection
  • Aseptic processing: terminal HEPA (ceiling-mounted), pressure cascade, unidirectional airflow at 0.45 m/s, 24/7 operation, 304SS ductwork. The highest-level HVAC requirements in ISPE
  • Aseptic potent powder: isolator + dedicated HVAC resolves the "positive vs negative pressure" conflict. Blow-through AHU is used for low-humidity control
  • Packaging/labeling: primary packaging is equivalent to the manufacturing area standard; secondary packaging needs only CNC + comfort conditions
  • Laboratories: VAV system + fume hood integration is the core. Chemical laboratories negative, clean laboratories positive. Minimum 6 AC/hr, recommended 8-12 AC/hr
  • Sampling/dispensing: HVAC grade should match the downstream process needs. Downflow booths provide operator protection
  • Warehouse: USP controlled room temperature 15-30°C / MKT < 25°C. Temperature mapping is a basic requirement. Biologics need a cold chain
  • Process equipment integration: the isolator is a "green technology" that allows the background environment grade to be lowered. Depyrogenation tunnels, capping and lyophilizers all have special HVAC considerations
  • Medical devices: HVAC follows patient risk level, from packaging area standards to aseptic processing standards, depending on the device's intended use and downstream sterilization method
3

Chapter 3: 4. Design Review

p81-p88

ISPE Good Practice Guide: HVAC | p81 - p88

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the definitions and purpose of Design Review and Design Qualification (DQ), and their role in the HVAC system lifecycle
  • Master the seven objectives of design review, and why reviewing before construction greatly reduces cost and risk
  • Understand the logic for separating GEP review from GMP review, and when a formal Design Qualification (DQ) needs to be launched
  • Become familiar with the use cases and key review items of the four design review checklists, Table 4.1 to Table 4.4
  • Learn how to assemble a cross-functional design review team and use risk tools such as FMEA to strengthen design robustness
4.1 Design Review (Design Qualification)

Original Text

This chapter provides guidance on verifying that the design as issued for construction will meet the user requirements.

It is easier and more cost effective to change a design before it is constructed than during or after construction, and therefore, there is less impact on capital cost and schedule. As the design develops, input from all interested parties should be considered to avoid later changes.

The process of reviewing a design (drawings and specifications) as it develops from concept to issued-for-construction status has several objectives:

  • to ensure that a design follows preferred custom and practice
  • to ensure that the concepts proposed are capable of meeting the requirements defined in the User Requirement documentation, i.e., user expectations
  • to ensure that a design minimizes risk to product quality/patient safety
  • to ensure that a design is robust and will perform reliably and that performance can be documented
  • to ensure that a design proposed is cost effective
  • to ensure that design options, the life cycle costs, and the risks have been identified and addressed
  • where an end user has preferred suppliers, the review should confirm that these have been specified

Common practice is for a design to receive comments for the designer (engineer of record) to incorporate or provide a rationale for not incorporating. Users usually do not approve a design to avoid making design responsibility unclear.

For systems that may affect product quality, it is a common practice to split design reviews into two categories:

  1. engineering or technical reviews
  2. quality (or GMP) focused reviews

A final specific "quality" review usually is performed to confirm that the HVAC system (and the specified related conditions for the areas it serves (temperature, humidity, classification, DPs, etc.) comply with GMP regulations/organizational standards. This review may be called Design Qualification, allowing the statement to be formally made that the design as reviewed is fit for its intended use, as well as confirming that the user requirements are met.

It should be noted that there are regulations requiring this review. ICH Q7 suggests a design review and the European regulations state:

"The first element of the validation of new facilities, systems, or equipment could be design qualification (DQ)."
"The compliance of the design with GMP should be demonstrated and documented."

The process of reviewing and accepting a design to be released for construction or the overall review process also may be considered a qualification of the design, because it confirms that the user organization has reviewed the design (documented through the design review process) and agrees to release the design for implementation.

Once a design has been accepted as fit for its intended use, formal change control should be applied. Formal change control should ensure the system remains in compliance and is fit for its intended use. Individual change requests may be reviewed or a single review of the system and all changes may be performed during installation qualification.

Figure 4.1 shows (diagrammatically) an overview of a typical design/design review process.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Design Review vs. Design Qualification

Design Review: a systematic review of drawings and specifications by a cross-functional team during design development, to ensure the design meets user needs and engineering best practice. It is an ongoing activity that runs from the concept stage through to construction tender.

Design Qualification (DQ): the final "quality review" step that formally confirms the design meets GMP regulatory requirements and declares the design "fit for intended use". DQ is the first step of the V-Model qualification lifecycle.

How the two relate: Design Review is the broader engineering activity; DQ is the subset of it that focuses on GMP compliance.

Analogy: Reading the Blueprint Before Building a House

Imagine you are building a new house. Before breaking ground, you get the architect, the plumber/electrician and the interior designer to go through the blueprint together:

  • The architect confirms structural safety (= engineering review)
  • The fire department confirms escape routes meet regulations (= GMP review)
  • The homeowner confirms the layout meets their needs (= URS comparison)

Changing a line on the blueprint takes minutes, but tearing out walls to reroute pipes after the house is built costs a fortune. HVAC design review follows exactly the same logic: a problem found before construction costs about 1/10 of one found afterwards.

Key Point: DQ Is a Regulatory Requirement, Not Optional

ICH Q7 and EU GMP explicitly require DQ. Many companies mistakenly think DQ is merely "good engineering practice", but in fact:

  • EU GMP Annex 15 explicitly lists DQ as the first step of validation
  • FDA expects to see documented evidence that the design complies with GMP
  • The DQ report is the first qualification document an inspector reviews

In a CDMO environment DQ is even more critical, because the HVAC system must meet the environmental needs of several clients' products at the same time.

Key Point: Design Approval vs. Design Review

The source text states specifically: "Users usually do not approve a design to avoid making design responsibility unclear."

This is an important regulatory concept: users review the design but do not approve it. Design responsibility remains with the design engineer (the engineer of record). The user's role is to give comments and confirm that requirements are met, not to take on design responsibility. This is critical for determining accountability when problems arise.

Practical Application: Design Review Strategy for a CDMO

For an aseptic filling CDMO, HVAC design review must pay particular attention to:

  • Multi-product flexibility: different clients' products may need different temperature and humidity ranges. Does the design leave room for adjustment?
  • Cross-contamination control: can the pressure differential cascade and airflow direction prevent cross-contamination between products?
  • Multi-regulator compliance: the same facility may need to meet FDA, EMA and PIC/S requirements at the same time
  • Capacity expansion: does the design reserve HVAC capacity for future production lines?

We recommend writing these CDMO-specific needs explicitly into the URS, to avoid discovering gaps only at design review.

Practice Questions

  1. A CDMO's HVAC design passed engineering review, but construction started before any GMP review was done. If an inspector finds this, what observation might they raise?
  2. After DQ is complete, a client asks to upgrade a cleanroom from ISO 8 to ISO 7. What process should this change follow, and why?
4.1 (cont'd) Knowledge Capture & Review Methods

Original Text

Organizations may develop knowledge capture systems such as:

  • design review checklists (see Table 4.1 to Table 4.4)
  • design guides: defining the preferred way of designing a given system type, e.g., HVAC systems or compendial water systems

These approaches should ensure that organizational experience and preferences are both captured and considered. They also should consider novel concepts.

The review method to be used should be defined and review participants should agree to the method. The method and participants may vary depending on the system type.

A preferred approach for design review is for a multi-disciplinary team to ensure that key viewpoints are considered with SMEs in HVAC, controls, commissioning, and regulatory requirements.

For areas where high system reliability is required, e.g., vivariums, a formal review may be conducted, such as using a Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA) to ensure that the design is adequately robust. A simplified version of this approach may be beneficial, considering the effect of system failures on adjacent areas to ensure that the design is robust and that system failure will not compromise product.

Notes taken from the design review should be implemented through drawing and specification changes. If the revision cross references the notes, it may not be necessary to formally close out all actions in a GEP environment. SMEs who sign off drawings for construction are expected to check that necessary changes have been incorporated in the drawing.

Large projects usually have multiple reviews at key stages, e.g., a review at the concept stage (to ensure that the user team agrees with the proposals from the A&E design company), interim design reviews, and a final review. These may focus on individual systems, or on specific areas of the design, e.g., HVAC systems or chilled water systems.

For smaller projects, e.g., with one system, there may be fewer reviews, but there should be one review before design release, as a minimum. The project team should agree the approach to be applied to a specific project.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Knowledge Capture

What ISPE emphasizes here is the institutionalization of organizational knowledge: do not let experience stay only in the heads of senior engineers. Two key tools:

  • Design Review Checklists: standardized review lists that make sure every review covers all key aspects (see Tables 4.1 to 4.4)
  • Design Guides: in-house design standards that define the "usual practice" for HVAC systems

The value of these two tools is that organizational knowledge is retained even when senior engineers leave. For a CDMO, they are also key to ensuring consistency across sites.

Analogy: The Pilot's Checklist

Before a Boeing 737 takes off, no matter how experienced the pilots are, they must complete the pre-flight checklist item by item. This is not because pilots are unprofessional, but because:

  • The human brain easily misses things when handling complex systems
  • A checklist ensures the same quality standard every time
  • It distills hard lessons learned from past accidents

The HVAC design review checklists (Tables 4.1 to 4.4) are the HVAC engineer's "pre-flight checklist".

Key Point: Applying FMEA in HVAC Design

The source text notes that areas with high reliability needs (such as a vivarium) can be reviewed formally using FMEA (Failure Mode and Effects Analysis).

In an aseptic manufacturing environment, FMEA is particularly useful in the following scenarios:

  • The effect of a single AHU failure on the pressure differential of adjacent cleanrooms
  • The risk of temperature excursion when the cooling system fails
  • The effect of a HEPA filter leak on cleanliness
  • Whether the fail-safe design is adequate when the control system fails

Even without a full FMEA, at least consider "the effect of system failure on product quality". This is the simplified version mentioned in the source text.

Design Review Stage Planning

Large project (multiple systems):
  Concept stage review → Mid-design review → Final review (before construction)
  ├── Concept stage: confirm the A&E firm's proposal meets user needs
  ├── Mid-design review: examine the detailed design and identify risks
  └── Final review: confirm the construction drawings are complete and issue the DQ

Small project (single system):
  At least one design review → issue before construction
  └── Scope and depth of review determined by the project team

Practice Questions

  1. Your company has no HVAC Design Guide, so every new project is designed from scratch. What problems might this cause? How would you build the first version of a Design Guide?
  2. A senior HVAC engineer is about to retire, and most of his 20 years of design experience is in his head. What method would you use to "institutionalize" this knowledge before he leaves?
4.2 Design Review Process

Original Text

Typically, the review process is formalized to make it more efficient and to ensure that all interested parties are involved the process.

The review may be structured to cover all design aspects or divided into two:

  1. A GEP review: to ensure that GEPs are incorporated; this may include a review of maintainability of the systems.
  2. A GMP review: to ensure that compliance requirements are adequately addressed by the proposed design.

(A Health and Safety review also may be justified for facilities handling potent or flammable compounds.)

The GEP review may be complex, (a significant amount of knowledge and experience within an organization can be captured and used in the review process). A formal audit trail usually is not required for GEP observations. Typically, reviewers ensure that comments have been addressed; therefore, there may be a benefit in keeping separate reviews.

The GMP review typically is simple and consistent; observations should be tracked to ensure that they are addressed and an audit trail established.

A series of typical categorized design challenges may be developed. See Table 4.1 to Table 4.4.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: GEP Review vs. GMP Review

This is the most important structural concept in this section. ISPE recommends splitting design review into two tracks:

  • GEP review (Good Engineering Practice): covers engineering best practice, maintainability, reliability, energy saving and other "doing it well" aspects. Observations do not need a formal audit trail.
  • GMP review: focuses on regulatory compliance (temperature and humidity, classification, pressure differentials, cross-contamination and so on), the "must be met" aspects. Every observation must be tracked and given an audit trail.

Why separate them? GEP observations can number in the dozens or even hundreds (including many engineering preferences). If they were all mixed into the GMP audit trail, they would dilute the GMP compliance issues that really matter.

Analogy: Two Layers of Acceptance for a Restaurant

When a new restaurant finishes fit-out, acceptance happens at two levels:

  • Engineering acceptance (= GEP): are the wires tidy, do the pipes leak, does the extraction work well, is the equipment easy to repair? These are questions of how well it is done
  • Health department inspection (= GMP): is kitchen temperature controlled, is the food storage area segregated, does the drainage system meet food safety law? These are questions of compliance

Engineering acceptance produces many suggestions ("this socket would be more useful in another spot"), but the health department looks only at the regulatory red lines ("if refrigeration temperature is out of range, no permit is issued"). Handling them separately is the most efficient.

Key Point: Do Not Forget the EHS Review

The source text mentions in passing: "A Health and Safety review also may be justified for facilities handling potent or flammable compounds."

This is especially important in a CDMO environment, because:

  • High-potency compounds need negative pressure control and dedicated exhaust
  • Handling flammable solvents requires explosion-proof design (ATEX zoning)
  • Biologics may involve biosafety level (BSL) requirements

During HVAC design review, always confirm whether an additional EHS review is needed; otherwise fixing it after construction is extremely costly.

Practice Questions

  1. In a GEP review, you find the design engineer has squeezed AHU maintenance space to only 40 cm wide. This violates no GMP regulation, but you believe it will make maintenance difficult. How would you record this observation in the review? Is an audit trail needed?
  2. A GMP review finds that the drawings show a pressure differential of 10 Pa between a grade B cleanroom and a grade C corridor, lower than the recommended 15 Pa. How would you handle it?
Table 4.1: Typical Design Concept Stage GMP Review

Original Text

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: A "Big Picture" Review at the Concept Stage

Table 4.1 is the checklist used at the earliest design stage (concept stage). The focus here is not on details but on whether the big direction is right:

  • Are the critical parameters defined? If not even the design targets for temperature, humidity and pressure differential are defined, all later design work is wasted
  • Is the zoning reasonable? AHU zoning must be based on process needs, not building convenience
  • Is the airflow direction correct? Air always flows from the cleaner area to the less clean area; this is the most basic GMP principle

Key Point: Risk Assessment Is the Foundation of DQ

The first Design Challenge asks: "Is the rationale for selecting the critical parameters (risk assessment) documented?"

This reveals a key logic: the starting point of DQ is not the design itself but the risk assessment. You must first use risk assessment to identify which parameters are "critical", and only then can you review whether the design meets them.

A DQ without risk assessment behind it will be seen at inspection as "window dressing with no scientific basis".

Analogy: Confirming School District Planning Before Building a School

Concept stage review is like confirming the following before building a school:

  • How many students will this district serve? (= process needs determine AHU zoning)
  • Do the classrooms need air conditioning? Does the library need independent temperature control? (= defining temperature and humidity requirements)
  • Are the fire escape routes pointing the right way? (= airflow direction / pressure differential direction)

If these big decisions are wrong and only discovered after the school is built, the cost of rebuilding can reach 30 to 50% of the original construction cost.

Practice Questions

  1. You are reviewing the HVAC concept design for a new plant. The drawings show a single large AHU serving all manufacturing areas. From a GMP perspective, what concerns would you raise?
  2. The design document says "temperature range 18-25°C" but does not define which areas need tighter control. How should this be handled in a concept stage review?
Table 4.2: Detail Design or Issue for Construction Stage GMP Review

Original Text

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Comprehensiveness of Detailed Design Review

Table 4.2 is the longest and most detailed checklist in the whole design review, covering every GMP-relevant aspect of an HVAC system from external conditions to internal details. It can be divided into several thematic groups:

  • External environment: weather conditions, locations of air intakes and exhausts, prevailing wind direction
  • Internal environment: temperature, humidity, pressure differential, classification, sensor locations
  • Air handling: AHU design, filter specifications, ductwork material
  • Monitoring and alarms: recording systems, alarm limits, control security
  • Failure modes: power loss, AHU failure, cross-contamination risk

Key Point: Know the Key Numbers

Table 4.2 contains several extremely important design figures:

  • 15 Pa: the minimum design pressure differential for airlocks between different cleanliness grades
  • 20 Pa: the recommended design pressure differential (leaving a margin for construction tolerance)
  • 99.97% (H13/H14): the required HEPA filter efficiency for classified areas
  • 4 feet (about 1.2 m): the maximum permitted length of flexible hose in non-classified areas; flexible hose is prohibited in classified areas

These numbers are often asked about during inspections, so you must be able to answer immediately and cite the source.

Key Point: Representativeness of Sensor Locations

The source text discusses monitoring sensor locations in great detail, which deserves special attention:

  • Large spaces (such as warehouses) need multi-point mapping and monitoring
  • In small spaces 1-2 monitoring points are usually enough, but their representativeness must be demonstrated during qualification
  • Sensor location must consider "where the product is exposed"; for example, sensors in a filling area should be close to the point of product exposure
  • Sensors must be easy to maintain and calibrate

Poor sensor placement is one of the commonly cited FDA 483 observations.

Analogy: A Thermometer at the Fridge Door vs. Next to the Food

If you put a thermometer at the door of your home fridge (where temperature fluctuates most every time it is opened), the reading cannot represent the true temperature of the food storage area.

Cleanroom sensors are the same: if one is placed next to a ceiling return air grille, its reading reflects return air temperature, not the temperature at the product exposure point beside the operator. The "representativeness" of sensor location is a key point of challenge in review.

Practical Application: Key Review Points of Table 4.2 for a CDMO

For a CDMO, several questions in Table 4.2 deserve particularly deep review:

  • Availability requirements: different clients' products may have different production scheduling needs, and the HVAC design external condition percentage (for example 99.6% availability = ASHRAE 0.4% design conditions) directly affects equipment selection and cost
  • Multiple AHU failure modes: a CDMO usually runs several lines at once. Would one AHU failure affect the pressure cascade of other lines?
  • Containment provisions: if a client's product is a high-potency compound, the exhaust filtration design must be upgraded
  • 21 CFR 173.310 steam additives: the water quality of steam humidifiers is often a focus in FDA inspections

Practice Questions

  1. Your plant is in central-southern Taiwan, with hot and humid summers. The design engineer used Taipei weather data as the external design conditions. What problems would this cause, and how would you correct it?
  2. The design drawings set the pressure differential for all airlocks at 15 Pa. Considering possible deviations after construction, would you suggest changing it? Why does ISPE recommend 20 Pa?
  3. A new aseptic filling line has no mention of a fail-safe mechanism for AHU failure in the design. What would you recommend in the design review?
Table 4.3: GEP Design Review High Level Challenges

Original Text

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The "Strategic" Questions of GEP Review

Compared with a detailed checklist like Table 4.2, Table 4.3 has only 5 questions, but each is a high-level strategic question. They do not ask "is a given specification met" but "is the overall thinking behind the design right":

  • Reliability: can the system run stably over the long term?
  • Best practices: does it use current industry best practice?
  • Maintainability: is routine maintenance convenient? Is calibration feasible?
  • Failure modes: what happens when the system fails? Does the design consider fail-safe?
  • Cleanability: how is the ceiling plenum cleaned?

Analogy: Five Core Questions When Buying a Car

Table 4.3 is like the five fundamental questions you ask before buying a car:

  • Is this car durable? (= reliability)
  • Does it have the latest safety features? (= current best practices)
  • Is servicing convenient? Are repairs expensive? (= maintenance/calibration)
  • What if a tyre blows or the battery dies? (= failure modes)
  • Are the seat covers easy to wash? (= cleanability of ceiling plenum)

These are "car buying decision" level questions, not detail questions like "should this screw be chrome plated".

Key Point: Cleaning the Ceiling Plenum Return

The last Design Challenge deserves particular attention: "Are ceiling plenum returns proposed; if so, how would the ceiling void be cleaned?"

To simplify the design, many plants use the space above the ceiling (ceiling plenum) as the return air path. But this raises serious cleaning problems:

  • The space above the ceiling is hard to inspect visually
  • Dust and particles accumulate there
  • In classified areas, if the ceiling plenum cannot be cleaned effectively, particles may fall into the cleanroom through gaps

The GEP view is: if cleaning is not feasible, this design should not be adopted, even if it is cheaper.

Practice Questions

  1. Your design team proposes a ceiling plenum return to reduce construction cost. The quality department raises cleaning concerns. As project manager, how would you evaluate this trade-off?
  2. Table 4.3 asks "Does the design proposed demonstrate current best practices?" What standard would you use to define "current best practices" for HVAC? Which guidelines or standards would you refer to?
Table 4.4: Detail Design or Issue for Construction Stage GEP Review

Original Text

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The "Operations-Oriented" View of GEP Review

Table 4.4 and Table 4.2 share many review items (such as sensor locations, ductwork material and power failure handling), but their starting points differ:

  • Table 4.2 (GMP): "Does this design meet regulatory requirements?"
  • Table 4.4 (GEP): "Is this design easy to operate and maintain, and can it run reliably over the long term?"

GEP review looks at the system's long-term sustainability: a system that is technically compliant but hard to maintain will eventually become non-compliant through poor maintenance.

Analogy: A Legal but Hard-to-Use Kitchen

Take a kitchen that passed the health department inspection (GMP compliant), but where:

  • The sink faucet in the wash area is too low, so the chef gets back pain from bending over for long periods
  • The refrigerator sits in a cramped corner, making it hard to move ingredients
  • The exhaust duct has no cleaning access, so grease builds up and blocks it over time

None of this is illegal, but it makes the kitchen run inefficiently. GEP review is there to catch these "compliant but hard to use" design blind spots.

Key Point: Building Sickness Syndrome

Building Sickness Syndrome, mentioned in Table 4.4, is an often overlooked but increasingly important topic:

  • Poor HVAC design can cause headaches, fatigue, allergies and other symptoms in staff
  • Common causes: insufficient fresh air proportion, poor return air filtration, and improper condensate drainage leading to microbial growth
  • For a CDMO, operator health directly affects operating quality and staff turnover

GEP review looks not only at equipment but also at people: how friendly the system is to operators.

Key Point: Future-Proofing

Table 4.4 has a unique question: "How does the design allow for future changes in the room layout in terms of sensor locations and zoning?"

This question would not appear in a GMP checklist, but it is extremely important for a CDMO:

  • The client mix will change, and process needs may change
  • Rezoning or additional monitoring points may be needed in future
  • If flexibility is not built in at design, every change will require major rework

A good GEP design solves not only today's problems but also leaves room for tomorrow's changes.

Practical Application: GEP vs. GMP Review in Practice

In practice, the recommended approach is:

  • GEP review: led by HVAC engineers, with the facility maintenance team invited. Held as a workshop, recorded in engineering documents, with no formal CAPA tracking needed
  • GMP review: led by QA, with the HVAC SME and process engineers invited. Every observation must be tracked to closure in the DQ report
  • Run them separately: to prevent the many GEP engineering suggestions from swamping the key GMP regulatory issues

Practice Questions

  1. Compare the review questions on "sensor location" in Table 4.2 and Table 4.4. How do their starting points differ? How would you record the observations of the GMP and GEP reviews separately?
  2. Your plant is 10 years old and no GEP review was done originally. You are now upgrading the HVAC system. Which GEP review items would you suggest adding to make up for the shortfalls of the original design?

Section Summary

  • Design Review is the systematic review process that ensures the HVAC design meets user needs before construction; Design Qualification (DQ) is the formal step within it that focuses on GMP compliance, and is required by regulation
  • Design review should be split into GEP review (engineering best practice, no formal audit trail needed) and GMP review (regulatory compliance, audit trail required), to avoid obscuring key issues
  • Table 4.1 (concept stage GMP) focuses on the big picture: definition of critical parameters, reasonableness of AHU zoning, correctness of airflow direction
  • Table 4.2 (detail design GMP) is the most complete checklist, covering all GMP aspects including environmental design, monitoring, filtration and failure modes. Key numbers: pressure differential at least 15 Pa (20 Pa recommended), HEPA efficiency 99.97% (H13/H14)
  • Table 4.3 (GEP high level) uses 5 strategic questions to review the design's reliability, currency of practice and maintainability
  • Table 4.4 (GEP detail) looks at the long-term sustainability of operations, including cleanability, future expansion and staff health (Building Sickness Syndrome)
  • The design review team should be cross-functional (HVAC SME, controls engineer, commissioning staff, regulatory expert), and for high-risk areas FMEA can be used to strengthen design robustness
  • After DQ is complete, formal Change Control must be initiated to ensure any later design change is reviewed
4

Chapter 4: 5. Equipment Spec & Qualification

p89-p136

ISPE Good Practice Guide: HVAC | p89 - p105

Learning Objectives for This Chapter

  • Understand the design specifications and construction requirements for pharmaceutical-grade AHUs (air handling units), including key components such as casing, panels, floors and drain pans
  • Understand the key factors in fan selection: type, drive method, bearing life, vibration control and redundancy
  • Understand the central role of motors and variable frequency drives (VFDs) in energy saving and precise control
  • Become familiar with the specification parameters of heating coils and cooling coils, including face velocity, tube diameter and row-depth limits
  • Understand the different technology options for humidifiers and dehumidifiers (steam injection, desiccant wheels, dual-path systems, etc.)
  • Understand the GMP requirements for ductwork design, damper selection, exhaust systems and dust collection
5.1.1 Introduction

Original Text

This section focuses on the design and specification of components that deliver conditioned air to GMP spaces. The equipment should meet safety, product, and regulatory requirements, while providing environmental comfort and protection to employees. Generally, to optimize life cycle cost, equipment should have:

  • robust capabilities for achieving initial, continuous, and long-term operation
  • ease of maintenance
  • low energy use

The guidance in this section suggests materials and construction that may help to assure reliability and uptime, leading to lower operating and maintenance (life cycle) costs. Economic analysis may justify the use of less expensive or "off the shelf" HVAC equipment.

Installation, startup, and ongoing maintenance aspects should be considered. See Sections 6.3 and 6.4.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Life Cycle Cost: Not just the purchase price, but the total cost from installation, operating energy, maintenance and downtime losses through to final disposal. ISPE states up front that the core criterion for HVAC equipment selection is "lowest total life cycle cost", not "lowest initial purchase price".

Conditioned Air: Air whose temperature, humidity and cleanliness are controlled; it is the basic safeguard of a GMP environment.

Analogy

It is like buying a car: a cheap car with high fuel consumption that breaks down often ends up costing more in the long run. HVAC equipment is the same: investing more in quality up front buys lower energy use, less downtime and repair, and a longer service life. This is the TCO (total cost of ownership) way of thinking.

Key Notes

ISPE specifically notes that "off the shelf" equipment can be acceptable in some cases. This means GMP does not necessarily require the most expensive "pharma-specific" equipment. What matters is performing an economic analysis to show that the selected equipment meets the User Requirements. This is a pragmatic, risk-based attitude.

Practice Questions

  1. When your site purchases HVAC equipment, does it perform a life cycle cost analysis, or does it look only at the figures on the quotation?
  2. What proportion of the equipment at your site is "off the shelf", and what has your experience with it been?
5.1.2 Air Handler Unit

Original Text

HVAC equipment manufacturers may specialize in "pharma grade" air handlers, particularly in large capacity custom units. Smaller HVAC systems have been successful using "off-the-shelf" HVAC equipment from acceptable manufacturers. As both options can satisfy product requirements, the driver usually is economics, not GMP. The selection of equipment should satisfy user requirements; less elaborate equipment may require more maintenance and may be less energy efficient, but may be acceptable.

Aspects that should be considered in creating purchase specifications for bespoke HVAC systems include:

  • GMP air-handlers should be constructed to meet stringent performance, improved reliability, and maintenance requirements for critical areas
  • Air handler components, such as coils, humidifiers, dehumidifiers, dampers, fans, motors, and filters should be designed and constructed to provide 115% of design capacity to accommodate potential increased demand or future expansion

5.1.2.1 Cabinet Construction

In geographic regions of moderate to high ambient humidity levels, condensation on the exterior of the AHU casing may be an issue. Where high humidity is relatively persistent, this condensation may lead to exterior rust, mildew, and mold growth. Consideration should be given to no through metal (a thermal break) on wall, floor, doorframe, ceiling sections, and doors. If thermal breaks are not correctly designed and implemented, there is a potential for exterior condensation.

To minimize leakage of expensive conditioned air, total air leakage rate from the casing may be specified at no greater than 0.5% of rated flow at 150% of the design pressure or 50 CFM (1.42 m³/min), whichever is greater, or the requirements stated in EN 1886 standard for the most severe "leakage class" operation. As eventual deterioration of seals on doors, dampers, and other components will lead to increased air leak rates, the initial measured air tightness can be used as a gauge to identify future loss of air flow.

5.1.2.2 Insulated Wall Panel Construction

For larger air handlers, the roof, floor, and ceiling may be constructed of "sandwich" panels that are insulated with foam (polyisocyanurate) that is approved by the insurers and meets local fire ratings. Foam should not be exposed to the air stream and should be covered to isolate it from the surrounding area. Other insulating materials may be used, but foam panels are:

  • structurally superior
  • eliminate migration of moisture and air
  • less subjected to deflection due to air pressure
  • have better insulating properties

The interior panel surfaces and joints should be smooth and continuous, constructed of a material such as aluminum, galvanized steel, or stainless steel that can be wiped clean and will not easily rust or corrode. In AHU compartments serving cooling coils or steam humidification injection, 304L SS should reduce rusting effects. Insulation or sound attenuation lining should not be exposed inside an air handling system serving a GMP area because of the potential of providing an area for mold and bacteria growth.

To minimize leakage, interior joints may be sealed with food grade RTV silicone sealant caulk, with exterior joints sealed with caulking having at least a 25 year life with a mold inhibitor.

5.1.2.3 Removable Wall Panels

Removable panels in large AHUs provide a method to remove large components, such as fan assemblies and coils that would not fit through the AHU access door. The panel should be removable with simple hand tools to avoid cutting or sawing and creating a leakage problem after reassembly.

5.1.2.4 Flooring

Flooring in large AHUs should be of a sufficient thickness to prevent "oil canning" (deformation) when walked upon and damage from dropped tools or equipment. The floor may be designed to have a capacity of 100 pounds per square foot (psf) live load to accommodate a service mechanic working inside the unit. Flooring should have a non-slip texture for the safety of personnel standing within the unit. Floor seams should be sealed to the wall for a watertight floor system.

5.1.2.5 Condensate Pan

The cooling coil condensate drain pan (upstream and downstream) should be of 304L SS to maximize its life. The pan should slope to enhance total drainage (minimum 1.5%) with a minimum depth to prevent overflow during normal operation. Its length should extend beyond the coil's downstream face a minimum of 12 inch (30 cm) or half the height of the coil, whichever is greater, and a minimum of 6 inch (15 cm) beyond its upstream face. Refer to the ASHRAE – Systems and Equipment Handbook, Chapter 21.4.

Each stacked cooling coil should have a drain pan with drainage into the lower coil section(s). The length of a stacked cooling coil should extend beyond its downstream face a minimum of 12 inch (30 cm) or half the height of the coil, whichever is greater, and a minimum of 15 inch (40 cm) beyond its upstream face.

Condensate drain pans should not leave puddles (which can lead to biological growth). Drain pans should slope a minimum 1:100 (1%) toward the drain outlet. Connections should be piped through the casing wall and sealed. Condensate drain traps should be tall enough to prevent air movement into or out of the air handler during operating conditions.

5.1.2.6 Wash Down Capability

In specific applications, the interior of the air handler may require cleaning and wash down. In these applications, AHU sections (excluding condensate pans) requiring drainage capability for wash down should have a drain opening fully sealed around its perimeter and fitted with a secured/removable, flush-mounted, airtight cover plate or plug to prevent entry of contamination during operation.

5.1.2.7 Roof

AHUs located outdoors should be provided with roof panels sloped to drain. The entire roof should be fully insulated without gaps at the peak. If deemed necessary, all outside AHUs should be fitted with a perimeter roof gutter and down spouts, along with rain guards above all exterior access doors.

5.1.2.8 Hardware

Hardware (i.e., screws, nuts, washers, etc.) should be corrosion resistant (e.g., 300 series SS) with flexible washers to minimize air leakage in the exterior. Materials that oxidize or promote rust should not be used in the construction of equipment. Adequate materials of construction along with painting of components (valves, fittings, etc.) should help protect against deterioration (i.e., corrosion) dependent on the environment the unit will encounter.

5.1.2.9 Doors

Access doors should be installed on each section of the AHU (i.e., coils, filters, fan, humidifier, etc.), sufficiently wide (e.g., minimum 24 inch = 610 mm) to allow entry by an operator for cleaning and maintenance. Coils should have an access door upstream and downstream. Access doors should open against the direction of higher relative pressure for safe use and positive air seal. Positive pressure sections of the air handler should have doors labeled as such to protect operators if opened during AHU operation. Doors should be of a double gasket compression design to minimize leakage. Each access door may be fitted with an instrument test port to allow temperature and pressure readings to be collected without drilling into the cabinet during air balancing commissioning.

It is considered advantageous to be able to visually inspect the interior without opening casing doors. Doors may have impact, mar-resistant, clear view ports (such as double pane wire, Mylar-backed glass, or polycarbonate (Lexan)), usually sized 12 inch x 12 inch (305 mm x 305 mm), or 12 inch (305 mm) diameter.

Doors should have latch handles located inside of the AHU to prevent personnel becoming trapped inside of the unit. Doors may have static pressure ports with threaded caps. The port should not rotate when tightening or loosening the cap.

5.1.2.10 Mixing Plenum

The mixing plenum is where outdoor air is mixed with return air. Outdoor air louvers in mixing plenums should be aligned to promote mixing with return air to avoid stratification.

5.1.2.11 Duct Connections

Cabinet duct connections can significantly reduce the system's delivery capacity if sized to match the size of ductwork mains. It is recommended that return and supply duct connections be sized sufficiently large to ensure lower air velocity at the connection (e.g., no greater than 1,100 fpm = 5.5 m/s). Suitable transitions can then be connected to the main ductwork to ensure smooth transfer of air to/from duct mains.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: AHU Design Philosophy

AHU (Air Handler Unit): The heart of the HVAC system. It filters, heats/cools and humidifies/dehumidifies air before supplying it to the clean spaces. ISPE stresses an important point here: both "pharma grade" and "off-the-shelf" units can comply with GMP, and the choice depends on economic analysis, not on brand labels.

115% design capacity: Every component is given 15% spare capacity, a golden rule. Ageing of the system, rising filter pressure drop and future capacity expansion will all consume this margin. A system with no margin is running at its limit from the first day of production.

Thermal Break: In humid regions, condensation forms on the outside of the AHU casing. A thermal break interrupts the conductive path through the metal and prevents condensation caused by the temperature difference between inside and outside.

Analogy

An AHU is like an "air factory", with each section serving a specific function: the mixing plenum is the food preparation area, the cooling coil is the refrigerator, the heating coil is the oven, the humidifier is the steamer, and the fan is the conveyor belt. The casing as a whole is the shell of this factory and must be sealed, insulated, corrosion-resistant and easy to maintain. The 115% capacity is like a restaurant that never has exactly as many seats as guests: some flexibility must always be kept in reserve.

Key Notes: Materials and Corrosion Protection

Note the layers in the material specification:

  • General areas: galvanized steel or aluminum
  • Cooling coil / steam humidifier sections: must be 304L stainless steel, because these sections are exposed to high humidity over long periods
  • Hardware: 300-series stainless steel; even the screws must not rust
  • Sealant: food-grade RTV silicone (internal), mildew-resistant sealant with a 25-year life (external)

These details may look trivial, but in the hot and humid climate of Taiwan, if corrosion protection is neglected an AHU can start to rust and leak in as little as three years.

Specifications Quick Reference

Casing leakage: ≤ 0.5% of rated airflow @ 150% of design pressure
             or ≤ 50 CFM (1.42 m³/min)
             whichever is greater
Standard reference: EN 1886 most stringent leakage class

Drain pan slope: ≥ 1.5% (collection pan) / ≥ 1% (drainage direction)
Drain pan extension: downstream ≥ 12" (30 cm) or half the coil height
             upstream ≥ 6" (15 cm)
Stacked-coil drain pan, upstream: ≥ 15" (40 cm)

Door width: ≥ 24" (610 mm)
View port: 12" x 12" (305 mm x 305 mm)
Floor loading: ≥ 100 psf

Duct connection velocity: ≤ 1,100 fpm (5.5 m/s)

Key Notes: Door Design Logic

Doors must open against the pressure, that is, toward the high-pressure side. This has two benefits:

  • Safety: A door in a positive-pressure section that opens with the pressure could be blown open and injure someone
  • Sealing: Positive pressure helps hold the door closed and reduces leakage

In addition, a handle must be fitted on the inside of the door to prevent maintenance personnel from being trapped inside the AHU. This is a basic personnel safety requirement.

Practical Application

In CDMO facilities in Taiwan and Southeast Asia, the high humidity makes condensation on the outside of the AHU casing especially severe. In practice we recommend: (1) use a thermal break construction; (2) always use 304L SS for drain pans; (3) inspect regularly for sealant deterioration. Many plants overlook these "small details", and a few years later the casing is moldy and the piping corroded, with repair costs far exceeding the construction savings made originally.

Practice Questions

  1. Does your plant's AHU casing have a thermal break design? Do you have external condensation problems in the humid season?
  2. Do the drain pan material and slope meet the recommendations in this section? Has there ever been standing water or microbial growth?
  3. Do the AHU doors open in the correct direction (against the pressure)? Are the view ports clear and usable?
5.1.3 Fans

Original Text

Fan selection is critical to efficiently moving the proper quantity of air (supply, return, and exhaust/extract) and creating required pressure to overcome losses because of:

  • dampers
  • coils
  • filters
  • silencers
  • ductwork

When selecting fans to operate smoothly over their intended life, aspects to consider include:

  • materials of construction (rigidity, weight, corrosion, cleanability) determined for the type of operation (clean/contaminated air, humidity, temperature, severity)
  • bearing
  • lubrication
  • direct versus belt driven
  • static pressure flow sensing
  • safety guards

Air handlers are configured as either a draw-through or blow-through operation; draw-through typically are used. Draw-through units have the fan located downstream of the pre-filters, coils, and humidifier. Their advantages include a shorter unit length, negative pressure on all access doors except the fan discharge section, and reheating of air leaving the fan section, which will reduce reheat coil requirements.

Fan pressure performance and construction are identified as Class I, II, III, or IV by AMCA, based on certain minimum operating criteria. A Class I fan offered by any particular manufacturer has a lower allowable minimum operating range than its Class II counterpart. As a result, a Class I fan has less mechanical design strength and with less first cost than a Class II fan. Typically, Class II and Class III fans are sufficient to handle pharmaceutical applications. Fans should not be sized too small, such that they operate above 1800 RPM, shortening bearing life. High fan RPM also has a risk of dangerous vibration (operating too near a fan's critical speed) and has more noise.

Fans typically used in air handlers on the supply side are either plug/plenum fans or centrifugal fans fitted with a drain plug and cleanout panel. Fans can be direct driven or belt driven. Exhaust/extract operations typically use direct or belt driven vane axial or centrifugal fans.

Plenum fans should be selected for high efficiency with non-overloading airfoil aluminum wheels. They should include inlet cones matched to the wheel intake rim to ensure efficient and quiet operation.

Vane axial fans are used where large volumes of air need to be moved at low to moderate pressures. The tubular design, high efficiency rotor, and integral straightening vanes provide high performance using minimal space. These fans are considered a suitable choice for HVAC systems using variable air volumes, high airflow to cleanrooms, and exhaust/extract. They are efficient as return fans to air handlers and for exhaust/extract applications (fume hoods, bio-safety cabinets.) These units should be configured for direct drive (motor in the air stream) although a belt drive could be used.

Another variation of the direct drive fan configuration is an array of smaller plug fans (commonly called a "fan wall") to replace a traditional single large fan. This arrangement reduces the overall footprint of the air handler, allows design flexibility, simplifies maintenance, reduces downtime, reduces low-frequency noise (rumble) within the air handler, and usually saves energy. Such use of multiple direct-drive fans operating in parallel improves reliability by providing redundancy.

Direct driven fans eliminate belt replacement, guards, and belt shedding and alignment. In addition, there are no shaft bearings present, which eliminates lubrication requirements.

Belt-driven fans should have their motors and fan belt/sheave assemblies completely enclosed (front and rear) in a rigid 304 SS or painted steel guard that protects personnel from injury, while providing for tachometer readings. These guards should be removable without the use of tools, but should include a warning label to notify the operator to secure the equipment prior to opening. The fan motor base should automatically control belt tension and be permanently aligned to allow belt changes without realigning. For multiple belt systems, belts should be matched sets. Entire fan assembly should be centered in the air stream both vertically and horizontally to assure efficient airflow. Fan inlets and discharges should have operator protective screens.

Belt driven fans may be laser aligned to decrease bearing, shaft, and belt failures and to reduce energy consumption. Correct fan belt tension should be maintained and requires special attention, particularly when installing new v-belts. Once new belt(s) have operated for a short time, they usually will need to be readjusted because of belt wear-in. Improper under-tensioning will result in premature failure and increased energy usage. Over-tensioning can reduce bearing life. Synchronous belts can reduce energy consumption, as they do not slip during startup and operation.

The best fan housings are continuously welded to provide strength and durability and extended service life. They have a primer with at least one coat of industrial strength or epoxy paint finish to eliminate rusting. For centrifugal fans, a drain connection should be located at the bottom of the fan housing for fluids that may accumulate, such as in a draw-through fan downstream of a condensing cooling coil.

If possible, fan wheels should be of aluminum construction to reduce weight and rusting and be fully welded and non-overloading. Wheels should be both statically and dynamically balanced. Fan shafts should be precision ground, polished, and sized so that the first critical speed is at least 25% over the maximum operating speed. A shaft seal should be included to reduce leakage or to protect the bearings from a contaminated air stream.

To minimize bearing problems, fan shaft bearings should be selected for a minimum average life of ABMA L10 200,000 hours. Automatic bearing lubricators may be installed to increase bearing life and reduce maintenance. This will eliminate the possibility of over/under lubrication, resulting in premature bearing failure. The lubricator should be installed directly on the bearing housing and be sized to supply lubricant for a minimum of 6 months without refill or replacement. The fan supplier should work closely with the lubricator supplier to provide the proper lubricant and device for the intended operation of the air handler. Note: The lubricator should not be mounted or activated until the fan is put into full operation to eliminate automatic excessive lubrication and damage.

Removable inlet and outlet fan guards should be included to provide protection for personnel and equipment meeting OSHA or local safety standards.

Fan inlets should be centered in both the horizontal and vertical planes within the air handler to promote more even airflow through filters and coils.

Bearing failure is the most common failure encountered within air handlers. Unbalanced fan wheels increase stress on bearings, leading to increased vibration and the likelihood of early bearing failure. Vibration should be minimized to conform to ANSI/AMCA Standard 204-05, "Balance Quality and Vibration Levels for Fans" and have a maximum balance and vibration BV-4 category. Balance readings should be checked by electronic type equipment in the axial, vertical, and horizontal directions on each of the bearings.

Fans and motors for critical applications should be provided with vibration sensors to provide early warning and trending of bearing performance with signal wiring brought out to a vibration interface enclosure mounted on the outside of the AHU.

One method of reliably measuring fan airflow without impeding air movement in or near the fan inlet is to install a combination piezometer ring and static pressure tap integrated into the fan inlet cone. The inlet cone of the fan is then used as the flow nozzle. The flow sensor should be provided with the fan.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Fan Types and Selection Logic

Draw-through vs Blow-through:

  • Draw-through: The fan is downstream of the coils/filters and "pulls air through" the treatment components. Advantages: shorter casing, most sections under negative pressure (doors are less likely to be blown open), and fan heat can reduce the reheat requirement
  • Blow-through: The fan is upstream and "pushes air through" the treatment components. Less commonly used

Fan Wall: Multiple small fans in parallel replace one large fan. This is a recent trend: it lowers noise, reduces footprint, provides redundancy and simplifies maintenance. Even if one fan fails, the others can keep running.

AMCA Class II/III: The pharmaceutical industry typically uses Class II or III, meaning moderate to high mechanical strength. Class I is too weak, and Class IV is usually over-designed.

Analogy

The fan is like a heart, driving the "blood circulation" of the whole HVAC system. Draw-through is like drinking through a straw (suction downstream), and blow-through is like blowing bubbles (push upstream). A fan wall is like replacing one big heart with several small hearts in parallel: if one pauses, the others can still keep circulation going. That is the value of redundancy.

Key Notes: Bearings Are the Biggest Point of Failure

ISPE states explicitly: "Bearing failure is the most common failure encountered within air handlers." This sentence is very important. Bearing life management is at the core of AHU reliability:

  • Fan bearings: ABMA L10 ≥ 200,000 hours (about 22.8 years of continuous operation)
  • Motor bearings: ABMA L10 ≥ 100,000 hours (see section 5.1.4)
  • Automatic lubricators: at least 6 months without refilling, mounted on the bearing housing
  • Vibration monitoring: BV-4 grade, electronic detection in three axes

Speed should not exceed 1800 RPM: higher speeds shorten bearing life and produce dangerous vibration.

Key Fan Specifications

Fan bearing life: ABMA L10 ≥ 200,000 hours
Motor bearing life: ABMA L10 ≥ 100,000 hours
Critical speed margin: first critical speed ≥ maximum operating speed × 125%
Recommended maximum speed: ≤ 1,800 RPM
Vibration grade: ANSI/AMCA 204-05, BV-4
Automatic lubricator refill interval: ≥ 6 months

Key Notes: Belt Drive vs Direct Drive

Direct drive has clear advantages:

  • No belt replacement, no belt guard, no alignment
  • Sealed bearings = lubrication-free maintenance
  • Combined with a VFD, speed can be adjusted precisely

Points to note for belt drive:

  • Belt tension must be readjusted after a new belt has run in
  • Insufficient tension → slippage → early failure + wasted energy
  • Excessive tension → shortened bearing life
  • Synchronous belts do not slip and save energy
  • Laser alignment can extend the life of belts, bearings and shafts

Practical Application

In a CDMO facility, AHU downtime directly affects the pressure differential and cleanliness of the cleanrooms, which forces production lines to stop. For this reason, fan wall designs are increasingly popular in pharmaceutical plants with high reliability requirements. We also recommend installing vibration sensors on critical AHUs and connecting them to the BMS (Building Management System), so that bearing condition can be monitored in real time and trended, allowing preventive maintenance before the bearing fails completely.

Practice Questions

  1. Is your plant's AHU a draw-through or blow-through configuration, and why?
  2. Do you currently use a fan wall design? If not, in which applications would it be worth considering?
  3. Are the fan bearings fitted with automatic lubricators? Is the vibration monitoring data connected to the BMS?
5.1.4 Motors and Drives

Original Text

Variable Frequency Drives (VFDs) are recommended to control the volume of air delivered to the various spaces. The advantages of the VFD in place of variable inlet guide vanes include:

  • better volume control
  • better energy usage
  • less maintenance
  • soft start of fan motor reducing the in-rush of electrical current and stress on the fan
  • positive control feedback to the building automation system

Invertors should include line and load reactors to eliminate motor failure.

The cost of VFD controls may allow VFDs to be used on small air systems. Motors that will operate at various loads should be inverter duty, rated NEMA premium efficiency, and should comply with NEMA MG1, Part 31. A shaft grounding system or isolated bearings should be installed to prevent bearing failures caused by induced electrical current.

Motor bearings should have a minimum average life of ABMA L10 100,000 hours. Automatic bearing lubricators should be installed for the same reasons and with the same requirements as for fan bearings. For further information see Chapter 5 of this Guide.

Fans with belt drives use a synchronous belt with matching sprocket in place of v-belts and sheave. The advantages include:

  • non-slip operation
  • longer life
  • less maintenance
  • little to no belt shedding
  • single synchronous belt versus multiple v-belts for same operation
  • reduced energy consumption

The one disadvantage is that it may produce higher noise levels.

A disconnect inside the AHU casing is recommended for maintenance personnel use, as motors usually are controlled remotely.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: The VFD Is Standard in Modern HVAC

VFD (Variable Frequency Drive): Regulates motor speed by changing the supply frequency, and thereby controls airflow precisely. Compared with traditional variable inlet guide vanes, the VFD is an all-round upgrade:

  • Significant energy saving: a 20% reduction in airflow can cut power consumption by about 50% (fan law: power ∝ speed³)
  • Soft start reduces current surge and mechanical stress
  • Can be integrated directly with the BAS (Building Automation System)

Shaft Grounding: The high-frequency current produced by a VFD discharges through the bearings, causing an "electrical erosion" effect (EDM, Electrical Discharge Machining), which in severe cases can destroy a bearing within a few months. A shaft grounding ring or insulated bearings must be installed.

Analogy

A VFD is like a car's accelerator. A fan without a VFD is like an electric fan with only "full on" and "off", whereas with a VFD it becomes infinitely variable. You do not need to run at full speed all the time and then block the surplus air with a damper (which is what inlet guide vanes do); instead the fan simply turns at the speed required, saving energy and running more quietly.

Fan Laws

Airflow Q ∝ speed N
Static pressure P ∝ N²
Power W ∝ N³

Example: airflow reduced by 20% (N = 0.8)
Power = 0.8³ = 0.512 → about 49% energy saving

This is the mathematical basis of VFD energy saving!

Key Notes: Bearing Electrical Erosion Caused by VFDs

The high-frequency pulse width modulation (PWM) of a VFD induces a voltage on the motor shaft. If this voltage discharges through the bearing, it creates "pits" on the surfaces of the balls and raceways, like tiny bolts of lightning striking the bearing. Solutions:

  • Install a shaft grounding ring (such as AEGIS SGR)
  • Use ceramic insulated bearings
  • Add line-side and load-side reactors (Line and Load Reactors)

This is an often overlooked problem with serious consequences: many "unexplained" early bearing failures are in fact caused by VFD electrical erosion.

Practice Questions

  1. Are all the AHU motors at your plant fitted with VFDs? Do you use "Inverter Duty" rated motors?
  2. Are shaft grounding rings installed to prevent VFD-induced electrical erosion?
  3. Are the VFDs fitted with line-side and load-side reactors?
5.1.5 Electrical

Original Text

For operator ease, particularly in larger AHUs, interior lights may be more convenient than portable lighting. Lighting may include vapor tight fluorescent fixtures (typically 4 ft (1200 mm)) tubes with two T8 lamps and electronic ballasts with one fixture in each section. The lighting should be controlled with a one 6-hour maximum waterproof, light switch timer, as a minimum.

Junction boxes should be weatherproof and conduit penetrations should be sealed airtight.

Electrical components, wiring, and terminals should be tagged. High voltage terminals must be labeled as such. Internal power cabling should be shielded.

Materials and installation methods should comply with NFPA and NEC or the local electrical code.

Sections with fans and moving parts should have warning signs, such as 'isolate before entry' affixed to doors. AHUs manufactured for Europe should have a Conformite Europenne (CE) mark. A Canadian Standards Association (CSA) rating should be placed on electrical devices.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Electrical Safety Inside the AHU

The interior of a large AHU casing is big enough for maintenance personnel to enter and work in, so electrical safety design is critical. Key points include:

  • Waterproof lighting: airtight, waterproof fixtures with a 6-hour automatic shut-off timer (to prevent lights being left on, wasting energy or creating a safety risk)
  • Waterproof junction boxes: conduit penetrations must be sealed airtight
  • Labeling: all electrical components and terminals must be labeled, and high-voltage terminals must carry warning markings
  • Safety warnings: a "Isolate before entry" sign on the fan section door

Key Notes

The 6-hour maximum timer is an easily overlooked detail: if maintenance personnel switch on the light when entering the AHU and forget to switch it off, the timer ensures it does not stay on indefinitely. Inside a humid AHU, long periods of lighting not only waste energy but can also raise the local temperature and affect the local environment.

Practice Questions

  1. Is there fixed lighting inside your plant's AHUs? Are the fixtures waterproof rated?
  2. Do the fan section doors carry a safety sign requiring isolation before entry?
5.1.6 Heating and Cooling Coils

Original Text

Coils should be fully drainable with vent and connections extending outside the AHU or ductwork. Full port shut-off valves with hose connection with cap and chain should be included. Steam coils should be fitted with vacuum breakers. Water coil velocities should be kept between 2 and 6 fps (0.61 and 1.83 m/s) to provide turbulence, but to minimize erosion. Without turbulence, reduced heat transfer can result.

Coils exposed to salt or corrosive conditions should use a fin material of copper rather than aluminum, which degrades in corrosive atmospheres, or be coated with a protective film. Cooling coils in condensing service may be coated to minimize corrosion and reduce biological growth.

Coil performances should be rated in accordance with ARI Std. 410.

Coil sizing, configuration, and installation will affect the ability to meet the requirements for delivery of conditioned air. Peak moisture load should be considered for cooling coil design using the climatic data from the ASHRAE Fundamentals Handbook or CIBSE Guide A.

Air handler cooling coils should have a maximum average face velocity of 450 fpm (2.29 m/s) to eliminate condensate carry over and optimize heat transfer capacity. Cooling coil face velocities should be fairly uniform. Steam and hot water coils should have a maximum face velocity of 600 fpm (3.0 m/s) to minimize static pressure drop, resulting in a lower (coil to energy) cost ratio compared to coils having velocities of 800 fpm (4.06 m/s) and higher.

Air handler coil tubing should be of nominal 0.035 inch (0.89 mm) thick seamless copper with aluminum fins of at least 0.0095 inch (0.24 mm) thickness. Coil casings and frames of 304L SS have better longevity and no rust. A center tube support for coils greater than 48 inch (1.2 m) in width is advised. Cooling coils should be no more than 10 rows deep and 10 fins/inch to enhance cleaning and heat transfer. Preheat steam and hot water coils should have no fewer than 2 rows to minimize downstream face temperature variation.

Duct mounted coil tubing should be 0.025 inch (0.64 mm) thick seamless copper with aluminum fins of at least 0.008 inch (0.20 mm) thickness.

Coil piping should have shut off valves and union fittings to facilitate coil removal for repair.

Steam supply should be taken off the top of the steam main.

For better control of liquid flow and proper venting through coils, control valves should be placed in the return piping.

Supply and return line shut-off valves should be provided to facilitate service and maintenance.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: The Three Balances in Coil Design

Coil design must balance three factors:

  1. Heat exchange efficiency: the more tube rows and the denser the fins, the larger the heat exchange area
  2. Cleanability: with too many rows (>10 rows) or fins too dense (>10 fins/inch), the interior is hard to clean and microorganisms can grow easily
  3. Pressure drop control: excessive face velocity increases resistance and also "blows" condensate downstream

    4. Face Velocity: The average velocity of air across the front face of the coil. Cooling coils are limited to 450 fpm to prevent condensate carry-over, in which water droplets are carried by the airstream to downstream filters and ductwork, creating a microbial risk.

Analogy

Think of a cooling coil like a bathroom exhaust fan after a shower: if the airspeed is too high it blows water droplets everywhere (condensate carry-over), and if it is too low it cannot carry the moisture away. 450 fpm is the "just right" balance point. The same logic applies to the water velocity of 2-6 fps inside the tubes: too slow and there is no turbulence, so heat exchange is poor; too fast and the tube walls erode.

Coil Specifications

Cooling coil face velocity: ≤ 450 fpm (2.29 m/s)
Heating coil face velocity: ≤ 600 fpm (3.0 m/s)
Water velocity in tubes: 2 - 6 fps (0.61 - 1.83 m/s)

AHU coil copper tube wall thickness: 0.035" (0.89 mm) seamless copper tube
AHU coil aluminum fin thickness: ≥ 0.0095" (0.24 mm)
Duct coil copper tube wall thickness: 0.025" (0.64 mm)
Duct coil aluminum fin thickness: ≥ 0.008" (0.20 mm)

Cooling coil: ≤ 10 rows deep, ≤ 10 fins/inch
Preheat coil: ≥ 2 rows (reduces downstream temperature non-uniformity)
Center support: required when coil width > 48" (1.2 m)
Frame material: 304L SS (corrosion resistant, long life)

Key Notes: Vacuum Breakers on Steam Coils

Steam coils must be fitted with a vacuum breaker. The reason is that when the steam control valve closes, the residual steam in the tubes condenses and creates a vacuum. Without a vacuum breaker:

  • Condensate cannot drain properly → standing water → water hammer
  • The vacuum can deform or even rupture the coil tubing
  • Water hammer causes violent vibration and noise, and over time damages the piping and supports

In addition, steam must be taken from the top of the steam main; taking it from the bottom carries condensate into the supply and degrades heating performance.

Practice Questions

  1. Is the face velocity of your cooling coils kept within 450 fpm? Have you ever had condensate carry-over problems?
  2. Are the steam coils fitted with vacuum breakers? Does the condensate drain freely?
  3. Do the coil row count and fin density meet the upper limits recommended by ISPE (10 rows, 10 fins/inch)?
5.1.7 Steam Humidifier

Original Text

Low-pressure steam is preferred over water for pharmaceutical HVAC humidification, because it is bacteria free and often available. Humidifiers should have steam injection dispersion/sparge tubes and accessories to provide drip-free steam absorption without downstream condensate droplets. When clean steam is required for humidification, such as for humidity controlled product dryers and coating pans, sanitary tri-clamp connection control valves, and thermostatic steam traps, along with other components made of 316L SS, should be used. Modulating steam control valves should be included to provide accurate control. A wye (Y) strainer should be installed upstream of the control valve to protect it from dirt. See Appendix 2 for a discussion of steam sources.

When located in the air-handling unit, the humidifier section should be located directly upstream of the cooling coil section (which should be off in the winter) to ensure efficient distribution and absorption of vapor into the air stream. The humidifier condensate drain pans (up and downstream) should be 12 gauge 304L SS, and at least 2 inch (5 cm) deep. Its length should extend beyond its downstream face to the upstream side cooling coil pan, and also extend a minimum of 6 inch (15 cm) beyond its upstream face. Connections should be piped to exterior of unit casing.

When the humidifier is located within ductwork, the ductwork should be constructed of fully welded 304L SS, 2 ft (0.6 m) upstream, and 5 ft (1.5 m) downstream of the humidifier for corrosion control. Humidifier ductwork sections should pitch downstream of the humidifier to a drain in the stainless section with a sufficiently tall trap to prevent air leakage through the trap.

Steam supply should be taken off the top of the steam main rather than off the bottom to ensure the driest steam is provided to the distribution manifold.

A high limit humidity sensor should be located within a relatively short distance of the humidifier, but after absorption of the steam has occurred to shut the humidifier control valve if air stream RH typically exceeds 85%, preventing accumulation of moisture onto downstream surfaces or air filters.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Advantages and Cautions of Steam Humidification

Why is steam preferred over water spray?

  • Sterility: Steam itself is sterile (bacteria free), whereas water-spray humidification introduces the microorganisms present in the water
  • Availability: Pharmaceutical plants usually already have a steam system, so no extra investment is needed
  • Control accuracy: A modulating valve can control the amount of steam injected precisely

Clean Steam vs Plant Steam: Plant steam is generally acceptable for HVAC humidification. However, when the humidified air comes into direct contact with the product (for example in coating pans or dryers), Clean Steam must be used, with 316L SS components and sanitary tri-clamp connections.

Analogy

Steam humidification is like using a steam iron, while water-spray humidification is like using a spray bottle. The steam from an iron is "clean" (the water is heated and evaporated), but a spray bottle sprays the water out directly, and if the water is not clean the impurities are sprayed onto the clothes as well. In pharmaceutical HVAC, those "impurities" may be microorganisms, which is why ISPE explicitly prefers steam humidification.

Key Notes: Humidifier Location Matters

The humidifier should be placed upstream of the cooling coil, for these reasons:

  • When humidification is needed in winter, the cooling coil is usually off, so there is no interference
  • In summer humidification is not needed, and the cooling coil is on to dehumidify
  • The space upstream of the humidifier provides the distance needed for the steam to be fully absorbed

High-limit humidity sensor (shuts off at RH > 85%): This is a safety protection mechanism. If the steam is not fully absorbed, excess moisture will condense on downstream filters and surfaces, creating a microbial risk and damaging the filters.

304L SS requirement for in-duct humidification: Fully welded 304L stainless steel must be used for 0.6 m upstream and 1.5 m downstream, because the steam condensation zone is extremely corrosive.

Practice Questions

  1. Does your plant's HVAC humidification system use steam or water spray? Is it Plant Steam or Clean Steam?
  2. Is the humidifier located upstream of the cooling coil? Is a high-limit humidity sensor installed?
  3. If you have in-duct humidification, is the ductwork fully welded 304L SS?
5.1.8 Dehumidification

Original Text

Where standard chilled water or glycol systems are not available or unable to sufficiently reduce RH levels, several dehumidification systems are available to provide lower relative humidity. These include:

  • run-around coil systems – provide humidity levels equal to standard chilled water/glycol, but at lower energy cost
  • heat pipe systems
  • dual-path systems
  • desiccant systems

Desiccant systems have been the most widely used method for dehumidification in the pharmaceutical industry, because they are capable of delivering air at much lower dew point than coils.

Layout of dehumidification equipment should include filters upstream of the coils and fans downstream of coils (in draw-through systems) to provide a small amount of reheat. Lower face velocity will reduce air pressure drop and improve the coil's dehumidification performance.

When dehumidification is integrated into a cooling system, attention should be given to:

  • Selection and size HVAC equipment (coils, fan, pump, damper, etc.) for sensible and latent cooling at peak load conditions. These usually do not occur simultaneously (highest temperature day usually is not the most humid day).
  • Designing for energy efficiency at part-load conditions because peak load usually occurs only about 2% of the operating time.

A desiccant dehumidification wheel should be upstream of final air filters to capture loose desiccant and contaminants deposited from reactivation air that may be shed from the wheel. Prefiltration of the reactivation air should be matched to the prefiltration of the process air to minimize the load on the final filters.

Cooling is required downstream of a desiccant wheel to remove the heat gained in the wheel. Pre-cooling (and even condensing) the air entering the wheel can enhance the drying capacity and energy efficiency of a desiccant wheel.

5.1.8.1 Run-around Coil System

A run-around coil system is a simple piping loop with an upstream pre-cooling coil and a downstream reheating coil that sandwiches the main cooling coil. A circulating fluid is pumped to transfer heat from the warm mixed air to the reheat coil, which heats the cold supply air coming off the main cooling coil. The run-around system reduces the cooling load on the main cooling coil; reheat energy is provided by the heat picked up by the circulating fluid in the pre-cooling coil instead of by an external source of energy.

The run-around loop requires a fractional horsepower pump and a three-way valve or a Variable-Frequency Drive (VFD) for the pump. For bigger systems, an expansion tank with air vent may be needed.

5.1.8.2 Static Refrigeration / "Heat Pipe"

Heat pipes increase the effectiveness of air conditioning systems by helping to decrease the total cooling load of the air. The typical design consists of a refrigeration loop with two connected heat exchangers, (or one heat exchanger divided into two sections) one upstream (evaporator coil section) and the second one downstream (condenser coil section) from the main cooling coil. As the air passes through the first heat exchanger it vaporizes the refrigerant and is pre-cooled. This allows the main cooling coil to more effectively cool the air to a point below the dew-point temperature and to extract more moisture. The air then passes through the second heat exchanger and is reheated by the warm refrigerant coming from the first exchanger, cooling and liquefying the refrigerant, causing it to flow back to the first heat exchanger. Single heat exchanger type heat pipe systems are hermetically sealed, using a wicking action, and requires no pump. The increased dehumidification capacity provided by heat pipes allows for a smaller cooling system. However, the addition of heat pipes will increase the pressure drop and fan power should be adjusted accordingly.
