For air dew points below 32°F (0°C), there is a risk of freezing condensed moisture from the air onto the surface of the main cooling coil with ice building up and reducing airflow over time. Often, a second cooling coil is installed in parallel to the first with dampers to switch over to the de-iced coil, while the first (iced) coil thaws.

5.1.8.3 Dual Path System

A dual-path system uses two coils (either chilled water or direct expansion-refrigerant) to separately cool the incoming outside air and return air. The hot and humid outdoor air is cooled by a 'primary' coil to 42 to 45°F (5 to 7°C) for dehumidification. The 'secondary' coil furnishes the sensible cooling of part of the relatively cool and dry return air. A portion of the return air may bypass the secondary coil and mix with the cooled return air stream. These two air streams (outside and return air) are then mixed into supply air with appropriate temperature and humidity.

Dual-path systems offer competitive energy efficiency with run-around loop systems and provide better control of the outside air ventilation rate. Dual-path systems decouple sensible cooling and latent cooling for easy control of the supply air temperature and humidity. Dual-path systems can be installed separately or integrated with additional HVAC/return equipment. The outside air cooling coil should be sized for peak latent load, while the return air cooling coil should be sized for peak sensible load. The outside air path controls the humidity of the mixed supply air by modulating the chilled water flow, while the return air path controls the mixed supply air temperature by adjusting the bypass damper position. As with the heat pipe, there is a risk of ice buildup for dew points below 32°F (0°C).

5.1.8.4 Desiccant Systems

Desiccant systems are applicable and commonly used when operations require large dehumidification and low space humidity levels (dew points at or below 37°F/3°C) that would be difficult to achieve with cooling-type dehumidification. They can be configured to condition part or all of the incoming air depending on percentage of outside air versus return air, outside and space RH levels, and the quantity of air flow for the conditioned spaces.

Desiccant materials have an affinity for water vapor greater than that of air. They can either be solid or liquid, as absorbents or adsorbents. Both solid and liquid desiccants are used in cooling systems, but solid desiccants are the most widely used for HVAC operations and less difficult from a corrosion perspective.

Absorbents generally are liquids or solids that gradually become liquid as they absorb moisture, i.e., they undergo a physical or a chemical change when they collect too much moisture. Typical absorbents include Lithium Chloride (LiCl) and Sodium Chloride (NaCl).

Adsorbents are mostly solids and do not undergo physical or chemical change when they contact moisture. Water is adsorbed or held on the surface of the material and in its pores. Typical adsorbents include Silica Gel, Molecular Sieve, and Activated Alumina with Silica Gel being the most widely used.

The choice of desiccant material should take into account the amount of moisture to be removed, the degree of air filtration following the desiccant, and operating and maintenance costs. LiCl and silica are most commonly used in pharmaceutical HVAC.

The choice of a desiccant system affects the sizing of the main cooling coil, because the cooling coil needs to handle only the sensible (dry heat) load of the supply air, which permits higher chilled water temperature and more efficient operation. However, the total sensible cooling load will be higher, because of the hot dry air leaving the desiccant wheel (due to heat of adsorption).

Typically, the space RH controller modulates a bypass damper around the dehumidifier, such that a need for lower room RH causes more air to pass through the desiccant wheel. Because of variability of airflow caused by the multiple paths, pressure and air volume controls are needed in the duct system to maintain constant airflow at the main AHU. Attempts to control RH by modulating the steam flow to the reactivation coil have been made, but this method is less effective because of the long time lag before a change in room RH and because of potential damage to absorptive desiccants through under-drying.

When the dehumidifier is idle (such as in cold winter weather when humidity is needed), it should be bypassed fully, but the wheel should be kept dry (i.e., keep the wheel running and the heat on). This is particularly true for absorptive desiccants (such as LiCl) that can "self-destruct" if allowed to absorb moisture without being regenerated.

The addition of a desiccant wheel increases the overall air pressure drop, fan power, and maintenance, and an additional small motor is required to rotate the wheel. This extra energy usage affects the overall life cycle cost. Desiccant systems may use steam, electricity, natural gas, low-cost surplus heat, waste heat, or solar heat for desiccant reactivation. Typical reactivation temperatures exceed the boiling point of water and usually exceed 250°F (122°C).

Units should be capable of sustained operation without damage to the desiccant. The dehumidifier often is a fully factory assembled package unit, complete with:

  • desiccant rotor
  • desiccant rotor drive assembly
  • reactivation heat source
  • filters
  • motors
  • reactivation fan
  • access panels
  • volume dampers
  • dust-tight electrical enclosure
  • component auxiliaries (recommended by the manufacturer for safe, unattended automatic operation)

The fan for the process airflow, needed to overcome the pressure drop induced by the wheel, is often purchased separately. The unit should be fully automated and equipped with DP gauges and temperature transmitters to measure and display the pressure drop across the desiccant wheel and the reactivation and pre-cooling air discharge temperatures.

The unit casing should be fabricated of strain-hardened aluminum for torsional rigidity and corrosion resistance. The casing should be welded, gasketed, and sealed to be air and vapor tight at design pressures and airflows. Air seals and internal partitions should separate the process and reactivation air streams at operating pressure differentials of up to 8 inch wg (1.99 kPa). The dehumidifier should have full-face seals on both the process air entering and the process air leaving sides of the wheel. These should seal the entire perimeter of both air streams as they enter and leave the wheel. The seals should have a minimum working life of 25,000 hours of normal operation.

The desiccant wheel medium should be bacteriostatic, non-toxic, non-corrosive, and nonflammable, and fabricated entirely of inert, inorganic binders and glass fibers with the desiccant uniformly and permanently dispersed throughout the matrix structure to create a homogenous media. The desiccant wheel should have the capability of delivering nearly 100% of its drying capability for a minimum of 5 years.

Desiccant systems are more competitive when:

  • a low supply air dew-point temperature is required
  • latent load fraction is high
  • low or no-cost reactivation heat from steam, hot water, or waste heat is available
  • electricity costs (for refrigeration dehumidification) are high when compared to gas or steam costs

There are several circumstances that may favor desiccant systems rather than cooling-based dehumidification systems. These include:

  • economic benefit from low humidity in the facility (often product-driven)
  • high moisture loads with low sensible load
  • need for more fresh dry air
  • exhaust air available for desiccant post cooling using energy recovery
  • low thermal energy (steam, gas) available or high electrical cost
  • economic benefit and bioburden benefit of dry supply air duct work
  • low-cost heat available for desiccant regeneration

Tutorial Commentary

Analogy

The four dehumidification technologies are like four different "dehumidification strategies":

  • Run-around Coil: Like using the cold air blown from an air conditioner to pre-cool the fresh air first, then using the heat "taken" during pre-cooling to reheat the supply air. It is moving heat from one hand to the other, saving the cost of reheating
  • Heat Pipe: Like a "magic wand" that conducts heat automatically across the temperature difference between its two ends: the cold end absorbs heat and the hot end releases it, fully automatically with no electricity
  • Dual Path: Like the two traffic flows in a restaurant: takeaway orders (outside air) go through a dedicated channel for intensive dehumidification, while dine-in guests (return air) go through another path that only cools
  • Desiccant: Like placing a basin of "super dehumidifier" at the door: air passing through has its moisture removed, and the saturated desiccant is then periodically heated with hot air to drive the water out (regeneration)

Key Notes: Critical Points for Desiccant Systems

  • Absorbent vs Adsorbent: An absorbent (such as LiCl) turns liquid after absorbing water and will "destroy itself" if not regenerated in time; an adsorbent (such as silica gel) does not change physical state and is more stable
  • The desiccant wheel must be upstream of the terminal filters: Any desiccant particles that may be shed will be caught by the filters
  • The wheel must not be stopped when idle: Even when no dehumidification is needed (winter), the wheel must keep rotating and regeneration heating must be maintained; otherwise an absorbent desiccant will take up too much water and be damaged
  • Regeneration temperature is usually > 250°F (122°C): A stable heat source is required
  • Desiccant wheel life: at least 5 years maintaining close to 100% dehumidification capacity
  • Seal life: at least 25,000 hours (about 2.85 years of continuous operation)

Key Notes: Icing Risk

With Heat Pipe and Dual Path systems, ice forms on the cooling coil surface when the target dew point is below 32°F (0°C). The solution is to install parallel dual coils with damper changeover: when one coil ices up, switch to the other and let the iced coil defrost. This is common in pharmaceutical applications that need very low humidity (such as powder formulations and inhalation products).

Dehumidification System Specs

Desiccant system applicable dew point: ≤ 37°F (3°C)
Seal pressure rating: maximum 8" wg (1.99 kPa) differential pressure
Regeneration temperature: usually > 250°F (122°C)
Seal life: ≥ 25,000 hours
Desiccant wheel life: ≥ 5 years (close to 100% capacity)
Casing material: strain-hardened aluminum

Peak load design notes:
  - The hottest day ≠ the most humid day (they usually do not occur together)
  - Peak load accounts for only about 2% of operating time
  → Part-load efficiency matters more!

Practical Application

In a CDMO, product characteristics often determine the dehumidification requirement:

  • Oral solid dosage (OSD): A low-humidity environment (typically RH < 30%) is critical for powder flow and stability → desiccant systems are the first choice
  • Sterile liquid products: Usually only standard cooling dehumidification is needed → Run-around or Heat Pipe is sufficient
  • Inhalation products: Very low humidity requirement (RH < 15%) → a desiccant system is essential

Always carry out a life cycle cost analysis when selecting: a desiccant system has a higher initial investment, but if cheap steam or waste heat is available for regeneration, the long-term running cost can be lower.

Practice Questions

  1. Which areas of your plant require low-humidity control? What dehumidification technology is currently used?
  2. What is the regeneration heat source for your desiccant system? Is it possible to use waste heat?
  3. Are there areas with a dew point requirement below 0°C? Is there a parallel-coil design to prevent icing?
  4. Has the energy performance at both peak load and part load been considered?

Key Concept: Comparison of the Four Dehumidification Technologies

ISPE describes four dehumidification systems, each suited to different scenarios:

5.1.9 Ductwork Design

Original Text

Ductwork should be in accordance with SMACNA and HVCA standards. Local standards may be similar to these US standards. Supply and general return air ductwork should be constructed of galvanized steel. Stainless steel should be used when corrosion or continual cleaning occur, such as inside a cleanroom. There should be no interior insulation that can add particles or harbor growth. Ductwork should be adequately supported so as to easily carry its weight and insulation along with in-line equipment and controls. If noise is a concern, in-line silencers may be installed ahead of HEPA filters. If vibration is an issue, flexible support and connections should be considered. When flexible ductwork is required to tie the branch to the terminal air device, its length should be kept to a minimum and should not exceed 10 feet (3 m).

Abrupt changes in the size and direction of ductwork can lead to increased noise, vibration, and pressure drop. Duct leaving fans and air handlers should be straight for as long as possible, and if elbows are required near the fan, they should not cause "system effects" that can greatly reduce system performance and consume horsepower. Sufficiently sized duct access doors should be provided at appropriate locations to equipment (e.g., at coils, humidifiers, control boxes, dampers). To preclude leakage of expensive conditioned air and to avoid larger leakage in the future, ductwork should be sealed with approved fire and smoke rated sealant in accordance with NFPA 255 or UL 723 or equivalent. Ductwork leakage percentages will vary from site-to-site, air system, and areas served. In general, ductwork should have no more than 1% leakage (with 0% leakage on positive pressure exhaust duct and positive pressure duct carrying hazardous materials), 4 inch wg (1 kPa) minimum static pressure class, and a SMACNA seal class A. Duct sealant should be carefully chosen to ensure long-term adherence to galvanized steel. Solvent or oil-based sealants are more difficult to work with and may have environmental restrictions, but they have usually provided good long-term service.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: GMP Principles for Ductwork Design

Ductwork: The piping system that carries conditioned air from the AHU to each clean space. It looks simple, but ductwork design directly affects system performance and GMP compliance:

  • No insulation inside the duct: Exposed insulation generates particles and provides a breeding ground for mold
  • Material selection: Galvanized steel is generally used, and stainless steel inside cleanrooms
  • Flexible duct length limit: ≤ 3 m; the uneven walls of flexible duct collect dust easily

Analogy

Ductwork is like a city's water supply network: the tightness of the pipes determines how much "good air" actually reaches its destination. The 1% leakage limit is like requiring that a water pipe leak no more than 1%. And "System Effect" is like a water pipe suddenly turning through a 90-degree elbow: water pressure is greatly lost and efficiency drops. So after leaving the fan, ductwork should be kept as straight as possible.

Ductwork Specs

General ductwork leakage: ≤ 1%
Positive-pressure exhaust ductwork / hazardous material ductwork: 0% leakage
Minimum static pressure class: 4" wg (1 kPa)
Sealing class: SMACNA Seal Class A
Maximum flexible duct length: 10 ft (3 m)
Sealant standard: NFPA 255 or UL 723

Key Notes

Positive-pressure exhaust ductwork must have zero leakage: If exhaust ductwork (carrying hazardous substances or chemical vapors) leaks in a positive-pressure section, the hazardous substances will spread into the equipment room or ceiling space, which is a major risk for personnel safety and cross-contamination.

Long-term durability of sealant: The sealant must stay bonded to the galvanized steel over the long term. Water-based sealants are easy to apply but may have inadequate adhesion; solvent-based sealants are harder to apply but perform better in the long run. This is a trade-off between "ease of installation" and "long-term reliability".

Practice Questions

  1. Has your plant's ductwork system been leak tested? What is the leakage rate?
  2. Is stainless steel ductwork used inside the cleanrooms? Is the flexible duct length kept within 3 m?
5.1.10 Dampers and Louvers

Original Text

Dampers redirect, stop, or vary the amount of air traveling within an HVAC system. Damper blade movement can be either parallel or opposed. Parallel blade dampers rotate in the same direction, staying parallel to each other throughout their travel from fully open to fully closed. Opposed blade dampers operate such that adjacent blades rotate in the opposite direction from each other.

Opposed blade dampers are preferred for their smooth throttling flow with more linear performance because of less turbulence. More sophisticated designs are available to provide better control, but at more cost. See Section 2.7 of this Guide.

For mixing applications, parallel blade dampers are preferred since they deflect air streams to encourage mixing. It is preferred to orient the locations of the outdoor air and return air entry points into the mixing plenum to direct the air streams into each other.

Louvers usually have no moving parts, and typically, are used for outside air intake. Outside air inlet velocities should prevent drawing in rain (recommended maximum of 3.05 m/s (500 fpm) through the louver's free area). For areas that experience significant snow, openings should be equipped with a 90-degree gooseneck inlet sized for a maximum of 1.02 m/s (200 FPM) and be equipped with an inlet louver sized for the same velocities. Louvers should be drainable and may be constructed of anodized aluminum or stainless steel with 304 SS hardware and include 304 SS bird screens.

Wind driven rain can be forced into outside air intakes with such force that the rain can be pulled through the air handling sections and then sent down the supply ductwork. A storm louver for outside air intakes to handle unseasonable weather should be selected to avoid pulling moisture into the system.

The outdoor air intake, return, exhaust, and relief dampers should be rated for low leakage to prevent the infiltration of air when the systems are off or during hostile weather conditions. Low leakage dampers should have vinyl seals that are mechanically attached (not glued) to the damper blade and jamb seals to prevent leakage around the ends of the damper blades.

Sufficient space should be provided to remove and install damper actuators without the need to remove dampers or other equipment. Dampers should be made of corrosion-resistant materials, such as aluminum or 304 SS. Damper jackshaft should be extended to the exterior of the AHU casing for actuator mounting.

The placement of outside air intake louvers for an air handler must take into account the location of fume and exhaust stacks, sewer vent pipes, and cooling towers that can affect Indoor Air Quality (IAQ). Avoid intake locations near where trucks may be running, such as loading docks. Local and regional codes provide minimum separation distances.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Damper Types and Selection Principles

Damper: A key component for controlling airflow and air direction. There are two basic types:

  • Opposed Blade: Adjacent blades rotate in opposite directions → more linear flow control and less turbulence → suited to airflow modulation
  • Parallel Blade: All blades rotate in the same direction → good air deflection → suited to mixing applications

Louver: A fixed air intake device. The design focus is to prevent rain and foreign objects from entering the system.

Analogy

An opposed blade damper is like two sets of shutters crossing in opposite directions: the air is "sliced" into even thin sheets and flow control is very smooth. A parallel blade damper is like all the blades turning the steering wheel together: the air is deflected to one side, which suits making two airstreams "collide" and mix. Using the wrong one is like installing a switch that offers only "high flame or low flame" where precise temperature control is needed.

Key Notes: The Intake Location Is the First Line of Defense for IAQ

The choice of intake location directly affects indoor air quality. It must be kept away from:

  • Exhaust stacks and exhaust outlets
  • Sewage vent pipes
  • Cooling towers (Legionella risk)
  • Truck loading docks (diesel exhaust)

The maximum louver intake velocity of 500 fpm (3.05 m/s) is intended to prevent rain from being drawn in. Storm louvers provide extra protection against extreme weather.

Low-leakage damper seals: Seals must be "mechanically fastened" rather than "glued": adhesive ages and peels off, whereas mechanical fastening (screws/clips) is more reliable and durable.

Damper/Louver Specs

Maximum louver intake velocity: 500 fpm (3.05 m/s)
Gooseneck intake velocity in snow regions: 200 fpm (1.02 m/s)
Damper material: aluminum or 304 SS
Louver material: anodized aluminum or SS + 304 SS hardware
Bird screen: 304 SS
Sealing method: mechanically fastened vinyl seals (not glued)

Practice Questions

  1. How far are your plant's outside air intakes from exhaust outlets, cooling towers and truck routes? Do they meet the minimum distances required by regulations?
  2. Are the airflow modulating dampers opposed blade or parallel blade? Has the correct type been selected?
  3. When the system is shut down, how much do the outside air and exhaust dampers leak? Are the seals intact?
5.1.11 Diffusers and Registers

Original Text

These devices are critical to the air distribution in and out of rooms/spaces. Proper positioning is vital for providing good distribution and a sweeping action of the air from the supply to the return side of the space to deliver uniform air patterns that cleanse the environment and displace contaminants. Poor positioning can result in either dead zones with increased local particulate levels or excessive airflow with unwanted air turbulence. For classified spaces requiring low in-use air counts, it usually is better to have more air outlets at low flow than to have one air outlet at high flow.

Since these devices are located at the perimeter of the space (usually in the ceilings), the choice of materials should be compatible with the room's function. For cleanroom operation, stainless steel is preferred, to eliminate corrosion and rusting resulting from wash downs with aggressive cleaning agents.

Terminal filtration modules (boxes) are used with room side accessible HEPA filters to supply clean air and to prevent contaminated air from leaving the room when the AHU is not running. Refer to the Filtration section for more detail.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: The Key to Air Distribution Quality

Sweeping Action: The ideal airflow pattern is a uniform "sweeping" effect from the supply side to the return side, carrying away particles and contaminants. This is one of the core principles of cleanroom design.

Dead Zone: An area the airflow does not reach. Particles accumulate in dead zones and can push local cleanliness out of limits. The remedy is to increase the number of diffusers and reduce the airflow at each point.

"Many points, low flow" is better than "single point, high flow": This is a very practical design principle. A high-flow outlet creates turbulence that stirs up particles, whereas many low-flow points can form a stable laminar-type flow.

Analogy

Imagine sweeping dust in a room: if you aim one very large high-pressure air gun in one direction, dust flies everywhere (turbulence). But if you use several small fans to create an even "waterfall of air" from ceiling to floor, the dust is carried steadily to the return and removed. That is the principle of "many points, low flow".

Key Notes

A Terminal Filtration Module with a HEPA filter not only supplies clean air but also has an easily overlooked function: when the AHU is shut down it prevents contaminated air in the room from flowing back into the duct system. This is especially important in a multi-product CDMO facility: if contaminants from one production line spread through the duct system to another line, that is a cross-contamination incident.

Practice Questions

  1. Does your cleanroom have any "dead zones"? Have you performed a smoke study to verify the airflow pattern?
  2. Are the diffusers and registers made of stainless steel? Is there any corrosion after cleaning?
5.1.12 Ultraviolet (UV) Light

Original Text

Ultraviolet light is an emerging bioburden control technology that may continuously supplement the existing filtration device(s) in a building's HVAC system, where biological growth can lead to energy losses because of heat transfer reduction caused by fouling on the cooling coil. This growth may be released into the air stream. Safety of maintenance personnel and materials in proximity are a concern. Manufacturer's recommendations should be followed.

To protect personnel from UV exposure, the UV power supply should be de-energized when the lamp access door is opened or when the door of the air handler is opened.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: The Dual Benefits of UV Lamps

UV lamps (ultraviolet germicidal lamps): Installed near the cooling coil, they have two benefits:

  1. Microbial control: Inhibits mold and bacterial growth on the coil surface
  2. Energy efficiency maintenance: Prevents biofilm from attaching and degrading heat exchange efficiency

Key Notes: Safety Interlock

UV light is harmful to people (skin burns, corneal damage), so a safety interlock must be provided: when the AHU door is opened, the UV power must be cut automatically. This is a non-negotiable safety design. ISPE called UV an "emerging technology" in 2009, and it has since been widely adopted in many modern pharmaceutical plants.

Practice Questions

  1. Are UV lamps installed in your plant's AHUs? Is there a door interlock safety design?
  2. Do the cooling coils have a biofilm problem? Could UV lamps improve it?
5.1.13 Fume Exhaust/Extract System Design

Original Text

5.1.13.1 Dust Collection Systems

There are three methods of controlling contaminant levels:

  1. dilution ventilation
  2. LEV (Local Exhaust Ventilation)
  3. containment inside the process

LEV uses the concept of extracting the contaminant as soon as it is generated as close as possible to the release point, removing it before it can be inhaled or become a source of contamination. It is generally less expensive to operate than an equivalent dilution ventilation system.

The system usually consists of a local hood or enclosure, a ductwork system, a filter (typically a self cleaning bag filter), a fan, ductwork to discharge the cleaned air from the system, and often for pharmaceutical applications, a "policing" (usually HEPA) filter to provide a final protective filter before air is discharged to atmosphere. This filter and seal should be routinely leak tested at change-out, at least annually or at intervals designated by local codes or internal company policies.

The design of the local hood is critical to obtaining the correct capture velocity for the size of particle and its means of dispersal. The design should also strive for reasonable noise levels and exhaust volumes.

The ductwork design should be based on constant velocity to ensure that particles remain suspended and do not accumulate in ductwork.

Ductwork is usually made of electrically conductive material, grounded (earthed) to prevent risk of explosion, and designed to either withstand or vent an explosion if one should occur. Duct for corrosive vapors may be non-metallic with conductive filler if the conveyed powders or vapors are flammable. Where positive pressure duct conveys hazardous material, zero leakage should be specified.

Duct thickness should account for erosion from solid impingement and incorporate smooth transitions with minimum bends to minimize energy consumption, erosion, and the potential of dust deposit build up. Access doors can facilitate routine inspection and cleaning.

The system may be designed for continuous operation to minimize risk of contamination due to cross flow within the facility if the HVAC system is turned off (thus influencing room pressures). Exhaust air volumes should be considered during balancing of the HVAC system. If the main dust collector is self cleaning, using a reverse flow of compressed air; the design and commissioning should consider the effect of the periodically reduced flow in the system ductwork to ensure that it does not present contamination risk due to momentary changes in room DPs when the exhaust flow is reduced during the cleaning cycle.

Dust collectors should normally be located outside the building served, typically in a separate building, to facilitate dust control during maintenance, and should be provided with explosion relief. Dust collectors may be located inside buildings if adjacent to an exterior wall, are vented to the outside through straight duct, typically not exceeding 10 ft (3 m) in length, and have explosion vents (depending on local regulations). Dust collectors may be located anywhere in a building if protected with an explosion suppression system. For further information, see NFPA Standard 654. The dust filter arrangements should be considered with safe change (bag in – bag out) housings provided where necessary.

Considerable information on the design of capture hoods and duct systems is found in the Industrial Ventilation Manual, ACGIH.

5.1.13.2 Exhaust to Atmosphere

Laboratory and process fumes should be directly exhausted to a safe location outside the building. The effective stack height (exhaust stack height plus plume height) should be sufficiently large to avoid re-entrainment of exhaust air into air inlets or onto roofs and to disperse the exhaust effectively. The effective stack height should be used when analyzing design issues. Local regulations may limit stack heights, requiring more stack velocity or exhaust treatment.

Wherever an occupational or environmental risk may be attributed to the LEV system installation, a building airflow wake simulation (wind tunnel test) may be performed to verify the effective dispersal of aerosol contaminant. Factors affecting the wake flow study include: toxicity of the material, quantities, and frequency of generation, inlet and exhaust placement, discharge filtration and velocities, prevailing wind directions and velocities, proximity of adjoining buildings or structures, and area topography.

Discharge velocities from exhaust stacks should be equal to or greater than 3,000 fpm (15.24 m/s) if exhaust air is contaminated.

Exhaust from capture hoods, bio safety cabinets (BSCs), or process equipment can be achieved by ducting each piece of equipment to a dedicated fan or by manifolding the ducts to a centralized fan system that may have a number of fans to handle varying airflow, each with its own stack operating at more than minimum stack velocity.

The manifolded system is preferred as it has full fan redundancy (with one additional fan needed) and reduced energy and maintenance costs. When only a few hoods exist and hood locations are remote from one another, or exhausted materials are incompatible, then individual dedicated fans may be justified.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Three Contaminant Control Strategies

ISPE lists three methods of controlling airborne contaminants, from weakest to strongest:

  1. Dilution Ventilation: Uses large volumes of fresh air to "dilute" the contaminant concentration. High cost and low efficiency, but simple to design
  2. Local Exhaust Ventilation (LEV): Extracts the contaminant directly at the point of generation. High efficiency, low airflow and low cost
  3. Containment in the process: The contaminant never leaves the equipment. The ideal solution, but with the highest equipment cost

    4. Capture Velocity: The minimum air velocity required at the hood opening to ensure airborne particles are "captured". The heavier the particles and the faster they are thrown off, the higher the capture velocity required.

Analogy

The three methods differ like ways of handling kitchen cooking fumes:

  • Dilution ventilation: Open all the windows to let the fumes disperse (the whole house smells of it)
  • LEV: Install a range hood above the wok (the fumes are pulled away as soon as they are produced)
  • Containment: Use a sealed induction cooker with a sealed lid (no fumes are produced at all)

The pharmaceutical "range hood" (LEV) must have a HEPA filter added before discharge, just like passing the fumes through an activated carbon filter before release, to ensure the environment is not contaminated.

Key Notes: Safety Design of Dust Collection Systems

Dust collection systems carry an explosion risk: many pharmaceutical powders (such as lactose and APIs) are combustible at certain concentrations. Key safety design points:

  • Ductwork must be grounded (to prevent ignition by static electricity)
  • Dust collectors must be fitted with explosion relief vents
  • Dust collectors are best located in a separate space outside the building
  • If inside the building: they must be on an exterior wall + a direct exhaust duct to the outside ≤ 3 m + explosion relief
  • Or install an explosion suppression system (suitable where an exterior wall location is not possible)
  • Use a Bag-in/Bag-out safe bag change design

Pressure differential effect of self-cleaning dust collectors: During reverse-pulse cleaning, the momentary drop in airflow can affect room pressure differentials, which is a serious problem in GMP manufacturing areas. This effect must be evaluated during design and commissioning.

Exhaust Specifications

Minimum exhaust stack discharge velocity: ≥ 3,000 fpm (15.24 m/s)
(applies to exhaust containing contaminants)

Minimum conveying velocity (by contaminant type):
  Gases: no minimum
  Vapors/smoke/fumes: 10 m/s (2,000 fpm)
  Light/medium-density dust: 15 m/s (3,000 fpm)
  Average-density dust: 20 m/s (4,000 fpm)
  Heavy/moist dust: 25 m/s (5,000 fpm)

HEPA "police" filter: the final line of defense before discharge to atmosphere
  → Leak test required when the filter is changed
  → Tested at least once a year

Key Notes: Manifolded vs Independent Exhaust Systems

ISPE explicitly prefers manifolded exhaust systems, because:

  • Fan redundancy: N+1 configuration, so one failure does not affect operation
  • Lower maintenance cost
  • Higher energy efficiency

However, when the exhausted substances are incompatible with each other (such as acidic and alkaline vapors) or the exhaust points are widely dispersed, independent fans are a reasonable choice.

Practical Application

In a CDMO environment, multi-product shared lines mean that a dust collection system may handle the dust of different APIs. Key considerations:

  • Cross-contamination: Are the dust collectors for different products completely segregated?
  • Product changeover: How is the dust collection ductwork cleaned and the cleaning validated at product changeover?
  • OEL considerations: Dust collection for highly potent drugs requires tighter containment and HEPA filtration
  • Effective stack height: Has a wind tunnel simulation been done to confirm the exhaust will not be drawn into the air intakes?

Practice Questions

  1. Is your plant's dust collection system manifolded or independent? Is the ductwork grounded?
  2. Are the dust collectors fitted with explosion relief? Are they located outside the building?
  3. How often are the exhaust HEPA filters leak tested? Is a Bag-in/Bag-out system used?
  4. Could the reverse-pulse cycle of self-cleaning dust collectors cause fluctuations in room pressure differential?

Section Summary

  • Core principle of equipment selection: Base decisions on life cycle cost, not initial purchase price. "Off the shelf" equipment is acceptable when supported by economic analysis; the key is to meet the User Requirements
  • AHU casing design: 115% capacity margin, thermal break against condensation, 304L SS for corrosion resistance, leakage ≤ 0.5%, doors opening against pressure with an interior safety handle
  • The fan is the most critical mechanical component: bearing failure is the most common fault (ABMA L10 ≥ 200,000 hr), a fan wall provides redundancy and energy saving, vibration monitoring to BV-4 grade, RPM ≤ 1800
  • The VFD is standard: precise airflow control, significant energy saving (power ∝ speed³), and shaft grounding must be addressed to prevent electrical erosion
  • Coil design balances three factors: heat exchange efficiency vs cleanability vs pressure drop control. Cooling coil face velocity ≤ 450 fpm, ≤ 10 rows, ≤ 10 fins/inch
  • Steam humidification first: because it is sterile and available. Place the humidifier upstream of the cooling coil, with automatic shut-off at a high limit of 85% RH
  • Each of the four dehumidification technologies has its own application: Run-around (energy efficiency), Heat Pipe (maintenance-free), Dual Path (precise control), Desiccant (very low dew point ≤ 3°C)
  • Duct sealing is critical: generally ≤ 1% leakage, zero leakage for positive-pressure hazardous material ductwork, SMACNA Seal Class A
  • Damper selection: Opposed Blade for airflow modulation, Parallel Blade for mixing. Louver intake ≤ 500 fpm, kept away from exhausts, cooling towers and truck areas
  • Exhaust system safety: dust collectors must be explosion protected, grounded and preferably located outside the building. Exhaust velocity ≥ 3,000 fpm. A manifolded exhaust system provides redundancy and is preferable to independent systems
ISPE Good Practice Guide: HVAC | p106 - p116

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the four levels of air filtration in HVAC systems (Level I to Terminal) and the correct selection and installation location of the filters at each level
  • Understand how HEPA (High-Efficiency Particulate Air) and non-HEPA filters are classified under ASHRAE 52.2, EN 779/1822 and IEST RP-CC001, and how those classifications correspond
  • Understand the physical mechanisms of air filtration (diffusion, interception, inertial impaction, electrostatic deposition) and the concept of MPPS (Most Penetrating Particle Size)
  • Become familiar with HEPA filter performance issues, namely gel seal degradation and bleed-through, and with strategies to prevent them
  • Understand the design and application considerations for terminal filter modules, bag-in/bag-out housings and fan-filter units (FFUs)
5.2.2 Filter Installations

Original Text

Each filter bank within air handling units and ductwork should have a DP gauge (Magnehelic or manometer) to monitor increase in pressure drop because of loading. Filters may be replaced based when an established optimal DP limit is reached. Changing filters based on time only can result in excessive change out costs or possibly insufficient change out frequencies that can result in excess energy costs, possible filter failure (blowout), and reduction in delivered air flow. Where filters can load quickly, a high DP alarm to the BAS may be justified. In general, alarms on every filter remove the need for the HVAC system operator to visit the AHU. This may save labor, but also may prevent noticing other problems at the AHU.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Differential Pressure Monitoring and Filter Replacement Strategy

DP gauge (differential pressure gauge): Installed across each filter bank to monitor in real time the pressure drop that builds up as dust loads the filter. When the differential pressure reaches the preset upper limit, the filter is approaching the end of its service life and should be replaced.

Pressure-drop-based vs. time-based replacement: The guide explicitly recommends using differential pressure, not just a time schedule, as the basis for replacement. "Scheduled replacement" can go wrong in two ways: changing too early wastes money, while changing too late causes energy consumption to soar, airflow to fall short, and even filter blowout.

BAS high differential pressure alarm: In environments where dust loads quickly, a high DP alarm can be connected to the Building Automation System so that maintenance staff are notified automatically.

Analogy

Monitoring filter differential pressure is like the oil-life indicator in a car. You would not change the oil every 3,000 km (too wasteful), nor wait until the engine starts making odd noises (too risky). A modern vehicle calculates the best time to change the oil from actual driving conditions (temperature, engine speed, distance). DP monitoring in an HVAC system works the same way: it uses the actual loading condition to decide when to change the filter.

Key Notes

The guide points out an interesting trade-off: fitting an alarm to every filter saves operators from walking the plant to check, but it may also cause other AHU problems (such as belt wear or poor condensate drainage) to be overlooked. This is a reminder that automated monitoring cannot fully replace in-person walk-downs. In a GMP environment in particular, regular visual inspection remains very important.

Practice Questions

  1. Does your site currently replace filters on a "fixed schedule" or "based on differential pressure"? Which approach gives the lower TCO?
  2. If the BAS high differential pressure alarm triggers frequently, what might it indicate? How would you carry out a root cause analysis?
5.2.3 Air Filter Nomenclature

Original Text

Table 5.3 and Table 5.4 provide the various filter classifications, ratings, and comparisons from ASHRAE 52.2 and EN 779/1822 standards, and IEST RP-CC001 recommended practice (References 22, 6, and 12, Appendix 12).

Table 5.3: Filter Comparison – Pre-filters

These comparisons of filter rating systems are only approximate as the test methods are different.

*All EN 1822 tests at MPPS. H = HEPA; U = ULPA

Table 5.4: Filter Comparisons – HEPA/ULPA

These comparisons of filter rating systems are only approximate as the test methods are different.

*All EN 1822 tests at MPPS. H = HEPA; U = ULPA. HEPAs = H10-H14, A, B, E, C, D, K; ULPA = U15-17, F, G. **All tested with thermally generated DOP aerosol (0.3 mm MMD; i.e., CMD is near MPPS). F, G and K type filters are tested at either 0.1–0.2 or 0.2–0.3 mm. K type filters are 99.995%.

Filters typically are classified by IEST Recommended Practice RP-CC001, ASHRAE Standard 52.2, or EN 779/1822 (European standards for general ventilation filters and HEPA/ULPA filters) (Reference 12, 22, and 6). As the grading systems are based on different challenge materials and sizes and use different measurement methods, comparisons between the grading systems are not exact.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Three Major Filter Classification Standards

Pharmaceutical HVAC engineers worldwide need to understand three different filter classification systems:

  • ASHRAE 52.2 (US): Uses the MERV (Minimum Efficiency Reporting Value) rating, from MERV 1 to MERV 16. Testing is based on the composite average efficiency over different particle size ranges (E1: 0.3-1.0 μm, E2: 1.0-3.0 μm, E3: 3.0-10.0 μm).
  • EN 779/1822 (Europe): For general ventilation filters, G1-G4 (coarse) and F5-F9 (medium/fine) are used; for high-efficiency filters, H10-H14 (HEPA, High-Efficiency Particulate Air) and U15-U17 (ULPA, Ultra-Low Penetration Air). EN 1822 testing is carried out at the MPPS (Most Penetrating Particle Size).
  • IEST RP-CC001 (international): Uses letter grades (A, B, C, D, E, F, G, K), mainly for cleanroom applications.

Key Notes

Comparisons between standards are approximate only! Because each standard uses different challenge aerosols, particle size ranges and test methods, a comparison table is a reference only and must not be treated as an exact equivalence. For example, MERV 14 corresponds roughly to EN F8, but the efficiency figures are not fully identical.

Practical impact for a CDMO: When clients cite different standards in the URS (User Requirements Specification), you must be able to map between them correctly. A European client may ask for an H14 HEPA, while a US client may ask for 99.995% @ 0.3 μm. These are essentially similar requirements, but the test conditions differ.

Analogy

The three standards are like three different exam systems used to assess students: the SAT in the US, A-Levels in Europe, and the GSAT in Taiwan. Each tests broadly similar core abilities (reading, math, reasoning), but the question style, scoring method and difficulty distribution all differ. You cannot say directly that "SAT 1400 = A-Level AAA"; you can only say they are "at roughly the same level". The same applies when comparing filter standards.

Table Analysis

Key points of Table 5.3:

  • MERV 1-4 (G1-G2): The most basic pre-filters, with efficiency below 20% for 3-10 μm particles, mainly stopping large particles (insects, plant debris)
  • MERV 7-8 (G4-F5): The common first-stage pre-filter, and a commonly used Level I specification in pharmaceutical HVAC
  • MERV 13-16 (F7-F9): High-efficiency medium filters, with 0.3-1.0 μm efficiency of 75-95%, commonly used for Level II and Level III

Key points of Table 5.4:

  • H13 (99.95% @ MPPS) and H14 (99.995% @ MPPS) are the HEPA grades most commonly used in pharmaceutical cleanrooms
  • ULPA (U15-U17) has higher efficiency, but because of its high pressure drop and cost it is less often used in typical pharmaceutical environments
  • EN 1822 testing is performed at the MPPS, which represents the most stringent condition; efficiency in actual use will be higher

Practice Questions

  1. What MERV/EN grades are the pre-filters and medium-efficiency filters in your site's AHUs? Do they meet the recommendations of this guide?
  2. When a European client asks for an "H14 HEPA" and your supplier only provides an IEST rating, how do you map the grades?
  3. Why does EN 1822 test at the MPPS rather than at 0.3 μm? What effect does this have on the test results?
5.2.4 How Air Filters Work

Original Text

Particles are captured within the depth of filter media as the air follows a convoluted flow path through a series of interconnected void spaces formed by the micro filter structure (e.g., fibers, membrane). As the air flows around the structural elements, particles are removed from the air stream via the particle collection mechanisms of diffusion, interception, inertial impaction, and an enhancement through electrostatic deposition. Mechanisms of lesser importance include sieving and gravitational sedimentation. The particle capturing effectiveness of each mechanism is primarily dependent on the particle size, air velocity, and size of the filter structure (e.g., fiber diameter).

Figure 5.5 shows the cumulative effect of the various collection mechanisms. The lowest filter efficiency occurs at the most penetrating particle size (MPPS), which is typically in the 0.1 to 0.2 micron size range.

[Figure 5.5: Effect of Particle Capture Mechanisms on Filter Efficiency — Used with permission from the American Filtration & Separations Society (AFS)]

Figure 5.6 provides a composite of various MERV rated prefilters and their initial fractional efficiencies verses particle size. They are all least efficient at the MPPS. They are most efficient as the particle size increases from the MPPS and efficiency increases again as the particle sizes decrease, but they do not achieve the same efficiencies as compared to the larger size particle capture rate and decrease rapidly once particle sizes are reduced below what is shown on the left side of the graph.

[Figure 5.6: Prefilter Efficiencies for MERV Rated Filters — Used with permission from the National Air Filtration Association (NAFA)]

Figure 5.7 shows HEPA/ULPA filter particle removal efficiencies verses particle size. The MPPS is around 0.1 μm, and most HEPA filters maintain very high efficiencies down into vapor size particles at 0.0005 μm and even some gases. The particles of interest in this Guide are either larger than 0.1 μm (dusts, bacteria, and spores) or smaller (viruses) and can be captured effectively.

[Figure 5.7: HEPA/ULPA Filters: Particle Removal versus Size — Used with permission from Camfil Farr]

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Four Particle Capture Mechanisms

Air filters capture particles through four main mechanisms:

  • Diffusion: Very small particles (< 0.1 μm) are bombarded by gas molecules (Brownian motion), so their paths deviate randomly and they contact and are captured by fibers. The smaller the particle and the lower the air velocity, the more effective this is.
  • Interception: As particles follow the airstream around a fiber, their own radius is large enough that they touch the fiber surface. This is most important for medium particle sizes (0.1-0.3 μm).
  • Inertial impaction: Larger particles (> 0.5 μm) cannot follow the airstream around a turn because of their inertia and hit the fiber directly. The larger the particle and the higher the air velocity, the more effective this is.
  • Electrostatic deposition: Charged particles are attracted to opposite charges on the fibers. Some synthetic filter media carry a static charge themselves.

Core Concept: MPPS, the Most Penetrating Particle Size

MPPS (Most Penetrating Particle Size) is a key concept every HVAC engineer must understand. It is the particle size at which filter efficiency is lowest, typically in the range of 0.1-0.2 μm.

Why does an MPPS exist? Because each of the four capture mechanisms is effective for a different particle size: diffusion works for very small particles, while interception and inertial impaction work for larger particles. At the crossover point, no single mechanism dominates, so the total efficiency is at its lowest.

This is why EN 1822 tests HEPA filters at the MPPS, because it is the most stringent challenge condition. If a filter achieves 99.95% at the MPPS (H13), its efficiency at every other particle size will be higher.

Analogy

Imagine catching fish with a net. Large fish (inertial impaction) are simply too big and get stuck in the net. Tiny plankton (diffusion) drift randomly in the water and sooner or later bump into the strands. But medium-sized fish (the MPPS) neither crash into the net like the big fish nor wander about like the plankton; they can follow the current around the strands, which makes them the hardest to catch. The MPPS is this "hardest-to-catch middle size".

Figure Analysis

Figure 5.5 (capture mechanism efficiency curve): This classic figure shows a U-shaped curve. On the left (small particles), diffusion dominates and efficiency rises as particles get smaller; on the right (large particles), interception and inertial impaction dominate and efficiency rises as particles get larger. The bottom of the U is the MPPS.

Figure 5.6 (MERV pre-filter efficiency): Pre-filters of different MERV ratings differ enormously in efficiency at the MPPS. MERV 7 may achieve only 20-30% at the MPPS, while MERV 16 can reach 95%. Note that pre-filter efficiency falls off quickly at the small-particle end.

Figure 5.7 (HEPA/ULPA efficiency): A HEPA filter maintains efficiency above 99.97% even at the MPPS (about 0.1 μm), and its efficiency is actually higher for even smaller particles (virus size, 0.002 μm). This is a common misconception: many assume HEPA is ineffective for ultra-small particles, when the opposite is true.

Key Notes

A common misconception is that "a HEPA filter can only filter particles of 0.3 μm and above". In fact, 0.3 μm is merely the challenge particle size used in US standard testing, not a lower limit of filtration. A HEPA filter is actually more efficient against particles of 0.01 μm or smaller, because Brownian motion (the diffusion mechanism) is very active at extremely small sizes.

Practice Questions

  1. If you need to capture 0.05 μm virus particles, will the efficiency of an H13 HEPA filter be higher or lower than its rated 99.95%? Why?
  2. When air velocity increases, does the MPPS shift toward smaller or larger particle sizes? What does this mean for filter selection?
5.2.5 Filter Applications

Original Text

Level I through Level III and Terminal Filtration parameters are outlined.

5.2.5.1 Level I Filtration (Pre-filter)

Level I Filtration is the lowest efficiency (and lowest cost) level used for pre-filtration, intended to capture larger particles (3 μm and larger such as insects or vegetation) typically found in the outside air. It also is used as a pre-filtration to extend the life of Level II filtration. MERV 7 (EN G4) filter is recommended.

5.2.5.2 Level II Filtration (Intermediate Filter)

This more expensive filter typically is located directly downstream of Level I filtration to capture smaller sized (0.3 microns and larger) particles to protect the coils and fan in AHUs, ductwork, and personnel. A MERV 14 (EN F8) filter is recommended.

5.2.5.3 Level III Filtration (Final)

This filtration is located at the discharge section of the AHU downstream of Level I and Level II filtration and fans/coils, and may use either ASHRAE or HEPA type filters.

ASHRAE Type: captures released mold and other material, which may have grown or been collected on the condensing (wet) cooling coils as well as dust from belts, etc. Movement of this material through the ductwork and its possible contact with personnel is prevented. A MERV 14 (EN F7/8) efficient filter is recommended.

HEPA Type: used when the controlled space requires a cleanroom classification (typically limited to Grade 8 (Grade C) if used alone without terminal filtration), when redundancy (with a terminal HEPA) is deemed necessary, or to extend the life of downstream terminal HEPA filters, which by themselves are capable of providing acceptable supply air quality, but because of their cost and limited accessibility, should have a service life as long as possible. (For further information on redundant HEPA filtration, see Appendix 9). These filters should have a seamless sealing gasket (preferred) or a silicone gel seal on the downstream side of the filter to form a positive seal to eliminate air bypass around the filter perimeter. Permanent upstream and downstream media protective screens (media guards) should be considered to prevent physical damage to the filter media. Individual HEPA filters should be able to be replaced without disruption of adjacent filters. H12 (99.5%) to H14 (99.995% at MPPS) filter is recommended. High efficiency filters should precede HEPA filters to extend their service life.

5.2.5.4 Terminal Filtration

This point of filtration uses HEPA filters typically at the supply air terminal and is associated with cleanrooms classified as cleaner than ISO 8 in use (such as EU Grade C) and where particles generated in ductwork could adversely contaminate supply air. A terminal-style filter also may be used on return/exhaust air when process room air is contaminated with environmentally sensitive particulate (hazardous airborne materials). Caution is advised, as return air filters can adversely affect room air pressure values, requiring more complex pressure controls for room or return ductwork.

These filters should have a silicone gel seal on the downstream side of the filter to form a positive seal to eliminate air bypass around the filter perimeter. Permanent downstream media protective screens (media guards) should be included to prevent physical damage to the filter medium. Individual HEPA filters in filter banks should be capable of replacement without disruption of adjacent filters. H13 (99.95%) to H14 (99.995% at MPPS) filter is recommended.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Four-Level Filtration Architecture

The ISPE guide establishes a clear four-level filtration hierarchy, with each level having a defined functional role:

  • Level I, pre-filter: MERV 7 / EN G4. Stops large particles (insects, plant debris, coarse dust) and protects the life of Level II
  • Level II, intermediate filter: MERV 14 / EN F8. Captures particles of 0.3 μm and above and protects the coils and fans in the AHU
  • Level III, final filter: ASHRAE type (MERV 14) or HEPA type (H12-H14), located at the AHU outlet, protecting the ductwork and downstream spaces
  • Terminal filter: H13-H14 HEPA, located on the supply side (ceiling), directly protecting the cleanroom space; suited to cleanliness requirements of ISO 8 or better

Analogy

The four levels of filtration are like a multi-stage drinking water purification system:

  • Level I (coarse filtration) = the screen at the waterworks, stopping stones, leaves and other large debris
  • Level II (medium filtration) = the sand filter bed, removing finer suspended matter and sediment
  • Level III (fine filtration) = the activated carbon filter, removing organics and trace chemicals
  • Terminal (ultra-fine filtration) = a household RO (reverse osmosis) unit, the last line of defense at the tap where you drink the water directly

Each level extends the life and improves the efficiency of the next. If the pre-filter is removed, the life of a HEPA filter could drop from 5 years to 6 months!

Key Notes

Choosing between Level III HEPA and Terminal HEPA:

  • With a Level III HEPA only (no Terminal), the best you can reach is Grade 8 / Grade C cleanliness
  • To reach Grade 7 / Grade B or better, a Terminal HEPA is normally required
  • A "double redundancy" configuration of Level III HEPA plus Terminal HEPA can extend the life of the expensive Terminal HEPA, which is worth considering on cost-effectiveness grounds

Gel seal requirement: Terminal HEPA filters must use a silicone gel seal to ensure air tightness and prevent air bypass around the filter perimeter. This is a key element of cleanroom integrity.

Practical Application

CDMO scenario: A CDMO is building a new aseptic filling line, and the design team is discussing whether to install a Level III HEPA (H14) in the AHU for redundancy.

  • Argument in favor: Replacing a Terminal HEPA requires a shutdown and a full integrity test, so each replacement is costly (the filter itself + downtime losses + requalification cost). A Level III HEPA can extend Terminal HEPA life by 2-3 times, giving a lower TCO in the long run.
  • Argument against: A Level III HEPA adds about 1 inch w.g. of system pressure drop and increases fan energy consumption. HEPA filter maintenance is also more complex than for ASHRAE filters.
  • Recommended strategy: For Grade A/B areas handling high-value products, redundant HEPA is almost essential. For Grade C/D areas, decide after performing a TCO analysis.

Practice Questions

  1. In your site, how many levels of filtration are used in each cleanliness grade area? Does this meet ISPE's four-level recommendation?
  2. Why would installing a Terminal HEPA filter on a return air duct affect room pressure differential control? How would you deal with it?
  3. How much real-world difference is there between using H12 (99.5%) and H14 (99.995%) at Level III? How would you quantify it?
5.2.5.4 Terminal Filtration: Modules, Bag-in/Bag-out & FFU

Original Text

A Terminal Air Filter Module is constructed either as a single or multiple HEPA filter housing structure. Terminal filters should be positioned at the entry (ceiling) of a room to supply clean air into the space.

A terminal module usually houses a single filter. The module should be complete with:

  • insulated housing (if ambient conditions surrounding the module would result in external condensation)
  • filter
  • filter aerosol and pressure test ports
  • damper adjustment
  • grille
  • trim
  • hardware

The body of the module should be solidly constructed of cleanable rigid material (such as stainless steel or aluminum) with the exposed trim usually being stainless steel. It should be designed for room side filter replacement, unless the terminal unit is a self-contained (throwaway) lay-in enclosure with filter sealed inside, in which case, it is installed from above the ceiling.

A terminal plenum module or unidirectional air flow unit is intended to house at least 2 filters to distribute unidirectional airflow over a specific area (typically a Grade 5 – Grade A classified space). It is a fabricated structural plenum that houses the air inlet opening with:

  • prefilter
  • HEPA filters
  • dampers
  • challenge dispersion manifold
  • test ports
  • optional sprinkler system
  • an integral grid for support of gel seal filled framed filters
  • flush mounted lighting and perforated grill

A HEPA/ULPA filter used in UDAF hoods or to capture hazardous materials is usually "pinhole scanned" over 100% of its face area with a penetration not exceeding 0.01%. If the challenge aerosol is oil (DOP, PAO), it will be captured and absorbed into the filter medium, and the filter needs to be permitted to "dry out" for some time after testing to let the oil evaporate and pass through as a vapor. If upstream challenge concentrations are high, or if the test takes many minutes, a significant quantity of aerosol oil can be absorbed, perhaps to the point of "wetting" the filter medium. For this reason, it is recommended that aerosol testing be brief (one filter at a time, if possible), and that upstream aerosol concentration be kept at the low end of the sensitivity range of the photometer. Other filters (such as in air handlers) usually are not scanned, and the test of the entire filter bank efficiency may take but a few minutes.

Bag-in/bag-out housing is a side-serviced filter housing to capture dangerous or toxic biological, radiological, cytotoxic, or carcinogenic materials. It prevents hazardous airborne materials from escaping into the exhaust or return duct system. It typically is positioned at the perimeter (near floor) of the room where the material is generated, but may be located in a central site.

The housing is constructed of stainless steel, should have zero leakage, and uses a control barrier to isolate personnel from hazardous materials during change-out of the HEPA filter. The housing should have a silicone gel seal and be adequately reinforced to withstand a negative or positive pressure of 15 inch wg (3.75 kPa).

A fan-filter unit (FFU) is a self-contained filter assembly similar to a small UFH with fan, prefilter, speed control, and a single shallow-medium HEPA filter (99.97 or 99.99% scanned) sealed into a lightweight enclosure. Preferred construction is stainless or aluminum. Fan-filters can be used as "clean air projectors" to protect small areas (sample points, manways, etc.), to augment movement of HEPA filtered air in a cleanroom, and to add air changes for dilution. Capacity is adjustable, often from 70 fpm (0.35 m/s) to 150 fpm (0.75 m/s). Some FFUs have extra fan capacity that permits the unit's air inlet to be ducted from floor level, making it usable as a retrofit for small rooms (such as older poorly-ventilated gowning rooms and airlocks) needing HEPA filtered airflow. When selecting FFUs, consideration should be given to:

  • service life
  • replacement of filter media
  • electrical ratings
  • excess capacity

Many low cost FFUs are meant for "throw-away" applications, while some other units may provide years of service with replaceable filters. Although several FFUs may be used together to serve as a Grade 5 UFH, care is needed to assure that the entire filter assembly provides acceptable airflow patterns. For this reason, few have been used as Grade 5 hoods. As an FFU is self-powered (it has its own fan), it may be used where the addition of a HEPA filter to a duct system would add unacceptable pressure drop or create imbalance in the system, such as a return air filter in a room. If mounted in a wall, an FFU can be used to create a DP between the two areas separated by the wall (such as the retrofit of an OSD facility to improve cross-contamination protection).

During commissioning of a clean space, areas of high particle concentration, slow recovery, or poor airflow patterns may be discovered. Prudent placement of an FFU may significantly reduce the issue. A lightweight FFU may be kept for troubleshooting to be replaced with a more expensive stainless unit for permanent use.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Three Types of Terminal Filtration Equipment

1. Terminal Air Filter Module: A ceiling-mounted HEPA filter housing, the last line of defense for cleanroom supply air. Single-filter modules are used in general cleanrooms; multi-filter plenum modules are used in Grade A/Grade 5 areas that require unidirectional airflow.

2. Bag-in/Bag-out (BIBO) Housing: A side-service filter housing designed for hazardous materials. It uses a plastic bag sealing technique so that maintenance staff can change HEPA filters without coming into contact with the contaminated filter. It is used for exhaust treatment of biohazardous, radioactive, cytotoxic or carcinogenic materials.

3. FFU (Fan-Filter Unit): A self-contained HEPA filtration device with its own fan, which can be deployed flexibly. It suits protection of small areas (sampling points, manholes, etc.), increasing the air change rate of a cleanroom, or serving as a retrofit solution for older facilities.

Analogy

A Terminal Module is like a central air-conditioning outlet: fixed in place and supplied by the larger system. An FFU is like a portable air purifier: it has its own fan, works when plugged in, and can be moved wherever needed. A BIBO Housing is like the exhaust outlet of a negative-pressure isolation ward in a hospital: it must ensure hazardous material never escapes at any time, so even the filter change is fully sealed.

Key Notes

Points to note for pinhole scan testing:

  • HEPA filters in UDAF (unidirectional airflow) hoods and hazardous-material containment units require a 100% area Leak Test, with penetration not exceeding 0.01%
  • When testing with oil-based aerosols (DOP test or PAO), the oil is absorbed by the filter media. The test should be as brief as possible, and the upstream concentration kept at the low end of the photometer's sensitivity range
  • After testing, the filter needs to be allowed to "dry" so that the absorbed oil evaporates. If the media becomes excessively "wet", its filtration performance will be affected

Limitations of FFUs: Although multiple FFUs could in theory be combined into a Grade 5 laminar flow hood, this is rarely done in practice because it is difficult to guarantee a consistent overall airflow pattern. FFUs are better suited as a supplementary or emergency solution.

Practical Application

CDMO retrofit scenario: A CDMO's gowning room was designed 20 years ago, has poor ventilation, and its particle counts frequently fail to meet the limits. A full HVAC rebuild would require a 3-month shutdown.

The quick FFU solution:

  • Install 2 stainless steel FFUs on the gowning room wall, drawing air from floor level and delivering HEPA-filtered air from the ceiling
  • Adds about 20 air changes per hour
  • Installation time: 1-2 days, with no need to stop production
  • Cost: about 1/10 of the HVAC rebuild cost

This is a typical application of what the guide describes as a "retrofit for small rooms needing HEPA filtered airflow".

Key Note: Room Side Replacement

The guide stresses that a Terminal Module should be designed for room side filter replacement. This matters because:

  • It avoids maintenance above the ceiling (the technical interstitial space), which is usually a non-cleanroom area
  • The replacement can be performed in a controlled environment, reducing contamination risk
  • It makes it easier for QA personnel to observe and record the replacement

Exception: disposable ceiling-recessed filters, where the entire module is removed from above and replaced together with the filter.

Practice Questions

  1. Does your site use Bag-in/Bag-out housings? If you handle highly potent APIs (HPAPI), how should the filtration design of the exhaust system be upgraded?
  2. In which scenarios is the FFU's "self-contained fan" an advantage, and in which is it a disadvantage?
  3. If a pinhole scan finds local penetration above 0.01% on a HEPA filter, how would your SOP handle it?
5.2.6 Airborne Particle Sizes

Original Text

Airborne particles can range for sub-micron size (0.01 micron) to many microns.

Viable particles (viruses, spores, and bacteria) are present as a very small fraction of total particles. For example, in outdoor air, there may be a million particles in a cubic foot (35 time more per cubic meter), but only a few hundred or a few thousand viable particles per cubic foot).

It is estimated that over 90% of airborne particles in outdoor air are under 0.5 micron in size and comprise less than 1% of the mass. Fewer than 2% of particles are over 1 micron in size and comprise 97% of the mass, meaning that pre-filters do most of the mass removal. Typical approximate particle sizes include:

  • viruses – 0.002 to 0.05 micron
  • bacteria – 0.4 to 20 micron
  • plant spores – 10 to 40 micron
  • smoke – 0.01 to 1 micron
  • test aerosol (DOP, PAO) – most particles are 0.1 to 0.7 micron
  • dust and ash – mostly 0.5 to 1000 micron (the large particles fall out quickly)

A filter with an MPPS of 0.1 to 0.3 microns should perform well against viable particles, capturing them at efficiencies greater than its rating at MPPS.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The 80/20 Rule of the Particle World

This section reveals a surprising fact:

  • 90% of particles by number are below 0.5 μm, but they make up < 1% of the mass
  • Fewer than 2% of particles by number are above 1 μm, but they make up 97% of the mass

This means that although a pre-filter has "low" efficiency, it carries the vast majority of the mass load. Without a pre-filter, large quantities of dust would hit the HEPA filter directly and greatly shorten its life.

Core Concept: Viable vs. Non-viable Particles

Viable particles (viruses, bacteria, spores) make up only a tiny fraction of total particles. Outdoor air contains about 1 million total particles per cubic foot, but only a few hundred to a few thousand viable particles.

This is why Particle Count can serve as an indirect indicator of microbial contamination: if total particles are controlled to a very low level, viable particles will naturally be greatly reduced as well. The reverse is not necessarily true, however: passing the particle count does not guarantee passing the microbial count.

Analogy

Imagine the crowd at a large music festival: 90% of the people (equivalent to submicron particles) are slight spectators who together take up little space, but the 2% made up of large equipment trucks and stage gear (equivalent to large particles) take up 97% of the floor area. The pre-filter is like the wide entrance gate that mainly stops large vehicles, while the HEPA is the final security checkpoint that makes sure every single person is carefully screened.

Particle Size Reference

Particle type          Size range        Pharma relevance
─────────────────────────────────────────────
Viruses              0.002 – 0.05 µm   ★★★★★
Bacteria             0.4 – 20 µm       ★★★★★
Plant spores         10 – 40 µm        ★★★
Smoke                0.01 – 1 µm       ★★
Test aerosol (DOP/PAO)   0.1 – 0.7 µm      (for testing)
Dust/Ash             0.5 – 1000 µm     ★★

HEPA MPPS range: 0.1 – 0.3 µm
→ Capture efficiency for all viable particles > the MPPS rating

Key Notes

Key insight: The last sentence of the guide is very important: "A filter with an MPPS of 0.1 to 0.3 microns should perform well against viable particles, capturing them at efficiencies greater than its rating at MPPS."

This means that the MPPS rated efficiency of a HEPA filter (such as 99.95% for H13) is the worst-case efficiency. For bacteria (0.4-20 μm) and viruses (0.002-0.05 μm), the actual capture efficiency is higher than the rated value. This gives us greater confidence in the role of HEPA filtration in sterility assurance.

Practice Questions

  1. If you had to explain to a regulatory inspector "why a HEPA filter is effective against viruses", how would you explain it using the concept of MPPS?
  2. Why do the "efficiency" figures of a pre-filter look so low (e.g. MERV 7 at only about 50-70% @ 3-10 μm), yet its contribution to the whole system is so large?
5.2.7 HEPA Filter Performance Issues

Original Text

Specific issues with HEPA filters have been observed in pharmaceutical cleanrooms, two of which are:

  1. HEPA filter gel seal degradation
  2. HEPA filter bleedthrough

5.2.7.1 HEPA Filter Gel Seal Degradation

Degradation of gel seals has been observed in cleanroom applications as the silicone (siloxane) gel seal material appears to revert to a liquid state and begins dripping out of the gel track. This may be accompanied by a color change, such as fading to a clear or translucent appearance. This usually does not result in a measurable integrity failure of the filter, but does present sterility, appearance, and safety issues. Studies have determined that this failure is because of the migration of unbonded polymer components out of the gel matrix, forming a slimy liquid on the surface of the gel. Factors which contribute to this include:

  • Crosslinking of the gel components:
    • the more complete the crosslinking, the less unbonded polymer that can migrate to the surface
    • the specific gel type and the mixing (ratio of components, environmental conditions, time to complete the reaction, etc.) are key to amount of crosslinking
  • Molecular weight of the gel:
    • higher molecular weight reduces the diffusion and migration of unbonded polymers
    • narrow weight distribution is desired at the higher molecular weights
  • Certain challenge aerosols (PAO, DOP, etc.):
    • accelerate the rate of unbonded polymer diffusion
    • aerosol acts as a solvent, increasing migration of unbonded polymers to the surface
  • Typical pharmaceutical cleanroom cleaning and sanitizing agents (such as bleach or hydrogen peroxide) do not seem to affect the rate of unbonded polymer diffusion

It is recommended that miter joints and penetrations in the filter gel track are sealed with a material proven to be impervious to the silicone gel components (i.e., silicone gel components will penetrate silicone caulk).

Urethane gels are not recommended as replacements for silicone gels in pharmaceutical cleanroom applications that will be exposed to cleaning and sanitizing chemicals, as their performance is affected by those chemicals, as well as being affected by aerosol challenge materials, such as PAO and DOP. Filter manufacturer should be able to help determine the appropriate silicone gel that maximizes crosslinking and molecular weight, and that provides satisfactory sealing characteristics (resiliency, adhesion, etc.). Reducing the amount of aerosol challenge to which the filters are exposed will also reduce the risk of gel degradation.

Since urethane gels are hydrophilic, high humidity can affect the ability of the gel to cure properly.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Mechanism of Gel Seal Degradation

Gel Seal Degradation is one of the most troublesome HEPA maintenance problems in pharmaceutical cleanrooms. The root cause is that incompletely cross-linked polymer components in the silicone (siloxane) migrate out of the gel matrix and form a sticky, slippery liquid on the surface.

Key influencing factors:

  • Degree of cross-linking: The more complete the cross-linking, the less unbonded polymer there is and the lower the migration risk. Mixing ratio, ambient temperature and reaction time all affect cross-link quality.
  • Molecular weight: Gel seal materials of higher molecular weight diffuse and migrate more slowly, and a narrow distribution is preferable.
  • DOP/PAO test aerosols: These oil-based aerosols act as solvents and accelerate the migration of unbonded polymer. Ironically, the very test performed to verify Filter Integrity itself accelerates gel seal degradation!

Analogy

Gel seal degradation is like the "white bloom" (fat bloom) on chocolate stored too long. If the cocoa butter in the chocolate has not crystallized well (similar to incomplete cross-linking), it slowly migrates to the surface over time and forms a white film. The chocolate can still be eaten (the filter integrity test may still pass), but its appearance and texture have deteriorated (a hygiene and appearance issue). And if the chocolate is exposed to a warm environment (similar to the solvent effect of DOP/PAO aerosol), the bloom appears even faster.

Key Notes

Three key warnings:

  1. Do not use silicone caulk to repair the seams of the gel seal track! The gel seal components will penetrate silicone caulk (silicone gel components will penetrate silicone caulk). A qualified material that is impermeable to the silicone components must be used.
  2. Do not substitute urethane gel for silicone! Urethane gel is sensitive to cleaning and disinfecting agents, and it is hydrophilic, so a high-humidity environment will affect cure quality.
  3. Reduce DOP/PAO exposure: Every integrity test accelerates gel seal degradation. Tests should therefore be brief and efficient: test one filter at a time and keep the upstream aerosol concentration at the lowest effective range.

Practical Application

Scenario: During a routine walk-down, plant maintenance staff find translucent fluid seeping from the gel seal of a HEPA filter in the ceiling of a Grade B area and dripping onto the floor below.

How should you handle it?

  • Immediate action: Initiate a deviation investigation, increase the frequency of environmental monitoring, and assess whether a temporary production stop is needed
  • Root cause analysis: Check the gel seal supplier's batch, confirm the mixing ratio records, and investigate the recent DOP test frequency and concentration
  • Corrective action: Replace with new HEPA filters that have a highly cross-linked silicone gel seal, work with the supplier to confirm the best gel seal specification, and adjust the integrity test SOP (lower aerosol concentration, shorter test time)
  • Preventive action: Establish an SOP for visual inspection of the gel seal, and bring the gel seal supplier specification under change control

Practice Questions

  1. How often does your site perform HEPA integrity tests? What DOP/PAO concentration is used in each test? Can it be optimized to reduce damage to the gel seal?
  2. If gel seal degradation has not caused an integrity test failure, does the filter still need to be replaced? How would you decide from a GMP perspective?
5.2.7.2 HEPA Filter Bleed-through

Original Text

HEPA filter bleed-through is a phenomenon in which a filter appears to fail a field integrity (leak) scan test using an aerosol challenge and a photometer with an observed leakage across the entire face of the filter media (not localized as with a pinhole or tear). This often occurs with filters that had previously passed a factory efficiency and scan test. It has been observed worldwide and is not limited to one filter or paper manufacturer. Further, it appears to be limited to HEPA (not ULPA) filters and to applications in which thermo-pneumatic (hot-block) aerosol generators were used for testing.

Bleed-through of HEPA filters occurs when they are subjected to field testing conditions that are more stringent than their factory test conditions. This may occur when:

  • actual field velocities are higher than factory tests
