  • actual field aerosol challenge particle sizes are smaller than factory tests
  • HEPA filter is not specified appropriately for actual field conditions

Studies into the nature of this problem have resulted in determining that the following factors are fundamental to understanding and avoiding bleed-through issues:

  • particle size distribution of the challenge aerosol from the generator
  • impact of velocity on filter efficiency and bleed-through
  • specifying and testing HEPA filters

Particle Size Distribution of the Challenge Aerosol from the Generator

Aerosol particle sizes generated by pneumatic Laskin-nozzle type generators are larger than those from hot-block generators (mean diameter – MMD – size of 0.5 to 0.7 microns versus 0.2 to 0.3 microns). Although HEPA filters often are efficiency tested and rated at 0.3 microns, the filters' actual MPPS is less than 0.3 microns, often in the 0.12 to 0.25 micron range. HEPA filters which may pass an integrity scan test in the factory with a Laskin nozzle generator (at 0.5 to 0.7 microns) may fail a scan test in the field with a hot-block generator because of bleed-through of too many small particles at the MPPS. The filter supplier should know the field test challenge method to be used in the field so that the appropriate filter paper can be provided. Many issues can be avoided by stating the efficiency of the filter at the filter's MPPS.

Impact of Velocity on Filter Efficiency

Air velocity has a significant impact on filter performance. Increasing the velocity will decrease both the filter efficiency and the MPPS for that filter (more smaller particles will pass). For example, factory testing a specific filter for efficiency and integrity at 100 fpm face velocity and then field integrity testing at 150 fpm likely will result in different results. Filter performance should be specified for the intended face velocity.

Figure 5.8 indicates a decrease and shifting of efficiencies at the MPPS points as air velocities increase. Note that the air velocity through the medium is much less than the face velocity through the filter, because of the added medium area created by numerous folds in the medium.

[Figure 5.8: Efficiency shift at MPPS with increasing air velocities]

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Root Cause of Bleed-through

Bleed-through is not a hole or crack in the filter (that is a pinhole leak). Instead, the entire filter face shows uniformly high penetration. This is a systemic problem whose root cause is a mismatch between factory test conditions and field test conditions.

Two key factors:

  • Type of aerosol generator: A Laskin-nozzle (pneumatic) generator produces larger particles (MMD 0.5-0.7 μm), while a hot-block (thermal) generator produces smaller particles (MMD 0.2-0.3 μm). If a filter passes the factory test with a Laskin-nozzle, it may fail in the field with a hot-block, because the hot-block particles are closer to the MPPS.
  • Difference in air velocity: Increasing air velocity lowers efficiency and shifts the MPPS toward smaller particle sizes. A filter that passes at 100 fpm at the factory may fail at 150 fpm in the field.

Analogy

Bleed-through is like a car that passes its brake test perfectly on a flat test track (factory test conditions) but cannot stop on a real mountain road (field conditions). The brakes are not broken; the test conditions simply do not represent the actual operating environment. On the track the speed is lower (the larger particles of a Laskin-nozzle) and the road is clean; on the mountain road the speed is higher (the smaller particles and higher air velocity of a hot-block) and the bends are sharper (a challenge closer to the MPPS).

The solution is simple: require the supplier to test under conditions close to actual use.

Key Notes

Three key strategies to avoid bleed-through:

  1. Specify filter efficiency at the MPPS, not at 0.3 μm. For example, specify "H14: 99.995% @ MPPS" rather than "99.995% @ 0.3 μm". This ensures the filter still meets the requirement under the most stringent conditions.
  2. Tell the supplier the field test method: Let the supplier know whether you will use a hot-block or a Laskin-nozzle generator, so that they can supply a suitable media grade.
  3. Specify the face velocity: Ensure the air velocity used in factory testing is no lower than the actual field velocity. If the design velocity is 90 fpm, the factory should test at no less than 90-100 fpm.

Comparison: Two Aerosol Generators

Generator type     Particle size (MMD)   Relationship to MPPS      Bleed-through risk
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Laskin-nozzle      0.5 – 0.7 µm   Much larger than MPPS (0.12-0.25)  Low
(pneumatic)                           → filter efficiency is higher

Hot-block          0.2 – 0.3 µm   Close to MPPS              High
(thermal)                           → filter efficiency is at its lowest point

Actual HEPA MPPS: 0.12 – 0.25 µm (not the 0.3 µm commonly quoted as standard)

Figure Analysis

Figure 5.8 (effect of air velocity on efficiency): As air velocity increases, the MPPS trough of the efficiency curve becomes deeper (lower efficiency) and shifts to the left (smaller MPPS). This double effect greatly increases the bleed-through risk at high air velocity.

The guide also mentions an important detail: the media velocity of the filter media is far lower than the face velocity, because HEPA media is heavily pleated, which increases the effective filtration area. For example, at a face velocity of 100 fpm, the media velocity may be only 3-5 fpm.

Practical Application

Scenario: Your QC team uses a hot-block generator to perform integrity tests on newly installed HEPA filters, and 2 of the 3 new filters fail, yet the factory test certificates from the supplier show that all of them passed.

Analysis and handling:

  • Step 1: Confirm the aerosol generator type and upstream concentration used in the field test. If a hot-block was used, its particle size distribution may differ significantly from the supplier's Laskin-nozzle test.
  • Step 2: Confirm whether the field test air velocity matches the air velocity of the supplier's factory test.
  • Step 3: Communicate with the supplier and request: (a) test data under hot-block conditions, (b) MPPS efficiency data rather than only 0.3 μm efficiency, and (c) if necessary, an upgrade to a higher media grade.
  • Long-term corrective action: Update the URS/purchasing specification to state clearly that filter efficiency is based on the MPPS, and specify the field test method.

Practice Questions

  1. What type of aerosol generator does your site use? What does the supplier use for factory testing? Are the two consistent?
  2. If all HEPA specifications were changed to "efficiency @ MPPS" instead of "efficiency @ 0.3 μm", what would be the effect on purchasing cost and supplier selection?
  3. Bleed-through occurs only in HEPA and not in ULPA filters. How does this relate to the structure of ULPA media?

Section Summary

  • Differential pressure monitoring is better than scheduled replacement: Monitor filter loading with a DP gauge and decide when to replace based on differential pressure rather than a time schedule; this lowers TCO and avoids the risk of blowout
  • The three major standards must be cross-referenced: ASHRAE 52.2 (MERV), EN 779/1822 (G/F/H/U) and IEST RP-CC001 (A-G/K) are three classification standards with different test methods, and comparisons are approximate only
  • The MPPS is the lowest point of filter efficiency: It lies in the 0.1-0.2 μm range and is the "blind spot" where the effectiveness of diffusion, interception and inertial impaction crosses over. EN 1822 tests at the MPPS, which represents the most stringent challenge
  • Each of the four filtration levels has its own role: Level I (MERV 7/G4) stops large particles and extends filter life, Level II (MERV 14/F8) protects equipment, Level III (HEPA or ASHRAE) protects the ductwork, and Terminal (H13-H14) protects the cleanroom
  • FFUs are a flexible supplementary solution: Self-contained HEPA units with their own fans, suited to protecting small areas, retrofitting older facilities and troubleshooting during commissioning
  • Gel seal degradation needs active prevention: Ensure the silicone is fully cross-linked, use a high-molecular-weight gel seal, and reduce DOP/PAO exposure. Do not substitute urethane gel for silicone.
  • Bleed-through stems from mismatched test conditions: It is caused by differences between factory testing (Laskin-nozzle, low air velocity) and field testing (hot-block, high air velocity). The solution is to specify the MPPS efficiency and the actual test conditions clearly in the URS
  • The decision hierarchy for sterility assurance: In all filtration system design decisions, sterility assurance always comes first, followed by product CQAs, and cost and flexibility come last
ISPE Good Practice Guide: HVAC | p115 - p136

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the key inspection points for each HVAC component during installation and startup: AHUs, fans, coils, humidifiers, dehumidifiers, HEPA filters, ductwork, etc.
  • Understand the difference between commissioning and qualification, and how the V-model applies to HVAC systems
  • Learn how to perform cleanroom particle counts, recovery tests, pressure differential verification and pressure alarm delay tests
  • Be familiar with the scope and content requirements of HVAC system personnel training
  • Understand preventive maintenance (PM) and predictive maintenance (PdM) strategies for the various types of HVAC equipment, including recommended maintenance frequencies
  • Understand spare parts strategy, so that critical components can be restored quickly when they fail
5.2 (cont.) Specifying and Testing HEPA Filters

Original Text

Recommended practices to avoid the bleed-through problem:

  • specify the filter for the maximum velocity it will see in operation
  • factory test for efficiency and leakage at that velocity at the filter's MPPS
  • If the filter will be field integrity tested with a hot-block generator, the filter should meet (as a minimum) the requirements for an IEST Type K or an EN-1822 Type H14 with a local penetration limit of two times the global penetration (i.e., 0.01%) instead of the standard five times (0.025%) as called for in EN-1822.
  • If bleed-through presents an insurmountable obstacle, ULPA filters may be used. In addition, HEPA filters that use Teflon media (ePTFE) can give better performance than other HEPA filters, but may present their own testing problems in the field. As ULPA and Teflon filters are more expensive than HEPA filters, their use should be justified and manufacturers consulted before specifying.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Bleed-through

Bleed-through: At high air velocities, particles that would normally be captured are "blown through" the HEPA filter media, reducing filtration efficiency. This is not a damaged filter; it is a physical loss of efficiency.

MPPS (Most Penetrating Particle Size): Typically between 0.1 and 0.3 µm, this is the particle size range at which a HEPA filter is least efficient. Factory testing is only meaningful if performed at this particle size.

Key Point: Local Penetration Limit

If a hot-block generator is used for on-site integrity testing, the requirement is stricter than the EN-1822 standard: the local penetration limit is tightened from 5 times the global penetration (0.025%) to 2 times (0.01%). This is because the aerosol particle size distribution produced by a hot-block generator differs from DOP/PAO, so a tighter specification is needed to ensure an equivalent level of safety.

Analogy

Imagine a fishing net: when the water flows slowly it catches every fish, but if the current is too fast, some of the small fish are swept through. HEPA filter bleed-through works on the same principle: the higher the air velocity, the more easily particles penetrate. That is why a filter must be tested at the actual maximum air velocity, not at an ideal low velocity.

5.3 Equipment Installation and Startup

Original Text

5.3.1 Introduction

The guidance in this section should be considered for HVAC design drawings, as well as in the construction specification.

Care should be taken during installation and startup to preclude operational and maintenance problems. It usually is helpful for the HVAC system installer to follow "build clean" practices, such as cleaning duct and components prior to installation, cleaning after installation, and sealing installed ductwork to prevent ingress of contamination. A "white glove test" may not be specified, but systems should be capable of passing this test.

This section is not all-inclusive, and the user should consult with the equipment manufacturer for detailed specifics and procedures. Guidance for startup also may apply to ongoing operation and maintenance.

Air system startup usually is contracted to trained and certified professionals. Organizations such as NEBB have offered specific cleanroom certification. Occasionally, a "facility HVAC engineer" may be called upon to solve an immediate problem. The solution depends on the engineer's skill and access to specific tools:

  • hot-wire anemometer
  • pressure sensor, 0.01 inch (2.5 Pa) accuracy to 0.5 inch full scale (125 Pa). Higher pressure range is needed to troubleshoot fan and duct problems.
  • flow hood (used to measure supply outlet or return airflow)
  • hand-held thermometer, RH meter
  • particle counter
  • cold aerosol generator (for HEPA test)
  • smoke source (smoke sticks, smoke candles) for air pattern visualization
  • duct tape and cardboard (used to temporarily block openings, divert airflow patterns, change the shape of equipment under UDAF hoods, etc.)

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Build Clean

Build Clean: Control cleanliness from the construction phase onward: clean components before installation, clean the system after installation, and seal completed ductwork to keep contamination out. This matters because dirt left during construction becomes "embedded" in the system and is very hard to remove completely after startup.

White Glove Test: Wipe the inside wall of the duct with a white glove and check for dust residue. Although it may not be formally written into the specification, ISPE expects system quality to be good enough to "pass" this test.

Analogy

It is like renovating a new house: if the construction dust is not cleaned up before painting and laying floors, it stays hidden between the walls and floors forever. The same is true of an HVAC system: metal shavings, grease and dust left over from construction will be blown into the cleanroom after startup, and can even puncture the HEPA filters.

Practical Application for a CDMO

As a CDMO, how rigorously build clean is carried out during a facility renovation or expansion directly affects how smoothly later qualification goes. Recommendations:

  • Write build clean requirements into the construction contract, with clearly defined acceptance criteria
  • Carry out an area cleanliness inspection at the end of each construction day
  • Seal HVAC ductwork immediately after completion and assign a dedicated person to patrol it
  • Prepare the basic measuring equipment from the tool list above, and build the troubleshooting skills of in-house HVAC engineers
5.3.2 Air Handling Units Shipping, Storage, Installation

Original Text

Larger air volume AHUs typically are disassembled after factory testing, and each section is separately wrapped for shipment. The unit or sections should be lifted vertically on a level plane by their lifting lug bracket arms to prevent distortion and stress on the components. It is recommended that an experienced rigger supervise the lifting and installation of the equipment.

The air-handling units should be stored in a dry area to protect components (fan-shaft, bearings and wheel, coils, humidifiers, and filters) against dust and corrosion. If a unit is idle for more than one month prior to startup, equipment with bearings should have their shafts manually rotated every two weeks to prevent premature bearing failure and redistribution of the lubricant.

The AHU position should allow sufficient free space for servicing its utility connections (steam, chilled and hot water, and electric) and internal components (e.g., coils, motors, filters). It should be mounted on a rigid, level foundation for correct alignment of the fan and drive equipment, for freedom from excessive vibration, and for the removal of condensate. It should be set sufficiently high to allow for correct condensate drainage using a P-trap and cap for ease of the trap's priming, removal, and cleanout.

When reassembling sections of the AHU, gaskets, and RTV sealant should be used to eliminate air leakage. Minimal sealant should be applied to produce a clean, smooth, and level bead surface.

Procedures during the installation and startup of the unit should preclude dirt and debris accumulating within and around the unit. The interior of the air handler should be wiped down to remove residual oil and grease.

Prior to startup, a checklist can encourage smooth operation. Items that may be considered are covered in ASHRAE Guideline 1.

Fasteners, bolts, wheel hub set screws, and bearing locking collars should be checked for tightness before equipment startup.

Shipping tie down bolts and shims also should be removed before air handler startup.

Dampers on air handlers should operate freely and blades close tightly.

When supplied with a variable frequency drive, the unit should be started at low rpm and its speed increased slowly up to its maximum capacity. Unusual noise should be listened for and inspection should be performed for increased vibration and overheating of bearings.

Tests to be considered include:

  • a pressurized leak test to ensure joints/connections are correctly aligned and the air handler cabinet is not leaking in excess of the specified value
  • condensate drain pans and traps should be filled with water to confirm correct drainage, while the unit is operating

Tutorial Commentary

Key Point: Bearing Protection for Idle Equipment

This detail is easy to overlook but costly: if an AHU sits idle for more than a month, the bearings can suffer dry wear because the lubricant settles under gravity. Manually rotating the bearings every two weeks is the simplest preventive measure. This is especially important when projects are delayed, since equipment that arrives on site and then waits months for installation is far from unusual.

Key Concept: Five Key Points of AHU Installation

  • Lifting: Lift vertically and level using lifting lugs and brackets to prevent deformation. Lifting must be supervised by an experienced rigger.
  • Foundation: A rigid, level base ensures fan alignment, reduces vibration and allows smooth drainage.
  • P-trap height: The condensate drain P-trap must be tall enough to prevent air from being drawn back in during operation.
  • Sealing: Use gaskets plus RTV sealant between sections; use as little sealant as possible and keep the surface smooth.
  • VFD startup: Ramp up slowly from low speed, and listen, look and feel as you go (listen for noise, look for vibration, feel the bearing temperature).

Analogy

Installing an AHU is like assembling a large, precision engine: the tightness of every bolt, the flatness of every sealing surface and the lubrication of every bearing all affect final performance. Just as a new car needs to be driven slowly during its break-in period, a VFD-driven AHU should also be "run in" from low speed and gradually brought up to design speed.

Practice Questions

  1. Does your facility have a procedure for periodically rotating the bearings while an AHU is stored after delivery and before installation?
  2. Does the pre-startup checklist for AHUs include leak testing and condensate drain testing?
5.3.3 - 5.3.5 Fans, Coils & Humidifiers Installation

Original Text

5.3.3 Fans

Correct fan installation and startup are critical to providing sufficient airflow in a safe manner, as a tremendous amount of kinetic energy is produced, and potentially, catastrophic results can result.

Laser alignment on the fan and motor shafts should be performed after the fan has been installed at the site, because shipping and installation can alter the factory alignment.

Drive belts should be adjusted to their proper tension prior to startup. Following 24 hours of operation, the belts should be re-tensioned.

Bearings should be checked for correct lubrication. If automatic lubrication units have been installed, they should be activated only at the time of startup.

Fan wheels should be turned over by hand to see that they run free and do not strike fan housings. The location of wheels in relation to fan inlets should be checked and fan housings should not be distorted. The fan should be jogged electrically to check for correct rotation.

Vibration testing should be performed following installation and startup to promote longevity and reliable operation of the equipment. It should be verified that the fan will not operate near its critical speed.

5.3.4 Heating and Cooling Coils

Coils should be inspected for concealed or visible damage prior to acceptance of delivery. The coil fins should be combed after installation to foster good air distribution and heat exchange.

Piping to the coil should be independently supported to avoid deforming the coil nozzle, headers or tubes, and stressing the brazed joints.

Insulation with protective jackets should be installed on hot and cold piping to eliminate hazard to personnel, reduce surface condensation, and reduce heat loss/gain.

Coils should be vented of air on initial startup and should include a manual or an automatic air vent.

For cooling coils, the term "moisture carry-over" describes the action of condensate being blown off the coil's surface with cooled air. Following startup when condensing occurs, observation should be made for moisture carry over. If carryover occurs, then the following resolutions are available:

  • reduce the coil face velocity (may not be possible if rooms need more airflow)
  • install a perforated screen upstream of the coil to evenly distribute air across the coil, producing a more even face velocity
  • install a mist eliminator after the coil

5.3.5 Steam Humidifiers

The steam distribution manifold should be placed where the supply air temperature is sufficiently warm to absorb steam being discharged without causing condensation at or after the unit. Inside an AHU, this may be downstream of the pre-heating coil and upstream of the cooling coil (which acts as a mist eliminator). Do not place the steam distribution manifold too near to the face of air filters where saturation of the filters will greatly shorten their life. Avoid placing the steam distribution manifold where visible discharge mist will impinge directly on a metal surface.

Another common location is in the ductwork after the reheat coil and air filters. When the humidifier is located in ductwork, a downstream section of the ductwork should be constructed of stainless steel to eliminate the possibility of rusting. Access panels should be located both upstream and downstream of the humidifier for servicing.

Drain pans and condensate piping should catch and carry away water that can occur from humidification 'spitting' during startup. The drain and trap should flow and the water column will not drain completely when the duct is pressurized.

Uniform airflow over the cross section of the steam distribution manifold should be verified to assure absorption of steam.

The airflow sensor ("sail switch" or a signal from the AHU airflow monitor) should prevent the steam valve from opening unless air is moving in the duct.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Point: Safety Warnings for Fan Installation

ISPE uses words such as "catastrophic" and "life threatening", which is very rare in this guide. A rotating fan carries a great deal of kinetic energy, and if it is installed improperly (unbalanced impeller, misaligned bearings, incorrect belt tension), it can cause serious accidents such as blades flying off or bearings bursting.

  • Laser alignment: Factory alignment shifts during transport and must be redone on site.
  • Belt tension: Adjust before startup, and readjust after 24 hours (new belts stretch).
  • Bump (jog) test: First turn by hand to confirm there is no contact with the housing, then jog electrically to confirm the direction of rotation.
  • Critical speed: Confirm that the operating speed is well away from resonance points.

Key Concept: Moisture Carry-over

Moisture Carry-over: Condensate on the cooling coil surface is blown off by the airflow and carried with the air into downstream equipment and ductwork. This leads to rust on the duct walls, microbial growth and wetting of the HEPA filters. There are three solutions, in order of priority: reduce the face velocity > install drain eliminators (baffles) > install mist eliminators.

Key Point: Where Not to Place a Steam Humidifier

There are three "do nots" for the location of the steam distribution manifold:

  • Not near filters: Steam saturation greatly shortens filter life.
  • Not facing metal surfaces: Visible steam impinging directly on metal surfaces causes corrosion.
  • Not where the temperature is insufficient: If the air is not warm enough, it cannot fully absorb the steam, and condensation results.

In addition, when a humidifier is installed inside a duct, the downstream ductwork must be stainless steel, because the steam continues to condense until it is fully absorbed.

CDMO Practical Reminder

Taiwan's climate is hot and humid, so steam humidifiers are mainly used in winter and the dry season. However, moisture carry-over from cooling coils is a potential problem all year round. It is recommended to watch specifically for moisture carry-over during the first hot summer period after the AHU is started up, and to make it an inspection item in the PM records.

5.3.6 - 5.3.8 Desiccant Dehumidifiers, Air Filtration & Ductwork

Original Text

5.3.6 Desiccant Dehumidifiers

Desiccant dehumidification systems are the most common means of achieving low RH for the pharmaceutical industry.

Desiccant units should be clear of surrounding obstructions to allow removal and replacement of the desiccant wheels, fans, filters, etc.

The air from the reactivation portion of the wheel should be ducted (sloped to the outside, if horizontal path) to the exterior of the building due to its high moisture and heat content. The intake and outlet for the process and reactivation air streams should not be located close together to avoid short cycling that can reduce overall dehumidification capacity.

Operation of bypass and humidity control dampers should be verified.

Manufacturer's recommendations should be followed for starting up their particular dehumidifier. This includes verifying wheel rotation and reactivation discharge temperature to dry the wheel before applying load to the wheel.

Wheels using lithium chloride should be kept hot and rotating, even when dehumidification is not required, to avoid damage to the desiccant due to over-absorption.

5.3.7 Air Filtration

Temporary filters should be installed during construction to keep the AHU, components, and ductwork clear of contaminants if the system is energized to provide temporary conditioning to the workspace. Once construction of the building and spaces has been completed, these filters should be replaced with clean filters.

HEPA/ULPA filters should be handled with special care. Consideration needs to be taken in the selection of the method and carrier used for filter shipment. Each pallet of filters should be checked before accepting shipment from the carrier. Pallets of filters that have been damaged or broken down should not be accepted without a thorough inspection and appropriate comments noted on the shipping documentation.

The filters should be stored to prevent damage or intrusion of foreign matter. Storage should be indoors, under roof, within 40 to 100°F (4 to 38°C) and 25 to 75% RH and be thoroughly protected from moisture.

Competent personnel and proven techniques and procedures should be employed for the installation of the filters. Prior to installation of HEPA/ULPA filters, duct and filter housings should be checked for cleanliness and obstructions that might impair filter operation. Filters should be unpacked and inspected for damage. Damaging the filter media should be avoided. If the media are damaged or have visible holes, filters should not be installed.

Filter clamping mechanisms should ensure that air does not bypass around filters or their supporting grid. This is particularly important at terminal filters mounted in ceiling frames.

Penetration (pinhole) testing is usually performed on only filters that provide direct contact air over product and critical locations, i.e., Grade A/Grade 5 hoods, and on occasion, for filters used to capture hazardous materials. There is little value in testing for pinholes in HEPA filters installed in ductwork and air handlers, where overall capture efficiency testing is more valuable. For further information see ISO 14644-3.

5.3.8 Ductwork

Ductwork typically is found in locations difficult to access. Sufficient access to service components, such as volume control devices and reheat coils, should be provided. Protection of the ductwork during construction and access to and around it should be provided; otherwise, damage to the ductwork may result in airflow leakage or increased air pressure drop and velocity. In addition, ductwork insulation that has been compromised will result in condensation and rusting and loss or gain in heat.

The use of flexible ducting should be limited to minimum lengths, properly supported, and securely fastened at each end. Sharp bends and turns, which will reduce the cross-sectional area of the flexible duct and result in reduced air volume delivery, should be avoided.

Ductwork should be wiped and cleaned of oil, dirt, and metal shavings prior to field installation. A solution of alcohol and lint free wipes may be used to remove oils or grease that may have accumulated during the fabrication and installation of the ductwork.

After ductwork is cleaned, openings should be covered with plastic sheeting and tape to keep them clean.

Avoiding the use of self-drilling sheet metal screws is recommended, as they generate small metal chips inside the cleaned ductwork. Self-piercing (zip) screws are preferred when there is concern for loose contamination inside the ductwork.

Installation of pressure test ports, smoke detectors, temperature sensors, and duct traverse testing ports at a later date can contaminate interior of ductwork with metal chips as a result of their field penetrations into a duct. Penetrations of the duct wall should maintain ductwork interior cleanliness. Where metal shavings or debris may have been produced, the interior of ducts should be cleaned, providing access as required, and the access opening sealed. Failure to follow these practices can result in sharp metal fragments being blown into the delicate HEPA filter media, causing filter integrity failures.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Point: Special Requirements for LiCl Desiccant Wheels

Lithium chloride desiccant has a fatal weakness: if it is left alone when shut down, it absorbs too much moisture from the environment, swells and "bursts" off the wheel. So even when dehumidification is not needed, a LiCl wheel must be kept heated and rotating. It is a piece of equipment that cannot be stopped even when it is not in use.

Key Concept: The HEPA Filter Handling Chain

ISPE's requirements for handling HEPA filters cover the entire "supply chain":

  • Transport: Choose an appropriate shipping method and vehicle, and inspect every shipment on arrival.
  • Receipt: Damaged pallets are not acceptable and must be noted on the delivery documents.
  • Storage: Indoors, under a roof, 4-38°C, 25-75% RH.
  • Before installation: Check the cleanliness of the filter housing and mounting frame.
  • During installation: Avoid damaging the filter media, and confirm that the clamping mechanism has no bypass.

Negligence at any one step can scrap a HEPA filter worth tens of thousands of NT dollars before it is ever put into service.

Key Point: The Knock-on Effect of Metal Debris in Ductwork

This is an underestimated risk: when sensors and smoke detectors are installed late in duct construction, the metal shavings from drilling stay inside the duct. After system startup they are blown toward the HEPA filters, and sharp metal fragments puncture the filter media, causing the integrity test to fail.

Preventive measures: Use self-piercing (zip) screws instead of self-drilling screws. Clean the inside of the duct whenever holes are made late in construction. Seal the duct with plastic sheeting immediately after cleaning.

Practice Questions

  1. Does your HEPA filter supplier have clear transport and storage requirements? Does the receiving inspection procedure cover packaging integrity?
  2. Do your ductwork construction specifications prohibit self-drilling screws? Do they require the duct to be cleaned after late-stage hole drilling?
  3. Are temporary filters installed during construction to protect the AHU and ductwork?
5.3.8.1 Duct Leakage Test

Original Text

Pressure testing is recommended for ductwork systems serving a GMP system to avoid:

  • increased use of outside air to overcome supply air losses and maintain adequate flow
  • increased energy costs to operate system
  • operating equipment at its maximum capacity with no reserve capacity
  • unwanted air leaking into surrounding (mechanical) spaces from positive pressurized ductwork or room air leaking into negatively pressurized ductwork, requiring more airflow through fans

The "Total Percentage Leakage Method" is recommended: a percentage of total air delivery of duct section under test at a specific static pressure for performing duct leakage. See SMACNA or HVCA DW143. Typical leakage percentages for various operations include:

  • 0% (essentially) leakage for positive pressure exhaust duct on hazardous operations to avoid release of harmful materials to the plant room
  • no more than 1% for product processing areas

Evaluation of leakage versus energy cost should be performed for laboratory supply systems and support and administrative areas.

Other leakage testing methods may be employed. It is generally not a GMP requirement for ducts to be leak-free; energy savings are a bigger driver for lower leakage. Risks associated with leakage should be assessed.

Table 5.5: Ductwork Testing Requirements

Duct leakage testing should be performed with traceable calibrated test instruments and documented with signed approvals.

Leakage from non-duct components (fire dampers, smoke dampers, air flow monitors, duct heating coils, manual volume damper quadrants, and access doors) is an integral part of the overall system leakage, and these components should be included in the duct leakage tests.

Once construction is completed, the system should be blown down for at least 1 hour to purge the ductwork of loose and light debris that may have accumulated. Blow down will not flush the system of metal fragments that result from poor ductwork cleanliness control.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Layers of Impact from Duct Leakage

Duct leakage is more than simply "air leaking out"; it causes a chain of effects:

  • Insufficient airflow: Downstream rooms do not receive the design airflow, and air change rates fall.
  • Loss of pressure control: Leakage changes the pressure balance of the system.
  • Higher energy consumption: The fan has to work harder to compensate for the leakage.
  • Exhausted capacity: The system runs at full load with no reserve capacity.
  • Cross-contamination risk: Air from positive-pressure ducts leaks into the mechanical room, or mechanical room air leaks into negative-pressure ducts.

Specifications Quick Reference

Hazardous material exhaust ductwork: leakage rate = 0% (essentially zero leakage)
Product processing areas: leakage rate ≤ 1%
General areas: determined by energy economic analysis

Blow-down after construction: ≥ 1 hour
Test instruments: traceable calibration
Documentation: signed and approved

Key Point: Blow-down ≠ Cleaning

ISPE specifically notes that blowing down the duct removes only loose, light debris and cannot remove metal fragments left by poor construction practice. The implication is: do not expect blow-down to make up for shortcomings in build clean. Build clean is the foundation; blow-down is only a supplement.

5.3.9 - 5.3.15 Dampers, Diffusers, UV Lights, Exhaust, UDAF, Controls & Building

Original Text

5.3.9 Dampers and Louvers

Actuators should be accessible for service and maintenance. Drive linkages should be secure and should operate without binding over their full range of travel.

Assemblies should be sealed to the framing of the opening to reduce bypass around damper perimeters.

5.3.10 Diffusers and Registers

Diffusers and registers should prevent poor distribution of air and to minimize drafts and short-circuiting of supply air.

5.3.11 Ultraviolet Lights

UV wavelength lighting degrades many plastics, including: synthetic air filter media and frames, plastic coated wires, gaskets, grommets, and duct insulation. These materials should be at least 3 ft (~1 m) from the light source.

UV power supply circuits should be interrupted upon the loss of airflow past the lighting elements.

There should be no escape of UV light through direct or indirect transmission. In addition, warning signs should be placed in the area to advise personnel.

Gloves should be worn when handling emitters. Oil from fingerprints can permanently etch emitter glass and weaken its structure. If necessary, emitter should be cleaned using isopropyl alcohol and lint free wipe.

5.3.12 Exhaust/Extraction Systems

Ductwork or stacks should be independently supported, as the additional weight may stress the fan housing and result in vibration that can transmit to building structures. Guy wires (supports) may be needed for adequate stack bracing.

Positive pressure process ducts handling contaminated exhaust inside a building should be leak-free.

Install fire dampers and explosion vents in accordance with the US National Fire Protection Association Codes and other applicable codes and standards.

Fans and filtration equipment should be located, such that maintenance access is serviceable.

5.3.13 Unidirectional Airflow

UDAF hoods should be commissioned and then verified fit for use:

  • Airflow face velocity is usually measured 6 to 12 inches (15 to 30 cm) from the filter face. Uniformity of velocity is expected to be within 20% of the target value.
  • HEPA filters should be integrity tested at accepted velocity. The casing of the hood also should be scanned for leaks at this time.
  • Pressure drop across HEPA filters should be recorded at the accepted velocity.
  • Airflow patterns at rest (no operators, production equipment not running) at the optimal average velocity. If not 90 ft/min (0.45 m/sec), it may be advisable to test at the lowest and highest velocities that create acceptable airflow patterns to justify a different velocity from 90 ft/min.
  • Flow alarms should be tested. The alarm should not be a motor sensor, as the motor may continue to operate after the supply fan has failed.

The science of fluid dynamics says that air turbulence increases with velocity and with distance. For these reasons, optimal airflow patterns may occur at lower velocity and closer to the filter face. It is not uncommon, during the commissioning phase, to create temporary curtains and aerodynamic shields to improve airflow patterns at critical sites.

5.3.14 Controls and Instrumentation

Instrumentation should be readily accessible for maintenance and replacement. Components should be calibrated prior to commissioning of the HVAC with calibration stickers applied.

5.3.15 Building

Construction activities typically occur at a tightly coordinated and accelerated pace to meet schedule commitments. The owner should inspect the site on a regular schedule to verify design intent, construction quality, and integration of systems occur as planned.

Typical construction issues include:

  • Air migration through the building caused by poorly sealed penetrations and finishes can lead to unacceptable control of space DPs. The following penetrations and openings should be checked: piping, ductwork, electrical conduit and receptacles, doors, diffusers and registers, architectural wall and ceiling joints, lighting fixtures.
  • During construction, cleaning procedures should minimize the accumulation of construction debris and dirt.
  • Procedures should be in place for personnel to wear appropriate gowning (i.e., booties, smocks) to keep out dirt from areas which have been designated and substantially complete. Before HVAC startup, equipment, walls, and cleanroom floors should have been wiped down and floors swept and vacuumed.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Key Points for UDAF Verification

UDAF (Unidirectional Airflow): The core equipment of Grade A/ISO 5 areas. Key verification points:

  • Face velocity measurement location: 15-30 cm from the filter face, not at the working surface.
  • Uniformity criterion: The velocity at each measurement point deviates from the target value by ≤ 20%.
  • Airflow visualization: Observe the airflow pattern under at-rest conditions (no operators, equipment not running).
  • The optimal velocity is not necessarily 0.45 m/s: Airflow patterns can be tested at different velocities to find the best balance.

Analogy: Turbulence and Distance

It is like a shower: close to the shower head the water stream is neat and straight, but the farther away you get, the more scattered it becomes. UDAF airflow behaves the same way: the closer to the HEPA filter, the more laminar it is, and the farther away, the more turbulent. That is why ISPE recommends using temporary curtains and aerodynamic baffles during commissioning to improve the airflow pattern in critical areas, much like adding a panel in a shower stall to guide the water.

Key Point: Hidden Risks of UV Lights

UV lights degrade plastic materials, including filter media and frames, wire insulation, gaskets and duct insulation. During installation, make sure these materials are at least 1 meter from the UV source. In addition, finger grease permanently etches the glass of UV lamps, so gloves must be worn when handling them.

Key Point: The "Seven Leaks" of Building Tightness

ISPE lists the most common leakage sources behind loss of pressure differential control:

  1. Pipe penetrations through walls
  2. Duct penetrations through walls
  3. Electrical conduits and outlets
  4. Door gaps
  5. Supply and return air openings
  6. Wall and ceiling joints
  7. Light fixtures

Each of these locations must be checked and sealed during construction. Missing any one of them can cause pressure control to fall short of requirements and delay qualification.

Practice Questions

  1. Is your UDAF face velocity uniformity within ±20%? Has static airflow visualization testing been performed?
  2. During construction, is a dedicated person responsible for checking the sealing of wall penetrations?
  3. Do construction workers in cleanroom areas wear the designated protective clothing (shoe covers, coveralls)?
5.4 Commissioning and Qualification

Original Text

5.4 Introduction

It is considered GEP for HVAC systems to be commissioned to verify that they perform as designed. Commissioning protocols typically are developed during design and executed during and after construction. HVAC engineers often are involved in Factory Acceptance Testing (FAT) and Site Acceptance Testing (SAT) of major HVAC equipment and systems.

Qualification should be performed for HVAC systems which have a direct impact on product quality and of components which are critical to product quality. Qualification may leverage documentation from earlier steps or may require extra testing.

Note: the "what" that needs to be done to qualify the system is shown (user requirements and functional design requirements should be satisfied). For further detail, see ASHRAE Standard 1 on Commissioning, ISO 14644-3 on cleanroom commissioning, and various Recommended Practices (RP) from IEST.

Direct impact, indirect impact, and no impact systems should be identified, followed by identification of the critical components within the direct impact systems. Critical systems and components should be qualified; the remainder of the systems and components should be commissioned. See the ISPE Baseline® Guide on Commissioning and Qualification.

HVAC systems may be identified as direct impact systems with, e.g., the HEPA filters being critical components. An alternative approach may be to identify all the final HEPA filters as the "air quality system," drawing a boundary around them as a direct impact system to be qualified with the air handler and its prefilters being indirect impact.

Similarly, direct impact system boundaries can be defined for pressure monitoring, temperature monitoring, etc., allowing qualification documents to focus on the components presenting the greatest risk to product quality and patient safety.

5.4.1 Typical Commissioning and Qualification Activities

Typical commissioning activities may include:

  • ductwork leak testing
  • layout and device location verification
  • safety device testing (freezestats, firestats, smoke detectors, pressure switches, etc.)
  • verification of filter installation
  • AHU and duct cleaning
  • motor rotation, speed, and amperage verification
  • operational testing of all components (dampers, motors, switches, indicators, etc.)
  • rotating equipment balancing
  • vibration measurement
  • lubrication
  • static pressure setpoint adjustment
  • temperature setpoint adjustment
  • VFD adjustment
  • air balancing
  • coil performance verification (water and air side)
  • startup

Typical qualification activities might include:

  • air balancing
  • filter integrity testing
  • room classification testing
  • room pressurization or airflow direction testing
  • airflow visualization
  • face velocity testing

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: The Key Difference between Commissioning and Qualification

This is the most important conceptual distinction in HVAC qualification:

  • Commissioning: Falls under GEP (Good Engineering Practice) and verifies that the system "operates as designed". It should be done for all systems. It is verification at the engineering level.
  • Qualification: Falls under GMP and verifies the critical components of systems that have a "direct impact" on product quality. It is required only for direct impact systems. It is verification at the quality level.

The point where the two intersect is air balancing: it appears on both the commissioning and the qualification lists, because it is both an engineering adjustment and a quality verification.

Key Concept: Impact Assessment

ISPE's system classification framework:

  • Direct Impact: Direct effect on product quality, so it must be qualified. Examples: HEPA filters, pressure differential monitoring, temperature monitoring.
  • Indirect Impact: Supports direct impact systems, so commissioning is sufficient. Examples: the AHU itself, pre-filters.
  • No Impact: Unrelated to product quality, so basic commissioning only. Example: HVAC for office areas.

ISPE offers a clever "system boundary" approach: all terminal HEPA filters can be defined as an "air quality system" with a direct impact boundary drawn around it, while the AHU and pre-filters are classified as indirect impact. This lets the qualification documentation focus on the highest-risk components.

Analogy

Think of a restaurant hygiene inspection: "commissioning" is like checking that the kitchen equipment works properly (the stove lights, the refrigerator cools, the exhaust hood extracts). "Qualification" is checking that the equipment that directly contacts food meets food safety standards (cutting board sanitization, refrigeration temperature, cooking temperature). Not every piece of equipment needs a food safety inspection, but equipment that directly contacts food must pass.

Practical Application for a CDMO

In a CDMO environment, the outcome of the impact assessment directly affects the scope and rigor of change control. Correct system classification can:

  • Reduce qualification documentation: Only direct impact components need formal IQ/OQ/PQ.
  • Speed up change approval: Replacing indirect impact components does not require requalification.
  • Focus resources: Concentrate limited QA resources where product quality is truly affected.
5.4.1.1 - 5.4.1.4 Room Testing

Original Text

5.4.1.1 Room Particle Counting

Setup for particle counting in a room is described in ISO 14644-2.

5.4.1.2 Room Recovery Test

Procedures using a smoke generator and multiple particle counters are outlined in ISO 14644-3.

For further information on recovery testing, see the ISPE HVAC COP Web site.

5.4.1.3 Room DP

Procedures for verifying DP are described in ISO 14644-3.

5.4.1.4 Time Delay on DP alarm

If a classified space is not separated from a space of a lower classification by an airlock, it may be necessary to verify the time delay on low DP alarms; a test may involve:

  1. Raising particle levels in the space with lower classification with a smoke generator; monitoring these levels to assure that they do not drop on their own. They should be at the upper limit of the space's in-use air class.
  2. Setting a particle counter in the cleaner space, between the doorway and the critical site. (If the critical site is under a UFH, locating the counter away from the hood.)
  3. Opening the door and simulating normal traffic through the door. Measuring the time before particle counts start to increase beyond normal expected levels. This time period will be the maximum time delay permitted.
  4. Setting the time delay set point at a time much less (e.g., 50%) than the measured time interval.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Pressure Alarm Delay Test

This is a very practical test that is often overlooked. When there is no airlock between two rooms of different cleanliness grades, opening the door instantly disrupts the pressure differential. If the pressure alarm is set too sensitive, operators trigger an alarm every time they open the door (too many false alarms); if it is set too sluggish, a genuine pressure abnormality may not be detected in time.

ISPE's approach: Measure experimentally how long it takes for particle counts to exceed limits after the door is opened, then set the alarm delay at no more than 50% of that time. This avoids too many false alarms while still giving a timely warning when something is genuinely wrong.

Analogy

It is like setting a speeding alarm in a car: if it sounded every time you briefly exceeded the limit by 1-2 seconds on the highway, the driver would get annoyed and switch it off. But if it is set to sound only after "speeding for more than 5 seconds", it can distinguish "a brief acceleration to overtake" from "sustained speeding". The logic of the pressure alarm delay is exactly the same: allow a time window for normal operations (opening doors, walking through), but respond quickly to genuine abnormalities.

Key Point: The Clever Design of the Test Method

Note the thought behind this test design:

  • First raise the particle level in the lower-grade area to its "upper limit" to simulate the worst-case scenario.
  • Place the particle counter "between the door and the critical area", so that it monitors the "path" of particle ingress.
  • If the critical area is under a UDAF, keep the counter away from it, because the UDAF would interfere with the result.
  • Set the delay at no more than 50% of the measured value, leaving an ample safety margin.
5.5 Training

Original Text

Personnel who operate and maintain the HVAC system should be trained on its intended function (to satisfy the user requirements) and on the procedures needed to keep it running.

  • What the system is expected to do (the user requirements): effect on product and patient. Operator or maintenance personnel should understand why an HVAC system and its maintenance are important.
  • How do the HVAC systems maintain user requirements?
  • Qualification activities and documentation – what components are under change control (as few as possible, based on criticality), as-built drawings?
  • Operating SOPs: what are the access to set points, system startup, troubleshooting procedures?
  • Maintenance SOPs: what activities are needed and when?
  • Cleaning and precautions during maintenance activities
  • Instrument calibration: procedures, frequency
  • Where and how records are stored: records for GMP purposes may be stored separately. Who has access and control?

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: The "Why-How-What" Structure of HVAC Training

ISPE's training content structure fully matches the Golden Circle approach:

  • Why: The impact of the HVAC system on the product and the patient, so that maintenance staff understand the meaning of their work.
  • How: How the system maintains the User Requirements; understanding the principles is what allows people to do the right thing.
  • What: The specific SOPs, calibration procedures and record retention, which are the details of day-to-day execution.

Key Point: Scope of Change Control

ISPE specifically emphasizes that the components placed under change control should be "as few as possible", based on a judgment of criticality. This is consistent with the logic of the impact assessment above: not every HVAC component needs change control, only critical components with a direct impact. It reflects risk-based thinking in the training content.

Practical Application for a CDMO

In a CDMO environment, training of HVAC maintenance personnel is especially important because:

  • Different clients' products may have different environmental requirements (temperature, humidity, pressure differential, air change rate)
  • HVAC parameters may need to be adjusted at product changeover
  • Maintenance staff need to understand "why these parameters matter" rather than just "following the checklist"
  • Training records are always examined in GMP inspections
5.6 Equipment Operation and Maintenance

Original Text

5.6.1 Introduction

The maintenance of systems is fundamental to achieving correct operation, appearance, longevity, and safety. Inadequate maintenance can lead to unexpected and extended shutdowns. It also could lead to underperformance in maintaining the various environmental parameters (temperature, humidity, air quality, air flow, and pressurization) required for GMP facilities.

Predictive Maintenance (PdM) encompasses a range of technologies to detect degradation of equipment performance at an early stage before it can become a problem. This allows maintenance personnel to order parts, schedule manpower, and plan multiple repairs during a scheduled shutdown. The goal of PdM is to proactively correct problems before significant deterioration occurs.

Traditional (scheduled) Preventive Maintenance (PM) practices often cannot identify mechanical equipment failures that could have been detected through changes in operating temperature, vibration signatures, and bearing wear indicators. Equipment is susceptible to unplanned catastrophic failure that can interrupt production operations, cause risk to product, and result in reactive repairs that can be more expensive than planned repairs.

Physical appearance of equipment and its surroundings reflects the quality of the maintenance performed upon the equipment. Spent materials, extra parts, and trash could give a regulatory inspector the impression of poor maintenance practices. Maintaining clean HVAC systems is important to acceptable IAQ. Common contaminants include:

  • dust particles
  • active bacterial or fungal growth
  • debris from HVAC components (rust, belt shedding, grease)
  • loose duct lining
  • mold spores

Holes in the vapor barrier on exterior insulation can lead to condensation inside the insulation and eventual growth of mold and bacteria, as well as loss of insulating properties; good housekeeping practices should be followed.

Periodic walk downs of mechanical areas can ensure housekeeping is maintained at an acceptable level of quality. A new coat of paint may not improve HVAC performance, but it conveys a sense of attention to the state of the HVAC system.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: PM vs PdM Maintenance Strategies

The essential difference between the two maintenance strategies:

  • PM (Preventive Maintenance): Maintenance performed periodically on a schedule: "do it when the time comes", regardless of the condition of the equipment. Like changing engine oil at regular intervals.
  • PdM (Predictive Maintenance): Maintenance timing is decided from equipment condition monitoring (vibration, temperature, wear indicators): "do it when it is about to fail". Like deciding when to change the oil based on oil analysis results.

ISPE explicitly points out the limitation of PM: it cannot detect many mechanical failures in advance. The advantage of PdM is that it allows you to order parts ahead of time, arrange manpower, and combine repairs into planned shutdowns.

Analogy

PM is like changing the oil every 5,000 km regardless of its quality. PdM is like using an oil analyzer to measure how degraded the oil is and changing it just before it actually starts to fail. PM may replace too early (wasteful) or too late (damage), while PdM pinpoints the "optimal replacement time". In HVAC systems, vibration analysis is the best PdM tool: it can predict bearing failure weeks or even months ahead.

Key Point: Appearance Reflects Quality

ISPE makes a thoughtful point: "the appearance of the equipment reflects the quality of maintenance". Even though repainting does not improve HVAC performance, it conveys the message "we value this system". During an FDA inspection, scrap material, surplus parts and rubbish in the mechanical room make the inspector doubt the quality of the whole maintenance program. Good housekeeping is a hidden plus in a cGMP inspection.

5.6.2 - 5.6.5 AHU, Fans, Coils & Humidifiers Maintenance

Original Text

5.6.2 Air Handling Units

The AHU should be inspected periodically for air leaks, rusting, condensate drainage problems, and dirt accumulation, and to verify the proper operation of doors, drives, dampers and actuators, and lighting and switches.

Periodic cleaning of the unit's interior is recommended, particularly for units serving classified spaces, such as aseptic operation. A cleanliness inspection should consider the components within the unit, such as: filters, heating and cooling coils, condensate pans, condensate drain lines, humidification systems, acoustic insulation, fans, fan compartments, dampers, door gaskets, and general unit integrity.

Prefilters do not remove all air contaminants inside an AHU. Dirt accumulation over time can lead to microbial growth. Typically, the units are washed down with a solution that will kill microorganisms, while at the same time, eliminating grease and oil that may have been dispersed from bearings and other lubricated joints.

It is recommended that visible rust is removed and surfaces repainted to return their appearance to new.

Pools of standing water in condensate drain pans can lead to microbial growth and rusting of ferrous parts. Drainage should be checked during hot and humid periods when condensate generation is high.

Lighting fixtures with failed fluorescent tubes or ballasts result in poor lighting levels, affecting maintenance of AHU components and personnel safety.

Defective electrical switches and receptacles can lead to electrical hazards, poor operation of the components they serve, and increased maintenance.

Door maintenance is significant to the air tightness of a space. Gaskets, frames, hinges and latching handles tend to loosen and wear, leading to lower air delivery from the unit, energy loss, sweating, and infiltration of dirt.

5.6.3 Fans

Maintaining desired fan airflow is critical to providing adequate conditioned supply air into a space. If not appropriately maintained, fan components can lead to diminished airflow and eventual failure; components include: fan housings, wheels, bearings, belts, guards, and motors.

The fan wheel should be checked periodically for accumulation of dirt, mechanical fatigue, and imbalance that can result in increased vibration and noise, and ultimately catastrophic failure with life threatening potential (i.e., broken blades and housings).

Bearing failure is common, because of over- or under-lubrication and the use of lubricants that are not intended for the airstream environment. Personnel should have appropriate training from bearing manufacturers and lubrication suppliers. Vibration and temperature monitoring can assist in trending analysis to identify impending bearing failure.

Belt drives need extensive care and procedures for removing, installing, and starting-up equipment with belt drives. Improper belt tension is one of the most common root causes of premature failure; steps which should be followed include:

  • Check belt tension, using a tension gauge or Sonic Tension Meter. Adjust the belt drive's center distance until the correct tension is measured.
  • Rotate the belt drive by hand for a few revolutions. Re-check the belt tension and adjust as necessary.
  • Start the drive, looking and listening for any unusual noise or vibration. If the motor or bearings are hot, the belt tension may be too high.
  • V-belt Run-In Procedure: a run-in procedure is recommended for v-belt drives to optimize belt life. A run-in consists of starting the drive and letting it run under full load for up to 24 hours. After the belts have run-in, stop the belt drive and check the belt tension. Re-adjust as necessary. Failure to check and re-tension the belt will result in low belt tension, belt slippage, reduction of airflow, and eventual premature belt failure.

Motors should be capable of operating for more than 10 years without major problems. Since motors are expensive to purchase and their operating costs are high (e.g., 25 hp motor × 8760 hrs/yr × $0.075/kwh = $12,250/yr) maintenance is essential to keep operating costs at a minimum. The following activities should be performed:

  • Dirty motors run hot when thick dirt insulates the frame and clogs cooling air passages. Motor exterior should be periodically cleaned.
  • Check for signs of corrosion. Serious corrosion may indicate internal deterioration and a need for external repainting.
  • Lubricate the bearings only when scheduled or if they are noisy or running hot. Do not over-lubricate.
  • Feel the motor frame and bearings for excessive heat or vibration. Listen for abnormal noise.
  • Verify that belt and motor drive guards are securely fastened.

5.6.4 Heating and Cooling Coils

Coils, whether for heating, cooling, or dehumidifying, should be clean both internally and externally, and the fins for heat transfer should be intact and undamaged. Cooling coils typically reduce both the sensible (cooling) and latent (de-humidify) heat of the air, and they are more sensitive to loss in heat transfer capability than are heating coils. Cooling coils are more likely to accumulate dirt since they are usually wet.

Typically, coils (especially cooling coils) are externally cleaned once a year, as this side of the coil receives the most dirt. Internal cleaning typically is performed only when DPs of the heat transfer fluid increase beyond manufacturer recommendations. Coils may be periodically pressure tested for leaks. When face and bypass heat coils are used, the damper mechanisms should be inspected annually to ensure they correctly operate smoothly over their entire range of motion.

Control valves wear out over time due to constant modulation. These valves should be included in a regularly scheduled maintenance program.

5.6.5 Steam Humidifiers

There are a number of components that make up the humidifier system; items that should be inspected and maintained include:

  • the strainer screen: twice per year as a minimum (if fouled, steam flow will be reduced)
  • the control valve: annually to ensure that: (1) the steam valve closes tightly, (2) the stem packing is not leaking steam, (3) the diaphragm in the actuator is not leaking air
  • the sealing and O-rings to assure that no steam leaks into the surrounding area with the possibility of personnel injury
  • the nozzles for proper dispersion of steam into the airstream; if steam is not dispersing properly, capacity can be reduced or condensate can form downstream
  • the silencer: annually as a minimum for cleanliness

Tutorial Commentary

Key Point: Microbial Risk in AHU Maintenance

Sources of microbial risk inside an AHU:

  • Dust + humidity = microbial breeding ground: Pre-filters cannot capture all dust, so dust gradually accumulates inside the AHU; together with the humidity near the coils and humidifiers, this creates ideal conditions for microbial growth.
  • Standing condensate: Water standing in the drain pan is the most common microbial source. Pay particular attention to drainage during Taiwan's hot and humid summer.
  • Damaged insulation: A damaged vapor barrier on external insulation causes condensation inside the insulation, promoting mold and bacterial growth.

Countermeasure: Periodically clean the inside of the AHU with a germicidal solution, removing grease at the same time. Repaint after removing rust.

Key Concept: The "Five Senses" Rule for Fan Maintenance

Fan maintenance as described by ISPE is essentially a "five senses" inspection method:

  • Look: Check for belt wear, dust buildup on the impeller and signs of corrosion.
  • Listen: Abnormal noise may indicate bearing failure or imbalance.
  • Feel: Overheating or abnormal vibration of the motor and bearings.
  • Measure: Belt tension (using a tension gauge or sonic tension meter) and vibration values.
  • Calculate: Analyze the motor running cost to justify the maintenance investment.

Annual Motor Running Cost Calculation

Annual electricity cost = motor power (hp) × 8760 hr/yr × electricity unit price

Example: 25 hp × 8760 hr/yr × $0.075/kWh = $12,250/yr
(about NT$390,000/year)

This means the electricity cost of a single 25 hp motor
is close to NT$400,000 per year.
With good maintenance its life can be extended to more than 10 years,
while the cost of premature replacement due to poor maintenance
is far higher than the maintenance cost.

Key Point: V-belt Run-In Procedure

New belts must be "run in": readjust the tension after 24 hours of full-load operation. New belts stretch, and if the tension is not readjusted:

  • The belt slips → airflow decreases
  • Slipping generates heat → the belt ages faster
  • End result: premature belt breakage and unplanned downtime

This is one of the most common root causes in fan maintenance, yet it is also the step most easily overlooked.

Practice Questions

  1. How often is the inside of your AHUs cleaned? Is a germicidal solution used?
  2. Are there clear frequency and quantity specifications for bearing lubrication? Has over-lubrication ever caused bearing damage?
  3. After a belt is replaced, is there a procedure for the 24-hour run-in and tension readjustment?
5.6.6 - 5.6.9 Desiccant, Filtration, Ductwork & Dampers Maintenance

Original Text

5.6.6 Desiccant Dehumidifier

The maintenance of desiccant units includes: filters, wheel drive assembly, wheel support bearings, seals between process and regeneration sections, fans, belts, and controls.

Desiccant components should be maintained according to a recommended schedule.

As a desiccant system has incoming air on the supply side and a second air stream for reactivation, both sets of inlet air filters need regular replacement to prevent airflow being reduced. Clogged filters on the supply or process air will cause overheating because of reduced airflows, as well as wasted energy. Clogged filters on the reactivation side may cause problems, including insufficient airflow to remove the moisture from the desiccant wheel, reducing system performance. As filters load still further, there is insufficient airflow to safely absorb the heat from the reactivation heater, so the unit shuts down because the temperature of the reactivation air entering the wheel is too high. A large number of reported problems related to desiccant systems can be traced to clogged filters.

Seals between regeneration and process airflow sections should be inspected. Leakage will degrade performance.

Lithium chloride desiccant can absorb excess moisture, expanding and literally "exploding" out of the wheel. When not in use, LiCl wheels should be kept hot and rotating.

The drive belt around the desiccant wheel needs to be sufficiently tight to turn the wheel, but not so tight as to put an excessive load on the drive motor shaft bearings. Belt tension should be checked at least twice a year or when the filters are changed.

The desiccant wheel has bearings that should be inspected at the same time as the fan bearings, and should be greased based on the manufacturer's recommendation. Typically, greasing is needed only once a year because of the wheel's slow rotational speed.

Controls should be recalibrated regularly to assure a steady state of operation. Bypass dampers should be checked for proper operation and seating. Shut off damper seals should be checked.

5.6.7 Air Filtration

As filters load with particles, resistance to airflow increases (higher pressure drop) to a point where airflow could be reduced and the filters could collapse. Alternatively, as filters load with material, their efficiency increases. Ideally, filters should be replaced based on a predetermined DP drop and the cost of the filters. This optimizes the TCO for the filters.

5.6.7.1 ASHRAE Type Filters

ASHRAE type filters should be replaced after no more than two years of service, even if pressure differential change-out limits have not yet been reached. This eliminates potential microbial growth and filter degradation. Filters should be inspected twice per year as a minimum.

ASHRAE type filters (non-HEPA) should not be repaired nor require leak testing.

5.6.7.2 HEPA/ULPA

Depending on the testing method and product/process, leakage of the upstream aerosol concentration above an acceptable limit when tested in-situ may require that HEPA/ULPA filters be replaced or patched. The most commonly recognized limit for defining a filter leak is a localized leak rate equal to or greater than 0.01% of the upstream aerosol concentration when tested via an in-situ filter face leak scan.

In-situ leak testing normally is performed once a year for GMP operations, but aseptic manufacturing normally requires testing every six months for some areas.

HEPA/ULPA filter leaks can occur in several ways: rough handling or touching with instruments, tools, or hands may easily damage the filter medium. Leaks also may occur along the interface where the medium is sealed to the frame. Another major leak source is at silicone gel seals, where the filter housing meets the knife-edge of the filter grid system. Over time, the gel can deteriorate because of exposure to aerosols used in the testing of filters.

When leaks are detected, the filter may be replaced or repaired. HEPA filters should be replaced when the patched area is more than 3 to 5% of the net face area or when a single patch has a lesser linear dimension exceeding 1.5 inches (3.8 cm). Patching material should be RTV silicone sealant caulk, which meets the FDA 21CFR 177.2600 and USDA for food grade applications.

It is not recommended to attempt to caulk a leak between silicone gel and the filter frame knife-edge, nor to repair a filter leak in a Grade 5 – Grade A hood where airflow patterns need to be uniform.

Care should be taken when storing, handling, installing, and testing HEPA/ULPA filters. They should be stored within 40 to 100°F (4 to 38°C) and 25 to 75% RH.

Prior to installation, it is recommended that information on individual filters and filter housings is recorded (model number, serial number, performance, factory test data, etc.). This can resolve future questions regarding filter efficiency, replacement filters, or issues arising from a product recall.

5.6.8 Ductwork

Periodic inspection of HVAC ductwork can identify potential problems (dirt, debris, leaks, and corrosion) to be corrected before unexpected failure and extensive repairs are needed. Ductwork can lose its seal over time and can be a source of excessive leakage that can affect room pressurization. Ductwork that has been crushed leads to insufficient airflow, increased noise, and poor airflow control. Damaged or lost duct insulation should be quickly replaced.

5.6.9 Dampers and Louvers

These should be checked for dirt accumulation and free movement without binding of the linkages over the full range of operation (full open to close). Linkages should not be loose. Dampers for low leakage applications should be replaced if gaskets have become hardened or do not provide a good seal.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Point: The First Suspect in Desiccant System Failures Is Clogged Filters

ISPE states explicitly: "a large share of reported desiccant system problems can be traced to clogged filters". A desiccant system has two sets of inlet filters (process side + regeneration side), and a clog on either side causes problems:

  • Process side clogged: Insufficient airflow, leading to overheating of the system and wasted energy.
  • Regeneration side clogged: Moisture cannot be carried away, dehumidification performance drops, and the system eventually shuts down automatically on over-temperature protection.

Best practice: Check the belt tension every time the filters are changed, killing two birds with one stone.

Key Concept: HEPA Filter Repair Rules

A HEPA filter does not have to be replaced the moment it leaks. ISPE allows repair, but with strict limits:

  • Maximum repaired area: ≤ 3-5% of the filter's net area.
  • Maximum size of a single repair: shortest side ≤ 1.5 inches (3.8 cm).
  • Repair material: FDA 21CFR 177.2600 food-grade RTV silicone.
  • Cases where repair is not allowed: Leaks between the silicone gel and the knife-edge frame, and Grade A/5 hood-type HEPA filters (because repair would affect airflow uniformity).

HEPA Testing Frequency Quick Reference

GMP operations: on-site integrity test once a year
Aseptic manufacturing: once every 6 months in some areas
ASHRAE-type filters: inspect every 6 months, replace within 2 years at most
Leak criterion: local leak rate ≥ 0.01% (of upstream aerosol concentration)

Key Point: The Three Main Sources of HEPA Leaks

  1. Media damage: Holes caused by rough handling or contact with tools or hands.
  2. Seal between media and frame: The adhesive cracks or separates from the frame (usually due to poor quality control, or adhesive incompatibility with chemicals in the airstream).
  3. Silicone gel seal: The silicone gel between the filter housing and the knife-edge frame degrades from long-term exposure to the test aerosol.

The third source deserves particular attention: the aerosol used to "test" the filter actually accelerates the aging of the sealing material. It is an ironic but real problem.

Practice Questions

  1. Do your HEPA filters have individual tracking records (serial number, factory test data, installation date)?
  2. Have HEPA filters ever been repaired? Does the repaired area comply with the 3-5% limit?
  3. Is the filter replacement frequency for desiccant systems sufficient? Have you ever had a shutdown caused by clogged filters?
5.6.10 - 5.6.14 Other Equipment Maintenance & Air Balancing

Original Text

5.6.10 Diffusers and Registers

Dirt accumulation will result in insufficient air distribution and can be seen from a room. Registers and diffusers should be inspected and cleaned periodically.

5.6.11 Ultraviolet Lights

Maintenance required for ultra-violet lighting involves the replacement of the UV lamp or bulb. The bulbs typically last about 8,000 hours, but their life will be shortened by accumulation of dirt or fingerprints on them. Dirt limits the lamp's intensity and its ability to destroy microbes effectively.

UV lighting ballasts typically have a life of more than five years.

5.6.12 Fume Exhaust/Extraction Systems

Exhaust systems serving pharmaceutical operations need a high level of reliability, because of the impact on the process should they fail. Maintenance should ensure equipment up time, including:

  • The system should be inspected to ensure it is free of debris and dirt that may reduce airflow volume.
  • Control dampers should operate freely.
  • Flexible duct connections should be checked to assure they are not leaking air, often because of deterioration or wear.

Fume hood performance should be tested in accordance with ASHRAE Standard 110.

Fans are the primary component in fume exhaust/extraction systems.

5.6.13 Building

As buildings age, leakage through the room fabric increases over time and can result in loss of room pressure relationships, requiring frequent readjustment of pressure dampers. Ultimately, the source of the leakage will need to be located; periodic inspection of penetrations and seals is recommended.

5.6.14 Air Balancing

Testing, Adjusting, and Balancing (TAB) for HVAC systems should be performed at regular intervals to ensure system compliance, as well as to verify that systems are operating as efficiently as possible. When changes to the room configurations or HVAC equipment occur, TAB should be performed.

At a minimum, recalibration of monitoring instruments, verifying supply airflow to process spaces and recalculating air changes per hour (ACPH), and adjusting pressure relationships should occur at least annually for GMP spaces, or when terminal HEPA filters are tested. Full rebalancing should be considered every five years as a minimum and seven years for non-GMP spaces.

A total rebalancing can uncover unsuspected increases in energy consumption and potential equipment failures. There is a risk in performing partial re-balancing; as a change in airflow to one zone may cause the opposite change in other zones (increasing air flow to one room may reduce airflow to all other rooms).

Note that typical airflow measurement accuracy is in the order of ±10%. This should cause no concern as long as room conditions (and recovery if measured) are achieved. Flow hoods used for air balancing should be calibrated periodically, usually annually. Adequate lead time should be factored into the re-balancing schedule for calibration.

Table 5.6: Suggested Maintenance Frequency

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Risk and Frequency of TAB (Air Balancing)

TAB (Testing, Adjusting, and Balancing): Air balancing is not a one-time job but a cycle that must be repeated periodically. Key insights from ISPE:

  • Butterfly effect of local adjustment: Increasing the airflow to one room may reduce the airflow to all other rooms. It is like a water pipe with several branches: open one valve and the water pressure in the other branches drops.
