  • Building aging effect: As the building ages, the seals around wall penetrations gradually deteriorate, leakage increases and the pressure relationships go out of control.
  • Measurement accuracy ±10%: Do not over-pursue perfect numbers; it is enough that the room conditions (particles, pressure differential, temperature and humidity) and recovery performance meet requirements.

Maintenance Frequency Quick Reference

Aseptic operations (Grade 5-7):
  Instrument calibration + ACPH confirmation + HEPA testing = every 6 months

GMP clean operations (Grade 8):
  Instrument calibration + ACPH confirmation + HEPA testing = every 1 year

Other GMP spaces (pilot plant, animal facility, laboratory):
  Full air rebalancing = every 5 years

Non-GMP spaces (mechanical rooms, offices):
  Full air rebalancing = every 7 years

Airflow capture hood calibration: once a year

Key Point: UV Lamp Maintenance Pitfalls

A UV lamp lasts about 8,000 hours (about 11 months of continuous operation), but its life is shortened by dust buildup and fingerprints. Many facilities replace a lamp only when it stops lighting, overlooking the fact that even while the lamp is still lit, its UV intensity may have dropped below the level needed for effective germicidal action. It is recommended to measure periodically with a UV intensity meter rather than just checking whether the lamp is "on".

Practical Application for a CDMO

In a CDMO environment, air balancing is especially challenging:

  • Change of room use: Different clients' products may need different air change rates and pressure differentials.
  • Capacity expansion: Adding new equipment may change a room's heat load and supply air requirements.
  • Knock-on effects of local adjustment: Adjusting airflow for a new production line may affect all other rooms served by the same AHU.

Recommendation: any change involving airflow should be followed by a full-system TAB, not just a local adjustment.

5.7 Spare Parts

Original Text

GEP and the economics of keeping production on line require that spare parts are kept to minimize the effect of failures. A good PdM program should predict the need to replace parts before they fail, allowing time to order replacement parts. However, there are specific items that may be useful in case of sudden failure:

  • A spare desiccant wheel: a desiccant wheel may fail because of remaining idle for months (as during cold winters when dehumidification is not needed), and not be ready for service the first humid day. This is particularly true for LiCl wheels, but silica wheels also have been known to become less effective over time.
  • Sensors and transmitters for critical parameters. If all the temperature sensors in the system are the same specification, only one spare is needed; similarly for RH and DP sensors.
  • Terminal HEPA filter or UFH HEPA filter: over-zealous cleaning may damage a HEPA filter exposed to the room. Rips and tears in UFH filters may have an effect on a critical zone. Sudden failure because of dirt loading of a terminal filter should not be a concern, particularly if a high efficiency filter in the AHU precedes the HEPA filter. Failed HEPA filters in an AHU have much less effect, and it may be possible to repair the filter while replacements are on order.
  • High temperature HEPA filter: because of the gradual destruction of the binders in high temperature filters operated beyond their rated temperature, it is possible that the entire filter bank in a depyrogenation tunnel will need to be replaced at one time. Repairs are not possible.
  • Fan belts: a good inspection program should notice belt wear; cost is relatively low.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: The "Critical Five" Spare Parts Strategy

The five critical spares listed by ISPE reflect the most vulnerable points of an HVAC system:

  1. Desiccant wheel: May fail after sitting idle, especially LiCl wheels. Having a spare set ready allows immediate replacement on the first humid day.
  2. Sensors/transmitters: Using a "specification standardization" strategy, only one spare is needed for sensors of the same specification, which is smart spare parts management.
  3. Terminal HEPA filters: The components most likely to be damaged by "over-cleaning". A HEPA tear in a UFH directly affects the Grade A area.
  4. High-temperature HEPA filters: Used for depyrogenation tunnels; the whole set may need to be replaced at once and cannot be repaired. Lead times are long, so stock must be prepared in advance.
  5. Fan belts: Low cost, replaced frequently, and the replacement timing is predictable through regular inspection.

Analogy

Spare parts management is like a home first-aid kit: you do not need to stock every medicine, only those you are most likely to use: adhesive bandages (fan belts), fever reducers (sensors), gauze (HEPA filters). The key is to decide what to stock and how much based on "failure risk" and "downtime impact". High-temperature HEPA filters are like a special prescription drug: rarely used, but extremely urgent when needed, and it cannot be compounded on the spot.

Key Point: The Risk of "Over-Cleaning" HEPA Filters

ISPE uses the term "over-zealous cleaning", which is a counterintuitive risk in a cleanroom environment. To ensure cleanliness, cleaning staff may wipe the HEPA filter face exposed in the room too forcefully and tear the media. This is a reminder that cleaning SOPs must clearly specify how HEPA filters are to be cleaned, and the limits.

Practical Application for a CDMO

Additional factors a CDMO's spare parts strategy needs to consider:

  • Multi-product shared lines: Different products may need HEPA filters of different specifications or special sensors.
  • Supply chain risk: There are usually few suppliers of high-temperature HEPA filters, and lead times can be as long as 3-6 months.
  • Cost-benefit analysis: Spare parts inventory cost vs downtime loss. One day of production downtime can cost more than a whole year of spare parts inventory.
  • Specification standardization: Standardizing sensor specifications at the new facility design stage can greatly reduce the variety and quantity of spares.

Practice Questions

  1. Does your facility have an HVAC spare parts list? Does it cover the five critical spares recommended by ISPE?
  2. Is the quantity of spare high-temperature HEPA filters sufficient to replace the whole filter set of a depyrogenation tunnel at once?
  3. Have sensor specifications been standardized? If the existing system uses several specifications, is there a plan to standardize them in future modifications?

Section Summary

  • Build clean is the foundation: Clean before installation, seal after installation, and use zip screws rather than self-drilling screws. Metal debris from construction is one of the main causes of HEPA integrity failures.
  • Five key points of AHU installation: Correct lifting, level foundation, P-trap height, RTV sealing, slow VFD startup. Equipment idle for more than a month needs its bearings rotated every two weeks.
  • Fan installation is a high-risk operation: Laser alignment, belt tension, bump test and vibration test; every step affects safety and system life.
  • Commissioning vs Qualification: Commissioning = GEP (done for all systems); Qualification = GMP (only for direct impact systems). The impact assessment determines the scope of qualification.
  • Pressure alarm delay test: Measure experimentally the time for particles to exceed limits after the door is opened, and set the alarm delay at no more than 50% of it.
  • PdM is better than PM: Vibration and temperature monitoring can predict bearing failure in advance. A tidy appearance is also a hidden indicator of GMP compliance.
  • Key HEPA maintenance numbers: Leak criterion ≥ 0.01%, repaired area ≤ 3-5%, single repair ≤ 1.5 inches. Test once a year for GMP, every 6 months for aseptic areas.
  • The butterfly effect of TAB air balancing: A local adjustment affects the whole system. Full rebalancing every 6 months for aseptic areas, every year for Grade 8, every 5 years for other GMP areas and every 7 years for non-GMP areas.
  • Five must-have spares: Desiccant wheel, standardized sensors, terminal HEPA, high-temperature HEPA (stock the whole set), fan belts.
  • The main cause of desiccant system failure is clogged filters: Both sets of inlet filters (process side + regeneration side) need regular replacement. A LiCl wheel must be kept heated and rotating when idle.
5

Chapter 5: 6. Documentation

p137-p142

ISPE Good Practice Guide: HVAC | p135 - p139

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the life cycle of HVAC engineering documents: the progression from conceptual design to as-built drawings and then to master documents
  • Distinguish the three categories of HVAC documents: maintenance/operations documents (non-GMP), master/record documents, and GMP documents
  • Know the content of the Engineering Turnover Package (ETOP) and when to build it
  • Understand the definition of a Critical Master Document, the standard for maintaining it, and its role in CMC filings
  • Be familiar with the HVAC document lists required in the Commissioning & Qualification and Process Validation phases
6.1 Introduction

Original Text

On completion of qualification, the disposition of HVAC system documentation should be established. Documents may be used by maintenance and operations or required for periodic Chemistry Manufacturing Controls (CMC) filings, becoming critical master documents, i.e., engineering documents maintained as GMP records.

This section discusses documents which typically are required and provides guidance regarding classification and use of documents.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Dual Identity of HVAC Documents

HVAC documents are not just engineering data; they may also be GMP records.

Once qualification is complete, the HVAC system documents need to be "classified": which ones stay with the maintenance team for reference, which ones are upgraded to GMP record documents, and which ones become part of the CMC filing.

CMC (Chemistry, Manufacturing and Controls): the section of a marketing application that describes the manufacturing and quality control methods. HVAC-related items such as the area classification drawing and the P&ID (piping and instrumentation diagram) may be included in the CMC filing.

Analogy: Document Tiers When Buying a House

When you buy a house, you receive many documents: architectural drawings, electrical and plumbing diagrams, the renovation contract, the inspection report and the property title.

Some are useful only during renovation (such as the renovation contract), some must be kept long term (such as the title), and some must be shown when you resell (such as the inspection report).

HVAC documents work the same way. Construction drawings can be archived once they have served their purpose, but the as-built drawings and the area classification drawing must always be kept current, because an inspector may ask to see them at any time.

Key Point: When to Classify Documents

This section states clearly that document classification should be established "after qualification is complete". In practice, however, the earlier you plan the classification, the better. The best time is the conceptual design stage, when you define which documents will become GMP records. If you wait until qualification is complete to decide, you often find that much of the data has been lost or is in the wrong format.

Practice Questions

  1. If you are the engineering manager at a CDMO and have just completed HVAC qualification for a new aseptic filling line, how would you decide which documents go to the maintenance department and which are upgraded to GMP records? What criteria would you use?
  2. Why must a CMC filing include HVAC-related documents? How is this directly linked to product quality?
6.2 Engineering Document Life Cycle
6.2.1 Planning Life Cycle

Original Text

The life cycle of project documents should be defined during conceptual design and no later than Functional/Schematic design to help to reduce ambiguity and prevent loss of data.

The planning document should define, which documents are required for construction, which documents will be part of an Engineering Turnover Package (ETOP) for maintenance and operations, which documents will be leveraged into qualifications, and which documents will be maintained as record documents for Maintenance and GMP use.

Defining the contents of the ETOP early in a project also allows the easy capture of design calculations and risk assessments as they are generated. Document management and collaboration software, which will apply the appropriate life cycle to documents as they are generated and approved, may be used to capture design and construction information into an ETOP.

A "Traceability Matrix," (a documentation of the plan and progress of documentation and concepts through the sequence of design, construction, qualification, and eventually showing that the HVAC is fit for service through process validation) may be used for planning and updating of document life cycle. The traceability matrix shows this progress and maintains the chain of design intent, linking final documents to conceptual design documents (User Requirements and Functional Design).

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Planning the Document Life Cycle

Life Cycle: the complete process of a document from creation through archiving and maintenance to eventual retirement. ISPE stresses that the "fate" of each document must be decided at the very start of the project.

ETOP (Engineering Turnover Package): the document package formally handed over from the engineering team to the operations/maintenance team after construction is complete. It covers the design basis, as-built drawings, equipment manuals and so on.

Traceability Matrix: a tracking document that links the full chain of "user requirements → functional design → construction → qualification → process validation", ensuring that every design intent can be traced to its final verification result.

Analogy: Deciding the Warranty Records Before Building the House

Imagine you are building a house to live in. The smart approach is to decide before work begins which documents go to the contractor for filing, which you keep for future repairs, and which are submitted to the authorities.

If you wait until the house is finished to look for documents, you will find that the designer's calculations are missing, the plumbing and electrical drawings were never updated, and the structural calculations are still the first version. This is exactly why ISPE recommends deciding the destination of each document at the conceptual design or even the functional design stage.

Key Point: The Audit Value of the Traceability Matrix

The Traceability Matrix is not just a project management tool; it is also a defensive weapon in regulatory inspections. FDA inspectors often ask: "What design basis is your qualification protocol based on? What user requirement does that design basis answer?"

The traceability matrix lets you work backward step by step: qualification results → test protocol → design specification → user requirements. When this "traceable chain" is complete, the inspection will not raise concerns.

Practical Application: ETOP Best Practices for a CDMO

For a CDMO, clients often conduct technology transfer audits after a project is completed. If the ETOP is incomplete at that point, it creates a great deal of communication overhead.

  • Timing: Plan the ETOP content list at the P&ID review meeting
  • Tools: Use a document management system (such as MasterControl or Veeva) to apply the document life cycle automatically
  • People: Appoint a "document coordinator" to track the status of each document

Practice Questions

  1. If you only start planning the ETOP content once your project reaches the construction phase, what problems might you run into? Give a specific example.
  2. What is the relationship between the Traceability Matrix and the Validation Protocol? Can the two be combined into one document?
6.2.2 Typical Steps in the Document Life Cycle

Original Text

HVAC documents typically start their life cycle as conceptual documents, including:

  • AFDs
  • AF&IDs
  • room/zoning layouts
  • room condition tables (temperature, RH, area class, DP, etc.)
  • load calculations
  • design basis/assumption tables

These documents progress through the Engineering Process to:

  • calculations
  • plan drawings
  • detail drawings
  • specifications
  • tables

Plans, details, and diagrams should be updated throughout (or after) the construction process to an "as-built" state (corrected after construction to match the actual final configuration). The update to "as-built status" is essential to maintenance and particularly important for systems that monitor or control critical environments. Specifications and designer's calculations usually are augmented (or replaced) by manufacturer's submittals, details, and calculations.

Some documents should be converted into master documents (engineering documents with construction notes removed) as a record of the ongoing state of systems and equipment and to allow capture of future construction changes. Those master documents that define the critical attributes of the HVAC system should be maintained as critical master documents (master documents that are maintained in a constant state of inspection readiness). The AF&ID, HVAC zoning layouts, and area classifications should be kept up to date, as a minimum.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Three Stages of Document Evolution

The HVAC document life cycle can be divided into three distinct stages:

  • Conceptual: AFD (Air Flow Diagram), AF&ID (Air Flow & Instrument Diagram), room condition tables and so on. These are the blueprints of the early design phase.
  • Construction: detailed calculations, plan drawings, construction drawings and specifications. These are the basis for the actual build.
  • As-built / Master: after construction is complete, documents are updated to "as-built" status to reflect the actual installation. Key documents are then upgraded to "Master Documents" or "Critical Master Documents".

Analogy: Document Evolution Is Like a Building Completion Inspection

The architect's design drawings (conceptual documents) represent the ideal state. During construction, because of site constraints, pipe routing may be adjusted slightly and equipment locations may shift.

As-built drawings are like the "street view" in Google Maps: not the ideal route the designer drew, but the real layout after the building was completed.

If you look for pipework using the "design drawing", you may drill in the wrong place. This is why ISPE emphasizes that "as-built updates" are essential for maintenance.

Key Point: Master Document vs. Critical Master Document

This section defines two levels of "master document":

  • Master Document: an engineering document with construction markups removed, serving as a record of the ongoing state of the system.
  • Critical Master Document: a master document that defines the critical attributes of the HVAC system and must be kept in a constant state of inspection readiness.

"Constant state of inspection readiness" is the key phrase: these documents cannot wait to be updated until an inspection is announced, but must be updated immediately after every change.

ISPE states explicitly that, at a minimum, the AF&ID, the HVAC zoning layout and the area classification drawing must be kept up to date.

Document Evolution Flow Chart

Conceptual documents (AFD, AF&ID, room condition tables)
    |
    v  Engineering design phase
Construction documents (calculations, construction drawings, specifications)
    |
    v  Construction complete → as-built update
As-built documents (As-built Drawings)
    |
    +--→ Maintenance documents (ETOP)
    |
    +--→ Master Documents
    |         |
    |         +--→ Critical Master Documents
    |                   ↑ Constant state of inspection readiness
    |
    +--→ Qualification Documents

Practice Questions

  1. After construction, it is found that the AF&ID of an HVAC system needs an additional HEPA filter. What steps must this document go through to be correctly updated as a Critical Master Document?
  2. If a design calculation was replaced during construction by the equipment vendor's submittal data, does the original calculation still need to be retained? Why?
6.3 Documents for Maintenance and Operations (Non-GMP)

Original Text

A well-constructed (and concise) ETOP can save time during troubleshooting or when entering data into a Computerized Maintenance Management System (CMMS) and may be more beneficial to maintenance than a complete set of design and construction documents.

The list may contain items that have no GMP impact on laboratories, OSD, Packaging, API, etc. Typical Documents for an HVAC ETOP include:

  • user requirements/FRS/functional design specification
  • room condition tables – temperature, RH (and particle levels, DP, air changes, as required)
  • as-built airflow and instrument diagram
  • area classification diagrams
  • pressure or airflow direction “maps”
  • AHU zoning diagrams (what areas are served by each AHU)
  • filter integrity testing (classified spaces, cross contamination in other facilities)
  • air balance
  • face velocity testing (HEPA filters in classified spaces)
  • alarm testing
  • pressure relationships
  • equipment submittals
  • ductwork shop drawings
  • coordination drawings
  • as-built ductwork, piping, and equipment plans
  • control diagrams
  • commissioning documents

The ISPE Baseline® Guides (Reference 13, Appendix 12) for each facility type define the critical parameters for the facility.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Role and Value of the ETOP

ETOP (Engineering Turnover Package) is the core document set that the construction team hands over to the operations/maintenance team. Its design principle is "lean but complete".

Note: documents in the ETOP are not necessarily all GMP documents. This section is specifically labelled "Non-GMP", meaning these documents mainly serve maintenance and operational needs rather than regulatory compliance.

CMMS (Computerized Maintenance Management System): a system used to manage preventive maintenance schedules, work order tracking and spare parts inventory. The equipment data in the ETOP is the basis for building the CMMS database.

Analogy: The Document Pack When You Collect a New Car

When you buy a new car, the dealer gives you a handover pack: owner's manual, maintenance schedule, warranty card, emergency roadside assistance number and tire specification sheet.

You do not need the full engineering drawings; those are for the manufacturer's engineers. What you need is the essential information for daily use and maintenance.

The ETOP is the "handover pack" of the HVAC system. What goes to the maintenance team is not hundreds of pages of design documents, but the as-built drawings, equipment parameters, control logic and test records they actually need.

Key Point: The Practical Value of the ETOP List

The 17 typical ETOP documents listed in this section make an excellent checklist. In practice, we suggest:

  • AHU zoning drawing: the most frequently used during maintenance. Which AHU serves which areas? How large is the impact area when it is shut down?
  • Air balance: the baseline for system fine-tuning or troubleshooting
  • Control drawings: the physical representation of the BMS program logic and the starting point for fault diagnosis
  • Differential pressure/airflow direction drawing: the reference for routine rounds

Note in particular: ISPE says these documents "may have no GMP impact" for laboratory, OSD, packaging and API areas. In aseptic manufacturing areas, however, the same documents may be GMP-critical.

Practical Application: ETOP Management Strategy for a CDMO

The challenge for a CDMO is serving multiple clients at once, each of whom may have different requirements for HVAC documents. We suggest:

  • Build a standard ETOP template: use it for all new projects to ensure consistency
  • Manage electronically: put the ETOP documents in the document management system so they can be retrieved quickly during client audits
  • Review periodically: confirm at least once a year that the ETOP content still reflects the current state of the system

Practice Questions

  1. If the air balance data in the ETOP does not match the actual operating state of the system (because a change was made later but the document was not updated), what consequences might follow?
  2. This section notes that the ETOP is more useful for maintenance than the "complete design and construction documents". Why is "leaner" actually "more valuable"? Analyze this from the maintenance technician's working scenario.
6.4 Master/Record Documents

Original Text

Documents that typically are kept updated to become HVAC master documents (for maintenance and facility engineering) include:

  • as-built AF&IDs
  • area classification diagrams (if spaces are classified)
  • pressure or airflow direction “maps”
  • AHU zoning diagrams
  • filter test data
  • control diagrams and critical alarms calibration/test records
  • sequence of operation
  • equipment submittal drawings
  • as-built ductwork, piping, and equipment plans

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Scope of Master Documents

A Master Document is a "living document": not a historical record sealed away when construction ends, but a reference document that continuously reflects the current state of the system.

The difference from the ETOP is that the ETOP is a one-time handover package, whereas master documents must be continuously updated as the system changes.

Each of the 9 documents listed in this section corresponds to a core need of maintenance and facility engineering:

  • AF&ID: the "big picture" of the system and the most important master document
  • Sequence of Operation: records the control logic of the HVAC system, such as start-up/shutdown sequences and interlock conditions
  • Filter test data: HEPA integrity test records, which directly affect the area classification

Analogy: A Master Document Is Like a Medical Record

A master document is like a person's medical record: it is not written once at birth and left unchanged, but updated at every visit. Blood pressure, weight and medication records all need to reflect the latest status.

If the doctor sees a medical record from five years ago, a correct diagnosis is impossible. Likewise, if the maintenance engineer is holding an AF&ID that is still the version from three years ago, he or she may make the wrong judgment during troubleshooting.

Key Point: Change Management and Master Document Synchronization

The biggest challenge in maintaining master documents is the execution of change management. Every time the HVAC system changes (adding a filter, modifying airflow, adjusting a differential pressure setpoint), the related master documents must be updated at the same time.

A common failure mode: the engineering change has been completed and the qualification signed off, but the AF&ID is still at the pre-change version. This is a frequent deficiency in FDA inspections.

Practice Questions

  1. Compare the ETOP list in Section 6.3 with the master document list in Section 6.4. Which documents appear on both lists? Why do these documents need to exist in both systems?
  2. Why is the "sequence of operation" a master document? If the control logic changes but the sequence of operation document is not updated, what risks might result?
6.5 GMP HVAC Documents

Original Text

It is important to align with the risk assessment performed in the design process to determine the HVAC documents to be leveraged into commissioning and qualification or become Critical Master Documents. Since the risk assessment varies by project, the following lists of typical documents should be reviewed against project/product needs. See the ISPE Baseline® Guides (Reference 13, Appendix 12).

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Risk-Assessment-Driven Document Classification

This section is the most important turning point of the chapter, moving from "engineering documents" into the realm of "GMP documents".

ISPE's core logic is: which HVAC documents need to become GMP documents is not decided by a fixed list but driven by risk assessment.

This means that the same AHU zoning drawing may be only an ETOP document in an OSD facility but a Critical Master Document in an aseptic filling area. The difference depends on the risk the system poses to product quality.

Key Point: The Decision Hierarchy in Document Management

Returning to ISPE's decision hierarchy:

  1. Sterility Assurance: HVAC documents that directly affect sterility assurance (such as the area classification drawing for Grade A/B areas and HEPA test records) must be Critical Master Documents
  2. Product CQAs: HVAC parameter documents that affect product quality attributes (such as temperature and humidity records) require GMP control
  3. Operational flexibility: documents that affect only operating efficiency (such as AHU drawings for unclassified areas) can be non-GMP documents
6.5.1 Commissioning and Qualification Documents

Original Text

Documents that typically are leveraged into commissioning and qualification include:

  • as-built AF&IDs
  • room environmental conditions – tables/schedules
  • area classification diagrams (classified spaces)
  • pressure or airflow direction “maps”
  • GMP air filter location map
  • AHU zoning diagrams
  • control diagrams or functional design for direct impact systems
  • critical instrument specifications
  • commissioning documents:
    • filter integrity or overall penetration testing (HEPA/ULPA)
    • airflow patterns for Grade 5 (Grade A) hoods and Grade 7 (Grade B) rooms
    • air balance (air changes OK for classified spaces, airflow direction OK)
    • face velocity testing (HEPA/ULPA for Grade 5/Grade A)
    • pressure relationships (contamination control)
    • particle counts at rest
    • critical monitoring and alarm testing, including calibration and alarm delay verification
    • temperature
    • humidity (if deemed critical)
    • room DP or leakage air velocity (for contamination control)
    • supply airflow (classified spaces)
    • Grade A/Grade 5 hood air flow (DP, sail switch, velocity sensor)
    • temperature mapping (usually for warehouse) – see Appendix 2
    • test protocols and supporting information
    • evidence that acceptance criteria have been met

Documents that are typically produced during commissioning and qualification (or Process Validation) are:

  • airflow visualization for Grade 5 (EU Grade A) or local protection areas in use
  • total airborne particulate testing
  • viable airborne particulate testing
  • room recovery testing (classified spaces)
  • test protocols and supporting information
  • evidence that acceptance criteria have been met

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Two Categories of C&Q Documents

This section divides commissioning and qualification (C&Q) documents into two major categories:

  • Documents "leveraged into" C&Q: these were originally engineering/design documents and are now brought into the qualification system as evidence. Examples include the AF&ID and the environmental condition tables.
  • Documents "produced during" C&Q: these are the direct outputs of test activities, such as airflow visualization and particle counts.

"Leverage" is a characteristic ISPE term. It means existing engineering data can be cited directly as qualification evidence without repeating the tests. This is a concrete expression of the "do not repeat testing" principle.

Analogy: "Exemption from the Exam" vs. "Taking the Exam"

Leveraged documents are like "admission without an exam": tests you already performed during construction (such as the HEPA integrity test) do not need to be performed again in the qualification phase; you simply cite the results.

Produced documents are like "taking the exam": airflow visualization, microbiological testing and so on can only be performed in the qualification phase (or the process validation phase), because they must be tested in a state "close to actual operation".

Key Point: Key Details in the Commissioning Document List

  • Humidity "if deemed critical": ISPE specifically notes that humidity testing applies "if deemed critical". This means not every project needs humidity qualification; it depends on the product's sensitivity to humidity (such as hygroscopic powders).
  • Alarm delay verification: do not only test the alarm function, but also verify the alarm delay time. Too short a delay causes false alarms; too long a delay defeats the purpose of the protection.
  • Differences in testing between Grade A and Grade B: Grade A (unidirectional airflow zone) requires face velocity testing and airflow visualization; Grade B (background environment) is tested mainly for air change rate and differential pressure.
  • Particle counts "at rest": at-rest particle counts are performed in the commissioning phase; dynamic particle counts (in operation) are performed in the process validation phase.

Practical Application: C&Q Document Strategy for a CDMO

For a CDMO, the quality of C&Q documents directly affects client audit outcomes and the speed of regulatory filings:

  • Build a C&Q document template library: standardize the protocol format and acceptance criteria for each test
  • Make good use of the leverage principle: test data from the FAT completed at the equipment supplier's site can be cited directly as IQ evidence, saving on-site testing time
  • Sequencing "at rest" vs. "in operation": schedule static tests in the commissioning phase and dynamic tests in the process validation phase to avoid scheduling conflicts
  • Alarm delay verification: complete it with the BMS/SCADA supplier at the FAT stage to avoid repeated adjustments on site

Practice Questions

  1. This section lists two categories of documents, "leveraged into" and "produced during". If you discover in the process validation phase that a test was missed in the commissioning phase, how should you handle it? Would repeating the test count as Commissioning or Qualification?
  2. Why can "airflow visualization" not be completed in the at-rest state, and instead must be performed in the "in use" state? Explain from a contamination control perspective.
  3. A new aseptic filling area at a CDMO uses RABS technology. List at least 8 key test documents required for HVAC C&Q in this area.
6.5.2 Critical Master Documents

Original Text

Critical Master Documents provide HVAC information for the CMC section of a drug filing and are subject to regulatory review.

Documents that typically are maintained as critical master documents include:

  • as-built AF&IDs
  • risk assessments and traceability matrix
  • room environmental conditions – tables and schedules
  • area classification diagrams
  • pressure or airflow direction “maps”
  • AHU Zoning Diagrams
  • qualification documents:
    • filter integrity testing (HEPA/ULPA)
    • air balance
    • air change calculations or recovery testing for classified spaces
    • face velocity testing (HEPA/ULPA in critical zones)
    • pressure relationships (continuous logging for classified spaces or spot-check?)
    • critical alarm and delay testing (temperature, RH, DP, airflow, etc.)
    • airflow visualization for Grade 5 (EU Grade A) or local protection areas
    • total airborne particulate testing (classified spaces)
    • viable airborne particulate testing (classified spaces)

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Regulatory Significance of Critical Master Documents

A Critical Master Document is the highest-level category in the HVAC document system. It has two key characteristics:

  • It provides information for CMC filings: in a marketing application, the CMC section must describe the manufacturing environment conditions. The HVAC critical master documents are the data source for these descriptions.
  • It is subject to regulatory review: regulators such as the FDA and EMA have the right to ask to see these documents and expect them to always reflect the current state of the system.

Key Point: Critical Master Documents vs. C&Q Documents

Comparing the lists in 6.5.1 and 6.5.2, you will find that they overlap heavily but differ in important ways:

  • Added items: Risk assessments and the Traceability matrix. These two do not appear in the C&Q document list but must be included in the critical master documents. The reason is that inspectors need to see the rationale for "why these test items were chosen".
  • The question on pressure differential recording: "continuous logging for classified spaces or spot-check?" ISPE deliberately uses a question mark to show that this depends on the risk assessment. For aseptic areas, continuous logging is usually necessary; for non-aseptic classified areas, periodic spot-checks may be sufficient.
  • Removed items: temperature and humidity mapping, warehouse-related tests and so on are not in this list, because they usually do not fall within the "critical" scope.

Analogy: A Critical Master Document Is Like a Company's Business License

A critical master document has the status of a company's business license or key contracts: not something kept in a drawer and taken out occasionally, but a document that the authorities may ask to see at any time.

What happens if the address on the business license has changed but the license was not updated? You are fined and your integrity is questioned. The same is true of HVAC critical master documents. If an inspector finds that the equipment configuration on the AF&ID does not match the site, the consequence may be an FDA 483 observation or even a Warning Letter.

Practical Application: Good Documentation Practice (GDocP) for Critical Master Documents

GDocP (Good Documentation Practice) sets especially strict requirements for critical master documents:

  • Version control: every revision must carry a version number, revision date, reason for revision and approval signatures
  • Change tracking: all changes must go through the formal change control procedure
  • Periodic review: we recommend a review at least once a year to confirm that the content still reflects the current state of the system
  • Backup and archiving: both paper and electronic versions must be stored securely and meet Data Integrity requirements

Practice Questions

  1. If an FDA inspector asks to see your HVAC critical master documents, how quickly can you provide them? If you cannot provide the latest version within 24 hours, what does that reveal about your system?
  2. Why do the Risk Assessment and the Traceability Matrix appear only on the "Critical Master Documents" list and not on the "C&Q documents" list? What role do these two documents play in regulatory inspections?
  3. What factors determine the answer to "continuous logging or spot-check?" Design your differential pressure monitoring strategy for a CDMO aseptic filling area and explain your reasons.

Section Summary

  • Plan the document life cycle early: decide the final destination of each HVAC document (ETOP / Master Document / Critical Master Document) at the conceptual design stage; do not wait until qualification is complete to classify them
  • As-built drawings are the foundation: the starting point of all HVAC document management is updating design drawings to as-built status to reflect the actual installed configuration. The AF&ID, area classification drawing and pressure differential drawing are the minimum set that must be kept current
  • The ETOP is lean but complete: the design principle of the engineering turnover package is "give the maintenance team what they really need", not "throw all the documents at them"
  • Master documents are "living": a Master Document must be continuously updated as the system changes, and a Critical Master Document must be kept in a constant state of inspection readiness
  • Risk assessment drives GMP document classification: which documents must become GMP documents depends on the results of the design-phase risk assessment, not on a fixed list
  • The "leverage" principle for C&Q documents: make good use of the leverage concept by citing test data already completed during construction directly as qualification evidence, avoiding repeated testing
  • Critical Master Documents are the highest level: they provide information for CMC filings, are subject to regulatory review, include the risk assessment and traceability matrix, and must meet the strict requirements of GDocP (Good Documentation Practice)
6

Chapter 6: App 1: HVAC Fundamentals

p143-p158

ISPE Good Practice Guide: HVAC | p143 - p158

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the three basic tasks of an HVAC system (personnel comfort, product protection, environmental protection) and how they are prioritized in a GMP environment
  • Understand the cause-and-effect relationship between the three primary environmental variables that affect product quality (temperature, humidity, air contamination) and the secondary HVAC factors (differential pressure, air change rate, airflow direction)
  • Understand the differences between international classification systems for classified space (EU Grade A-D vs. FDA ISO 5/7/8) and ISPE's unified "Grade" nomenclature
  • Learn to distinguish between Air Change Rate and Air Flow Rate, and understand why an arbitrary air change rate can be either insufficient or excessive
  • Become familiar with the basic concepts of psychrometrics: sensible heat, latent heat, dry bulb, wet bulb, dew point, and their application in HVAC design
  • Understand how differential pressure controls airflow direction, and the basic formula for calculating crack airflow velocity
7.1 Introduction

Original Text

This Appendix introduces the fundamentals of HVAC systems that control a GMP workplace environment.

HVAC aims to make personnel comfortable and to protect both workers inside a facility and the environment outside a facility from airborne materials that could be hazardous. In pharmaceutical manufacturing facilities, there also is a specific requirement to control the impact of the environment on the finished product (to assure product quality).

Three primary room environment variables may affect product and processes (at "critical locations," i.e., locations where product is exposed or where cleaned product contact surfaces are exposed):

  • air temperature
  • RH
  • airborne contamination (viable and non-viable particles)

Some of these variables, such as local airborne contaminants, depend on secondary HVAC factors, for example:

  • room pressure
  • air changes
  • airflow volume
  • airflow direction
  • airflow pattern
  • exhaust location and air velocity
  • air filter efficiency

Tertiary HVAC variables, such as fan speed and duct pressure, may vary to satisfy these secondary HVAC factors, and therefore, have an effect on them.

This appendix explores these variables and how they affect product, patient, and personnel. It also introduces some basic HVAC terminology.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: The Three-Tier Variable Structure of HVAC

ISPE divides HVAC variables into three tiers. This tiered thinking is very important for system design:

  • Primary Variables: temperature, humidity, air contamination. These directly affect product quality and are the core focus of GMP regulations
  • Secondary Variables: differential pressure, air change rate, airflow direction, etc. These are the "means" of achieving control of the primary variables
  • Tertiary Variables: fan speed, duct pressure, etc. These are operating parameters at the engineering execution level

In day-to-day CDMO operations, QA personnel focus on the primary variables, facility engineers regulate the secondary variables, and maintenance technicians monitor the tertiary variables. If the cause-and-effect chain between the three is broken, OOS (Out of Specification) events will occur.

Analogy

Think of an HVAC system as the ventilation system of a restaurant kitchen:

  • Primary goal: keep the guests (the product) unaffected by cooking fumes (contamination) and at a comfortable temperature
  • Secondary means: the position of the exhaust hood, the exhaust airflow, and the pressure difference between the kitchen and the dining area
  • Tertiary execution: motor speed, duct size, damper position

You would never tell a guest "our motor runs at 3000 RPM"; you would say "the cooking fumes will not drift into the dining area." This is why regulations focus on the primary variables.

Key Notes

Critical Locations is one of the most important concepts in this section. It refers to locations where the product is exposed to the environment, or where cleaned product-contact surfaces are exposed. In aseptic filling, this is the area between the filling needle and the container opening. The HVAC system design must give priority to protecting these locations.

Practice Questions

  1. Which locations in your facility are "critical locations"? Is the environmental control of all these locations covered by the HVAC system?
  2. If the fan speed of the air-conditioning system drops (a tertiary variable), how will this affect the air change rate (secondary) and ultimately particle control (primary)?
7.2 What Is Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning?

Original Text

Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) is the generic name given to a system that conditions the environment through the control of temperature, RH, air movement, and air quality (including fresh air, airborne particles, and vapors). HVAC systems can:

  • increase or decrease temperature
  • increase or reduce the moisture or humidity of the air
  • decrease the level of particulate or gaseous contaminants in the air

These capabilities are employed to protect personnel and product and for human comfort. HVAC systems also can protect the outdoor environment from hazardous material removed from a workplace environment via HVAC exhaust.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: The Four Functions of HVAC

The name HVAC itself reveals three functions: Heating, Ventilation and Air Conditioning. In a pharmaceutical environment, however, we need to add a fourth, implicit function:

  • Temperature control (heating/cooling)
  • Humidity control (humidification/dehumidification)
  • Air quality control (filtering particles/gaseous contaminants)
  • Environmental protection (preventing harmful substances from being discharged to the outside environment)

The last point is easily overlooked, but in CDMO facilities handling highly potent active pharmaceutical ingredients (HPAPI), exhaust treatment is a focus of regulatory review.

Key Notes

Note that the original text says HVAC can "protect the external environment." This is especially important when handling highly potent compounds, hormones or anticancer drugs. The exhaust system must be fitted with suitable filtration (usually HEPA filters) to ensure that hazardous dust is not discharged into the atmosphere. This is also part of what environmental regulations (such as COSHH) require.

7.2.1 Personnel Comfort

Original Text

The primary role of HVAC systems is to protect personnel and product. The most common role is to make personnel comfortable.

Four criteria usually are considered for personnel comfort and safety:

  • Temperature
  • Humidity
  • Air quality (carbon dioxide (CO2) levels and odors)
  • Air movement (sense of air movement and unwanted "drafts")

7.2.1.1 Temperature and Humidity

Figure 2.1 shows two boxes that define comfort conditions (temperature and humidity) that personnel in the US generally find comfortable in winter and summer (ASHRAE Handbook). This standard varies across the world, e.g., in parts of the tropics, people prefer an office at 78°F (26°C) to one at 72°F (22°C).

Note: these are general guidelines; numerous factors affect these conditions, e.g., the type and variety of work being performed, the extent of personnel gowning, as well as individual preferences.

Generally, non-production areas should fall within the "comfort zone" shown in Figure 2.1.

Where gowning levels are heavier or where work is more intense, room conditions should be cooler and less humid than for office areas. Workers in industrial settings, especially those who are required to wear over-garments (gowning) in pharmaceutical facilities, could be uncomfortable working in office room conditions. Typically, room temperatures are cooler (about 20 to 21°C or 68 to 70°F) with room humidity below 60% to provide "comfort" conditions. In addition, the lower limit on comfort humidity often is set at 30% to minimize static charges and to avoid irritation of the throat that could lead to an increased risk of respiratory illness.

7.2.1.2 Air Movement

A sensation of gentle air movement often is preferable; a typical design figure of 0.1 m/s (0.3 ft/s) is used in an office environment. Greater air velocities (up to 1 m/s or 3.28 ft/s (200 ft/min)) usually are needed for product protection to capture airborne particles. In manufacturing environments, higher velocities may be needed where operators experience discomfort from heavier gowning.

7.2.1.3 Air Quality

Fresh air is required to dilute exhaled carbon dioxide, odors, and other environmental contaminants. The amount of fresh air required depends on personnel activities. Table 2.1 shows typical oxygen use for different levels of activity.

ASHRAE 62 states the amount of fresh air required to provide adequate IAQ in a non-contaminated workspace should be 15 to 20 cubic feet/min (CFM) or 24 to 32 cubic meters per hour per person; unless a complex ASHRAE analysis is performed. Local building codes may require different quantities.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: GMP Environment vs. Office Environment

The key insight of this section is that the "comfort" standard of a pharmaceutical cleanroom is different from that of an ordinary office. Operators wearing full cleanroom garments need a lower temperature (20-21°C) and lower humidity (<60%).

The ASHRAE Comfort Zone is the range of temperature and humidity that the American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers defines as comfortable for people. In a pharmaceutical environment, however, because protective garments hinder the dissipation of the operator's metabolic heat, additional cooling is needed.

Analogy

Imagine working for 8 hours in an office at 25°C wearing a winter down jacket. You would feel stiflingly hot. Operators in a GMP cleanroom wearing cleanroom garments (even double gloves and a face mask) are in the same situation as someone wearing a down jacket. This is why cleanroom temperatures must be 2-4°C lower than in an ordinary office to achieve the same level of comfort.

Key Notes

Design considerations for the 30% lower humidity limit:

  • Static electricity risk: below 30% RH, static charge build-up increases. In powder filling or areas with flammable solvents, static electricity can cause safety incidents
  • Personnel health: air that is too dry irritates the mucous membranes of the throat and increases the risk of respiratory illness, and a sick operator is a source of contamination in the cleanroom
  • Particle generation: uncomfortable operators generate more particles (rising from 100,000 per minute to several million)

Formula and Calculation

Fresh air requirement (ASHRAE 62 standard):

Fresh air required per person = 15-20 CFM (24-32 m³/hr)

Example: if there are 10 operators in the cleanroom at the same time
Minimum fresh air requirement = 10 × 20 CFM = 200 CFM
                              = 10 × 32 m³/hr = 320 m³/hr

Note: this is only the minimum IAQ requirement.
The actual supply airflow is usually much greater
(because the cleanliness requirements must also be met)

Practical Application

CDMO scenario: Operators in a CDMO's Grade B area complained of being too hot. Engineers found that the room temperature was set to 22°C (the office standard), but the operators were wearing level 2 cleanroom garments. After the temperature was lowered to 20°C, the operators' environmental particle monitoring data improved markedly, because comfortable personnel generate fewer particles. This case shows that personnel comfort is not just a welfare issue but a product quality issue.

Practice Questions

  1. What is the temperature setpoint of your cleanroom? Has the gowning level of the operators been taken into account?
  2. Why does ISPE say that "an uncomfortable operator may shed millions of particles per minute"? What does this mean for your environmental monitoring (EM) data?
  3. In an office environment an air velocity of 0.1 m/s is sufficient, but product protection requires 1 m/s. How is the balance between the two handled in your facility?
7.2.2 Product and Process Considerations

Original Text

Products may be sensitive to temperature, humidity, and airborne contamination from outside sources or cross-contamination between products.

Process operators may need protection from exposure to hazardous airborne materials.

When considered critical, product environmental requirements normally are listed in a New Drug Application (NDA). Data from process development of a new drug may be available. The affects of conditions outside these ranges will depend on the duration of exposure; prolonged exposure time may affect product quality. Safety requirements for personnel exposure normally are found in Material Safety Data Sheets (MSDSs).

Control of airborne contamination should be considered and frequently is associated with temperature and humidity, e.g., the effect of temperature:

  • Comfortable personnel work more efficiently and are more productive. They also produce fewer environmental contaminants: a typical worker will discharge 100,000 particles a minute doing relatively sedentary work (particles sized 0.3 μm and larger (a human hair is approximately 100 μm in diameter)). A worker who is hot and uncomfortable may shed several million particles per minute in the size range, including a greater number of bacteria.

Additional ways in which environmental conditions inside a building can influence the product include, e.g., high humidity may increase microbial and mold growth rates on surfaces.

If environmental conditions inside are significantly different from environmental conditions outside a building and the fabric of the building has insufficient integrity, condensation can occur in interstitial spaces and can lead to microbial contamination problems and deterioration of the building.

In addition, protection of personnel depends on airflow direction both within and between rooms. Airflow can entrain particles of product or other hazardous materials harmful to operators. DP and the airflow it produces frequently are used to control the migration of airborne particulate between two rooms (to prevent cross-contamination between products).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: The Two-Way Relationship Between Environmental Conditions and Product Quality

This section reveals a key "two-way logic" in HVAC design:

  • Environment → Product: temperature, humidity and particles directly affect product quality
  • Personnel → Environment: uncomfortable operators generate more particles, which indirectly affects the product

Cross-contamination is especially important in a CDMO, because the same facility may produce multiple products at the same time. Differential pressure (DP) control is the main HVAC means of preventing cross-contamination.

Analogy

Think of an isolation ward in a hospital: if the air pressure inside the ward is lower than in the corridor (negative pressure), air flows from the corridor into the ward when the door is opened, preventing pathogens from spreading into the corridor. HVAC pressure differential control works on exactly the same principle: air always flows from the "cleaner" area to the "less clean" area. When a CDMO handles multiple products, each product area is like an "isolation ward."

Key Notes

Striking figures on human particle emission:

  • Sitting quietly: about 100,000 particles/minute (≥0.3 µm)
  • When hot and uncomfortable: millions of particles/minute

This means that an uncomfortable operator can increase particle generation by 10-50 times! This is why personnel comfort is not only a human resources issue but also a quality management issue. A considerable proportion of the environmental monitoring (EM) excursions in a CDMO can be traced back to improper temperature control.

Key Note: Risk of Condensation in the Building

The original text mentions an easily overlooked problem: interstitial condensation. When the temperature difference between indoors and outdoors is large and the building is not sufficiently sealed, water vapor condenses inside wall and ceiling cavities. This not only damages the building but also becomes a breeding ground for mold and microorganisms. In a high-humidity climate such as Taiwan's, this problem is especially serious. Building maintenance inspections of a CDMO facility should include an assessment of condensation within walls.

Practice Questions

  1. Do your NDA documents (or quality agreements) clearly specify the environmental temperature and humidity ranges for the product? If not, how did you decide the temperature and humidity setpoints for your cleanrooms?
  2. In a multi-product CDMO facility, if two adjacent rooms both have exposed product, how should the differential pressure be set to prevent cross-contamination?
7.2.3 Control of Parameters by HVAC Systems

Original Text

7.2.3.1 Temperature and Humidity

HVAC systems control the temperature and humidity in a room by supplying that room with air in a condition that produces the desired temperature and humidity when mixed with the room air.

Thermal heat gains and losses to and from a space occur through three types of heat transfer:

  1. radiant
  2. conductive
  3. convective

These may occur as a result of the temperature from sunlight outside the facility and internal heat gains resulting from the process, equipment, lighting, and personnel.

Changes in humidity may arise because of processes, personnel, and the environment. Moisture migration through openings or porous walls into a controlled space from surrounding areas is governed by the difference in vapor pressure (as defined by Dalton's law) and may migrate against an air pressure differential.

7.2.3.2 Air Velocity

Air velocity in manufacturing spaces usually is higher than recommended for human comfort. Adequate velocity is vital to correct mixing (dilution) of air within the room and for the removal of airborne contaminants. The direction of airflow should protect operators as well as product. Air velocity that is too high can create eddies and vortices near operators and increase the risk of exposure to hazardous material.

7.2.3.3 Particulate, Fume, and Vapor Control

Filtration in HVAC systems usually is capable of removing almost the entire mass of particles. Filters vary in efficiency:

  • Low efficiency filters may remove much of the mass of particles, but this represents only 20 to 30% of the number of particles.
  • High Efficiency Particulate Air (HEPA) and Ultra Low Particulate Air (ULPA) filters remove almost the entire number of particles, but a very small number of nearly "massless" particles may pass through.

The majority of airborne particles are non-viable. A fraction (< 1%) of airborne particles are viable, e.g., bacteria and viruses; however, these can multiply. Viable particles travel with non-viable particles; therefore, controlling the total number of airborne particles also controls the number of viable particles.

Airflow patterns have a significant effect on the control of airborne contaminants, which may be removed by dilution or displacement (see Section 2.8), reducing contaminant levels through the use of exhaust and replacement (makeup) fresh air where necessary.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: The Three Modes of Heat Transfer

The basics of thermodynamics:

  • Radiant: sunlight heating a room through a window, or infrared radiation emitted from equipment surfaces
  • Conductive: heat transferred through solid materials such as walls and floors
  • Convective: air movement carrying heat away or bringing it in. This is exactly how an HVAC system mainly works

HVAC designers must calculate all heat sources (solar gain, equipment, lighting, people) in order to size the cooling capacity correctly.

Key Note: Water Vapor vs. Air Pressure Difference

A very important but easily overlooked point in the original text: water vapor can migrate against the air pressure differential. This is because water vapor migration follows Dalton's Law and is driven by vapor pressure difference, not air pressure difference.

Practical implication: even if your cleanroom is maintained at positive pressure, moisture can still infiltrate from a high-humidity outside environment. This is why, in high-humidity climates (such as Taiwan), good building sealing and a dehumidification system are needed in addition to differential pressure control.

Key Concept: HEPA vs. ULPA Filters

HEPA (High Efficiency Particulate Air filter): efficiency ≥ 99.97% (for 0.3 µm particles)

ULPA (Ultra Low Particulate Air filter): efficiency ≥ 99.999% (for 0.12 µm particles)

Key insight: a low-efficiency filter may remove most of the particle "weight" (mass) but only 20-30% of the particle "count." This is because large numbers of tiny particles have a low total mass but are extremely numerous. GMP regulations are concerned with particle count, not mass.

Analogy

Imagine using an ordinary kitchen strainer to filter a mixture of sand and water. The strainer stops the large grit (most of the weight), but the fine silt (large in number but light in weight) all passes through. A HEPA filter is like an extremely fine filter paper that catches even the smallest silt. This is why cleanrooms must use HEPA rather than ordinary filters.

Key Note: Viable Particles Hitch a Ride on Non-viable Particles

A key statement in the original text: viable particles (bacteria, viruses) attach to non-viable particles and travel with them. Therefore, controlling the total particle count is equivalent to controlling the viable particle count. This is why GMP regulations require monitoring both viable and non-viable particles; they are "travel companions hitching a ride together."

Practice Questions

  1. What are the main heat sources in your facility? Has a heat load calculation been performed?
  2. Why might an excessively high air velocity actually increase the risk of operator exposure to hazardous substances (hint: eddies and vortices)?
  3. If a low-efficiency filter removes 90% of the particle mass but only 25% of the particle count, what does this mean for GMP environmental monitoring?
7.2.4 Limitations of HVAC Systems

Original Text

HVAC systems are not a substitute for good process, facilities, and equipment design or for good operating procedures. HVAC systems are not able to:

  • clean surfaces that are already contaminated
  • adequately control processes that generate excessive contaminants
  • compensate for improperly designed or maintained facilities

As viable particles, such as bacteria and viruses, travel with non-viable particles, HVAC systems can only help control biocontamination in a room by delivering clean air to that room. Where an HVAC system has been properly designed, constructed, and maintained, that system is unlikely to be either the cause or the solution for persistent contamination problems.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: HVAC Is Not a Cure-All

This section is very important; ISPE clearly draws the boundary of what an HVAC system can do:

  • HVAC cannot clean surfaces that are already contaminated. That is the job of cleaning procedures (CIP/SIP)
  • HVAC cannot compensate for a poorly designed facility. If doors do not close automatically or walls have cracks, even the best HVAC cannot maintain cleanliness
  • HVAC cannot control a process that generates excessive contaminants. Control is needed at the source (for example, closed operations)

Analogy

HVAC is like an air purifier at home. If you do not sweep the floor or take out the garbage, an air purifier alone cannot make the room clean. An air purifier can only deal with particles in the air; it cannot wipe the table or mop the floor. Likewise, HVAC can only control air quality; it cannot replace proper facility design and operating procedures.

Key Notes

The last sentence of the original text implies an important investigation logic: if the HVAC system is correctly designed, built and maintained, then persistent contamination problems are unlikely to be caused by HVAC, and are unlikely to be solved by HVAC.

In CDMO deviation investigations, people often question the HVAC system as a first reaction. But if the HVAC maintenance records and performance data are all normal, the investigation should turn to operator behavior, cleaning procedures, equipment design or building integrity.

Practice Questions

  1. In your facility, of the environmental monitoring (EM) deviations over the past year, how many were ultimately traced to the HVAC system? How many were actually operational or cleaning problems?
  2. If a room frequently exceeds particle limits while the HVAC system is operating normally, which directions would you investigate?
7.3 Air Quality Fundamentals

Original Text

7.3.1 Introduction

Pharmaceutical HVAC should control airborne contamination and needs to help to ensure the "...purity, identity and quality..." of the product (21 CFR Part 211). By introducing conditioned clean air, HVAC can help control temperature, humidity, and airborne particulates in a space within the requirements for a product. In order to determine the equipment needed at the HVAC system level, the purpose of air supplied to a room needs to be predefined.

Both the quality (temperature, humidity, cleanliness) and quantity of air introduced into a room affect its ability to maintain environmental conditions. The effects of physical layout (geometry), air velocity, and air volume should be considered to ensure effective ventilation.

7.3.2 Fundamentals of Ventilation

Ventilation is the movement and replacement of air for the purpose of maintaining a desired environmental quality within a space. The term "Ventilation" has two common uses:

  • It may refer to the movement or exchange of air through a space, which is responsible for the transport of airborne particles, the mixing or displacement of masses of hot or cold air, and the removal of airborne contaminants (e.g., vapors and fumes). In this use, ventilation may supply all outdoor ("fresh") air or may recirculate air from the building combined with some fresh air.
  • It may refer to the supply of "fresh" oxygen-rich air.

This Guide uses the definition only for movement or exchange of air through a space.

For pharmaceutical spaces, both "air change rates" and "ventilation rate" may be used. Appropriate filtration and attention to the physical airflow patterns in a space tends to be successful where pharmaceutical HVAC design.

The locations of air inlets and outlets relative to the location of sources of contamination/heat and to expected airflow obstructions are crucial to controlling contamination. The relationship between these factors is expressed in the "effective ventilation rate" for a space. This measure expresses the efficiency of the dilution air supply at removing contaminants expressed as a percentage of the theoretical performance with perfect (complete) dilution. For further information and calculations, see Appendix 9.

A comparison of the ventilation rates of various designs indicates that good air supply layout, good return/exhaust layout, and effective supply filtration may produce desired airborne particulate levels and recovery rates with less air change rates than used traditionally. The importance of room level airflow patterns in the control of contamination and the performance of classified spaces has lead to the application of computer modeling (Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD)) and testing to assure effective design. The WHO guidance 937 Annex 2 suggest that this be performed for oral dosage spaces, but the practice is common only for the most potent products.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: The Two Meanings of Ventilation

Ventilation has two meanings in the pharmaceutical context:

  • Air exchange: moving and replacing the air in a room to control contaminants (the main definition used in this guide)
  • Fresh air supply: providing oxygenated fresh air

Effective Ventilation Rate is a key indicator of ventilation efficiency. It expresses the actual dilution effect as a percentage of theoretically perfect dilution. An effective ventilation rate of 60% means that 40% of the supply air is "wasted" on short-circuiting or in dead zones.

Analogy

Imagine opening a window to ventilate a smoke-filled room. If the windows are on the same side of the room (supply and exhaust too close together), most of the fresh air flows straight from one window to the other and the smoke in the corners of the room is barely affected. This is inefficient ventilation. If the windows are at diagonal positions, the fresh air passes through the whole room before leaving. This is efficient ventilation. The layout principle for HVAC supply and return grilles is exactly the same.

Key Note: The Value of CFD Simulation

Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) has become an important tool in modern HVAC design. Through computer simulation, engineers can predict the following before construction:

  • Airflow paths and velocity distribution within the room
  • Distribution maps of particle concentration (identifying "hot spots")
  • Comparison of the effects of different supply/return layouts
  • The disturbance of airflow caused by operators and equipment

For a CDMO, CFD can optimize the HVAC system at the design stage and avoid discovering problems after construction that require costly modifications.

Practice Questions

  1. Did your facility use CFD simulation at the HVAC design stage? If not, was a smoke study performed during commissioning to verify the airflow patterns?
  2. 21 CFR Part 211 requires that the "purity, identity and quality" of the product be ensured. Can you explain how HVAC supports each of these three requirements?
7.3.3 Contamination Control

Original Text

Pharmaceutical HVAC should help to:

  • prevent unwanted environmental contaminants from adversely affecting product
  • prevent products from contaminating each another
  • limit operator exposure to hazardous pharmaceutical compounds, ingredients, or reagent vapors
  • prevent hazardous materials being spread to the outdoor environment

Room contamination control generally is achieved by filtering the incoming air to ensure that it does not carry unwanted particles, and then introducing the air to the work space to mix with ambient air and dilute any contaminants. Contaminants may be removed more rapidly using displacement airflow of adequate velocity and direction (e.g., in a UFH, local extraction vent, or via non-aspirating diffusers) than with dilution ventilation.

The number and intensity of contamination sources in a room should be considered; if low, a displacement airstream may be more useful in controlling airborne contaminants than dilution.

The orientation of airflows can be aligned to protect product or personnel by sweeping across one or the other (or both) between the supply terminal and the extract point. Local (usually high level) supply or extraction, or complete enclosure of the process also can create a local environment that excludes or removes particulates. Local supply or extraction is considered most effective when located near the point of contaminant generation.

Pharmaceutical HVAC can help control contaminants within a space, but facilities should be designed with physical architectural features, such as airlocks, which limit the migration of contaminants.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Dilution vs. Displacement

HVAC has two basic strategies for controlling particles:

  • Dilution Ventilation: clean air is supplied and mixes with the contaminated air in the room, lowering the overall contaminant concentration. It is like continuously adding clean water to a glass of ink.
  • Displacement Airflow: clean air "pushes" the contaminated air out from one end, like flushing the ink out with clean water. It is more efficient but requires more precise airflow design.

A UFH (Unidirectional Flow Hood) is a typical application of displacement airflow. Air flows vertically downward or horizontally from a HEPA filter across the work area, "flushing" particles away from the critical location.

Key Note: The Four Areas of HVAC Protection

Note that the original text lists four aspects that HVAC must protect at the same time:

  1. Protecting the product from environmental contamination (the primary responsibility)
  2. Preventing cross-contamination between products (the core challenge for a CDMO)
  3. Protecting operators from exposure to hazardous substances (occupational safety)
  4. Protecting the external environment from discharge of hazardous substances (environmental protection)

When designing an HVAC system, these four needs sometimes conflict. For example, protecting the product requires positive pressure, but protecting operators from exposure to highly potent drugs requires negative pressure. How do you balance them? This is the core challenge of containment HVAC design.

Practical Application

CDMO scenario: Your CDMO manufactures a penicillin-class antibiotic for Client A and an injectable protein drug for Client B. These two products must never cross-contaminate (penicillin allergy can be fatal). The HVAC design must ensure: (1) completely independent air-handling systems for the two areas, (2) the corridor is kept at positive pressure relative to both areas, (3) an airlock acts as a physical barrier. This is a typical case of the "physical architectural features" mentioned in the original text working together with HVAC.

Practice Questions

  1. In your facility, which areas use displacement airflow and which use dilution ventilation? Why?
  2. Can you list at least three examples where "the contamination source should be near the local exhaust point"?
7.3.4 Classified Space

Original Text

The concentration of total airborne particles and microbial contamination within the space is a key measurement of room environmental conditions for pharmaceutical operations, particularly for sterile products and some biopharmaceutical APIs. The target maximum reading for these measurements is referred to as the "classification" of the space.

Several similar systems have been communicated for the classification of space; however, there is no consensus between international regulators on a single terminology for classification:

  • the EMEA uses "Grades A to D"
  • the FDA refers to ISO levels (5, 7 and 8), but only "in-use" (there are no "at-rest" limits), and further adds bioburden limits for each ISO class

It would be cumbersome to apply EU and FDA GMP nomenclature to facilities and to explicitly state "ISO X, in-use with colony forming unit (CFU) limits of Y per cubic meter."

This Guide uses the term "Grade" followed by an ISO level number. Therefore, "Grade 7" meets ISO 7 (10,000 0.5 micron particles per cubic foot or 352,000 per cubic meter) in use only with bioburden limits of 10 per cubic meter. By comparison, a Grade 7 space looks much like a European Grade B space, but the European Grade (A, B, C, D) also has at-rest limits.

Notes:

  • There are small differences in numerical values between the US and European air classes.
  • The US particle levels are for the 'in operation' state only, but it is considered GEP to measure periodic at rest particle levels to monitor the overall health of a facility.
  • The US has no equivalent to EU Grade D although the term Controlled Not Classified (CNC) has been used in the pharmaceutical industry and is discussed in the ISPE Baseline® Guides for Sterile and Biopharmaceuticals. A CNC space may meet ISO 8 at rest without the use of HEPA filters if the airborne challenge is low.
  • Air quality for facilities that do not require classified spaces, (e.g., oral dosage, packaging, warehousing, closed biopharmaceutical, most APIs (except aseptic processing), and API intermediates) is described in the relevant ISPE Baseline® Guide.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: International Cleanliness Classification Systems

Cleanliness classification systems in the pharmaceutical industry are a common source of confusion. ISPE attempts to simplify them with "Grade + ISO number":

  • Grade 5 = ISO 5 in-use = EU Grade A = old Class 100
  • Grade 7 = ISO 7 in-use = similar to EU Grade B = old Class 10,000
  • Grade 8 = ISO 8 in-use = similar to EU Grade C = old Class 100,000
  • CNC = Controlled Not Classified = similar to EU Grade D

Key Note: Key Differences Between EU and FDA

The practical impact on a CDMO is very large:

  • The EU has two sets of limits, "at-rest" and "in-operation", while the FDA has only "in-operation"
  • The EU has Grade D (the lowest grade of classified space), for which the FDA has no equivalent
  • If a CDMO manufactures for both European and US clients, it must meet the requirements of both sides, which usually means meeting both the at-rest and in-operation particle limits

Recommendation: when designing a CDMO facility, use the stricter standard as the baseline so that both EU and US regulatory requirements can be met.

Analogy

Think of cleanroom classification as hotel star ratings. The EU is like a rating system that evaluates both "after cleaning" (at-rest) and "with guests checked in" (in-operation). The FDA evaluates only "with guests checked in," believing that the actual state of use is what really matters. ISPE says, "We use ISO star numbers, but add the FDA's microbial limits," trying to establish a common language.

Table Analysis

Table 7.2 is a very important quick-reference table, and we recommend printing it and keeping it on your desk. Key observations:

  • The 0.5 µm particle limit for Grade A/ISO 5 is 3,520/m³ in both at-rest and in-operation, meaning that this grade allows almost no increase in particles from personnel activity
  • At rest, the Grade B particle limit is the same as Grade A (3,520), but in operation it allows up to 352,000, a 100-fold difference! This is why the concept of "recovery time" is so important
  • Viable microbial limit: Grade A requires <1 cfu/m³, which is almost zero tolerance

Practice Questions

  1. Which classification system does your facility currently use (EU Grade or ISO Class)? If you needed to convert to the other system, which differences would you need to watch for?
  2. Are the particle levels in your CNC areas (if any) monitored regularly? How does their performance compare with EU Grade D?
  3. If your CDMO needs to manufacture sterile products for both EU and US clients, to what grade should the HVAC system be designed to meet both sets of requirements?
7.3.5 Total Airflow Volume and Ventilation Rate

Original Text
