The relationship between air change rate, ventilation rate, the air particle concentration in the space, and recovery rates from in-use to at-rest conditions should be considered.

The process that will be operated in a given space should be understood in order to determine the air flow rate (not air change rate) required to meet the stated room air classification (see Chapter 5 of this Guide).

Arbitrary air changes may be either excessive or insufficient. The airborne particle level depends on several factors. After a facility is commissioned, particle levels and room recovery should be sufficiently below specified limits, rather than having an arbitrary number of air changes.

7.3.5.1 Air Change or Air Flow?

Arbitrarily set air change rates often drive decisions regarding room size and airflows. This can have significant cost implications, but does not relate directly to the particle count in a room. Air change rates are more related to a room's ability to recover from an upset, not the room classification. The following is an explanation of this difference:

  • Assume a 1 cubic foot room containing an aseptic process that generates 10,000 particles per minute. If the room is purged with 1 CFM of clean air, the steady state (equilibrium) airborne particle level will be 10,000 particles per cubic foot (PCF). This 1 CFM creates an air change every 1 minute or 60 air changes per hour. This value (60/hr) is often assumed to be more than enough to keep a space well below 10,000 PCF.

Now put the same process into a 100 cubic foot volume and keep the airflow at 1 CFM, assuming good mixing occurs inside the room. Now the room sees an air change every 100 minutes or about 0.67 ac/hr. However, when the dilution is calculated, the equilibrium airborne particle counts are still 10,000 PCF (10,000 particles per minute/1 cubic foot per minute = 10,000 particles per cubic foot). Hence, average airborne particle counts are not determined by the air changes, but by the three factors (assuming perfect mixing, see Appendix 9):

  1. particles generated inside a space (PGR)
  2. quantity of dilution air supplied to a space (cubic volume per time) assuming adequate mixing in the room
  3. cleanliness of dilution air (assumed to be negligible in aseptic processing based on HEPA filtration)

A room receiving only 1 air change per hour will take several hours to recover from in-use to at-rest conditions. With a clean air supply of 20 air changes per hour, a 100-fold reduction in airborne particle levels can occur with less than 20 minutes recovery time, satisfying the European GMP requirement. See the ISPE Sterile Manufacturing Facilities Baseline® Guide.

For recovery, air changes are important; a rate of 20/hr often is used as the minimum for classified spaces.

For applicable oral dosage facilities, the WHO 40th report suggests 6 to 20 AC/hr with recovery of 20 minutes from in-use to at-rest conditions (to be defined by the User and verified at building commissioning).

Although "air change rate" is important, for pharmaceutical HVAC system design, greater benefit may be obtained from correct air filtration and attention to the airflow patterns in a space.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Air Change Rate vs. Air Flow Rate, a Critical Distinction

This is one of the most important concepts in this appendix. ISPE uses an elegant mathematical example to illustrate it:

  • Air Change Rate = supply airflow ÷ room volume. It depends on the size of the room but does not directly determine particle concentration
  • Air Flow Rate = the actual amount of clean air supplied. This is what truly determines the steady-state particle concentration

Conclusion: the same airflow gives a low air change rate in a large room and a high air change rate in a small room, but the steady-state particle concentration is exactly the same!

Formula and Calculation

Steady-state particle concentration formula (assuming perfect mixing):

Steady-state particle concentration = PGR / Q

Where:
  PGR = Particle Generation Rate (particles/minute)
  Q   = Air Flow Rate (CFM or m³/min)

Example 1 (1 ft³ room):
  PGR = 10,000 particles/min, Q = 1 CFM
  Concentration = 10,000 / 1 = 10,000 PCF
  Air change rate = 1 CFM / 1 ft³ = 60 changes/hr

Example 2 (100 ft³ room):
  PGR = 10,000 particles/min, Q = 1 CFM
  Concentration = 10,000 / 1 = 10,000 PCF (exactly the same!)
  Air change rate = 1 CFM / 100 ft³ = 0.67 changes/hr

Conclusion: the air change rates differ by 90 times, but the particle concentration is exactly the same.
The airflow (Q) is the key to controlling steady-state concentration.

Analogy

Imagine dripping one drop of ink into a bathtub and into a swimming pool, then pouring in clean water at the same flow rate (for example, 1 liter per minute). The bathtub's "water change rate" is very high (because the volume is small) and the pool's is very low (because the volume is large). But in the end, if you keep dripping ink and pouring in clean water at the same rates, the equilibrium ink concentration is the same in both. The difference is that the bathtub returns to clear much faster than the pool. This is why recovery time is what relates to the air change rate.

Key Note: The Myth of Air Change Rates

The pharmaceutical industry has long held a myth: "the higher the air change rate, the better." ISPE clearly states that this is an expensive misunderstanding:

  • An excessively high air change rate means larger air-handling equipment, higher energy consumption, and higher HEPA filter replacement costs
  • The air change rate mainly affects recovery time, not the steady-state particle concentration
  • 20 changes/hr is a common minimum for classified space and can achieve a 100-fold particle reduction in 20 minutes
  • The correct approach is to first determine the PGR and the target concentration, then calculate the required airflow, and only then know the air change rate

Practical Application

Cost impact: A CDMO's Grade 7 room (50 m³) was designed with an air change rate of 40 changes/hr (airflow of 2000 m³/hr). After commissioning, it was found that at-rest particle levels were far below the limit and recovery took only 8 minutes. When the air change rate was reduced to 25 changes/hr (1250 m³/hr), the recovery time increased to 14 minutes (still within the 20-minute requirement), but air-conditioning energy consumption fell by about 35%. The annual savings in electricity and filter costs were several hundred thousand NT dollars.

Practice Questions

  1. What is the air change rate of your classified spaces? Was it derived from calculation or from "industry convention"?
  2. If the air change rate is reduced by 25%, by how much will the recovery time increase? Can the regulatory requirement still be met?
  3. Do you know the PGR (particle generation rate) of your cleanroom? If not, is there a way to estimate it?
7.3.5.2 Particle Generation Rate

Original Text

The PGR for an existing process may be calculated if the steady-state room particle count, the room supply airflow, and the supply airflow particle level are known (see Appendix 9). The calculated value of PGR can then be used for the same process in a new facility.

However, equipment manufacturers may not know the PGR of their equipment, necessitating HVAC designers to make conservative estimates and over-design room airflow. Data gathered during "water batching" (process simulation), but before actual production, may offer an opportunity to reduce airflow rates where in-operation airborne particle levels appear to be low (because of over-design).

When using empirical data for airborne particulate monitoring, it should be taken into consideration that particulate of the product being processed is not a contaminant. This is of particular interest in aseptic powder filling operations, where high particle counts may be associated with the filling process, but do not indicate failure of a cleanroom design. If an air volume reduction appears to be feasible, other critical HVAC parameters (temperature, RH, room DP, recovery, and at-rest levels) should be maintained.

Figure 7.2 gives an indication of particulates generated by personnel within a cleanroom. Although equipment in operation can generate many times more particles per minute, personnel are a primary source of viable contamination. Increased control of total particles released from personnel leads to an increased control of viable particles in a room.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: The Practical Significance of PGR

Particle Generation Rate (PGR) is a key input parameter for HVAC design. If you know the PGR, you can calculate the required airflow precisely. In reality, however:

  • Equipment vendors usually do not provide PGR data
  • HVAC designers are forced to make conservative estimates, leading to over-design
  • Over-design = larger equipment + higher energy consumption + higher cost

The good news is that PGR can be measured during water batching (a simulated batch with water), and if it turns out to be lower than estimated, there is an opportunity to reduce the airflow and save cost.

Key Note: Product Dust Is Not a Contaminant

This is a very important but easily confused concept. In aseptic powder filling operations, a particle counter may show very high readings, but these particles are the product powder itself, not environmental contaminants.

This does not mean the cleanroom design has failed. But note that even though product dust itself is not a contaminant, high dust concentrations can still interfere with the interpretation of environmental monitoring. A CDMO needs to establish clear data interpretation criteria that distinguish "product-related particles" from "environmental contaminant particles."

Analogy

PGR is like the rate at which a faucet leaks. If you know the leak rate (PGR), you can calculate how large a drain pipe (airflow) you need to prevent water from accumulating (particle excursions). If you do not know the leak rate, you can only install a drain pipe that is "supposed to be big enough," which is over-design. The commissioning phase is like turning on the faucet for the first time to test it: you finally know the actual leak rate and can decide whether a smaller (cheaper) drain pipe will do.

Practice Questions

  1. Does your facility collect PGR data during commissioning or APS (aseptic process simulation)? Are these data used to optimize the HVAC design?
  2. If the particle counts on your powder filling line far exceed the ISO 7 limit during operation but are all product dust, how would you handle these environmental monitoring data?
7.3.5.3 Impact of Unidirectional Airflow Hoods on Air Change Rates

Original Text

Air leaving the processing space inside a hood is often significantly cleaner than the air of the room into which it moves. The relatively clean air from the hood may help, along with the supply air from the HVAC system to dilute airborne particles in the room.

In addition to reducing airborne particles, air flow from a hood may accelerate the recovery time of a room from in-use to at-rest conditions. The entire air flow from a hood may not be available to include in air change calculations because:

  • Short-circuiting of the air leaving the hood zone back (upward) to the hood inlet; the added dilution will affect only areas near the airflow path. If the hood inlet is near a room air supply outlet, that air could also short circuit into the hood without helping to mix air in the room.
  • Hood air may not be as clean as HVAC supply air. Even though the critical location under the hood might be rated as ISO 5, the air leaving the Grade 5 work space has collected additional contaminants from equipment and personnel outside the critical zone before passing back into the hood inlet.
  • Similar increases in room air cleanliness and recovery can be accomplished with HEPA-equipped FFUs operating inside a room. Short circuiting of filtered air back to the air intake may create only localized "super-clean" areas, as with UFHs.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: The Contribution of UFH/FFU to Air Change Rates

Unidirectional Flow Hoods (UFH) and Fan Filter Units (FFU) create additional clean airflow within a room. However, this airflow cannot simply be added to the room's air change rate calculation, for three reasons:

  • Short-circuiting: air discharged from a UFH may be drawn straight back into its own intake without actually diluting the air in the whole room
  • Contaminant accumulation: air leaving the Grade 5 work area has already collected particles from equipment and personnel and is no longer "clean"
  • Local effect: an FFU may create an "ultra-clean" zone only directly beneath it rather than improving the whole room uniformly

Analogy

Imagine placing a desktop air purifier in a dusty room. The purifier makes the air near it very clean, but if its outlet and inlet are too close together, the clean air circulates around the purifier and the other end of the room stays dirty. You cannot say "purifier airflow + central air-conditioning airflow = total air change of the room," because the purifier's airflow is effective only locally.

Key Notes

During HVAC qualification, the actual effect of the UFH/FFU on the whole room needs to be verified:

  • Measure room particles with the UFH operating and with it switched off
  • Measure particle concentrations at different distances from the UFH outlet and plot a decay curve
  • Perform a smoke study to confirm whether short-circuiting exists

Practice Questions

  1. Does your cleanroom have UFHs or FFUs? When calculating the air change rate, do you include their airflow?
  2. Have you performed a smoke study to confirm whether the UFH airflow has short-circuiting?
7.3.6 Room Air Distribution and Quality of Incoming Air

Original Text

Optimal layout for air inlet and outlet, and adequate filtration, can produce desired airborne particulate levels and recovery rates using lower air change rates than those used traditionally.

Using the recovery example in Section 2.3.5.1 of this Guide, faster recovery can be accomplished in a classified room where clean air supply is distributed over a high percentage of the ceiling (or via multiple non-aspirating diffusers) than by supplying the same total supply volume from one conventional air outlet. It is not necessary to create a "laminar flow ceiling." Numerous air outlets equally spaced, with equal flow rates, can create a "plug flow," a situation where air generally moves downward from ceiling to floor, but not at constant velocity. This can lead to faster recovery (often less than 10 minutes for 20 ac/hr) and also prevent "hot spots" of high particle count in a room. The resultant downward velocities are much less than those used in a unidirectional flow (Grade 5) area, and activity in the room may cause undesirable airflow patterns that should be investigated during commissioning. Numerous well-located low wall air returns can help prevent "dead zones" near the floor. (Generally, pharmaceutical facilities do not use perforated floors for air returns.)

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Plug Flow vs. Laminar Flow

ISPE presents an important design philosophy: you do not need to build an expensive "laminar flow ceiling" to achieve good air distribution.

  • Laminar Flow: all air moves in the same direction at a uniform, constant velocity. It is expensive and requires the entire ceiling to be HEPA filters
  • Plug Flow: air moves roughly from the ceiling toward the floor, but at a non-constant velocity. It is achieved through multiple evenly distributed supply outlets and costs less

Non-aspirating Diffusers are the key devices for achieving plug flow. They discharge air vertically downward at low velocity without entraining the surrounding air.

Key Note: The Risk of Dead Zones

Dead Zones are areas of a room where the air barely moves, usually in corners and near the floor. Particles accumulate in these areas and become a potential source of contamination. Solutions:

  • Install multiple return grilles at low wall positions
  • Avoid stacking items in corners that block airflow
  • Use smoke studies during commissioning to identify dead zones

Note: pharmaceutical facilities generally do not use perforated floors as returns (unlike semiconductor fabs) because they are difficult to clean and maintain.

Practice Questions

  1. What type of supply diffuser does your cleanroom use? Conventional square diffusers or non-aspirating diffusers?
  2. Did your facility perform smoke studies during commissioning to identify dead zones?
7.3.7 Airflow Direction and Pressurization

Original Text

Constructing a space that is absolutely airtight is considered impractical using normal construction techniques; therefore, alternative approaches are required to prevent airborne particulate migrating into or out of a space. A continuous flow of air in the desired direction through the cracks in building construction (door gaps, wall penetrations, conduits, etc.) can reduce transport of airborne particulates. A velocity of 100 to 200 FPM (0.5 to 1.0 m/sec) usually will capture and transport light powders and bioburden, assuming there are no strong drafts nearby (such as a worker passing quickly in front of a laboratory hood).

One method to control the direction of airflow is to control the relative pressurization of adjacent spaces, i.e., the DP between the spaces.

A simplified method (neglecting the orifice coefficient for the opening) to calculate the expected velocity of airflow through a "crack" (e.g., around a closed door) resulting from a given pressure differential is:

V = 4005 √VP   or   VP = (V/4005)²

Velocity (V) can be broken down to volume divided by area, giving V = Q/A:

VP = (Q/4005A)²

For metric units: VP (Pascals) = (Q/110A)²
(where Q is in m³/hr and A is in square meters)

Where:

  • 4005 is a conversion factor
  • V is velocity in ft/min
  • VP is velocity pressure, here assumed to be the room DP in inches wg
  • A is area of the opening in square feet
  • Q is airflow in Cubic Feet per Minute

Assuming room DP converts fully to VP through an opening (a conservative assumption), calculating the opening area, such as the crack area around a closed door between rooms, allows calculation of the airflow (CFM) required to create a pressure across that door, or the velocity that results from a known DP.

For A=1 sq foot (0.1 sq m) opening, 890 CFM (about 1500 m³/hr or 0.45 m³/sec) will create 0.05 inch wg (12.5 Pa) DP (V = Q/A = 890 FPM = 4.5 M/s)

Other "cracks" in the fabric separating a pressurized room from lower pressure spaces may not be accounted for using this calculation. This often leads to a requirement for more airflow to the room than predicted by the calculation to satisfy DP requirements. A common method which accounts for this additional airflow is to allocate 0.05 to 0.5 CFM per square foot of room surface, depending on construction and DP. This airflow can be minimized by constructing rooms tightly and testing for (and correcting) leaks during commissioning.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Differential Pressure (DP) Control

Differential Pressure is one of the most important control parameters in pharmaceutical HVAC. The core principles:

  • A completely airtight room cannot be achieved with ordinary building methods
  • Door gaps, pipe penetrations through walls, conduit runs and so on all create "cracks"
  • By maintaining a pressure differential between rooms, air always flows from the high-pressure (clean) side to the low-pressure (less clean) side
  • The air velocity through cracks must reach 100-200 FPM (0.5-1.0 m/s) to effectively block the migration of particles and microorganisms

Formula and Calculation

Formula relating pressure differential, velocity and airflow:

Imperial:  V = 4005 × sqrt(VP)
           VP = (Q / (4005 × A))²

Metric:    VP(Pa) = (Q / (110 × A))²
           Q = m³/hr, A = m²

Worked example:
Assume a door gap area A = 0.1 m² (about 1 ft²)
Target pressure differential VP = 12.5 Pa (0.05 inch wg)

Q = 110 × A × sqrt(VP)
Q = 110 × 0.1 × sqrt(12.5)
Q = 110 × 0.1 × 3.54
Q ≈ 39 m³/min ≈ 1500 m³/hr

That is, a single door gap alone requires about 1500 m³/hr of
"extra" supply air to maintain a 12.5 Pa pressure differential!

Analogy

Pressure differential control is like a balloon: if the balloon has a small hole, you must keep inflating it to keep it inflated (positive pressure). The more or larger the holes, the higher the rate of inflation required. The door gaps and pipe penetrations of a room are the "small holes," and the supply air system is the "pump." The more tightly the building is constructed, the less "inflation" is needed and the more energy is saved.

Key Note: A Hidden Cost Factor

The "leakage make-up airflow" needed to maintain pressure differentials is an important but often underestimated source of HVAC energy consumption:

  • A common estimating method: allow 0.05-0.5 CFM of leakage make-up airflow per square foot of room surface area
  • The poorer the building's sealing, the greater the make-up airflow required and the higher the energy consumption
  • Commissioning is the best time to test for and repair leaks to reduce long-term operating costs

When a CDMO evaluates a building lease or new construction, the airtightness quality of the building directly affects HVAC operating costs.

Practice Questions

  1. What are the pressure differential setpoints (in Pa) between the cleanrooms in your facility? How were these values determined?
  2. Do you know the approximate area of the door gaps in your cleanrooms? What effect does this have on the airflow needed to maintain pressure differentials?
  3. During commissioning, did your facility perform airtightness tests and repair leaks?
7.3.8 Control of Operator Exposure to Potent and Hazardous Compounds

Original Text

Modern pharmaceutical processing increasingly requires handling of potent active ingredients, requiring small dosages to produce a pharmacological effect, and may require the handling of other materials that can be hazardous to human health. The prevalence of these challenges creates a burden on the HVAC system and process engineers to control operator exposure and possible environmental discharge. Worker protection standards vary by jurisdiction, but Control of Substances Hazardous to Human Health (COSHH) regulations (this is a terminology coined in the UK, but common in the industry) are ubiquitous. These standards may specify 8 hour Operator Exposure Limits (OELs) for commonly used substances and require that manufacturers specify OELs for proprietary compounds. A hierarchy of control is expected; with substitution and control at the source being considered before Local Exhaust Ventilation (LEV) and other HVAC methods, followed by Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) and administrative controls.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: The Hierarchy of Operator Exposure Control

When handling highly potent active pharmaceutical ingredients (HPAPI), ISPE emphasizes a Hierarchy of Control:

  1. Substitution: can a less hazardous substance be used instead?
  2. Source Control: closed vessels, isolators, closed transfer systems
  3. LEV (Local Exhaust Ventilation): exhaust points at dust-generating locations
  4. HVAC approach: pressure differential and air change control for the room as a whole
  5. PPE (Personal Protective Equipment): face masks, respirators, etc.
  6. Administrative Controls: shift systems, limits on exposure time

Key point: PPE is the last line of defense and should not be the first choice.

Key Note: The Relationship Between OEL and HVAC Design

The Operator Exposure Limit (OEL) directly affects HVAC design. The lower the OEL (the more potent the drug), the higher the level of protection the HVAC system must provide:

  • OEL > 100 µg/m³: general ventilation + basic PPE may be sufficient
  • OEL 10-100 µg/m³: LEV + negative pressure control required
  • OEL < 10 µg/m³: isolators or closed systems required
  • OEL < 1 µg/m³: fully enclosed isolator systems required

For a CDMO, before accepting an order for a highly potent drug, it must assess whether the existing HVAC system can provide sufficient protection.

Practical Application

CDMO business decision: A CDMO received a manufacturing inquiry for an HPAPI product with an OEL of 0.5 µg/m³. The existing facility has no isolators, only open workstations and LEV. Before bidding, it needs to assess: (1) the cost of modifying the HVAC system, (2) the investment in purchasing isolators, (3) the additional cost of operator health monitoring. These costs must be reflected in the quotation; otherwise the company will lose money or violate occupational safety regulations.

Practice Questions

  1. What is the lowest OEL band that your facility can currently handle? If a client requires a lower OEL, what upgrades would you need?
  2. In the hierarchy of controls, which level does your facility mainly rely on? Does it rely too heavily on PPE instead of engineering controls?
7.4 Psychrometrics

Original Text

7.4.1 Introduction

Psychrometrics is the science involving the properties of moist air (a mixture of dry air and water vapor) and the process in which the temperature or the water vapor content of the mixture are changed. A psychrometric chart is used to identify conditions of air and to illustrate the process of achieving the desired state of the controlled space. For further information, see Appendix 1. See sources such as the ASHRAE Fundamentals Handbook for a detailed discussion. This section contains a high level overview of psychrometrics.

7.4.2 Basic Properties of Air

Dry air is normally comprised of 78.1% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and has trace amounts of 10 additional elements totaling 0.9%. Air is normally a mixture of dry air and water vapor. When moist air reaches a level at which it cannot hold more moisture, it is said to be, "saturated." The colder the air, the less moisture it can hold. Warmer air can hold larger quantities of moisture.

The moisture in air (its specific humidity) is measured in:

  • grains of moisture per pound of air (7,000 grains equal 1 pound)
  • grams of moisture per kg of air (SI units)

Air at 75°F (24°C) and 60% RH has a specific humidity of 78 grains of water per pound (7000 grains) of dry air (11g/kg).

A psychrometric chart (see Appendix 3) provides an overview of thermodynamic properties of air-water mixtures. If any two properties of the air mixture are known, the chart allows an engineer to determine its remaining properties. Air-water vapor mixtures have interrelated psychrometric properties that can be plotted on the chart. The values on the chart are for a given barometric pressure (usually assumed to be at sea level); the values will be different at substantially different elevations.

7.4.2 (continued) Sensible and Latent Heat

Sensible (dry) heat causes a change in the temperature of a substance. Sensible heat can be "sensed" or felt and quantified by measurement with a dry bulb thermometer. Addition or removal of sensible heat will cause the measured air temperature to rise or fall.

On the psychrometric chart, sensible heat shows as temperature, as a horizontal line with a scale increasing from left to right. As mixed air is heated with only sensible heat, there is no resulting change in the amount of water vapor in the air.

Latent heat is the heat of vaporization carried by the moisture in the air/water mixture. Changes in latent heat are not detected with a dry bulb thermometer. The addition of water vapor to air may increase the humidity of the air without changing the temperature of the air, for example:

  • If sufficient latent heat is added to water in its liquid state, it will change state into a vapor (or steam) by evaporation:
    • The change of state caused by heating a liquid to steam is called the latent heat of vaporization.
    • The change of state caused by cooling from a steam to a liquid is called the latent heat of condensation.
    • The change of state from a liquid to a solid (ice) is called the latent heat of fusion.
    • The change of state from a solid to liquid is called the latent heat of melting.

Latent heat (mass of water per mass of dry air) appears on the psychrometric chart as horizontal lines on a vertical scale.

RH is the amount of moisture in the air versus the air's capacity to hold moisture. As warmer air can hold more moisture, sensible heating of air reduces the RH, and vice versa. Generally, at room temperature, it is assumed that each degree Fahrenheit change in temperature will yield a 2% change in RH. RH is a useful measure as it is related to the vapor pressure of water in the air, and therefore, reflects the tendency of water (in its liquid state) or moist surfaces to lose moisture to the air. Human comfort is more closely associated with RH than specific humidity, because of this drying effect on skin and mucus membranes.

7.4.3 Psychrometric Properties of Air

See Appendix 3 for a discussion of the terms used in Psychrometrics and for an explanation of the Psychrometric Chart.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concept: Psychrometrics

Psychrometrics is the science of the properties of moist air (dry air + water vapor). For HVAC engineers, it is the mathematical foundation for designing air-conditioning systems. Core concepts:

  • Dry Bulb Temperature: the temperature measured by an ordinary thermometer, reflecting sensible heat
  • Wet Bulb Temperature: the temperature measured by a thermometer wrapped in a wet cloth, reflecting the effect of evaporative cooling
  • Dew Point: the temperature at which air, when cooled, begins to condense water droplets
  • Specific Humidity / Humidity Ratio: how many grams of water vapor are contained per kilogram of dry air
  • Enthalpy: the total energy in the air (sensible heat + latent heat)
  • Relative Humidity (RH): the ratio of the current water content to the saturated water content

Key tool: the Psychrometric Chart. If you know any two parameters, you can read off all the others from the chart.

Key Concept: Sensible Heat vs. Latent Heat

This is the most fundamental and most important distinction in HVAC design:

  • Sensible Heat: heat that changes the temperature without changing the water content. You can "feel" the temperature change. It is a horizontal movement on the psychrometric chart.
  • Latent Heat: heat that changes the water content (a phase change) without changing the temperature. You cannot "feel" it; only a hygrometer can detect it. It is a vertical movement on the psychrometric chart.

The four forms of latent heat:

  • Latent Heat of Vaporization: liquid → gas
  • Latent Heat of Condensation: gas → liquid
  • Latent Heat of Fusion: liquid → solid
  • Latent Heat of Melting: solid → liquid

Analogy

The best analogy for sensible heat vs. latent heat:

Imagine boiling a pot of water. As it heats from cold water to 100°C, you can see the thermometer rising continuously. That is sensible heat. But once the water reaches 100°C and you keep heating, the thermometer stops moving! All the heat goes into turning the water into steam. That is latent heat. In HVAC, the cooling coil of an air-conditioning system must handle both sensible heat (cooling) and latent heat (dehumidification), which is why HVAC design requires separate calculations of these two heat loads.

Formula and Calculation

Approximate relationship between temperature and relative humidity:

Rule of thumb (room temperature range):
  Each 1°F rise in temperature → RH drops by about 2%
  Each 1°F drop in temperature → RH rises by about 2%

Example:
  Initial room conditions: 72°F, 50% RH
  Heated to 77°F (a 5°F rise)
  New RH ≈ 50% - (5 × 2%) = 40%

This is why the more the heating is turned up in winter,
the drier the air gets: as temperature rises, RH falls automatically.

Humidity ratio example:
  Air at 75°F (24°C), 60% RH
  Specific Humidity = 78 grains/lb = 11 g/kg
  (7,000 grains = 1 pound)

Key Note: The Effect of High Altitude

The original text mentions that the values on the psychrometric chart assume sea-level pressure. At high altitudes (such as Mexico City at 2,240 m or Kunming at 1,890 m), the air pressure is lower and the air density is smaller:

  • The same volume of air contains less oxygen and has less water vapor capacity
  • Fans need a larger volumetric flow to achieve the same mass flow
  • The values on a standard psychrometric chart need to be corrected

For a CDMO with plants at different altitudes, an HVAC design cannot simply be copied; it must be recalculated for the local air pressure.

Practical Application

CDMO scenario: dehumidification design: Your cleanroom must maintain 20°C / 45% RH. The outside air is 35°C / 80% RH (a Taiwan summer). The air-conditioning system must: (1) first cool the air well below the dew point so that the water vapor condenses (handling latent heat), (2) then reheat it to 20°C (handling sensible heat). This "cool first, then reheat" process consumes a great deal of energy and is a major source of energy consumption for CDMOs in Taiwan. Understanding psychrometrics helps you evaluate the energy efficiency differences between dehumidification strategies (desiccant wheel vs. cooling dehumidification).

Practice Questions

  1. Can you read the dew point temperature of 20°C / 50% RH air from the psychrometric chart? What does this mean for the design temperature of the cooling coil?
  2. Why is human comfort more closely related to RH than to specific humidity?
  3. In your facility's HVAC energy consumption, roughly what proportion goes to sensible heat handling and what proportion to latent heat handling?

Section Summary

  • The three-tier variable structure of HVAC: primary variables (temperature, humidity, particles) directly affect the product, secondary variables (differential pressure, air change rate, airflow direction) are the means of control, and tertiary variables (fan speed, duct pressure) are operating parameters. There is a clear cause-and-effect chain between the three.
  • The limitations of HVAC: HVAC cannot clean already contaminated surfaces, cannot compensate for poor facility design, and cannot control a process that generates excessive contaminants. HVAC is only one part of the contamination control strategy (CCS).
  • Air change rate vs. air flow rate: steady-state particle concentration is determined by the PGR (particle generation rate) and the airflow (Q), and is not directly related to the air change rate. The air change rate mainly affects recovery time. An arbitrarily set air change rate can lead to over-design and unnecessary cost.
  • Differences in cleanliness classification: the EU uses Grade A-D (with at-rest and in-operation limits) and the FDA uses ISO 5/7/8 (in-operation only). A CDMO serving both European and US clients should use the stricter standard as the design baseline.
  • Differential pressure control: by maintaining pressure differentials (DP) between rooms, air is forced to flow from clean areas to less clean areas. Building tightness directly affects the extra airflow and energy needed to maintain the pressure differential.
  • Psychrometrics: sensible heat changes temperature and latent heat changes water content. The psychrometric chart is the core tool of HVAC design; knowing any two parameters is enough to determine all the properties of the air.
  • Hierarchy of operator exposure control: from source control (substitution, containment) to engineering controls (LEV, HVAC) and then PPE; the higher in the hierarchy, the higher the priority. PPE is always the last line of defense and should not be the first choice.
7

Chapter 7: App 2: HVAC Applications

p159-p198

ISPE Good Practice Guide: HVAC | p158 - p178

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the components of an Air Handling Unit (AHU) and how each affects the environmental parameters (temperature, humidity, differential pressure, airflow, air cleanliness)
  • Master the function and design considerations of heating coils, cooling coils, humidifiers and dehumidifiers
  • Understand the grading of air filtration: the protection logic of Pre-filter → Intermediate Filter → Final Filter → Terminal HEPA
  • Compare the three basic HVAC system types, Once-Through (100% fresh air), Recirculated and Exhaust, in terms of advantages, disadvantages and applications
  • Understand the characteristics of the two AHU configurations, Blow-Through and Draw-Through
  • Master the pressure control strategies for airlocks: Cascade, Pressure Bubble and Pressure Sink
  • Understand supply air distribution design: choosing between Dilution and Displacement, and the GMP grade requirements

Table of Contents

8.1.1 Introduction 8.1.2 AHU 8.1.7 Heating Coil 8.1.8 Cooling Coil 8.1.9 Humidifier 8.1.10 Dehumidifier 8.1.11 Air Filtration 8.2.2 Number of AHUs 8.2.3 System Types 8.2.4 AHU Configurations 8.3 Pressure Control 8.3.3 Airlocks 8.3.4 DP & Air Leakage 8.4 Ventilation Strategies
8.1 Equipment / 8.1.1 Introduction (General Overview of Equipment)

Original Text

8.1.1 Introduction

HVAC equipment helps to meet the user requirements for room environmental conditions. HVAC equipment serving GMP areas is intended to work in conjunction with associated controls and sequences of operation systems to:

  • maintain room temperature
  • maintain room pressurization and DP relationships; therefore, assisting in the prevention of contamination and cross-contamination
  • minimize airborne contamination delivered to the conditioned space by HVAC systems
  • provide make-up air for ventilation and room pressurization
  • maintain RH by adding to or removing from the moisture content of the air
  • provide required air flow volumes to maintain room cleanliness classification and recovery rate, when required

Figure 8.1 illustrates the possible arrangement of components in an HVAC system for a draw-through, recirculating air handler with nearly all possible components. (Note that the arrangement is not considered preferable; it is for illustration only.)

8.1.2 Air Handling Unit

An Air Handling Unit (AHU) is an equipment package that includes a casing box (usually metal), a fan or blower, heating and cooling coils, air filtration, etc. to provide HVAC to duct systems and then to a building. Access doors or panels are usually provided for maintenance of each component.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Six Duties of HVAC Equipment

In a GMP environment, HVAC equipment does much more than "blow cold air". It performs six key duties:

  1. Temperature control - maintaining the temperature needed for the process and for personnel comfort
  2. Pressure differential maintenance - preventing cross-contamination through DP (Differential Pressure) relationships
  3. Air cleanliness - minimizing the particulate contamination introduced by the HVAC system itself
  4. Fresh air supply - providing the outside air needed for ventilation and pressurization
  5. Humidity control - controlling relative humidity (RH)
  6. Air change rate - maintaining the cleanliness classification and recovery rate

Core Concept: What Is an AHU?

An AHU (Air Handling Unit) is an integrated equipment package that includes:

  • A metal casing box
  • A fan or blower
  • Heating and cooling coils
  • Air filtration
  • Access doors/panels for maintenance

The AHU is the "heart" of the HVAC system: it conditions the air and then delivers it through the ductwork to each room.

Analogy: An AHU Is Like a Multi-Function Water Purifier

Picture a large water purifier: water comes in and is filtered first (air filtration), then heated or cooled to the right temperature (coils), and a pump (fan) sends the treated water to each tap (room). An AHU does to air exactly what the purifier does to water: filter, adjust temperature, adjust humidity and pressurize for delivery.

Practice Questions

  1. Why does ISPE specifically stress that an HVAC system should "minimize the particulate contamination it introduces itself"? What kinds of contamination can an HVAC system generate?
  2. Why are the AHU access doors/panels important for GMP? What are the consequences if maintenance is difficult?
8.1.3-8.1.6 Fan, Mixing Box, Energy Recovery, Fume Exhaust

Original Text

8.1.3 Fan

A fan is a driven air moving device used to supply, return, or exhaust/extract air to or from a room through ductwork to move air in sufficient amounts to provide ventilation, heating, or cooling or to overcome room air pressure losses.

8.1.3.1 Supply Fan: Air handlers have a supply fan to provide the motive force to distribute air throughout an HVAC system.

8.1.3.2 Return Fan: Most large recirculating air systems use a return air fan. This fan allows return duct pressure and flow to be managed independently from the supply. This is particularly important if the duct system has volume controllers on both the supply and return (such as for controlled supply air volume and room pressure control). It also allows the return air to be diverted to exhaust when outside air conditions are closer to desired discharge conditions than return air (economizer cycle) or when return air contains flammables.

8.1.4 Mixing Box

Common in recirculating air systems, the return air is mixed with outside air for pressurization and fresh air ventilation. The resulting air stream is referred to as mixed air. In very cold environments, the mixed air may "stratify" and not mix well with return air, leading to errors in temperature readings and potential for partial freeze-up of heating coils (even a steam heating coil can freeze). An internal turbulence-inducing device (air blender) can assure thorough mixing and avoid temperature stratification.

8.1.5 Energy Recovery Coil

Once-through air systems, or other systems with high amounts of expensive exhausted air, may employ an energy recovery coil to return a portion of the energy lost in the exhausted air to the incoming air. These coils typically are upstream of other supply air conditioning coils, and may be placed upstream of the intake air filters to melt snow in cold climates. These systems also may employ a bypass damper to decrease pressure drop caused by the coil when energy recovery is not advantageous.

8.1.6 Fume Exhaust/Extraction System

This is a system made up of ductwork, fans, and possibly air cleaners (filters, dust collectors, scrubbers, carbon adsorbers, etc.) that discharges unwanted or contaminated air to the outside atmosphere to a safe distance to avoid re-entrainment of exhausted materials in other HVAC systems, and to avoid exposure to people.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Supply Fan vs. Return Fan

The Supply Fan provides the motive force for airflow and sends conditioned air to each room. The Return Fan manages the pressure and flow on the return side independently.

Why is a Return Fan needed? In a large recirculated system, relying on the Supply Fan alone means the return-side pressure and flow cannot be adjusted independently. This matters especially when the system has variable air volume (VAV) controllers, because the return fan can respond independently to changes in room pressure differentials.

Economizer Cycle: when the outdoor air temperature and humidity are close to the required supply conditions, the proportion of outside air can be increased to reduce cooling energy, in effect using "free cooling". However, this mode is normally used only in areas without pressure control (offices, warehouses).

Key Point: The Risk of Temperature Stratification in the Mixing Box

In cold climates, the cold outside air and warm return air in the mixing box may not mix evenly, resulting in Temperature Stratification:

  • Warm air above + cold air below → inaccurate temperature sensor readings
  • Localized low temperature → local freezing of the heating coil (even steam coils can freeze!)
  • Solution: install an Air Blender, which forces mixing through turbulence

This is seldom encountered in Taiwan, but if your CDMO has sites in North America or Europe, winter freeze protection design is critical.

Analogy: An Energy Recovery Coil Is Like a Heat-Exchange Range Hood

In a once-through system, you spend a great deal of energy conditioning outdoor air to 22°C / 45% RH and then exhaust all of it, like pouring freshly heated water straight down the drain. An Energy Recovery Coil works like a household total heat exchanger (HRV/ERV): the exhaust air first "pre-heats" or "pre-cools" the incoming fresh air, recovering 50-80% of the energy.

Key Point: The Re-entrainment Risk of Exhaust Systems

Re-entrainment is the most easily overlooked risk in exhaust system design: contaminated exhaust air is drawn back in through the air intakes of other HVAC systems. ISPE requires that exhaust be discharged to a "safe distance", which in practice means:

  • Sufficient distance and height difference between exhaust outlets and air intakes
  • Exhaust outlets should be above the roof line and away from fresh air intakes
  • Consider the influence of the prevailing wind direction
8.1.7 Heating Coil

Original Text

A Heating Coil is a heat transfer device consisting of a coil of piping, covered with heat-transfer fins, which increases the sensible heat transfer into an air stream, using steam, hot water, glycol, or sometimes hot refrigerant gas as the heating medium. An electric air-heating element also can be called a "heating coil."

8.1.7.1 Preheat Coil

Once-through air systems or other systems with high amounts of cold outside air may employ a preheat coil to condition the incoming or mixed air. These coils are positioned upstream of cooling coils to protect them from freezing and may be placed upstream of the filters to melt airborne snow. As these coils do not typically impose a large pressure drop, a bypass damper is not common. Care should be taken to avoid freezing preheat coils if the temperature of the air mixture entering them is below freezing. In warm weather, the coil's heating is turned off.

8.1.7.2 Reheat Coil

Systems that require over-cooling for humidity control (in place of desiccant dehumidification) also may employ a reheat coil to avoid overcooling of the space. By heating air leaving cooling coils, reheat coils decrease the RH of air leaving the AHU to avoid condensation in air filters or in the ductwork.

Tutorial Commentary

Analogy: The Logic of Reheat - Cool First, Then Heat

"Cooling first and then heating" sounds wasteful, but think of it this way: after a shower the bathroom mirror is fogged up (high humidity). A dehumidifier (cooling coil) cools the air and condenses out the moisture, but the air becomes too cold. A Reheat Coil then warms it again, giving warm, dry air.

Many pharmaceutical processes (such as inhalation and dry powder products) have strict humidity requirements, and "cool first, then heat" is the simplest way to dehumidify.

Key Point: Freeze Protection Design for the Preheat Coil

ISPE specifically warns that if the air entering the preheat coil can be below freezing, freeze protection measures must be taken. Even steam coils (usually considered freeze-proof) can freeze locally because of a control valve failure or a drop in steam pressure. Common freeze protection methods include:

  • Using circulating glycol rather than plain water
  • Installing a Freezestat (freeze protection thermostat)
  • Ensuring the steam coil has sufficient condensate drainage capacity

Core Concept: The Three Roles of Heating Coils

Heating coils look simple, but they play three different roles in an HVAC system:

The heating medium can be steam, hot water, glycol, hot refrigerant gas, or electric heating elements.

8.1.8 Cooling Coil

Original Text

A cooling coil is a heat transfer device consisting of a coil of piping, covered with heat-transfer fins, which reduces the sensible heat and possibly latent heat (via condensation of water vapor) in the air stream using chilled liquid or refrigeration gas as the cooling medium. Cooling to maintain environmental conditions is common in pharmaceutical applications. Cooling coils may be located upstream or downstream of the fan (draw-through versus blow-through). A cooling coil is a common method of lowering air humidity; therefore, air velocity and drainage from these coils are key design issues. Mist eliminators may be employed to eliminate carryover of liquid water droplets that condense on the coil. These coils impose a large pressure drop, but a bypass damper (used when cooling is not needed) can add a risk of unconditioned air leakage around the coil when maximum cooling is needed.

8.1.8.1 Re-cool Coil (Post-cooling Coil)

These coils may be installed downstream of desiccant dehumidifiers to eliminate excess sensible heat in the supply air. They may provide additional dehumidification downstream of a condensing cooling coil, operating below chilled water temperature using a refrigerant or a low temperature brine (typically water and glycol (ethylene or propylene)). Mist eliminators may be employed on these coils. Coils operating at sub-freezing internal temperatures can eventually ice over, and an alternation bypass/de-icing scheme is normally needed.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Dual Duty of the Cooling Coil

A Cooling Coil handles two kinds of heat load at the same time:

  • Sensible Heat: lowering the air temperature
  • Latent Heat: condensing water vapor into liquid water, which lowers the humidity

This is why the cooling coil is the most common means of dehumidification in an AHU. Key design issues:

  • Air Velocity: if too high, it blows condensed water droplets downstream
  • Drainage: condensate must drain freely, otherwise microorganisms will grow
  • Mist Eliminator: intercepts water droplets carried by the airflow

Key Point: The Double-Edged Sword of the Bypass Damper

A cooling coil has a high pressure drop, so bypassing it with a Bypass Damper when no cooling is needed saves fan energy. ISPE warns, however, that when maximum cooling is required the bypass damper may allow uncontrolled air leakage: some air goes around the coil and directly into the supply system, causing temperature and humidity control to fail.

In a GMP environment, the preferred approach is either not to use a Bypass Damper or to ensure its sealing performance has been qualified.

Key Point: The Icing Risk of the Re-cool Coil

A Re-cool Coil operates below chilled water temperature (using refrigerant or low-temperature brine), so the temperature inside the coil may fall below freezing and ice can form on the coil surface. The solution is an Alternation Bypass/De-icing Scheme: two coil banks work in turn, so while one is de-icing the other continues cooling.

Practice Questions

  1. A dry powder inhaler (DPI) production room requires RH < 25%. Is the dehumidification capacity of a cooling coil sufficient? When does a Desiccant Dehumidifier need to be added?
  2. If the cooling coil condensate drain becomes blocked, what is the impact on GMP compliance?
8.1.9 Humidifier

Original Text

Humidifiers increase the humidity within a controlled space by the discharge of water vapor (steam or water mist) into a supply air stream or directly into a room. Systems in cold or arid climates may employ a humidifier to inject water vapor to increase the moisture level of the air supply. These devices typically are downstream of the preheating coil, and may be mounted in ductwork where air turbulence and high velocity promote absorption of water vapor. When employed in an AHU, mounting upstream of a cooling coil provides a natural baffle to prevent carryover of liquid water droplets, as it is unlikely that both humidifier and dehumidification through cooling will be in use at the same time.

Generally, the water source is steam, potable water, or demineralized water (produced via reverse osmosis (RO), ion exchange resins, or distillation) that will not introduce objectionable contaminants into a room. It is common practice to use steam that is free of volatile additives in pharmaceutical manufacturing HVAC systems. Volatile additives that meet USP requirements can be considered, allowing direct use of plant steam in pharmaceutical manufacturing HVAC systems. Plant steam (which may contain amines or other volatile additives, necessary to prevent corrosion in steam piping) frequently is used for non-production spaces.

Facilities may use clean steam, generated from USP purified water or Water For Injection (WFI) (also called pure steam) for humidification. This practice is considered wasteful, as steam of adequate cleanliness for classified spaces may be obtained from copper, brass, or stainless steel re-boilers fed with water of adequate quality and heated by higher pressure plant steam. However, it may make sense to use clean steam if it is the most readily available form of steam. Maintenance should be considered, as purified steam or steam free from additives can corrode piping. Softened or demineralized water are commonly used for this service, as minerals in potable water can be left behind in the steam generator.

Water mist humidifiers are usually fed with deionized or purified water to prevent the carryover of dissolved mineral solids into an air stream. When a humidifier is not in use, additional care is required to prevent growth of bacteria in an unprotected water system.

It is common practice to install a length of welded, liquid tight stainless steel (or other corrosion resistant) ducting downstream of in-duct humidifiers to prevent damage and rust from condensation. Generally, duct humidity should be kept significantly below saturation level; 80% RH is a common upper limit.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Humidifier Water Source - A Key GMP Decision

A humidifier injects water vapor or water mist into the air, so water source quality directly affects product safety. The water source options listed by ISPE (from most to least stringent):

  1. Clean Steam: generated from USP purified water or WFI. ISPE considers its use for HVAC humidification wasteful
  2. Re-boiler steam: generated in a copper/brass/stainless steel re-boiler, using water of appropriate quality as feed and heated by plant steam. This is the compromise ISPE recommends
  3. Plant steam without volatile additives: can be used directly in pharmaceutical production areas
  4. Plant Steam with additives: contains amine-based inhibitors and may be used only in non-production areas

Analogy: Steam Quality Is Like Drinking Water Standards

Imagine spraying a water mist to cool a restaurant: tap water is fine, and there is no need for bottled mineral water. But in an operating theatre you would need at least RO water. Using WFI steam for HVAC humidification is like washing the floor with Evian: the quality is more than good enough, but it is a waste. ISPE recommends steam from a re-boiler, which is like using RO water of sufficient quality in the operating theatre: safe and economical.

Key Point: Microbial Risk When the Humidifier Is Not in Use

ISPE specifically points out that when a humidifier is not in use, residual water in the system readily supports bacterial growth unless it is properly protected. This is especially dangerous for seasonally used humidifiers: after use in winter, the idle piping through spring and summer becomes a microbial culture dish.

Best practice: drain the system when not in use, disinfect it regularly, or use a SIP (Steam In Place) design.

Key Point: The In-Duct Humidification Limit - 80% RH

The relative humidity in a duct must not approach the saturation point, otherwise condensation forms on duct walls and filters, leading to:

  • Corrosion of metal ductwork (so stainless steel ductwork should be used downstream of the humidifier)
  • Reduced filter efficiency once the filter absorbs water, and possible microbial growth
  • A common design upper limit: 80% RH

Practical Application

A CDMO finds the supply air humidity insufficient in winter (RH < 20%) and is considering installing a humidifier. Key decision points:

  • Water source: does the site have amine-free steam? Is a Re-boiler needed?
  • Installation location: inside the AHU upstream of the cooling coil, or in the duct?
  • Downstream duct material: use welded, sealed stainless steel ductwork for at least 3-5 meters after the humidifier
  • Idle management: an SOP for disinfection and draining when not in use in summer
8.1.10 Dehumidifier

Original Text

A dehumidifier is a device that removes water vapor from the air to reduce humidity, either by condensation of water vapor from the air using a cooling coil or by absorption or adsorption using a desiccant (when room RH below 30 to 40% is required). Desiccant dehumidifiers often are located downstream of a cooling coil that removes much of the moisture challenge at lower energy cost and increases RH to increase desiccant efficiency. However, care should be taken to assure saturation or carryover of liquid water droplets does not damage the desiccant.

The choice of desiccant depends on the application. Desiccants are regenerated using heat; therefore, air leaving the dehumidifier is both drier and hotter than upon entering. A re-cooling coil may be needed. It may be necessary to keep the wheel regenerated even when dehumidification is not needed to prevent damage to some desiccants. Appropriate expertise is required to design and commission the control of desiccant dehumidifiers. Manufacturers should be consulted before attempting a dehumidification control scheme.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Crossover Point Between Two Dehumidification Methods

An HVAC system has two ways to dehumidify, and the choice depends on the target RH:

  • Cooling coil dehumidification: economical, but can only bring RH down to about 30-40%. Principle: the air is cooled below its dew point and the moisture condenses on the coil
  • Desiccant dehumidification: can bring RH below 10%. Principle: an adsorbent (such as silica gel or molecular sieve) absorbs moisture from the air and is then regenerated with hot air

Best practice is to use both in series: the cooling coil first removes most of the moisture (low cost), then the desiccant provides precision dehumidification.

Key Point: Three Things to Watch with a Desiccant Dehumidifier

  1. Higher outlet air temperature: adsorption of moisture by the desiccant releases heat, so the outlet air is hotter and drier than the inlet air → a Re-cool Coil is usually needed
  2. Desiccant protection: liquid water droplets will damage the desiccant, so the upstream cooling coil needs a Mist Eliminator
  3. Regeneration while idle: some desiccants must be kept in regeneration even when not in use, otherwise they will be damaged

ISPE stresses that designing and commissioning the control system of a desiccant dehumidifier requires specialist expertise, and the equipment manufacturer should be consulted.

Practice Questions

  1. A room producing dry powder inhalers (DPI) requires RH < 15%. Is a cooling coil alone enough for dehumidification? Why or why not?
  2. Why does ISPE recommend placing the desiccant dehumidifier downstream of the cooling coil rather than upstream?
8.1.11 Air Filtration

Original Text

Air filters remove particulate material from an airstream by means of various media types. Pre-filters typically are provided upstream of coils in an air handler to protect the coils from fouling with dirt or debris. Pre-filters use low efficiency dust stop filters followed by a medium or high efficiency intermediate filter. For further information, see Chapter 2 of this Guide.

Air filters of activated carbon or other materials may be used to absorb some vapors. This is common where objectionable aromas or small quantities of volatile organics need to be decreased.

8.1.11.1 Final Filter

Filters may be provided as the last air treatment step in an air handler. The use of high efficiency filters (typically 95% DOP or HEPA) can assure air quality (with reference to particles) inside supply air ductwork and can protect terminal (ceiling mounted) filters from fouling with dirt or debris; therefore, extending the life of the terminal filters and preventing differential blinding. See the ISPE Baseline Guide on Sterile Manufacturing Facilities.

In systems without terminal filtration, final filters in AHUs can provide adequate filtration, perhaps for some classified spaces, as long as ductwork is clean. High efficiency final filters are more commonly used in systems that employ fan drive belts that shed particulate into the airstream.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Three Lines of Defense in Air Filtration

The HVAC air filtration system uses a layered protection strategy:

  1. Pre-filter: low-efficiency coarse dust filter, located upstream of the coils to protect them from dust clogging
  2. Intermediate Filter: medium-to-high efficiency, further reducing particulates
  3. Final Filter: 95% DOP or HEPA (High Efficiency Particulate Air), ensuring the quality of the air in the supply ductwork
  4. Terminal HEPA: the last filtration stage, installed in the ceiling, ensuring the air entering the room meets the cleanliness classification

Each layer protects the next: extending its life, lowering replacement cost and preventing Differential Blinding.

Analogy: A Filtration System Is Like Multi-Stage Water Purification

Think of a household water purifier: the PP cotton cartridge (Pre-filter) stops large particles → activated carbon (Intermediate) removes odors → the RO membrane (Final Filter) removes trace impurities. Each layer protects the finer one after it. If you skip the PP cotton and go straight to the RO membrane, the membrane clogs quickly and costs soar.

Key Point: Special Uses of Activated Carbon Filters

ISPE mentions that activated carbon filters are used to absorb odors and volatile organic compounds (VOCs). In a CDMO environment, this might be used to:

  • Treat exhaust from solvent-based processes (such as the isopropanol and ethanol used in fluid bed granulation)
  • Prevent odor cross-influence between different products
  • Protect operators from exposure to low concentrations of hazardous vapors
8.1.12-8.1.15 Ductwork, Damper, Diffuser, UV Light

Original Text

8.1.12 Ductwork

This is a network of air conduits distributed throughout a building, connected to a fan or AHU to supply, return, or exhaust/extract air to or from zones and rooms in a building. These ducts may be constructed of metal, plastic, building construction materials, fiberglass boards, or a combination of these materials. Metal ductwork is recommended for most pharmaceutical applications.

8.1.13 Damper and Louver

8.1.13.1 Damper: A damper is a valve for controlling airflow in ductwork, which consists of a movable element plate, plunger, or bladder that opens and closes to regulate airflow. Dampers may be used to regulate airflow to and from specific rooms (to "balance" airflow) and to control fresh air or return air to the AHU.

8.1.13.2 Louver: A louver is an assembly of sloping vanes, usually fixed in position, intended to permit air to pass through, while inhibiting passage of water droplets from outdoors into air systems. A louver also may be found in return air ductwork at room interfaces.

8.1.14 Diffuser, Register, and Grille

Air distribution inlet or outlet grilles are composed of a combination of blades, plates, or vanes intended to direct airflow entering or leaving a space in a desired pattern. Grilles generally are characterized by their pattern of distribution from 1 to 4 directions and projection distance at a given airflow (the throw).

Registers are grilles with an added airflow control damper close coupled to the concealed side.

Diffusers are air outlets, assembled from a series of vanes and plates, generally designed to mix supply air with room air to minimize drafts and maximize dilution. An exception is the non-aspirating diffuser, which is designed to provide equal velocity of discharge in all directions with minimal mixing. Diffusers are usually found at ceilings and located to distribute the air as uniformly as possible throughout a space.

8.1.15 Ultraviolet Light

Ultraviolet (UV) lights (a form of ionizing radiation) at 254 nm may be employed in an airstream to disrupt microorganisms. The energy flux required to achieve destruction at typical duct or AHU velocities is prohibitively high, because of the relationship between the energy level and exposure time needed for this purpose. UV lights may be mounted in conjunction with filters to increase exposure time; however, this is considered of little value in pharmaceutical HVAC systems.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Point: UV Lamps Have "Almost No Value" in Pharmaceutical HVAC

ISPE's position is clear: UV lamps are of limited value in pharmaceutical HVAC. The reasons are:

  • Air velocity in the duct is too high (typically 5-15 m/s), so microorganisms spend too little time in the UV irradiation zone
  • Achieving an effective germicidal dose requires a very high UV energy density, which is uneconomical
  • Even with filters added to increase exposure time, the effect is limited

Microbial control in a pharmaceutical plant should rely on HEPA filtration and differential pressure control, not UV lamps.

Key Point: Why Is Metal Ductwork Recommended for Pharmaceutical Plants?

ISPE recommends Metal Ductwork for the following reasons:

  • It does not shed fibers: fiberglass duct board releases fiber particles
  • Smooth interior walls: easy to clean, reducing adhesion of particles and microorganisms
  • Durable: does not degrade with cleaning agents or disinfectants
  • Does not absorb moisture: plastic or fiberglass materials may absorb water

Core Concept: The Difference Between Grille, Register and Diffuser

In Chinese these three English terms are often used interchangeably, but they are defined differently:

In a cleanroom, the Non-Aspirating Diffuser is particularly important: it provides uniform downward airflow with minimal mixing, and suits places needing unidirectional flow or low mixing (such as HEPA filter panels).

Table 8.1: System Components and Their Influence on Environmental Parameters

Original Text

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: How to Read This Matrix

This table is the "cheat sheet" for understanding HVAC system design: which environmental parameters each component influences is clear at a glance.

Key observations:

  • The Air Handler (AHU) is the only equipment that affects all five parameters, which is why it is the core of the system
  • The Cooling Coil affects both temperature and humidity, making it the most "multi-functional" component in the AHU
  • The Air Filter affects only Air Cleanliness, but that is the most critical parameter for GMP
  • Ductwork and dampers affect pressure and airflow: they are the "delivery system" and do not condition the air

Practice Questions

  1. If the temperature in a cleanroom is high but the humidity is normal, which component is the most likely cause of the problem? What if the temperature is normal but the humidity is high?
  2. Using this table, design a "minimal" HVAC system (controlling only differential pressure and air cleanliness). Which components are needed?
8.2 HVAC System Configuration / 8.2.2 Number of Air Handling Units (Deciding the Number of AHUs)

Original Text

8.2.1 Introduction

This section gives a brief overview of the key factors to consider, the options available in HVAC system design, and the factors influencing decisions to choose a particular system type. This section should be read in conjunction with Chapter 3 of this Guide.

8.2.2 Number of Air Handling Units

A manufacturing area often is divided into zones with a separate AHU for each zone. In the pharmaceutical industry, a zone is usually considered to be an area with one type of manufacturing process or area cleanliness classification, e.g., a tablet compression suite in an oral solid dosage facility or all classified areas for aseptic product.

When dividing a facility into zones, advantages include:

  • Use of multiple AHUs improves reliability of the total area; it would be unusual for all zone units to fail. If one unit fails, other zones may continue to operate.
  • The use of multiple smaller AHUs may make air balancing (commissioning) easier and reduce the need for automated balance or pressure controls.
  • Total energy costs may be lower, as each zone uses only what it needs and may be turned down to use much less energy if idle, without the use of automated balancing controls.
  • The use of multiple smaller AHUs allows the main distribution ducts to be smaller, and therefore, easier to route in smaller ceiling voids.
  • Modifications to parts of a facility should be easier. Upgrades to a small AHU serving a single zone should be easier than changing a large single AHU, which serves many zones, without automated balancing controls.
  • The use of multiple AHUs allows easier separation of areas within a multi-product concurrent manufacturing plant. The potential for cross contamination of products via the HVAC system is minimized, hazardous materials can be isolated, and upstream processes for a single product can be isolated from those downstream. Air filtration also can address this issue.

Disadvantages include:

  • If once-through air is desired for all zones, there is less justification for more zoning of AHUs to reduce risk of cross-contamination between products. A single large system may be sufficient.
  • If an automated air balancing control system is employed, most of the advantages are offset by the ability of the control system to manage system changes.
  • Increased initial cost (more of the same controls for more systems).
  • Increased maintenance (more labor, more parts, more protocols).

The decisions regarding AHU system zoning are important factors in subsequent facility commissioning, qualification, and related documentation. The decisions for zoning should be based on risk to product and to operators, taking into account the preferred air filtration and monitoring technology.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Point: Special Considerations for a CDMO

For a multi-product CDMO, how the AHUs are zoned directly affects operational flexibility:

  • Cross-contamination control: products of different clients should not share an AHU; even with HEPA filtration, regulators and client audits will question it
  • Concurrent Manufacturing: ISPE states explicitly that multiple AHUs make it easier to achieve concurrent manufacturing of multiple products
  • Product-specific differences: some products need low humidity, others need contained exhaust; separate AHUs can be set independently
  • Decision principle: base the decision on "product risk and operator risk", which is consistent with the spirit of ICH Q9 risk management

Practical Application

A CDMO is planning a new facility with three production lines: oral solid dosage, aseptic filling and highly potent API formulation. The best AHU zoning strategy:

  • Aseptic filling area: dedicated AHU + once-through air or high-efficiency filtered recirculation
  • Highly potent API formulation area: dedicated AHU + full exhaust (Once-Through) + exhaust treatment
  • Oral solid dosage area: can be divided into sub-areas such as compression, coating and packaging, each with its own AHU

Each additional AHU increases initial and maintenance cost, but in the CDMO business model the reduced cross-contamination risk and increased operational flexibility are worth more.

Core Concept: AHU Zoning - Several Small Units vs. One Large Unit

This is the first major decision in HVAC design. ISPE's analysis framework:

8.2.3 Basic System Types

Original Text

8.2.3.1 Once-Through HVAC Systems

Once-through HVAC systems supply treated outside air to satisfy the design conditions for a space. This air is then extracted from the space and exhausted to the atmosphere.

Advantages:

  • Provides an abundance of oxygen rich fresh air to dilute contaminants and assure the health of personnel.
  • Can handle hazardous materials without recirculation into supply air; however, the extracted air may need treatment before it is discharged to the atmosphere.
  • Lower risk of cross contamination of products from another room, via HVAC system ducting.
  • Exhaust fans may be located remote from the AHU making exhaust duct routing simpler.
  • As there are fewer concerns about noise in the extract ductwork, it can usually be sized for a high velocity and smaller diameter, making it easier to route.

Disadvantages:

  • More expensive to operate than an equivalent recirculating system, particularly when cooling and heating. Energy recovery often is justifiable.
  • Air filter loading will be very high leading to frequent replacement.
  • Potential need for air treatment for exhausted air contaminated by the process.
  • Room conditions may be more difficult to control as the system needs to be sized to handle extreme outdoor air conditions, but may operate most of the time under much less load.

8.2.3.2 Recirculating Systems

This system type is widespread; the room supply air is made up of a portion of treated outside air mixed with some of the air returned from the space. An equivalent portion of the air supplied to the room is either discarded or lost through leakage to adjacent areas, due to local area pressurization. The amount of outside air is driven by:

  • IAQ requirements (see ASHRAE 62), about 20 CFM (35 cuM/hr) per occupant
  • the need to offset exhaust from the area
  • the need to provide excess air to pressurize the area

Advantages:

  • A smaller range of challenge to HVAC systems may result in better control of parameters, as heating/cooling equipment may be smaller.
  • Usually, less AHU air filter loading is required; therefore, less filter maintenance is required.
  • Usually, lower heating/cooling energy cost than once-through air systems.
  • A single once-through AHU may pre-treat outdoor air for numerous individual recirculated systems, concentrating pre-heating and humidity control in one unit, with potential energy savings.

Disadvantages:

  • Return air ductwork routing back to the AHU may complicate congestion above ceiling and make duct chases larger.
  • Potential for cross contamination, via the HVAC system. Requires adequate supply air filtration.
  • Potential for recirculation of odors and vapors. Poor design may result in inadequate fresh air supply for the health of personnel and room pressurization.

8.2.3.3 Exhaust (Extract) System

Exhaust systems may be stand-alone systems that remove airborne contaminants from a work space. They may be interlinked to a once-through or recirculated air supply system. Used alone, the extract/exhaust system will create a negative DP in a room or space, drawing in air from the surroundings.

Advantages:

  • Simple to operate. Makeup air for the fan is pulled from surrounding spaces.
  • It can be used to draw fresh air into an unventilated building, such as a warehouse, that does not require heating or cooling.

Disadvantages:

  • If used to capture large quantities of contaminants, such as from open processes, high energy costs will be associated with conditioned air being discarded. Exhaust system energy is greatly reduced if emissions from processes are contained within process enclosures.
  • If exhaust air is not adequately cleaned, stack height and velocity should be adequate to prevent re-entrainment in HVAC systems and to prevent personnel hazards.
  • Temperature and humidity are influenced by the surrounding area.

Tutorial Commentary

Analogy: Three System Types Are Like Three Ways of Ventilating

  • Once-Through (100% fresh air) = all the windows open + an exhaust fan: fresh air keeps coming in, but all the heating and cooling is blown away, and the electricity bill is huge
  • Recirculated = an ordinary household air conditioner: most of the air circulates indoors and only a little outside air is added, the most energy-efficient option
  • Exhaust = a kitchen range hood: it only extracts the dirty air and draws in surrounding air through gaps around doors and windows

Actual pharmaceutical plants usually use a combination: recirculated systems for clean areas (saving energy), once-through for high-hazard areas (safety), and local exhaust systems (capturing contaminants).

Key Point: The Hidden Cost of Once-Through Systems

Once-through systems are particularly expensive in tropical climates (such as Taiwan and Southeast Asia):

  • Summer outdoor air at 35°C / 80% RH → requires large cooling and dehumidification capacity
  • Dry winter outdoor air → may require humidification
  • Outdoor air carries a large particle load all year round → pre-filters must be replaced far more often

ISPE recommends: if once-through air is used, Energy Recovery is usually justified, since it can recover 50-80% of the energy in the exhaust air.

8.2.3.4-8.2.4 AHU Parallel/Series & Blow-Through vs. Draw-Through

Original Text

8.2.3.4 Use of Air Handling Units in Parallel or Series

AHUs may be placed in series, e.g., if a higher air pressure is required to offset the pressure drop through HEPA filters in ductwork to just one area served by the primary HVAC system. A common series configuration uses an AHU to precondition outdoor air as makeup air to one or more 'local' AHUs downstream. This minimizes or eliminates condensation at local AHUs, simplifies installation, and saves energy at the local AHU(s).

The use of parallel AHUs is common practice where large areas are being conditioned. This approach increases reliability allowing acceptable conditions in the area to be maintained if one unit fails or when the load on the system is light. Parallel fan installations may be configured for 100% or reduced redundancy. In a 100% redundant installation, multiple fans are sized to be capable of meeting the entire load with one fan out of service.

Example: A system with 2 fans each capable of delivering 50% of flow at design pressure may deliver as much as 70% of design capacity with one fan out of service because of a reduction in static pressure.

8.2.3.5 Series Configuration for Outside Air Pretreatment

In recirculating air systems, a separate, series air handler may be used to pre-treat incoming outside air rather than overcooling or chemical dehumidification of an entire recirculated air stream. This is a common configuration, particularly where the outside air conditions represent all or most of the latent load addressed by a system (e.g., in the tropics). In its most economical application, a central pre-conditioning unit may serve multiple recirculation systems.

8.2.4 Air Handling Unit Configurations

There are two basic types of AHU configuration: (1) blow-through and (2) draw-through. The term describes the relationship of the fan to the coils inside an AHU.

8.2.4.1 Blow-Through Units: In blow-through units, air is drawn into the AHU through pre-filters, then blown through the coils. Advantages: (1) AHU discharge temperature can be at the cooling coil discharge air temperature, because fan heat is removed in the cooling coil — useful when heat loads are particularly high. (2) If the drain trap runs dry, treated air will blow out through the trap, not allowing contaminants to enter the AHU. Disadvantages: (1) Unit typically needs to be longer to allow a diffuser after the fan. (2) Air leaving the cooling coil may be saturated with moisture that could collect on final filters.

8.2.4.2 Draw-Through Units: Pre-filters and coils are before the fan.
