Analogy

Imagine you are assessing the risk posed by an old tree near your home:

  • Hazard = the old tree might fall (the source of harm)
  • Harm = damage to the house or injury to people (the actual harm)
  • Severity = how serious is the harm? Hitting the garden versus hitting the bedroom gives completely different consequences
  • Risk = the "probability" of falling × the "severity" of the damage it causes

If the tree is healthy and far from the house, the overall risk may be acceptable even though the severity is high, because the probability is extremely low.

Key Notes

The nine elements listed in the source text make up the complete risk management process. In CDMO practice they usually correspond to the following:

  • Risk Assessment = includes three sub-steps: identification, analysis and evaluation
  • Risk Control = includes two decision paths: reduction and acceptance
  • Risk Communication = information sharing across departments
  • Risk Review = ongoing monitoring and updating
10.2 Overview of the Quality Risk Management Process

Original Text

Quality risk management is a systematic process for the assessment, control, communication, and review of risks to the quality of the drug (medicinal) product across the product lifecycle.

A model for quality risk management is outlined in Figure 10.1, which is taken from ICH Q9.

The emphasis on each component of the framework might differ from case to case, but a robust process will incorporate consideration of all the elements at a level of detail that is commensurate with the specific risk.

Figure 10.1: Overview of a Typical Quality Risk Management Process – from ICH Q9

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Risk Management Across the Product Lifecycle

Quality risk management covers the entire product lifecycle, from development and technology transfer through commercial manufacturing to product discontinuation. This means:

  • Design stage: identify the risks that the HVAC system design may introduce (such as airflow direction and pressure differential settings)
  • Validation stage: assess whether installation and operational qualification adequately verify the risk control measures
  • Routine production: continuously monitor environmental parameters to confirm that the risk controls remain effective
  • Change management: any system change requires the risk to be reassessed

Analogy

The ICH Q9 risk management process is like a "risk management GPS". It has three core functions:

  1. Positioning (Assessment): where are you? How big is the risk?
  2. Navigation (Control): where should you go? How do you reduce the risk?
  3. Real-time update (Review): have road conditions changed? Does the route need re-planning?

"Commensurate with the specific risk" is like a GPS adjusting its guidance to road conditions: on a motorway it does not need to remind you of a turn every 50 metres, but on complicated city streets more frequent guidance may be needed.

Key Notes

Figure 10.1 is the classic ICH Q9 flow chart (cited here in text form). In practice, this flow chart is usually turned into an internal company SOP and integrated into the quality management system. A CDMO should make sure the risk management process for every client product follows this framework, although the depth of the assessment can be adjusted to the product risk level.

10.3 Initiating Quality Risk Management

Original Text

Quality risk management should include systematic processes designed to coordinate, facilitate, and improve science-based decision making with respect to risk.

The following steps should be considered when initiating and planning a quality risk management process:

  • Define the problem and/or risk question, including pertinent assumptions.
  • Identify the potential for risk.
  • Assemble background information and/or data on the potential hazard, harm, or human health impact relevant to the risk assessment.
  • Identify a leader and necessary resources.
  • Specify a timeline, deliverables, and appropriate level of decision making for the risk management process.

Determining the risks associated with maintenance requires a common and shared understanding of factors such as:

  • impact of operational tolerances on patient safety and product quality
  • impact of design of facilities and equipment on maintenance activities
  • impact of methods and materials used during maintenance activities
  • maintenance programs and maintenance plans
  • training

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Five Steps to Initiate Risk Management

Risk management is not something done "whenever it comes to mind". The source text provides structured steps for initiating it:

  1. Define the problem: clearly define which risk is to be assessed (for example, "the impact of an AHU failure on the cleanroom environment")
  2. Identify the potential for risk: what could go wrong?
  3. Gather background information: historical data, theoretical analysis, expert opinion
  4. Assign a leader and resources: who will lead? Which departments need to take part?
  5. Set a timeline and deliverables: when will it be completed? What documents will be produced?

Application

Examples of maintenance-related risk assessment:

The source text specifically highlights risk factors related to maintenance activities. In CDMO HVAC maintenance, these factors show up as follows:

  • Operational tolerances: is a pressure differential deviation of ±5 Pa from the set point still acceptable? How large a temperature deviation will affect product quality?
  • Impact of facility design on maintenance: is the AHU installed where it can be serviced easily? Does the HEPA installation method allow replacement without interrupting production?
  • Impact of maintenance materials: are the lubricants food grade? Have spare parts been confirmed for material compatibility?
  • Personnel training: have maintenance technicians received GMP training? Do they understand cleanroom behavior rules?

Practice Questions

  1. If you were to initiate a risk assessment for an AHU serving a Grade B area in a CDMO, how would you define the "problem/risk question"? Which key assumptions would you list?
  2. Which departments should be represented on your risk assessment team, and why?
  3. What specific risk scenarios arise from the "impact of maintenance materials and methods" in an aseptic filling environment?
10.4 Risk Assessment

Original Text

Risk assessment consists of the identification of hazards and the analysis and evaluation of risks associated with exposure to those hazards, and consists of identification, analysis, and evaluation activities.

Risk assessment addresses the following questions:

  • What might go wrong?
  • What is the likelihood (probability) it will go wrong?
  • What are the consequences (severity)?

Risk identification is a systematic use of information to identify hazards referring to the risk question or problem description. Information can include historical data, theoretical analysis, informed opinions, and the concerns of stakeholders. Risk identification addresses "What might go wrong?" including identifying the possible consequences. This provides the basis for further steps in the quality risk management process.

Examples of CGMP risks include:

  • contamination of product caused by maintenance practices, e.g., use of inappropriate spare parts that contaminate product
  • facilities or equipment design that does not facilitate appropriate levels of maintenance
  • lack of CGMP training for maintenance technicians
  • maintenance activities causes (critical) equipment to be (unknown to production) out of service

Systems or equipment that may impact product quality or patient safety (CGMP systems or equipment) should be identified as part of the commissioning process.

Risk analysis is the estimation of the risk associated with the identified hazards. It is the qualitative or quantitative process of linking the likelihood of occurrence and severity of harms. The ability to detect the harm also should be considered in the estimation of risk.

Risk evaluation compares the identified and analyzed risk against given risk criteria. Risk evaluations consider the strength of evidence for all three of the fundamental questions.

Typically, the outcome of the risk assessment will be expressed using qualitative descriptors, such as "high," "medium," or "low." These terms and how they are used should be defined in as much detail as possible.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Three Questions of Risk Assessment

The essence of risk assessment can be distilled into three simple but profound questions:

  1. What might go wrong? → Risk Identification
  2. What is the likelihood? → Risk Analysis
  3. What are the consequences? → Risk Evaluation

These three questions correspond to the three sub-steps of risk assessment: identification → analysis → evaluation.

Terminology: Risk Identification vs Analysis vs Evaluation

  • Risk Identification: find all possible hazards, the "inventory" stage. Use methods such as historical data, theoretical analysis and expert opinion
  • Risk Analysis: assess the probability of occurrence and the severity of each hazard, the "quantification" stage. Note that the source text specifically mentions that detectability should also be considered, which is the D value in FMEA
  • Risk Evaluation: compare the analysis results against risk criteria, the "decision" stage. The result is usually expressed as "high/medium/low"

Key Notes

The four CGMP risk examples listed in the source text are all directly related to maintenance activities, which reflects this guide's (the HVAC Good Practice Guide) emphasis on the risks of equipment maintenance:

  • Contamination from improper spare parts: for example, using bearings with an incompatible lubricant, causing particulate or chemical contamination
  • Design that hinders maintenance: AHU panels that cannot be opened, or a HEPA filter located too high to reach
  • Inadequate training: maintenance personnel entering the cleanroom without understanding gowning procedures
  • Unknown equipment shutdown: the maintenance department shuts equipment down without notifying production, so production continues without environmental control

The last point is especially dangerous in a CDMO: if maintenance turns off pressure differential control without production knowing, an entire batch of product may have to be scrapped.

Practice Questions

  1. The source text says risk analysis should consider "detectability". In an HVAC system, which risks are "high severity but low detectability"? How should this type of risk be managed?
  2. Risk evaluation results are expressed as "high/medium/low". How does your company define these three levels? What follow-up actions does each level trigger?

Application

Specific examples of HVAC risk assessment:

10.5 Risk Control

Original Text

Risk control includes decision making either to reduce risks or accept them, or both. The purpose of risk control is to reduce the risk to an acceptable level. The amount of effort applied to risk control should be proportional to the significance of the risk.

Risk control addresses the following questions:

  • Is the risk above an acceptable level?
  • What can be done to reduce or eliminate risks?
  • What is the appropriate balance among benefits, risks, and resources?
  • Are new risks introduced as a result of the identified risks being controlled?

Risk reduction focuses on processes for mitigation or avoidance of quality risk when it exceeds a specified (acceptable) level. Risk reduction might include actions taken to mitigate the severity and probability of harm. Processes that improve the detectability of hazards and quality risks also might be used as part of a risk control strategy. The use of PdM technologies can increase the detectability of an equipment failure and might be implemented where the associated risk warrants such an approach.

The implementation of risk reduction measures can introduce new risks into the system or increase the significance of other existing risks. For example, frequent maintenance on equipment increases the probability of error in disassembly or reassembly. Hence, the results of risk assessment should be revisited to identify and evaluate any possible change in risk after implementing a risk reduction process.

Risk acceptance is a decision to accept risk. Risk acceptance can be a formal decision to accept the residual risk or it can be a passive decision in which residual risks are not specified.

For some types of harms, even the best quality risk management practices might not entirely eliminate risk. In these circumstances, it might be agreed that an appropriate quality risk management strategy has been applied and that quality risk is reduced to a specified (acceptable) level. This (specified) acceptable level will depend on many parameters and should be decided on a case-by-case basis.

Procedural and technical controls available to reduce risks to an acceptable level include:

  • Establishing a Maintenance Program, including:
    • system inventory and risk assessments
    • maintenance plans
    • change management
    • clearly defined roles and responsibilities
    • documentation requirements
    • spare parts
    • training

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Decision Logic of Risk Control

Risk control is essentially a decision-making process that needs to answer four key questions:

  1. Does the risk exceed the acceptable level? If not, no additional action is needed
  2. What can be done to reduce the risk? Identify feasible control measures
  3. Is there a balance between benefits, risks and resources? Putting too many resources into low-risk items is wasteful
  4. Does the control measure introduce new risks? This point is especially easy to overlook

Key Notes

"Control measures introducing new risks" is the most important insight in this section.

The source text gives a very practical example: frequent maintenance of equipment reduces the risk of failure, but every disassembly and reassembly increases the probability of human error. In an HVAC system this shows up as follows:

  • Frequent HEPA filter replacement → each replacement carries a risk of improper installation and leakage
  • Frequent sensor calibration → each removal and refitting may affect sensor accuracy
  • Frequent duct cleaning → the cleaning process itself may generate particulate contamination

Therefore, once risk reduction measures have been implemented, the overall risk status must be reassessed.

Terminology: Risk Reduction vs Risk Acceptance

  • Risk Reduction: actively take measures to reduce the probability or severity of the risk. The source text specifically mentions that PdM (Predictive Maintenance) can improve detectability, for example using vibration monitoring to detect fan bearing wear early and replace the bearing before it fails
  • Risk Acceptance: formally accepting the residual risk after reasonable control measures have been taken. This can be an explicit decision (documented residual risk acceptance) or an implicit one (residual risk not specifically designated)

Analogy

Risk control is like managing fire safety in a large building:

  • Risk Reduction: install sprinklers, smoke detectors and fire doors to reduce the probability and severity of a fire
  • Introduction of new risk: if the sprinkler system is triggered by mistake, it causes water damage instead, so the control measure itself brings a new risk
  • Risk Acceptance: even with all the protection in place, a small fire risk remains, and this is the "acceptable residual risk"
  • Commensurate effort: high floors need stricter fire protection measures, and a storeroom does not need the same level as an operating theatre

Application

The Maintenance Program is the core tool of risk control. The seven elements listed in the source text make up a complete framework for managing maintenance risk:

  • System inventory and risk assessment: list all CGMP-relevant HVAC equipment and classify it by risk level
  • Maintenance plan: set preventive/predictive maintenance frequencies based on risk level
  • Change management: any change to maintenance methods or materials must go through risk assessment
  • Roles and responsibilities: clearly define the responsibilities of the maintenance, production and quality departments
  • Documentation requirements: the scope and retention period of maintenance records
  • Spare parts management: critical spare parts stock levels and confirmation of material compliance
  • Training: GMP awareness training, equipment operation training and cleanroom behavior rules
10.6 Risk Communication

Original Text

Risk communication is the sharing of information about risk and risk management between the decision makers and others. Parties can communicate at any stage of the risk management process.

The output and result of the quality risk management process should be appropriately documented, and communicated, e.g., to regulators, to the patient, within a company.

The relationship between the Maintenance Unit and Operations should be a partnership with mutual accountability for asset care. Each department should communicate with the other to ensure errors are avoided. For example, operating departments need to provide detailed information about equipment when in need of repair rather than indicating "it is not working." Similarly, the Maintenance Unit should inform the operating department that they can resume use of the asset following completion of a repair to avoid partially repaired equipment from being placed into service.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Maintenance-Production Partnership

The core message of this section is that the maintenance and production departments should build a partnership rather than an upstream/downstream "customer-supplier" relationship. The source text gives two very practical examples of communication failure:

  • Insufficient communication from production: only saying "the machine is broken", without giving detailed information such as the specific symptoms of the equipment, when the abnormality occurred and the operating conditions
  • Insufficient communication from maintenance: not telling production after a repair, so equipment that has not been fully repaired is put back into use

Analogy

Imagine going to see a doctor and only saying "I don't feel well", without saying where it hurts, when it started or what the symptoms are; the doctor can hardly make a correct diagnosis. Likewise, a maintenance technician needs a detailed "description of symptoms" from the operator in order to troubleshoot effectively. Conversely, if the doctor finishes treatment and leaves without telling you, you will not know whether you can resume normal activity; completion of maintenance must be clearly communicated to production.

Key Notes

"Partially repaired equipment being placed into service" is a major risk in a GMP environment.

In a CDMO HVAC system, such scenarios may include:

  • An AHU repair restores only part of the function (airflow is normal but temperature control is not calibrated), and production starts using it without knowing
  • After a pressure differential sensor is replaced, calibration is not yet complete, but the room has already been "released" for production
  • The integrity test after HEPA replacement has not been completed, but the maintenance technician forgot to note this on the work order

Solution: establish a clear equipment release process, so that after maintenance the equipment can be returned to use only after sign-off by quality or production release personnel.

Practice Questions

  1. What mechanism does your CDMO currently have to ensure real-time communication between the maintenance and production departments? If there is none, what system would you recommend?
  2. The source text says that risk management outcomes should be communicated to regulatory authorities, patients and within the company. For routine HVAC maintenance risk management, what does each of these three types of communication contain?
10.7 Risk Review

Original Text

Risk management should be an ongoing part of the quality management process. A mechanism to review or monitor events should be implemented.

The output and results of the risk management process should be reviewed to take into account new knowledge and experience. Once a quality risk management process has been initiated, that process should continue to be utilized for events that might impact the original quality risk management decision, whether these events are planned (e.g., results of product review, inspections, audits, change control) or unplanned (e.g., root cause from failure investigations, recall).

Use the data gathered by the quality system to find opportunities to further minimize the CGMP risks.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Risk Management Is an Ongoing Activity

This section stresses that risk management is not a project that ends once it is done, but an ongoing part of the quality management system. The triggers for risk review fall into two categories:

  • Planned Events：
    • Annual Product Review
    • Results of regulatory inspections
    • Internal/external audit findings
    • Change Control: any system change should trigger a reassessment of risk
  • Unplanned Events：
    • Root Cause Analysis of failure investigations
    • Product recall
    • Deviations and CAPA

Key Notes

The last sentence of the source text, "Use the data gathered by the quality system to find opportunities to further minimize the CGMP risks", is the core spirit of continual quality improvement. In an HVAC system, this means:

  • Trend analysis: regularly analyze trends in environmental monitoring data; for example, a gradual rise in particle counts in a room may suggest declining HEPA filter efficiency
  • Retrospective review of maintenance records: analyze the correlation between maintenance frequency and equipment failures to optimize the preventive maintenance schedule
  • Deviation pattern recognition: if a certain type of deviation recurs, reassess whether the related risk control measures are sufficient

Application

Suggested annual process for HVAC risk review:

  1. Compile the HVAC-related deviations, CAPAs and change control records from the past year
  2. Analyze environmental monitoring data trends (particles, temperature and humidity, pressure differential, microbiology)
  3. Review maintenance records (preventive maintenance completion rate, number of unplanned repairs, spare parts usage)
  4. Update the risk assessment: are there new risks to add? Are the existing control measures still effective?
  5. Feed the review results into next year's maintenance plan and budget planning
10.8 Quality Risk Management Tools

Original Text

No one tool or set of tools is applicable to every situation in which a quality risk management process as described is applied. ICH Q9 provides a general overview of and references for some of the primary tools used in quality risk management by industry and regulators:

  • Predictive Maintenance (PdM)
  • Reliability Centered Maintenance (RCM) Analysis
  • Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA)
  • Root Cause Failure Analysis (RCFA)

Typically, the Maintenance Unit is involved in these types of processes and analysis.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Four Risk Management Tools

The four tools listed in the source text each suit different application scenarios:

  • PdM (Predictive Maintenance): uses sensor data (vibration, temperature, current, etc.) to predict when equipment is likely to fail, so that maintenance can be done before failure. It suits high-value, high-risk equipment such as AHU fans and chiller compressors
  • RCM (Reliability Centered Maintenance): systematically analyzes equipment functions, failure modes and consequences to define the most cost-effective maintenance strategy. RCM helps decide which equipment needs which level of maintenance
  • FMEA (Failure Modes and Effects Analysis): systematically lists all possible failure modes, assesses the severity (S), occurrence (O) and detectability (D) of each, and calculates the RPN (Risk Priority Number = S × O × D). This is the most commonly used risk assessment tool in the pharmaceutical industry
  • RCFA (Root Cause Failure Analysis): after an equipment failure, systematically traces the root cause. Common methods include fishbone diagrams, 5 Whys and fault tree analysis

Analogy

These four tools are like different functions in the healthcare system:

  • PdM = health check-up (regularly monitor indicators and find problems early)
  • RCM = health management planning (draw up a personalized health plan based on your health risk factors)
  • FMEA = preventive risk assessment (list every illness that could occur, assess severity and probability, and prepare prevention in advance)
  • RCFA = diagnosis of illness (after falling ill, find the real cause rather than just treating symptoms)

Key Notes

The source text stresses that "no single tool is suitable for all situations", which means a CDMO should build a toolbox and choose the most suitable tool for each situation. In practice:

  • New system design/change → use FMEA first
  • Investigation after an equipment failure → use RCFA
  • Defining a long-term maintenance strategy → use RCM
  • Routine monitoring of high-value critical equipment → introduce PdM

The maintenance department is usually the main user of these tools, but the quality and engineering departments should also take part to ensure the risk assessment covers the GMP perspective.

Practice Questions

  1. Which risk management tools does your CDMO currently use? Are there gaps in the toolset, for example is there any PdM capability?
  2. If you were to carry out an FMEA for a newly installed AHU, which main failure modes would you list? Roughly what would the S, O and D be for each mode?
  3. An RCM analysis may recommend a "run-to-failure" strategy for some HVAC components that are not GMP-critical. Which components do you think can be treated this way, and which absolutely cannot?

Application

Examples of how each tool is applied in HVAC systems:

Section Summary

  • Risk Management is a systematic, iterative process of identifying, assessing, controlling and monitoring risk; the goal is to reduce risk to an acceptable level, not to pursue zero risk
  • ICH Q9 provides the international framework for pharmaceutical quality risk management, with two principles: based on scientific knowledge, and commensurate with the level of risk
  • The four key terms must be distinguished precisely: Hazard (source of harm) → Harm, Risk = Probability × Severity, Severity (measure of consequences)
  • The three steps of Risk Assessment: Identification (find the problems) → Analysis (assess probability and severity) → Evaluation (compare against criteria to determine the level)
  • The key insight of Risk Control: control measures can themselves introduce new risks (for example, frequent maintenance increases the probability of human error), so they must be reassessed after implementation
  • Risk Communication emphasizes the partnership between maintenance and production: equipment repair requests must give detailed information, and completion of repairs must be clearly communicated to production before the equipment returns to use
  • Risk Review is an ongoing activity: both planned events (audits, change control) and unplanned events (failure investigations, recalls) should trigger risk reassessment
  • The four tools each have their strengths: PdM (predictive monitoring), RCM (maintenance strategy planning), FMEA (systematic preventive risk assessment), RCFA (failure root cause analysis); choose the tool that suits the situation
10

Chapter 10: App 5–8: Risk & Qualification Examples

p217-p232

ISPE Good Practice Guide: HVAC | p217 - p232

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the five elements of an HVAC risk assessment: risk description, probability, impact, detectability, and mitigation
  • Grasp the HVAC risk scenarios and countermeasures for different space types (classified spaces, pressure-controlled spaces, multi-product facilities)
  • Recognize the impact relationships between critical HVAC parameters and components, and distinguish direct from indirect impact
  • Understand ISO 14644-3 as a cleanroom verification document, including its test methods and pharmaceutical applications
  • Grasp science- and risk-based specification and verification methods, including the ASTM E2500 framework
  • Understand the structure and content of a Verification Report, and build an end-to-end qualification mindset from design to release
11 Appendix 5 – HVAC Risk Assessment Examples

Original Text

11.1 Examples – Risk Assessment for HVAC

These examples describe an approach to risk assessment and countermeasures for HVAC systems serving product handling spaces.

To perform a successful risk evaluation, the SME should consider:

  • risk description
  • risk probability
  • risk impact on product/patient
  • ability to detect
  • risk reduction steps

11.1.1 Example One – Classified Space

  • Risk – upset of room air balance due to failure of CV box on air supply.
  • Risk probability – medium: it does happen.
  • Risk impact – medium: changes in airflow will change room particle counts and room pressures. Adverse pressure relationships may follow.
  • Ability to detect – high: DP alarms will detect change in room DP due to airflow change if there are no DP controls in the room to mask the problem. Daily in-operation particle monitoring should detect room count changes due to changed airflow.
  • Risk reduction – risk to patient is low: for GEP, to avoid having the problem cause a loss of product; however, the use of low-quality CV boxes should be avoided. If air supply is held constant and double HEPA filters are used (primary HEPA in AHU and terminal filters), CV boxes should not be needed. Airflow to each room will follow airflow from HVAC AHU (which is monitored for fan control); alarm low AHU airflow. Summary: risk to patient is low 'as-is.' However, changing the design (e.g., replacing CV devices with terminal HEPA) may increase confidence in the air filtration, while eliminating the potential for CV failure.

11.1.2 Example Two – Classified Space

  • Risk – failure of UFH over Grade 5 (EU Grade A) area.
  • Risk probability – medium: either the fan must fail to run (medium probability) or a HEPA filter must fail (low probability).
  • Risk to product/patient – high: product is exposed under the hood.
  • Ability to detect – medium: operators may not notice a change in hood status.
  • Risk mitigation – airflow switch on fan (not a motor current switch) or airflow velocity monitoring (hot wire) at the hood filter face, but not in the path to critical sites. Periodic scan testing of HEPA filters should include velocity check. Summary: a hood flow monitor should reduce the risk and increase ability to detect. Periodic HEPA integrity and velocity checks also are advised.

11.1.3 Example Three – Pressure Controlled Space

  • Risk – pressure reversals due to improper action of room pressure control damper.
  • Risk probability – medium: usually a small system can be tuned such that active pressure control will not adversely affect pressure relationships, but large systems may be more difficult to maintain in control. In addition, controls may reset wind up because of doors being open too long: when doors close pressure relationships reverse.
  • Risk to product/patient – high: pressure reversal may upset air balance in depyrogenation equipment or introduce large quantities of contamination from room to room.
  • Ability to detect – high: pressure monitoring and alarm.
  • Risk mitigation – calibrate and challenge DP monitoring periodically and ignore momentary DP changes because of doors opening and closing (validate acceptable time delay). No further action will be needed, unless economics require minimal product loss due to upsets. If further action is needed to avoid loss of product (GEP), use airlocks between air classes. Alarm if DP = zero through an airlock (two doors are open). Choose which DP control dampers should be "fast" and which "slow." Consider eliminating automated pressure control by simplifying the air balance (no variable exhausts, constant supply, etc). Summary: if pressure monitoring can be trusted, no unacceptable product should result because of pressure control malfunction.

11.1.4 Example Four – Multi-Product Campaigned OSD Facility with One AHU

  • Risk – cross-contamination potential because of backflow in HVAC or residue from earlier product in air ducts or from other rooms running different product.
  • Risk probability – medium: power/HVAC failures are infrequent. Product contamination in air ducts is likely, but large amounts are not expected as each room has local process exhaust to keep airborne levels low.
  • Risk impact – could be high if sufficient quantities of deposited material break loose and contaminate another product.
  • Ability to detect – low.
  • Risk mitigation – 1. put processes under protective hood or (better) inside pressurized containment device. If product is potent, consider a double wall barrier to also protect operator. Do not recirculate process exhaust from isolator. 2. Terminal HEPA filters will capture in-duct material and keep cross-contaminants from entering the room via HVAC, even if air supply power fails. Filters should be tested periodically. 3. Rooms should be held negative to building to help prevent airborne cross-contamination from other concurrent processes. 4. Optional: a central return air duct filter bank will keep AHU clean and capture airborne product closer to the room. An alternative would be return air filters at each room with volume controls (possibly DP control) to compensate for air filter loading. Summary: process containment and terminal HEPAs will do the most to reduce the risk to low, probability to low.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Risk Assessment: The five-element framework ISPE presents here is highly consistent with ICH Q9 Quality Risk Management. The five elements map onto the logic of FMEA:

  • Risk description = Failure Mode
  • Risk probability = Occurrence
  • Risk impact = Severity
  • Detectability = Detection
  • Risk mitigation = Risk Control

Although ISPE does not use the quantitative RPN (risk priority number) method, a qualitative assessment across these five dimensions is equally valid. The point is to get SMEs (subject matter experts) to think systematically through each failure scenario.

Analogy

An HVAC risk assessment is like a Hospital Infection Control Plan:

  • Risk description = airflow in a patient room reverses and pathogens leak out of the isolation area
  • Probability = how often the door is left open too long
  • Impact = an immunocompromised patient becomes infected
  • Detection = a negative-pressure monitoring alarm system
  • Mitigation = double doors (airlock), automatic door closers, continuous differential pressure monitoring

The logic in a pharmaceutical cleanroom is exactly the same: protecting a "vulnerable product" is like protecting a "vulnerable patient".

Key Notes – Design Philosophy

GEP vs GMP: The examples repeatedly say "for GEP, to avoid having the problem cause a loss of product". This is very important:

  • GMP requirement: protect patient safety (the core of the risk assessment)
  • GEP requirement: avoid product loss (an economic consideration)

Even when the GMP risk is already "low", some additional measures are still worth investing in because they reduce the financial loss from rejected batches. This is where "good engineering practice" goes beyond "minimum compliance".

Practical Application

CDMO scenario: Your aseptic filling facility uses UFH (unidirectional flow hoods) to cover the Grade A areas. One day an operator says "the airflow doesn't feel as strong as it used to", but no alarm has sounded.

Under the analysis in Example 2, this is exactly the "medium detectability" problem: an operator's subjective impression is not reliable. You should:

  • Confirm whether an air velocity monitor is installed (rather than relying only on a motor current switch)
  • Check that the monitor is installed on the filter face and not in the path leading to the critical location
  • Confirm the frequency of periodic HEPA integrity testing and the result of the most recent test

Practice Questions

  1. Example 1 recommends replacing the CV box with a terminal HEPA. Why does this solve both the filtration efficiency problem and the airflow control problem?
  2. Example 3 mentions "ignoring the transient pressure differential caused by door opening". How would you verify an acceptable time delay?
  3. In Example 4, why is it recommended not to recirculate the process exhaust from the isolator? Which GMP principle is most relevant?
  4. If you had to perform an HVAC risk assessment for a new multi-product OSD plant, which SMEs would you invite?

Key Notes

Risk level and countermeasure matrix for the four examples:

Note that Example 4 has "low" detectability, which is the most dangerous situation. When detectability is insufficient, control must be strengthened at the source (sealed isolator, terminal HEPA) rather than relying on monitoring to find the problem.

12 Appendix 6 – Impact Relationships Example

Original Text

Figure 12.1 addresses the inter-relationships between critical HVAC parameters for Aseptic Processing (a classified space) and the HVAC components. Items in shaded boxes are more critical (i.e., direct impact) as determined by the Baseline® Guide on Commissioning and Qualification (Reference 13, Appendix 12). The three boxes showing the actual HVAC critical parameters are temperature/RH, room airborne contaminants, and process environment. Monitoring systems for temperature, RH, and particles should be qualified.

Secondary parameters (that can affect the HVAC critical parameters) are also usually included in HVAC qualification:

  • airflow to the room, affecting particle counts and recovery, monitored at the AHU
  • recovery (periodic test)
  • terminal HEPA filters (note that HEPAs in the air handler are for GEP to extend terminal filter life)
  • internal particle generation (requires control of people and process, outside the HVAC qualification scope, but may depend on local exhaust for particle removal)
  • room pressure (to keep contaminants out)
  • UFH airflow patterns
  • UFH HEPA filters
  • UFH airflow monitor

An HVAC system serving a non-classified area (oral dosage, non-sterile drug substance, packaging, etc.) would have fewer or different direct impact systems and critical components. Understanding the impact of components on product quality allows qualification efforts to focus on critical components (e.g., monitoring systems, HEPA filters).

Figure 12.1: Impact Relationships for Aseptic HVAC (figure not available in text extraction)

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Impact Assessment: This is a core tool of the ISPE Commissioning & Qualification (C&Q) framework. The impact assessment classifies each component of the HVAC system as:

  • Direct Impact: Failure of the component directly affects product quality or patient safety. Examples: terminal HEPA filters, temperature/humidity monitoring systems, particle monitoring systems
  • Indirect Impact: The component supports the operation of direct impact components but does not itself directly affect product quality. Examples: AHU fans, pre-filters, cooling coils
  • No Impact: Components with no relationship to product quality

This classification determines the scope and depth of qualification: direct impact components require full IQ/OQ/PQ, while indirect impact components need only GEP-level verification.

Analogy

Imagine an operating room:

  • Direct impact = sterile surgical instruments, the air filtration system, temperature control (these directly determine the success of the surgery)
  • Indirect impact = backup generators, the chilled water system (they support direct impact equipment but do not touch the patient)
  • No impact = corridor lighting, visitor lounge air conditioning

You would not perform surgical safety validation on corridor lighting, but you would certainly verify the sterile instruments and the air filtration system with great care. The logic of an HVAC impact assessment is exactly the same.

Key Notes

The three critical HVAC parameters (direct impact):

  1. Temperature/Relative Humidity (Temperature/RH) - affects product stability, microbial growth, and operator comfort (indirectly affecting bioburden)
  2. Room Airborne Contaminants - directly related to particle classification and sterility assurance
  3. Process Environment - includes the unidirectional airflow under the UFH and the air quality in product-exposed areas

All three must have Qualified Monitoring Systems. Note that the HEPA filter in the AHU is classified as a "GEP" application (extending the life of the terminal filters) rather than a GMP-critical component; only the terminal HEPA is a direct impact component.

Impact Hierarchy

Critical HVAC parameters (direct impact, require qualification)
├── Temperature/RH → monitoring system requires qualification
├── Airborne particles → monitoring system requires qualification
└── Process environment → UFH airflow requires qualification

Secondary parameters (indirect impact, usually included in the qualification scope)
├── Room supply airflow → affects particle counts and recovery
├── Recovery time → periodic testing
├── Terminal HEPA → periodic integrity testing
├── In-room particle generation → personnel and process controls
├── Room differential pressure → prevents ingress of external contamination
├── UFH airflow pattern → verified by smoke testing
├── UFH HEPA → integrity testing
└── UFH air velocity monitoring → ensures the Grade A environment

GEP components (good engineering practice)
├── AHU HEPA → extends terminal filter life
├── Fan control → maintains total airflow
└── Cooling/heating coils → temperature and humidity regulation

Practical Application

CDMO scenario: During a customer audit you are asked: "Have the HEPA filters in your AHUs been qualified?"

Based on the impact relationships in this appendix, you can answer clearly: "The HEPA in the AHU falls under GEP; its purpose is to protect the terminal HEPA and extend its life. We replace it periodically and verify it at the GEP level. What actually requires qualification is the terminal HEPA filter, for which we perform full installation verification, integrity testing, and periodic retesting."

This kind of answer shows a real understanding of impact assessment, rather than blindly qualifying every component to the same level.

Practice Questions

  1. Why would the direct impact components of non-classified areas (such as an OSD packaging room) be "fewer or different"? Name the HVAC parameters that could be direct impact in an OSD facility.
  2. "Internal particle generation" is listed as a secondary parameter but "outside the scope of HVAC qualification". Does this mean it is unimportant? Who is responsible for controlling it?
  3. If you were building an impact assessment matrix for an aseptic filling facility, how would you distinguish "monitoring systems that require qualification" from "monitoring systems that need only GEP-level verification"?
13 Appendix 7 – ISO 14644-3 – A Qualification Document

Original Text

The ISPE Baseline® Guide on Commissioning and Qualification (Reference 13, Appendix 12) suggests qualifying, while commissioning, without repetition of commissioning tests for qualification.

International Standard ISO 14644-3, Cleanrooms and Associated Controlled Environments – Part 3, Test Methods, (Reference 3, Appendix 12) outlines procedures for testing the performance of clean spaces, whether the space is a classified (such as ISO 7, Euro Grade B) cleanroom or a non-classified processing space (such as for oral dosage products). Incorporating ISO 14644-3 may help to create documents to qualify the performance of a cleanroom.

Procedures covered by Annex B of 14644-3 include methods and equipment for testing:

  • airborne particle counting for room classification (classified pharma spaces)
  • airborne particle counting, ultrafine particles (smaller than 0.1 micron) – not normally used in pharma
  • airborne particle counting, macroparticles (larger than 5 micron) – not a normal pharmaceutical test
  • airflow – velocity and uniformity – for unidirectional airflow spaces, airflow supply from filters and in ducts; also airflow to non-unidirectional spaces
  • air DP – may be used for classified and other process spaces. For classified space (as in sterile product manufacture), verify GMP DP values of 10 to 15 Pa between air classes.
  • installed filter leakage – total leakage, scan test, choice of aerosols (may be used for non-classified space, such as where hazardous products are processed). The sterile processing guidances may require a specific performance for HEPA filters serving classified spaces.
  • Airflow visualization (smoke testing) – common in Grade A (ISO 5) unidirectional spaces, but may be used where process containment is used. The "tracer thread" method is not commonly used in pharmaceutical environments, and videos are expected for most UFHs.
  • Temperature – usually a critical parameter where product is stored, may be critical to personnel comfort (and subsequent generation of bioburden) in classified spaces.
  • Humidity – not usually an issue for liquid products, and may be a personnel comfort issue. See the appropriate ISPE Baseline® Guide (Reference 13, Appendix 12) for the pharmaceutical dosage form.
  • electrostatic and ion generators – usually used for electronics manufacture, not pharmaceutical environments
  • particle deposition – electronics; pharma uses settling plates for CFU counting instead
  • room recovery – common test in European pharmaceutical cleanrooms, a good indicator of HVAC robustness; in the US recovery testing can justify as-built air changes. See ISPE Baseline® Guide for Sterile Manufacturing Facilities (Reference 13, Appendix 12).
  • containment leakage – to check integrity of the room "fabric," sometimes done in pharmaceutical environments, particularly where potent materials are exposed to the room environment

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

ISO 14644-3: This is the international standard for cleanroom test methods and an important tool document for HVAC verification. ISPE emphasizes a key principle here: "perform qualification concurrently with commissioning to avoid duplicate testing".

How the ISO 14644 series fits together:

  • Part 1: cleanroom classification (defines ISO 5, ISO 7, etc.)
  • Part 2: monitoring requirements (demonstrating continued compliance)
  • Part 3: test methods (the subject of this appendix: how to test)
  • Part 4: design, construction, and start-up

The pharmaceutical industry mainly uses Part 1 (classification) and Part 3 (test methods), but note that the ISO standards are "not pharmaceutical-specific": pharmaceutical-specific requirements (such as the 10-15 Pa pressure differential in EU GMP Annex 1) must be layered on top.

Analogy

ISO 14644-3 is like the "standard test center" for a driving license exam: it defines every possible test item (road test, reversing, parking, etc.), but you do not need to take every item every time. The pharmaceutical industry selects the items relevant to product quality to perform a cleanroom "health check".

It is like a medical check-up report that includes blood pressure (= differential pressure), blood oxygen (= particle count), and an ECG (= airflow pattern): each test has a standard method, but the doctor decides which items are mandatory based on your health risks.

Key Notes – EU vs US Differences

EU vs US differences in the Recovery Test:

  • Europe: EU GMP Annex 1 explicitly requires a recovery test, requiring the cleanroom to return to the specified particle level within a set time after a contamination event (typically 15-20 minutes)
  • United States: FDA has no explicit recovery test requirement, but ISPE notes that a recovery test can be used to "justify the as-built air change rate". In other words, if recovery is fast enough, it can support a design decision to reduce air changes

For a CDMO serving both EU and US customers, it is advisable to use the European standard as the baseline for recovery testing, which satisfies both sets of requirements in one pass.

Practical Application

CDMO scenario: You are planning the qualification program for a new cleanroom. An engineer asks: "Which ISO 14644-3 tests do we need to perform?"

Taking an aseptic filling Grade B environment as an example, your answer should include:

  • Airborne particle counts (at-rest and in-operation): the basis for classification
  • Differential pressure measurement: confirm the 10-15 Pa gradient
  • Terminal HEPA integrity test: DOP/PAO scan
  • Temperature and humidity confirmation: product and personnel needs
  • Recovery test: EU customer requirement + justification of air change rate
  • Grade A (UFH) areas additionally require: air velocity uniformity and airflow visualization (video recorded and archived)

The key is not to blindly perform every test listed in ISO 14644-3, but to select the items relevant to your product and process based on a risk assessment.

Practice Questions

  1. Why does ISPE recommend "performing qualification concurrently with commissioning"? What are the benefits? What are the risks?
  2. The "tracer thread" method in ISO 14644-3 is common in the electronics industry. Why does the pharmaceutical industry prefer smoke testing?
  3. If the cleanroom of an OSD (oral solid dosage) plant is a non-classified space, which ISO 14644-3 test items would you choose, and why?

Key Notes

Commonly used vs rarely used ISO 14644-3 test methods in the pharmaceutical industry:

14 Appendix 8 – Science- and Risk-Based Specification and Verification Approach

Original Text

14.1 Introduction

This chapter describes an enhanced science- and risk-based approach to verifying that a system is fit for intended use, based on recent regulatory and industry trends, and published guidance, specifically ICH documents, such as Q8 Pharmaceutical Development, Q9 Quality Risk Management, and Q10 Pharmaceutical Quality System, and various supporting industry consensus standards, such as the ASTM E2500 Standard Guide for Specification, Design, and Verification of Pharmaceutical and Biopharmaceutical Manufacturing Systems and Equipment (Reference 10, Appendix 12).

This approach is based on:

  • a thorough understanding of the product and process and the role of science
  • use of risk assessments to determine the scope and extent of required verification in the overall risk management process, which is related to patient safety
  • focusing on parameters that affect product quality and patient safety
  • focusing on practices that lead to achieving fitness for intended use

Key principles that provide the basis for developing engineering requirements include:

  • The assessment and designation of criticality should be primarily based on impact on the safety and efficacy of the drug product to the patient.
  • CQAs should drive the focus of the risk assessment along with CPPs.
  • The installation and verification process should focus on value added activities and should remove activities that are wasteful or do not add value.
  • Verification practices performed solely for regulatory compliance should be avoided.4
4 If a practice adds to the assurance that the equipment or system will work as intended, then that practice should be performed whether or not the system is part of GMP manufacturing operations. If it does not, then that practice should not be performed unless specifically required for compliance.

Well planned commissioning activities and documentation that follow GEP can contribute to meeting installation and verification requirements.

Acceptance of this approach by individual regulators (or even individual operating organizations) will likely vary. The operating company may wish to discuss the approach with appropriate regulators before defining detailed activities and documents for facility acceptance.

The appropriate ISPE Baseline® Guide (Reference 13, Appendix 12) covers regulatory expectations for HVAC performance. The extent of verification documentation may depend on the level of risk identified.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

The ASTM E2500 framework: This is the core reference standard of ISPE Appendix 8, and it represents a major shift in thinking in pharmaceutical engineering, from the traditional IQ/OQ/PQ validation model toward "science- and risk-based" verification.

Traditional model vs ASTM E2500 model:

  • Traditional: IQ → OQ → PQ (a fixed sequence in which all components are treated equally)
  • E2500: risk assessment → identify critical aspects → targeted verification (in-depth verification only for components that affect product quality)

Fitness for Intended Use: This is the central goal of the whole approach: not "passing the tests", but "demonstrating that the system is fit for its intended use". This subtle difference completely changes how verification is thought about.

Analogy

Traditional IQ/OQ/PQ is like making every student sit the same standardized exam, whether they want to be a doctor or an engineer. ASTM E2500 works differently: first understand what job you will do (product requirements), then assess which skills matter most (risk assessment), and finally verify only those critical skills (targeted testing).

The result? Medical students are tested in depth on anatomy and clinical reasoning, and engineering students on mechanics and design. Everyone spends their time on what really matters.

Key Notes

Footnote 4 is the most important sentence in this appendix:

"If a practice increases the assurance that equipment or a system works as intended, it should be performed, whether or not the system is part of a GMP manufacturing operation. If it does not, it should not be performed unless explicitly required by regulation."

This means:

  • A valuable test: should be done even if the system is not a GMP system (because of GEP)
  • A test with no value: should not be done even if the system is a GMP system (unless explicitly required by regulation)

This directly challenges a culture of "compliance for the sake of compliance". Many companies spend enormous amounts of time producing "validation documents" that add no quality assurance. ISPE says explicitly: stop doing this.

Key Notes – Regulatory Acceptance

ISPE honestly points out: "Different regulatory agencies (and even different companies) may differ in their acceptance of this approach." This is not an empty remark. In practice:

  • FDA: relatively open, encourages risk-based approaches
  • EU/PIC/S: Annex 15 still retains the IQ/OQ/PQ terminology but allows flexible interpretation
  • China NMPA: traditionally more conservative, prefers to see complete IQ/OQ/PQ documentation

Recommended CDMO strategy: internally, apply the scientific thinking of ASTM E2500 to plan verification activities, but keep the IQ/OQ/PQ framework language in the documentation to meet the audit expectations of the most conservative customers.

Practice Questions

  1. Where does the principle of Footnote 4 conflict with your company's current verification practice? Can you give an example of a test performed for "compliance for the sake of compliance"?
  2. Why does ISPE recommend "discussing with the regulatory agency before defining detailed activities"? Is this feasible in a CDMO context?

Original Text

14.2 Key Concepts of the Approach

This section addresses the application of the key concepts described in ASTM E2500 (Reference 10, Appendix 12) to the specification, installation, and verification of HVAC Systems.

The goal of this approach is to improve patient safety while controlling costs and reducing non-value adding effort.

It should be noted that these key concepts focus on patient safety and product quality (GMP). The verification of the specification and design impacts on worker safety, health, environmental, and other non-GMP concerns also should be considered.

14.2.1 Risk-Based and Science-Based Approach

The level of risk to product quality should be based on scientific knowledge that leads to protection of the patient. The level of effort expended in the quality risk management process should reflect the level of risk. Product and process information related to product quality and patient safety should be the basis of the science- and risk-based decision to ensure that manufacturing systems are designed and verified fit for their intended use.

Considerations include CQAs, CPPs, process control strategy, and prior production experience.

For HVAC Systems, the risks of system failures and interruptions should be addressed during the specification and design part of the process.

14.2.2 Critical Aspects of Manufacturing Systems

Critical aspects of manufacturing systems typically are functions, features, abilities, and performance characteristics necessary for the manufacturing process and systems to ensure consistent product quality and patient safety. HVAC systems may affect the manufacturing system and the critical aspects. Verification activities should focus on the critical aspects of the HVAC system's effect.

14.2.3 Quality by Design

Quality by Design concepts should be applied to the manufacturing system throughout its life cycle.

14.2.4 Good Engineering Practice

GEP is a set of established engineering methods and standards that are applied throughout the facility life cycle to deliver appropriate and effective solutions. For HVAC systems, GMP requirements, code requirements, including sustainability requirements and energy efficiency, safety, health environmental, ergonomic operational, and maintenance, should be addressed.

GEP covers all engineering activities and documentation and encompasses the following:

  • Design and installation that takes account of GMP, safety, health, environmental, ergonomic, operational, maintenance, recognized industry guidance, and statutory requirements.
  • Professional and competent project management, engineering design, procurement, construction, installation, and commissioning that demonstrates functionality in accordance with design specifications.
  • Appropriate documentation, including design concepts, design schematic drawings, as-installed drawings, test records, maintenance and operations manuals, statutory inspection certificates, etc.

14.2.5 Subject Matter Experts

SMEs have specific expertise and responsibility in a particular area or field. For HVAC systems, this could include the HVAC engineer, quality unit, automation experts, or operations.

14.2.6 Use of Supplier Documentation

Supplier documentation may be used in the verification process if a vendor with an acceptable quality system produces it. A risk- and science-based approach can be used to determine if the supplier's practices are aligned to manage the risks associated with the selected equipment or system.

14.2.7 Continual Improvement

Continual improvement can happen as information is gained from operations. Improvements can be based on periodic reviews and evaluation, operational data, and root-cause analysis of failures. Typically, for HVAC systems, energy optimization is reviewed.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

The seven key concepts of ASTM E2500 applied to HVAC:

  1. Science & Risk-Based - use scientific knowledge to determine the risk level, and the risk level to determine the depth of verification
  2. Critical Aspects - identify the functions, features, and performance of the HVAC system that affect product quality
  3. Quality by Design (QbD) - build quality into the system across its whole lifecycle, considering verification needs from the design stage
  4. Good Engineering Practice (GEP) - good engineering practice is the foundation, covering all aspects: GMP + safety + environment + maintenance
  5. Subject Matter Experts (SMEs) - a cross-disciplinary expert team, rather than a decision by a single department
  6. Supplier Documentation - make good use of supplier documentation (provided the supplier has a qualified quality system)
  7. Continual Improvement - improve continuously based on operating data, rather than "never touching it again once verified"

Analogy

These seven concepts are like the end-to-end thinking behind building a house:

  • Science and risk = the geological survey (understand the foundation risks before deciding the structural design)
  • Critical aspects = load-bearing walls (not every wall is equally important)
  • QbD = plan the routing of pipes at the design stage (rather than drilling holes afterwards)
  • GEP = compliance with building codes (the basic requirements for fire safety, utilities, and structure)
  • SMEs = teamwork between the architect, structural engineer, and utilities engineer
  • Supplier documentation = trusting the factory reports from a building materials supplier that holds quality certification
  • Continual improvement = improving based on actual use once people have moved in (such as adding energy-saving windows)

Key Notes

"Verification effort should be proportional to the risk level" - this is the core principle of resource allocation.

In practice, this means:

  • High risk (Grade A/B HVAC): a full verification plan, detailed test protocols, a formal verification report
  • Medium risk (Grade C/D HVAC): simplified verification, leveraging GEP commissioning documents
  • Low risk (non-classified space HVAC): GEP commissioning documents are sufficient; no additional GMP verification is needed

The problem at many companies is that every HVAC system gets the same depth of IQ/OQ/PQ. This wastes large amounts of resources on low-risk systems, and the quality of verification for high-risk systems then suffers from a lack of resources.

Key Notes – Leveraging Supplier Documentation

14.2.6 Leveraging supplier documentation is an often-overlooked efficiency opportunity:

  • If an HVAC equipment supplier has an accredited quality system (such as ISO 9001), its factory test reports can be used as part of verification
  • For example: AHU fan performance curves, control valve stroke tests, factory integrity tests of HEPA filters. These do not need to be repeated on site
  • The prerequisite, however, is that you assess whether the supplier's quality system is reliable (supplier audit)

This is consistent with the "leveraging supplier data" principle of EU GMP Annex 15.

Practical Application

CDMO scenario: Your quality department insists on full IQ/OQ/PQ for the warehouse HVAC system, on the grounds that "all GMP areas must have it".

Under the principles of ASTM E2500, you can propose that:

  • The only critical aspect of warehouse HVAC is temperature control (protecting product stability)
  • The temperature monitoring system (direct impact) requires qualification, but the AHU itself needs only GEP-level commissioning verification
  • Airflow, differential pressure, particle counts, etc. are not critical parameters for a warehouse
  • Recommendation: invest the resources saved in more in-depth verification of the aseptic filling area HVAC

Practice Questions

  1. GEP covers a broader scope than GMP (including safety, environment, human factors engineering, etc.). Can you give an example of an HVAC design decision that "GMP does not require, but GEP does"?
  2. 14.2.5 mentions that SMEs can be HVAC engineers, quality unit staff, automation specialists, or operators. In your experience, which SME is most often overlooked? Why is their participation important?
  3. Continual improvement mentions "energy optimization of the HVAC system". Why is this specifically raised under the ASTM E2500 framework? How does it relate to GMP?

Original Text

14.3 Design, Specification, Verification, and Acceptance Process

This section addresses the verification process as they relate to the overall specification, design, and verification process for the manufacturing system as well as the HVAC subsystem. For a more detailed description of the HVAC design process, see Chapters 2 to 4 of this Guide.

14.3.1 Requirements Definition

Product knowledge, process knowledge, regulatory requirements, and company quality requirements should be considered when determining the requirements for the HVAC system. The requirements definition should be driven by patient safety.

14.3.2 Specification and Design

For HVAC Systems, the design process should follow the process described in this Guide.

14.3.3 Verification

The verification process uses a multidisciplinary team focused on product and patient safety. Team members include process, product, and SMEs who may ask "What are the elements of this system that are critical to product quality and patient safety, and how can the team appropriately manage risks associated with those elements to maintain or improve our overall product quality?"

The interdisciplinary expert team forms the foundation for developing a risk management plan. Team members should decide on methodologies to determine acceptable levels of risk and appropriate tools to evaluate risk (e.g., FMEA) after establishing the User Requirements. User Requirements should identify the CPPs, CQAs, and other aspects related to product quality and patient safety.

Once the critical aspects have been identified and documented by the interdisciplinary team, this document becomes the basis for the Verification Plan to be developed. Engineers should know what acceptance tests the quality unit expects to be performed after the verification process is complete in order to prepare systems to pass these tests.

Verification covers the activities, testing, and documentation to confirm that systems, equipment, and environments are fit for their intended use. It is based on GEP coupled with the risk management plan developed in the risk assessment phase. The types of checks and tests to be performed are developed by the SME. For example, the HVAC SME would design a plan to verify the acceptance criteria that meet the critical aspects within the framework of the risk management plan.

For an overview of the verification process, refer to Figure 14.1.

Figure 14.1: Overview of Verification Process (figure not available in text extraction)

14.3.4 Acceptance and Release

The acceptance and release phase confirms that the manufacturing system and supporting HVAC system are fit for their intended use. This is the last check before initial operation.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

The four stages of the verification process:

  1. Requirements Definition - driven by patient safety, combining product knowledge, process knowledge, regulatory requirements, and company quality requirements
  2. Specification & Design - translate requirements into verifiable engineering specifications
  3. Verification - a cross-disciplinary team confirms that the system meets the acceptance criteria for the critical aspects
  4. Acceptance & Release - final confirmation that the system is fit for use, the last checkpoint before start-up

The core logic of the Verification Plan: User Requirements → identify CQAs/CPPs → risk assessment → identify critical aspects → define acceptance criteria → design verification activities. This is a clear logical chain from "requirements to evidence".

Analogy

The verification process is like the acceptance check when buying a new car:

  1. Requirements definition = what kind of car do you need? (seating, fuel economy, safety ratings)
  2. Specification and design = choosing the model and configuration options
  3. Verification = the pre-delivery inspection: does the engine start normally? Are the brakes responsive? Is the airbag tested? Is the air conditioning cold enough? You do not check every screw, only the "critical aspects"
  4. Acceptance and release = sign for the car and drive it away

You would not check the bolt torque on the door handle, but you would certainly confirm that the braking system works. That is "risk-based verification".

Key Notes

The key question in 14.3.3:

"What are the elements of this system that are critical to product quality and patient safety, and how can the team appropriately manage risks associated with those elements?"

This question should be the opening line of every verification meeting. It forces the team back to the essentials:

  • Not "What do we need to test?" (task-oriented)
  • But "What will affect product quality and patient safety?" (risk-oriented)

When quality and engineering disagree on the verification scope, returning to this question usually makes the answer clear.

Practice Questions

  1. Why does ISPE stress that "engineers should know the acceptance tests the quality unit expects"? What common problem does this imply?
  2. How do you make sure the "acceptance and release" stage does not become a formality? Give a specific HVAC release checklist item.

Original Text

14.4 Supporting Processes

The activities described here support the specification, design, and verification process. They occur throughout the process.

14.4.1 Quality Risk Management (QRM)

Quality Risk Management is the high level concept applied to all systems, including HVAC systems. QRM defines the risk assessment process for the manufacturer. Risk Assessment for the HVAC system should be addressed as part of the overall Risk Assessment activity.

14.4.2 Design Review

Design Reviews are planned systematic reviews of specifications, design, design development, and continuous improvement changes performed throughout the life cycle of the manufacturing system. For HVAC systems in the design phase, reviews typically occur at the BOD, schematic design, design development, and construction document phases. HVAC equipment specifications are often not available until the construction document phase, but their review is critical to system quality.

14.4.3 Change Management

Change Management controls changes that affect critical aspects of the manufacturing system, both before and after acceptance for use. After acceptance, changes that affect GMP critical parameters are usually approved by the quality unit prior to implementation. With continual improvement as a goal of the FDA initiative, it is expected that systems that have been verified and accepted for intended use will be later modified to achieve improved patient safety or to reduce operating costs as opportunities arise during the system's life cycle.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Three supporting processes run through the whole lifecycle:

  • QRM (Quality Risk Management): the overarching framework that defines the overall risk assessment process. The HVAC risk assessment is not standalone; it is part of the facility-wide risk assessment
  • Design Review: systematic reviews conducted at different stages of the design. Note that HVAC equipment specifications are usually not fixed until the construction documents stage, which means early design reviews may miss critical equipment-level details
  • Change Management: the control mechanism after verification. ISPE specifically notes that FDA encourages continual improvement, which means a "we dare not touch it once it is verified" mindset is wrong

Key Notes

The four stages of Design Review and their relationship to HVAC:

  1. BOD (Basis of Design): confirms the HVAC design premises: space classification, pressure strategy, air change rate targets
  2. Schematic Design: confirms the AHU configuration, duct routing, and control strategy
  3. Design Development: confirms the automation control logic, alarm settings, and monitoring points
  4. Construction Documents: confirms equipment specifications and installation details. This is the stage at which HVAC equipment specifications are first fixed, so the review is critical

A common problem: many projects overlook HVAC in early design reviews and only discover insufficient space or duct clashes at the construction stage.

Practice Questions

  1. Why should the HVAC risk assessment be "part of the overall risk assessment" rather than performed independently? What does this imply for team composition?
  2. Change Management says that "improvements after verification" require quality unit approval. If an improvement concerns only energy efficiency (such as reducing the air change rate during non-working hours), is quality unit approval needed? Why?

Original Text

14.5 Example Verification Report

The approach described is not prescriptive. One possible approach to the process for an OSD facility, intended as a basis for discussion, is presented.

14.5.1 Design Verification

The company has a single system for reviewing design proposals covering both GEP and GMP aspects. Once the company is satisfied that its comments have been either incorporated or responded to, they issue a memo to the design authority affirming that the drawings may be issued for construction. This document is the written confirmation that the design is, in the companies' opinion, fit for its intended purpose.

Concept: a design review quality system is in place and used in support of GEP – no additional requirements have been added to make this a "quality documentation" exercise. The formal communication to the designer is a contract requirement, not a GMP requirement.

14.5.2 Construction

In this example, the Construction Manager is responsible for getting the project built and commissioned to predefined robust specifications. The CM verifies that work has been completed to specification.

14.5.3 Risk Assessment

The company has identified two quality systems that affect the facility:

  1. The environmental monitoring program, including:
    • HEPA leakage testing
    • area airborne particle and microbiological monitoring
    • confirmation of the area monitoring system alarm history – temperature, humidity, and "critical" room DPs
  2. The HVAC calibration and maintenance system, to verify that monitors are correct

The system verification summary report covers both of these systems. It is supported by a review that releases the area and the supporting systems for use, incorporating a company quality, environmental impact, and EHS review.

For example, a company has completed a risk assessment of the HVAC system for a new OSD facility, and the following are considered to be critical aspects to allow operation:

  • installation of the correct grade of and leak testing of the AHU mounted HEPA filter (cross-contamination control)
  • the construction, testing, and verification of the environmental monitoring system
  • maintenance and calibration of monitoring systems for critical parameters
  • supporting procedures

14.5.4 The GEP Documentation Package from the CM should include the following:

14.5.4.1 Installation Verification

The installation documentation confirms that the HVAC system is installed to specification. In this example, it also is used to gather the information needed to populate a CMMS and is a check of the major components. As this document is also used to release the system for use, it will include:

  • verification of the key components
  • verification of the specified system construction quality checks, e.g., ductwork leakage testing, installation quality, HEPA certification
  • control system point-to-point cable testing, instrument calibration checking, and controlled component functional testing (e.g., control valves operate in the correct direction and over their entire range)

14.5.4.2 Automation Check Out/Functional and Performance Testing

Industry practice is inclined toward ACO and FPT:

Automation Check Out (ACO) – checking the BMS sequence of operation, alarms, and interlocks.

Functional and Performance Testing (FPT) – setting up the system for balance, tuning the control loops and setting system alarm points based on the performance achieved by the installed system. For a critical system, a simulated load test also may be carried out.

In the example, company practice is not to produce a "commissioning summary report," but a system installation and operation verification report that releases the system for use. In this case, the HVAC system release is a part of the requirements for the area release, together with the verification report for the facility and monitoring system.

The project team then checks that this documentation is adequate to confirm correct installation and performance and follows with a Verification Report.

14.5.5 Verification Report

The verification report for this example is less than 15 pages. It contains the following sections:

  • Summary
  • Purpose and Scope
  • System Description
  • Summary of Verifications Performed – confirming that installation, ACO, and FPT have been satisfactorily completed.
  • Risk Assessment Qualification Requirement Summary – confirming that requirements identified in the Risk Assessment have specifically been addressed in the commissioning; in this example, the correct grade of HEPA has been installed with certification (from installation) and has been leak tested, and the area has been able to maintain the specified conditions over a representative test period (FPT). (It should be noted that the pre-defined acceptance criteria are derived from the design specification, which is derived from User Requirements.)
  • System Operational Requirements – confirming the SOPs required to operate the system have been identified.
  • System Maintenance and Calibration – confirming the SOPs required to maintain the system have been identified.
  • Engineering Change Management Review – confirming that change of the design from the accepted "issue for construction" drawings has been managed and that the installed design remains acceptable.

Acronyms used in the Example Verification Report

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Structure of the Verification Report: ISPE provides an example verification report for an OSD plant, and the key point is that it is "under 15 pages", which is itself an important message. Traditional IQ/OQ/PQ documents can run to hundreds of pages, whereas a risk-based verification report can be far more concise.

The seven sections of the verification report:

  1. Summary - conclusion first
  2. Purpose and Scope - define the boundaries
  3. System Description - what is being verified
  4. Summary of Verification Activities - results of installation, ACO, and FPT
  5. Risk Assessment Requirements Confirmation - the most critical part, linking the risk assessment to the verification evidence
  6. Operational Requirements - confirm that SOPs are in place
  7. Maintenance and Calibration - confirm that maintenance SOPs are in place

There is also a Change Management Review, confirming that any design changes between "approved for construction" and "as installed" have been managed.

Analogy

This verification report is like a house handover inspection report:

  • Summary = "This house has passed inspection and is ready for occupancy"
  • Installation verification = whether the electrical, water, and gas lines were installed according to the design drawings
  • ACO = whether the central air-conditioning controller operates correctly (when set to 25 degrees, does it really blow 25-degree air?)
