  • FPT = overall performance test (with all rooms cooling at the same time, is the temperature stable?)
  • Risk requirements confirmation = is there evidence that your biggest worries (water leaks, structural safety) have been ruled out?
  • SOP confirmation = the homeowner's manual (how to operate the heating system, how to replace the filter)

The point is that you would not write a separate acceptance report for every door handle; you would write one consolidated report focused on the "critical aspects".

Key Notes

Identifying the critical aspects of the OSD plant: In the example, the risk assessment identified only four critical aspects:

  1. The correct grade and integrity of the AHU HEPA filters (to prevent cross-contamination)
  2. Construction, testing, and verification of the environmental monitoring system
  3. Maintenance and calibration of the critical parameter monitoring systems
  4. Supporting procedures (SOPs)

Note: for an OSD plant, the primary function of the HEPA filter is "cross-contamination control" (not sterility assurance), which differs from the risk focus of an aseptic filling facility. This is what "science-based" means: different product types have different risk priorities.

Key Notes – Leveraging GEP Documentation

"The design review quality system is used to support GEP; no additional requirements are added to make it a quality document"

This statement in 14.5.1 reveals an important principle: GEP documents themselves can satisfy part of the verification need, and there is no need to create a separate "quality document version" for GMP. Specifically:

  • Design review memoranda = evidence of design verification (no separate DQ report is needed)
  • The construction manager's installation verification = evidence for IQ (no separate IQ protocol is needed)
  • ACO + FPT records = evidence for OQ (no separate OQ protocol is needed)

This is the biggest difference between ASTM E2500 and the traditional approach: use existing engineering documents rather than creating duplicate documents for the sake of compliance.

Verification Process Mapping

Traditional IQ/OQ/PQ          ASTM E2500 verification
─────────────          ──────────────
DQ (design qualification)     ←→   Design Review + design review memoranda
IQ (installation qualification)     ←→   Installation Verification (GEP)
OQ (operational qualification)     ←→   ACO + FPT
PQ (performance qualification)     ←→   FPT (simulated load test)
Validation Report ←→   Verification Report (≤15 pages)

Key differences:
• Traditional approach: separate documents for each stage, with heavy duplication
• E2500: a unified document framework that leverages GEP commissioning records
• Result: fewer documents, more focused verification, higher efficiency

Practical Application

CDMO scenario: You are building a new OSD plant, and the HVAC contractor asks: "When will you give me your IQ/OQ protocols? I need to align my testing with your document format."

A response based on ASTM E2500: "We do not need separate IQ/OQ protocols. Complete installation verification and functional performance testing to GEP standards and provide complete test records. Our quality and engineering teams will review your documents and, combined with the results of our risk assessment, produce a verification report confirming that the system is fit for use."

This approach saves both sides a great deal of document back-and-forth while ensuring the testing is genuinely focused on the critical aspects.

Practice Questions

  1. If you were writing a similar verification report for an aseptic filling facility (rather than an OSD plant), which items would be added to the critical aspects?
  2. The example report is "under 15 pages". How many pages do you think a traditional IQ/OQ/PQ document of similar scope would run to at your company? Where does the difference come from?
  3. 14.5.5 states that "acceptance criteria come from the design specifications, and the design specifications come from the user requirements". If this traceability chain is broken (for example, the user requirements document is missing), what problems result?
  4. What is the difference between ACO and FPT? Why do they need to be performed separately?

Section Summary

  • Appendix 5 (Risk Assessment Examples): An HVAC risk assessment contains five elements (description, probability, impact, detectability, mitigation), and the four examples cover classified spaces, UFH failure, pressure reversal, and multi-product cross-contamination. Core principle: the lower the detectability, the more important source control becomes.
  • Appendix 6 (Impact Relationships): HVAC components are classified as direct impact (require qualification), indirect impact (usually included in qualification), and GEP level. The three direct impact parameters are temperature/RH, airborne particles, and process environment. The HEPA in the AHU is GEP; only the terminal HEPA is direct impact.
  • Appendix 7 (ISO 14644-3): Provides the international standard for cleanroom test methods, and the pharmaceutical industry should select the relevant test items based on risk. Core principle: "perform qualification concurrently with commissioning to avoid duplicate testing". Note the EU/US differences in recovery testing.
  • Appendix 8 (Science- and Risk-Based Verification): Based on the ASTM E2500 framework, moving from traditional IQ/OQ/PQ to "identify critical aspects → risk-based verification → confirm fitness for use". Core idea: verification effort should be proportional to risk, and GEP documents can satisfy verification needs, so there is no need to create duplicate documents for the sake of compliance.
  • Consistency of the decision hierarchy: The common theme of the four appendices is "patient safety as the highest priority", which is fully consistent with the decision hierarchy of Sterility Assurance → Product CQAs → Business Flexibility.
11

Chapter 11: App 9: Economics & Sustainability

p233-p246

ISPE Good Practice Guide: HVAC | p233 - p246

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the Total Cost of Ownership concept for HVAC systems, and how to balance capital expenditure against operating cost
  • Understand the financial impact of HVAC failure on drug manufacturing, and the cost-benefit analysis of redundant design
  • Learn the factors that make up Life Cycle Cost: energy, consumables, maintenance and reliability
  • Become familiar with the various Energy Recovery technologies and their limitations in pharmaceutical facilities
  • Understand the rating systems for Sustainable Design (LEED, Green Globes) and the special considerations for pharmaceutical HVAC
  • Learn the key role and contribution of the HVAC engineer in the green building design process

Table of Contents

15.1 HVAC System Economics 15.1.1 Risk to Product 15.1.2 Life Cycle Cost 15.2 Sustainable Design 15.2.3 Rating Systems 15.2.5 New Project Design 15.2.6 IAQ during Construction 15.2.8 Renewable Energy 15.2.10 Refrigerants
15.1 HVAC System Economics

Original Text

In addition to protecting the product and patient, production facilities need to consider economics (i.e., making a profit) to continue in business. Overall cost is a major factor in deciding which options to implement for an HVAC system. Life cycle cost usually is much greater than the initial (capital) cost of an HVAC system.

It is common practice to use methods, such as net present value or the rate of return to evaluate different design options. These concepts often are unfamiliar to engineers who strive for the most robust design regardless of cost. Organizations usually have internal accounting systems to facilitate the evaluation of different design concepts, evaluating payback against capital cost, (investment analysis) over the expected life of a facility. Typical systems include net present value and investment rate of return. A cost model should be developed early in a project to estimate the final maintenance, consumables, and energy usage of the facility. It should be the basis against which life cycle cost decisions are evaluated and can be used to challenge User Requirement decisions.

Cost models should be holistic and consider the impact of HVAC on production costs, down time, product or productivity losses, and other costs of doing business.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Life Cycle Cost: the sum of all costs from design, procurement, installation, operation and maintenance through to final decommissioning. ISPE stresses here that the operating cost of an HVAC system usually far exceeds the initial capital cost.

Net Present Value, NPV: the value of future annual cash flows discounted back to the present at a discount rate. It is the standard financial tool for evaluating long-term investment options.

Cost Model: a financial model built early in the project to estimate the maintenance, consumables and energy costs over the facility life cycle. This model should be built during the design phase, not added retrospectively.

Analogy

The Life Cycle Cost of an HVAC system is like the total cost of owning a car (TCO): a cheap car may cost 500,000 to buy, but if it uses a lot of fuel, needs frequent repairs and has expensive parts, it can cost 1.5 million over 10 years; a more expensive hybrid at 800,000 may cost only 1.2 million in total over the same 10 years. HVAC is the same: Capital Cost is only the tip of the iceberg, and Operating Cost is the real bulk.

Key Notes

ISPE specifically notes that "these concepts are often unfamiliar to engineers", which is a very important reminder. In a CDMO environment, engineering teams are used to pursuing the "most robust design" without necessarily considering cost-effectiveness. A good HVAC design must strike a balance between quality assurance and economic benefit.

The cost model should be "holistic": it must consider the impact of HVAC on production cost, downtime, product loss and loss of productivity, not just electricity and maintenance costs.

Practice Questions

  1. Did your facility build an HVAC cost model during the project design phase? If not, what problems do you think this causes?
  2. Why does ISPE recommend using NPV rather than simply comparing which option is cheaper? Over a facility life of 10-15 years, how do energy price fluctuations affect the decision?
15.1.1 Risk to Product and Associated Costs

Original Text

The production-related considerations described are additional to conventional economical considerations balancing capital and operating costs. See Appendix 2.

15.1.1.1 Impact of Failure

The impact of an HVAC system failure could be financially significant in the pharmaceutical industry, possibly causing loss of a batch of product or the loss of control of the conditions in a research laboratory and potentially invalidating the results of a long term test. The risk assessment of a system's failure should include product quality issues, as well as potential business issues. A clear definition of the potential impact of system failure can influence and justify the budget for a system.

The potential impact of a system failure on the area being conditioned and adjacent areas should be reviewed and consider potential modes of failure, such as:

  • airflow failure
  • air filter failure
  • failure of temperature control
  • failure of humidity control

15.1.1.2 Redundancy

If the cost and likelihood of failure are high, duplication of systems/equipment may be justified. Redesign the system or process to reduce the risk may be considered a better option. The potential impact of redundancy complicates HVAC system design, startup, and maintenance, along with design requirements for the supporting utilities. For example, duplex air handling systems may require duplex chillers and circulating pumps to decrease risk appropriately.

15.1.1.3 Aesthetics

Materials and systems that do not add functionality, but are provided for aesthetic reasons (e.g., screen walls, high cost materials) should be considered in the cost evaluation. For example, stainless steel and similar duct materials may provide lower life cycle costs when exposed to a rigorous cleaning regimen, but may not be justified in most applications.

15.1.1.4 Defining User Requirements

Range of internal conditions:

  • What are the critical parameters?
  • What are their Acceptance Criteria?
  • How much variation is acceptable?

A wider operating range may mean a lower cost system, both to install and operate. Specifying closer tolerances, may not provide a "better", (i.e., more robust) system. In order to maintain closer tolerances, a facility may be designed with greater capacity and faster responding sensors and actuators, which are more sensitive and require careful tuning and increased maintenance. Having specified closer tolerances, the larger and more complex system will need to be commissioned to operate to meet these specifications. The capital and operating costs of this more complex system are likely to be higher than a simpler smaller system, with no benefit to the product.

Design value for external conditions:

  • If a facility needs to be operable 365 days a year, it should be sized to handle extreme external design conditions. If it is acceptable to have a small percentage down time during peak seasons, the HVAC system and supporting utilities can be significantly downsized. Load shedding may be incorporated into the design of the support utilities, such as reduction of chilled water for office cooling, with only the process HVAC system components being sized to suit the extremes.
  • Area classification, air change rates, and DPs should not be over-specified, as this will result in higher life cycle cost with no extra value to the product. For further information, see the applicable ISPE Baseline Guide and Chapter 2 of this Guide.

15.1.1.5 Other Factors

Other factors can affect the system economics, for example:

  • Internal layout/design: this should keep the influence of major heat loads outside the conditioned area or use other systems to minimize the internal loads. For example, a dust extract unit also can remove heat from a motor in the room, reducing space heat gains. There may be benefits to grouping environmentally critical areas within a building, keeping them away from external walls to reduce external heat load variations.
  • The use of Computational Fluid Dynamics (computer airflow modeling) may be considered for optimizing air distribution design.
  • Sustainability (see Appendix 7)
  • Availability/uptime of HVAC systems: demanding high availability (little shut down or maintenance time) drives costs up.
  • Other Regulations: requirements of Building and Fire Codes, local zoning, worker protection (OSHA), environmental (EPA), and numerous other requirements must be met, in addition to GMP product/process requirements. These requirements may affect HVAC system design (transport of hazardous powders via HVAC systems to other rooms or outdoors, smoke ventilation, etc.).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Impact of Failure: the consequence of an HVAC failure in the pharmaceutical industry is not just "discomfort"; it can lead to the scrapping of an entire batch or the invalidation of long-term stability study data. Such losses can reach millions or even tens of millions of US dollars.

Redundancy: providing backup for critical systems. But redundancy is not a free lunch: dual AHUs also mean dual chillers and circulation pumps, which adds to the complexity of design, start-up and maintenance.

Over-specification: specifying overly narrow temperature and humidity tolerances does not make the product better. Instead it leads to a larger, more complex and more expensive system that is harder to maintain.

Analogy

"Over-specification" is like demanding that your home air conditioner hold a constant 22.0 ± 0.1°C. To reach that precision you would need industrial-grade sensors and controllers, and your electricity bill would soar, yet you could not feel any difference whether you wore short or long sleeves. In pharmaceutical manufacturing, if the product is acceptable anywhere in the 20-25°C range, why spend a lot of money to control the temperature at 22 ± 0.5°C?

Key Notes

Failure mode analysis is the basis of cost decisions: the four failure modes listed by ISPE (airflow, filters, temperature, humidity) all require risk assessment. In a CDMO, an AHU failure in an aseptic filling area can lead to the loss of an entire batch, and each batch of biologic may be worth more than USD 5 million. This is why aseptic areas are usually provided with redundant systems.

User Requirements should not be "the tighter the better": this is a common mindset trap for engineers. ISPE states clearly that a narrower tolerance does not mean a better system and may instead bring unnecessary extra cost.

Formula

Redundancy investment decision:

Annual expected loss from failure = P(failure) × Impact($)

If P(failure) = 2%/year, Impact = $5M/batch × 10 batches/year
Annual expected loss = 0.02 × $50M = $1M/year

Additional cost of redundant system = $500K capital + $50K/year maintenance
Payback Period = $500K / ($1M - $50K) = 0.53 year

Conclusion: payback in half a year, so the redundant system is clearly worth the investment!

Practical Application

In a CDMO environment, clients often specify very tight temperature and humidity ranges in the User Requirement Specification (URS). As the facility owner, you need to be able to explain to the client: "Our system capability range is X, your product specification allows range Y, and we recommend Z as the operating range." This kind of conversation requires both technical knowledge and commercial communication skills.

Practice Questions

  1. Which HVAC systems in your facility have redundancy? Do you think these redundancy investments are justified?
  2. If the HVAC system suddenly fails during batch filling, what is your SOP? From a financial perspective, how much protection does this SOP provide?
  3. Have you seen a case of "over-specification"? What was the total cost impact of that experience?
15.1.2 Life Cycle Cost Considerations

Original Text

Numerous factors influence the life cycle cost of a facility and should be considered in the design process to financially assess a project properly.

15.1.2.1 First Cost versus Life Cycle Cost

There is an optimal balance between first cost and operating cost that is unique for each organization and time period. Increased capital investment that yields reduced operating costs may not be the optimal solution, depending on cash flow issues. Additional factors that should be considered include:

  • the system design life
  • energy costs and trends
  • costs of consumables
  • ongoing reliability and maintenance costs

15.1.2.2 System Design Life

If the facility has a short life, it may be possible to save money on the equipment and not invest in plant of the quality that would be optimum for a facility with a long predicted operating life. Maintenance costs (as discussed below) extend over the entire facility life, becoming more cost-significant as the facility life increases.

15.1.2.3 Energy Costs and Trends

The type and cost trend of energy supply has a significant impact on HVAC system design choices. Where supply costs are high or expected to rise, systems can be configured to minimize demand and the "total cost of ownership."

Air Filtration

A low average filter pressure drop translates into reduced fan energy usage. Higher filtration efficiency also results in cleaner coils and equipment, optimizing heat transfer and reducing frequency of equipment cleaning. Lower velocities through the filter medium may translate into better capture efficiency. The optimum selection of pre-filtration systems will balance:

  • labor cost
  • filter cost
  • the contaminants to be captured
  • the capacity of the filter
  • energy costs and the cost of cleaning the AHU during changing of the filter: this may be a conventional panel/bag or a bag-in/bag-out filter combination.

Drive Belts

Up to 7% efficiency can be lost with traditional v-belt drives because of slippage by worn belts and improper tensioning. This can be reduced dramatically by using direct driven fans, where possible. Cogged or synchronous belt drives could improve the drive efficiency by 2% over v-belts. In addition to saving energy, synchronous belts and flat belts run cooler and tend to last longer than v-belts.

Makeup Air Pretreatment

Rather than cool the entire mixed air quantity to the desired dew point, it may be more economical (when outside air quantities are relatively high) to treat only the outdoor air (preheat or dehumidify for RH control) in a smaller AHU. This treated air, when later mixed with return air in the second AHU, may be of sufficiently low moisture content that further condensing cooling is not required, leading to savings in cooling and reheating energy. It also is possible to pre-treat outdoor air in a large AHU and send the pretreated makeup air to a number of AHUs serving separate areas. These pretreatment schemes are common in sterile facilities and in many OSD facilities with high levels of exhaust. In addition, when coupled with an exhaust air heat recovery system, better energy efficiency may be possible.

Economizer

An outside air economizer is a collection of air dampers and controls that allows more outside air and less return air to be drawn into the air handler. Some designs have incorporated a "blended" approach, attempting to create the ideal supply air temperature by mixing outdoor air and return air. Non-linearity of control dampers can lead to higher airflows than expected, requiring more fan control.

Some spaces (e.g., offices, laboratories, and warehouses) may have less rigid airflow requirements and will not be affected by variable airflow. An outside air economizer saves on cooling energy when outside ambient conditions (sensible and latent heat) are favorable (typically in the more temperate months of a year), rather than using warmer return air to reduce the load on the cooling section. When the outside ambient temperature conditions are lower than the inside space temperature, increased usage of the cooler and less humid outside air will reduce cooling energy that would come from mechanical cooling.

The supply, return, outside, and exhaust air quantities can change during the economizer cycle, leading to changes in facility room pressurization. If another AHU serves an adjacent area, it is possible for unwanted room pressure excursions to occur because of the changing air quantities resulting from varying positions of dampers in an HVAC system. The use of the economizer in areas that require pressurization control is not recommended. Additionally, the increased use of less clean outside air can shorten air filter life and consume more energy to overcome filter pressure. Outside air dampers should have a minimum stop position to assure adequate fresh air for personnel. The guidelines established in "ASHRAE 62.1, Ventilation for Acceptable Indoor Air Quality" should be followed to ensure a healthy indoor environment.

Energy Recovery: General

Wherever a significant amount of energy is lost as exhaust, the possibility of energy recovery should be explored. There are some limitations on energy recovery, such as excessive powders in the air stream, the use of scrubbers for pre-treatment, or the presence of significant quantities of condensable hazardous materials in the airstream. Many pharmaceutical facilities may benefit from some sort of recovery.

When evaluating energy recovery options, all costs (pumping, air pressure drops, etc.) on both sides of the equation should be considered. It is recommended that the efficiency of the system, with some level of performance degradation due to fouling, is included in the calculation.

In climates with high humidity during the summer months, energy recovery can be enhanced by employing evaporative cooling in the exhaust air stream; therefore, recovering a portion of the latent heat. Evaporative cooling may be achieved using an evaporative pad or by direct spray on the energy recovery coil.

Energy Recovery – Enthalpy Wheel

Similar in construction to a desiccant dehumidifier wheel, an "enthalpy" heat recovery wheel recovers total energy (sensible, as well as latent heat). Supply and exhaust ducting configuration should be adjacent at the heat recovery device. Purge section and labyrinth sealing system can limit cross contamination to 0.04% of the exhaust air concentration by volume. Specific contaminants in the exhaust stream may be retained in the wheel to be released into entering fresh air. Generally, such recovery units are used only rarely in pharmaceutical HVAC systems.

Energy Recovery – Air-to-Air Plate Exchangers

Air-to-air plate exchangers normally are used to recover only sensible heat from general and toilet exhausts, transferring it to the incoming outside air. Supply and exhaust ducting configuration needs to be adjacent. The reduced heating demand will reduce mechanical heating equipment sizing and operating costs. If recovery efficiency is too high, it could cause icing of the exhaust air in extremely cold weather, requiring a bypass around the unit. Additional fan energy is needed to overcome airside pressure drop.

Energy Recovery – Run Around Coil

Run around coils are normally used on 100% outside air units by transferring only sensible heat from an exhaust air stream to a makeup air stream, via coils and piping normally filled with a glycol solution to avoid freezing. They should be applied where exhaust and supply air handlers are separated by a suitable distance and usually perform best when heating requirements are more dominant than cooling requirements (greater temperature difference between the two air streams). The recovered heat can reduce demand from mechanical heating equipment, resulting in possible downsizing and reduced operating costs. Additional fan power is required because of increased airside static pressure drop through the coils. Refrigerant filled loops also may be employed; these are a hybrid of this system and a static refrigeration device. In these systems, the preload pressure is adjusted to allow the condensation of refrigerant at the temperature of the cooler airstream. These systems are not common and should be attempted only by experienced refrigeration engineers.

Energy Recovery – Refrigerant Coils

Similar in layout to air-to-air exchangers, requiring both air streams to be adjacent, a coil using passive refrigeration (no compressor) can transfer a high percentage of sensible heat from exhaust stream to outdoor (makeup) air. Precautions required are similar to those for air-air exchangers, but also close attention should be given to mounting details.

Component Selection

The cost of energy should be considered from both the system design concepts and the perspective of component selection, for example:

  • AHU housing: low cost (off the shelf) units may be made of pre-finished steel and have minimal insulation. The unit may suffer from high leakage of conditioned air, causing increased operating costs, and suffer from external sweating, leading to corrosion and a shorter working life. Custom units may cost appreciably more, but may incur lower energy losses and maintenance costs.
  • High-efficiency motors: these reduce energy usage. With proper installation, high-efficiency motors can run cooler than standard motors, and consequently, can have higher service factors, longer bearing life, longer insulation life, and less vibration. NEMA rated Premium Efficient motors have a slightly higher initial cost, but should pay for themselves because of reduced electrical consumption.
  • Building envelope: a low cost poorly insulated facility will mean a corresponding increase in the operating cost and capital cost of the HVAC system for a given set of internal conditions. Similarly, a review of the facility construction/insulation may be beneficial, e.g., improving the insulation may allow a warehouse facility to require only a heating system and no air conditioning.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

First Cost vs. Life Cycle Cost: the best balance point differs for every organization. A company with tight cash flow may prefer an option with low capital expenditure but higher operating cost, while a large, well-funded pharmaceutical company may prefer to invest fully up front in exchange for long-term savings.

Energy Recovery: recovering energy from the exhaust air and reusing it. ISPE describes four main technologies:

  • Enthalpy Wheel: recovers sensible and latent heat, but is rarely used in pharmaceutical facilities (cross-contamination risk)
  • Air-to-Air Plate Exchanger: recovers sensible heat only, and the supply and exhaust air streams must be adjacent
  • Run Around Coil: the supply and exhaust streams can be separated, with a glycol solution transferring the heat
  • Refrigerant Coil: a passive refrigerant loop with no compressor and high efficiency

Economizer: uses cooler outdoor air to reduce the mechanical cooling load. However, an economizer is not recommended for pharmaceutical cleanrooms that require pressure differential control, because changes in airflow affect room pressure differentials.

Analogy

Energy recovery is like a waste hot water heat exchanger: the waste water from your hot shower is still at 35°C, and if you use it to preheat the incoming cold water (15°C), your water heater no longer has to heat from 15°C to 42°C, only from 25°C to 42°C, saving about 60% of the energy.

An economizer, on the other hand, is like opening a window for ventilation: on a cool autumn day you do not run the air conditioner, and simply opening the window is cool enough. But in a space that needs "sterile operating theater" level control, you would not open a window casually, because it would affect pressure differentials and cleanliness.

Key Notes

V-belt efficiency loss of up to 7%: this is a very practical number. If the motor of an AHU fan is 30 kW, a 7% loss is 2.1 kW. Over 8,760 operating hours a year, that is 18,396 kWh, which at 4 per kWh comes to about 74,000 per year. Switching to a direct-drive fan or a synchronous belt saves most of this.

Makeup Air Pretreatment strategy: particularly important in a hot, humid climate such as Taiwan. Using a smaller AHU to treat the humidity of the outside air first, and then mixing it with return air, can greatly reduce the cooling and reheating energy of the main AHU. This is common practice in aseptic facilities and in OSD facilities with high exhaust volumes.

Enthalpy Wheels are rarely used in the pharmaceutical industry: although they can recover both sensible and latent heat, even a cross-contamination rate of only 0.04% may be unacceptable in a pharmaceutical environment, especially when handling highly potent drugs.

Formula

Belt drive energy saving calculation example:

V-belt efficiency = 93% (7% loss)
Synchronous belt efficiency = 98% (2% loss)
Direct-drive fan efficiency = ~100%

Annual energy consumption comparison for a 30 kW fan (24/7 operation):
  V-belt:    30kW / 0.93 = 32.26kW → 282,598 kWh/yr
  Synchronous belt:  30kW / 0.98 = 30.61kW → 268,150 kWh/yr
  Direct drive:      30kW / 1.00 = 30.00kW → 262,800 kWh/yr

Annual saving (V-belt → direct drive):
  19,798 kWh × $0.12/kWh = $2,376/yr
  10 AHUs = $23,760/yr saving

Practical Application

For CDMO facilities in Taiwan, because of the hot and humid conditions all year round, the following strategies give the highest return on investment:

  • Makeup Air Pretreatment: in Taiwan the summer outdoor air dew point often exceeds 25°C, and pretreatment can greatly reduce the dehumidification load of the main AHU
  • Run Around Coil: suitable for CDMO facilities with high exhaust volumes (such as powder filling and potent drug handling), because the supply and exhaust streams do not need to be adjacent
  • High-efficiency motors + direct-drive fans: initial investment increases by about 15-20%, but payback is usually within 2-3 years

Practice Questions

  1. Which Energy Recovery technology does your facility currently use? If none, which do you think is best suited to your facility conditions?
  2. Why is an Economizer not suitable for cleanrooms that require pressure differential control? If someone proposed this option at the design stage, how would you explain the risk?
  3. How would your HVAC equipment selection strategy differ between a clinical trial facility with an expected life of 5 years and a commercial manufacturing facility with a life of 20 years?
15.1.2.3-15.1.2.6 Setback, Consumables, Reliability & Other Factors

Original Text

Night Time or Off Hours (Unoccupied) Setback of HVAC

Typical pharmaceutical manufacturing spaces operate as at a constant airflow (CV and reheat system) to:

  • ensure adequate airflow to offset particle generation in-operation
  • maintain the space "cleanliness" or room classification

In the case of sterile filling areas, this also satisfies regulatory requirements for 20 AC/hr or 15 to 20 minute recovery time (in non-sterile filling these requirements do not apply, but are common in the industry). This approach results in high energy usage, particularly during periods when the space is not in use.

Designs may allow reduced airflow in manufacturing spaces during idle periods. This normally is achieved with airflow controls (dampers or boxes) with flow measurement and a trigger mechanism (push button, time of day function, timer, light switch, etc.) to change airflow to the space. Pressure relationships should be maintained during the setback period, regardless of flow. The time required take for the desired conditions to be achieved (typically 3 to 4 cycles of dilution) should be understood. Setback airflows should be designed to maintain critical conditions in the space as mandated by stored materials, equipment, closed product, etc. It is common to reduce flow to 6 AC/hr in a setback scheme.

Room temperatures and humidity levels may be set back (raised or lowered) periodically to save energy, but should be within the operating acceptance criteria for a room if:

  • closed product is present
  • corrosion is an issue
  • bioburden control is an issue

15.1.2.4 Consumables Costs

The life and cost of each consumable component should be considered. For example, air filters; the optimum selection of pre-filtration systems balances:

  • labor cost (for the replacement and the cleanup required)
  • filter cost
  • particle capture required
  • the capacity of the filter
  • rate of change of pressure drop
  • energy costs

The optimum may be a conventional panel/bag arrangement or may be a bag/bag filter combination to be more cost effective. More expensive, high capacity filters can last longer in service, and over time, require less replacement labor, while providing improved air filtration efficiency as they become dirty. The cost of ULPA filters or "scanned" HEPA filters, rather than ordinary HEPA filters, may be offset by less potential for "bleed-through" issues during routine testing, leading to fewer out-of-specification reports.

An additional example is a fan's drive belt; v-belts have a significantly shorter life than flat belts, but cost less. They are not as energy efficient as flat belts; therefore, the savings in maintaining a stock of spare belts, energy savings, and saving in labor costs to replace the belts and re-tension them, may make flat belts cheaper over the operating life of a facility.

15.1.2.5 Reliability/Maintenance Costs

The decision to invest in labor-saving features, such as performance monitoring and centralized lubrication systems, should consider the anticipated facility life and trends in the cost of labor.

The life cycle cost analysis also should consider reliability/maintenance aspects.

Examples

  • Consider the lowest cost material used for a cooling coil: aluminum fins on copper tube. In a poor environment (such as in drug substance facilities), there will be corrosion on the fin material, reducing the heat transfer efficiency of the unit with the fins eventually corroding to the extent that the unit will not perform adequately. Optional coil materials, e.g., copper tube with polyester coated aluminum fins or copper tube with electro tinned copper fins, will increase the first cost, but also will extend the operating life.
  • A fan specification with a long-life bearing design will allow for extended operating periods without maintenance. Grouped lubrication points will minimize costs and allow lubrication, while the facility is in operation.
  • The cost of routinely calibrating instrumentation should be considered; it may be cost effective to have one calibrated high DP switch across a bank of filters with un-calibrated "engineering information" manometers or pressure gauges across each filter. It also may be economical to install only pressure taps, using a portable calibrated gauge to take readings.

Robust HVAC equipment is more likely to perform reliably from the start and continue beyond its normal anticipated life when properly maintained. Good maintenance procedures performed in a timely manner will, over the life of the equipment, reduce total costs and have a positive effect on the uptime of the production process. For example, vivariums are extremely sensitive operations with long-term animal studies that require reliable and redundant systems to achieve steady environmental conditions. The loss of room conditions could mean the loss of years of data and delay of product introduction.

Reliability and maintenance items that should be considered include:

  • redundant fans (if 100% uptime is needed)
  • direct driven fans (no belt breakage/slippage, less adjustment needed)
  • vibration monitoring of blower and motor bearings (predicts failures, extends up time)
  • automated lubrication (reliability and labor cost savings)
  • bearing life of ABMA L10 200,000 hours (reliability)
  • lower rotation speeds of motors and fan wheels (extend life, lower noise, suggest 1800 RPM maximum)
  • high efficiency air filters (keep the HVAC system clean)

15.1.2.6 Other Factors

Factors to consider, which may vary the ratio of direct (capital) versus indirect (operating) cost include:

  • availability grants to assist with capital costs
  • incentives from utility providers to make a system more energy efficient
  • tax rates

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Night Setback: reducing the air change rate to save energy when there is no production. ISPE suggests reducing to 6 AC/hr (normal operation may need 20+ AC/hr), but the pressure differential relationships and critical conditions must be maintained. Returning to normal conditions usually takes 3-4 air dilution cycles.

ULPA vs. HEPA: ULPA filters (≥99.999% @0.12μm) are more expensive than ordinary HEPA (≥99.97% @0.3μm), but because their filtration efficiency is higher, "bleed-through" problems are less likely to appear during routine testing, which can reduce OOS (out-of-specification result) reports.

ABMA L10 200,000 hours: this is a bearing life specification. L10 means that at this number of operating hours, 90% of the bearings are still in good working order. 200,000 hours is equivalent to about 23 years of continuous operation, enough to cover the service life of most facilities.

Analogy

Night setback is like the air conditioning schedule of an office building: after work there is no need to hold a constant 22°C, and the temperature can drift up to 28°C. But if the building has a server room (analogous to a cleanroom storing product), the cooling cannot be shut off completely even after hours; only the airflow can be reduced while the temperature range is maintained.

Choosing ULPA vs. HEPA filters is like buying car insurance: comprehensive cover (ULPA) is more expensive, but the cost of handling an incident (bleed-through found in routine testing) is extremely low; basic cover (HEPA) is cheaper, but once a deviation report has to be handled, the investigation cost and downtime loss may far exceed the difference in premium.

Key Notes

Regulatory considerations for night setback: aseptic filling areas are required to have 20 AC/hr or a recovery time of 15-20 minutes. Although the air change rate can be reduced during setback, you must ensure there is sufficient recovery time before production starts. It is recommended to define the setback conditions and recovery procedure clearly in an SOP, supported by environmental monitoring data.

HVAC equipment reliability directly affects line utilization: ISPE gives the example of a vivarium: long-term animal studies need stable environmental conditions, and an HVAC failure can invalidate years of data and delay product launch. The same logic applies to stability testing rooms and microbiology research laboratories.

The economics of calibration strategy: not every pressure gauge needs to be calibrated. A calibrated high differential pressure switch (for GMP use) can be installed on a bank of filters, together with uncalibrated engineering gauges (for trending reference only). This is a pragmatic cost optimization strategy.

Formula

Night setback energy saving estimate:

Assume cleanroom area 500m², ceiling height 3m
Room volume = 1,500 m³

Normal mode: 20 AC/hr → 30,000 m³/hr supply airflow
Setback mode: 6 AC/hr → 9,000 m³/hr supply airflow
Airflow reduction ratio = 9,000/30,000 = 30%

Fan power is proportional to the cube of airflow:
Power ratio = (0.30)³ = 0.027 = 2.7%

Assume normal fan power 15kW:
Setback power = 15 × 0.027 = 0.41kW
Saving per night = (15 - 0.41)kW × 12hrs = 175 kWh
Annual saving = 175 × 365 = 63,875 kWh
Cost saving = 63,875 × $0.12/kWh ≈ $7,665/yr per room

Practical Application

In a CDMO, a setback strategy is especially valuable for multi-product shared facilities:

  • Non-filling days: cleanroom reduced to 6 AC/hr, maintaining pressure differentials while saving a large amount of fan energy
  • Changeover and cleaning days: a higher air change rate may need to be maintained to support particle recovery after cleaning
  • Weekends/holidays: all non-critical areas set back, maintaining only pressure differentials and basic temperature control
  • Integration with BMS (Building Management System): set schedules for automatic switching, together with environmental monitoring alarms

A typical CDMO facility that implements night setback in 10 cleanrooms can achieve annual savings of $70,000-$100,000.

Practice Questions

  1. Does your facility implement night setback? If so, what is the air change rate in setback mode? How do you ensure the recovery time meets regulatory requirements?
  2. Is your filter replacement strategy time-based (fixed schedule) or pressure-drop-based (condition-triggered)? Which approach is more economical?
  3. Calculate: if all the AHU fans in your facility were changed from V-belt to direct drive, what would the annual energy saving be?
15.2 Sustainable Design for HVAC Systems

Original Text

15.2.1 Introduction

For a facility that is aiming to be considered as 'green' or sustainable, HVAC systems are an important component. Many pharmaceutical HVAC SMEs may be asked to follow sustainable design and construction guidelines or standards. The requirements may come from a company standard, industry guideline, a design and construction regulation, or a regulation imposed on an already operating facility. Compliance with sustainability guidelines has been optional and considered progressive, and provided market differentiation for the building owner. Compliance with sustainability guidelines and standards may be required in some regions.

15.2.2 Basics – Personnel, Planet, Profit

Many products, technologies, and buildings have claimed to be "green" and many facility owners and personnel want to be considered in line with this concept:

  • The first goal is to make the facility and its impact good for society and the people that are affected.
  • The second is that the environment should not be disturbed in a way that would cause change, such as global warming or toxic pollution that would affect nearby inhabitants or the plant and animal environment.
  • The third goal is that this should all be done in a way that allows the economic system to thrive and return a profit to shareholders.

In an effort to meet these goals, a number of groups have formed to develop guidelines and standards.

There have been claims that green buildings also increase the productivity of personnel. This is beyond the scope of this Guide, but be may be a key driver of the movement toward sustainability.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Sustainable Design: taking environmental sustainability into account in HVAC system design while meeting GMP requirements. ISPE stresses that this has changed from a "bonus question" to a "compulsory question" in some regions.

Triple Bottom Line: Personnel, Planet, Profit:

  • People: the positive impact of the facility on society and employees
  • Planet: reducing environmental disturbance, lowering carbon emissions and toxic pollution
  • Profit: maintaining economic benefit and shareholder return while being sustainable

Analogy

Sustainable design is like a healthy diet: you would not give up tasty food (functionality and GMP compliance) or take on a price you cannot afford (economic benefit) just because you are pursuing health (sustainability). The best strategy is to find the balance among the three: nutritionally balanced (good for the environment), tasty (meets user needs), affordable (reasonable cost).

Key Notes

The sustainability challenge in the pharmaceutical industry: pharmaceutical HVAC systems are inherently energy-intensive, with high air change rates, strict temperature control and large volumes of outside air to treat. This makes pharmaceutical facilities harder than ordinary commercial buildings to bring up to green building standards. But for that very reason, the benefit of HVAC energy-saving improvements is especially significant in pharmaceutical facilities.

The impact of ESG trends on CDMOs: today in 2026, more and more large pharmaceutical clients require their CDMO partners to provide sustainability reports. A facility with LEED certification or a similar green building certification may have a market differentiation advantage in CDMO bidding.

Practice Questions

  1. Does your company have a sustainability strategy or targets? What role does the HVAC system play in it?
  2. Of the "Personnel, Planet, Profit" triple bottom line, which do you think is most easily overlooked in a pharmaceutical CDMO, and why?
15.2.3-15.2.4 Rating Systems & Building Energy-Labeling

Original Text

15.2.3 Rating Systems – Project Based

New buildings and large renovation projects can be graded through the use of third party ratings systems. These rating systems are prepared by green building groups. The largest umbrella organization is currently the World Green Building Council (WGBC), represented in the United States by the United States Green Building Council (USGBC). There are equivalent groups throughout the world. There are other organizations that also are developing standards for sustainable construction.

The USGBC produces the Leadership in Environmental and Energy Design (LEED) rating systems. In addition, in the US, the Green Building Initiative (GBI) is a group referenced by many local jurisdictions. The GBI manages the "Green Globes" rating system. There is a move to make either or both of these systems part of a sustainability building code, and some jurisdictions have adopted these guides as regulations.

Both groups are actively working on code language versions (USGBC with ASHRAE and GBI internally) and there is likely to be wider acceptance as time progresses. For pharmaceutical facilities, there may be exceptions for specific spaces, such as cleanrooms. These spaces are important as they consume a lot of energy per unit area.

Each rating system gives points or credits for going beyond the norm compared to similar facilities. There is no credit given for more profit. There are prerequisites that must be met by every building that strives to be considered a green building.

The USGBC has developed an internet-based tool to help teams submit information to achieve certification, using third party reviewers of each building certification application. This review will be run by a separate entity and provides an independent review of prerequisite and credit submissions. The prerequisites and credits needed to achieve the building rating cover a wide variety of green building issues. The overall green building submission and approval process is usually not managed by the HVAC SME. The HVAC SME's involvement is important, but the HVAC SME cannot deliver a building rating alone.

The USGBC also has established a professional credential, the LEED Accredited Professional (LEED AP) based on passing a test related to the sustainable building design and construction process.

15.2.4 Building Energy-Labeling

There are also building energy-labeling systems to address the efficiency of existing building stock. These energy-labeling programs also may be applied to new construction.

Global plans are being developed to label each existing building. Directive 2002/91/EC (EPBD, 2003) of the European Parliament and Council on energy efficiency of buildings is being implemented; ultimately, all buildings in the EU will have an energy rating that can be compared to other buildings. In the UK, each building will be required to post a placard with a letter rating of A to G at the main entry. In the US, the rating system is in development by ASHRAE. One optional label available to buildings is from the US EPA Energy Star Program. The Energy Star program identifies top performing buildings and provides guidance on how to design and operate an "Energy Star building." The Energy Star program also provides additional guidance on designing a green building.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

LEED (Leadership in Environmental and Energy Design): the world's best-known green building rating system, developed by the USGBC (U.S. Green Building Council). It has four levels: Certified, Silver, Gold and Platinum. The HVAC system is one of the key areas for earning LEED credits.

Green Globes: another rating system, administered by the GBI (Green Building Initiative), which has been adopted as regulation by some local governments in the United States.

EPBD (Energy Performance of Buildings Directive): the EU directive on building energy performance, which requires all buildings to have an energy performance rating (A-G), similar to the energy efficiency labels on household appliances.

Cleanroom exceptions: ISPE specifically points out that green building rating systems may contain exception clauses for cleanrooms, because the energy density of a cleanroom (energy consumption per square meter) is far higher than that of ordinary spaces, so applying the standard directly is not reasonable.

Analogy

LEED certification is like a Michelin star for a restaurant: you do not need a Michelin star to open a restaurant (you do not need LEED to build a factory), but having a star rating lets you stand out from the competition and attract more discerning customers (ESG-oriented large pharmaceutical companies). And just as Michelin has different star levels, LEED also has the grades Certified → Silver → Gold → Platinum.

Key Notes

The HVAC engineer cannot deliver the building rating alone: ISPE reminds us that green building certification is a cross-disciplinary team effort, involving the architect, structural engineers, MEP engineers, the owner and the contractor. HVAC is an important part of it, but not the whole.

The trend from "optional" to "mandatory": sustainable design standards are evolving from voluntary guidelines into regulatory requirements. In some jurisdictions, LEED or Green Globes have already been incorporated into building codes. This means that future new-build or major renovation pharmaceutical facility projects may have to comply with green building standards.

Practice Questions

  1. Does your region have green building regulations or incentive policies? How do they affect your facility design decisions?
  2. If your CDMO wants to pursue LEED Gold certification, the high energy consumption of the cleanrooms is the biggest challenge. What energy-saving strategies would you propose to earn credits?
15.2.5 New Project Design Process and Considerations

Original Text

15.2.5.1 Sustainable Design Process

For new projects, the sustainable design process starts with an event called the Design Charette. The project team members (including HVAC SMEs, architects, other designers, owner, and builder) participate in selecting the sustainable features of a facility. Team members are assigned specific prerequisites and credits to review and provide feedback to the team on cost, schedule, and impact to occupants. A goal is then established and the team prepares materials for submission.

The design team completes the design in an accepted manner. A submission can be made at the end of the design process using LEED to give the team feedback on how many credits can be achieved. After the design is released for the construction, the team constructs and commissions the facility in preparation for occupancy.

Once prerequisites and an adequate number of credits have been achieved, the building can be considered a green building with a specific level. The LEED program identifies certified, silver, gold, and platinum levels of building certification.

15.2.5.2 Energy Consumption

Rating systems for new projects have a major focus on Energy Consumption with much effort placed on selecting the right system and on selecting design criteria (either occupied space or outdoor conditions) that do not require excessive capital and energy to achieve the desired conditions. Building HVAC systems are normally designed to comply with the local energy sub-code that are usually developed by HVAC centered organizations (such as ASHRAE) and require a minimum level of energy performance. Energy performance can be proven through modeling or prescriptive methods. The level of energy consumption allowed by code is being progressively lowered as technology progresses. The building rating systems expect superior performance for a building to be classified as green. For further information, see Section 3.6.3 of this Guide.

15.2.5.3 Day Lighting – Impact on HVAC

One element of sustainable design is for a building to have natural lighting and views for personnel to see outside. This generally results in larger window areas and potentially the need to increase heating and cooling capacities. In pharmaceutical clean space design, this may require that a series of windows permit a view from a clean space through less clean adjoining spaces to the outside.

Commissioning

Commissioning for sustainable buildings is focused on HVAC, lighting controls, on-site renewable power generation, and domestic hot water systems. Pharmaceutical projects focus on patient safety and product quality and include HVAC systems, as well as critical utility and processing equipment. Pharmaceutical plants normally are commissioned using a process that covers HVAC systems in a GMP manner that complements the sustainable approach.

Sustainable commissioning practices include the development of an Owner's Project Requirements (OPR) document, a commissioning plan, and a summary commissioning report, similar in practice (if not in name) to pharmaceutical commissioning and qualification. The use of the user requirements document in manufacturing systems is similar to the owner project requirements document in sustainable commissioning practices.

Several useful documents, which may be used as a basis for creating commissioning protocols for a specific project or referenced in project protocols without re-writing are listed in the references.

The ASHRAE Guidelines may be used to define the commissioning process activities and scope; they do not describe how to perform hands-on activities.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Design Charrette: an intensive working meeting at the start of the project attended by all stakeholders (HVAC specialists, architects, the owner, the contractor and others) to determine the facility's sustainable design goals and strategies. This is a key decision point: the choices made here shape the direction of the whole project.

OPR (Owner's Project Requirements): the owner requirements document in sustainable design, equivalent to the URS (User Requirement Specification) in the pharmaceutical industry. ISPE notes that the two concepts are similar and can be used in an integrated way.

Day Lighting: sustainable design encourages bringing in natural light and views, but this increases window area and therefore the HVAC heating and cooling load. In pharmaceutical cleanrooms, special consideration is also needed on how to let personnel see outside from the clean area through adjacent spaces.

Analogy

A Design Charrette is like a family meeting before building a house: the whole family sits down to discuss how many rooms, which way the kitchen faces, whether to have solar panels, and what the budget is. If you wait until the house is half built to say "I want a green building", changes are expensive and slow. Sustainable design must be built in from the start and cannot be remedied afterwards.

Key Notes

Pharmaceutical Commissioning and Qualification (C&Q) naturally complements sustainable Commissioning (Cx): the IQ/OQ/PQ process in the pharmaceutical industry is more rigorous and comprehensive than commissioning for ordinary commercial buildings. ISPE notes that the pharmaceutical commissioning process already covers most of the requirements of sustainable commissioning, needing only minor additions.

Energy Modeling: modern building codes (such as ASHRAE 90.1) require that energy performance can be demonstrated either by modeling or by a prescriptive method. For facilities pursuing green building certification, modeling is almost essential, because it quantifies how much energy your design saves compared with the baseline.

LEED certification levels: Certified (40-49 points) → Silver (50-59 points) → Gold (60-79 points) → Platinum (80+ points). Because of the high energy consumption of cleanrooms, pharmaceutical facilities usually target Silver or Gold.

Practical Application

If your CDMO is planning a new building, here are practical recommendations for incorporating sustainable design into HVAC:

  • Hold a Design Charrette at the concept design stage: ensure the HVAC team takes part in setting sustainability goals from the start
  • Integrate the URS and OPR: avoid two parallel requirements documents, and use one integrated document to meet both GMP and sustainability requirements
  • Carry out energy modeling early: compare the energy consumption of different HVAC options to provide data support for cost decisions
  • Use the C&Q process: add sustainable commissioning checks into the existing IQ/OQ/PQ framework

Practice Questions

  1. Has your company held a workshop similar to a Design Charrette in a new-build or renovation project? Did the HVAC team take part in setting sustainability goals at the start of the project?
  2. What do the pharmaceutical URS and the sustainable design OPR have in common, and how do they differ? How can the two documents be integrated?
15.2.6-15.2.9 IAQ, Measurement, Renewable Energy & Materials

Original Text

15.2.6 Indoor Air Quality during Construction and Prior to Occupancy

It is considered a sustainable practice to monitor the interior of buildings to ensure that there is proper ventilation during construction to avoid the buildup of toxic materials in the building that could affect construction workers and occupants. There also is concern for mold growth if materials are moist and promote growth. An IAQ Management Plan for the construction phase can assist with:

  • keeping ductwork sealed
  • installing temporary filters to reduce dust in equipment and systems
  • isolating work areas
  • keeping the construction site clean

At the end of construction, buildings can be tested for contamination or flushed out to prepare for move-in of the building occupants.

15.2.7 Measurement and Verification of Utility Services

It is considered a sustainable practice to install metering equipment on utility services, including steam and chilled water on large sites. This data is considered useful in understanding peak demand and identifying options that can lower energy consumption.

15.2.8 On-site Renewable Energy Sources

Certain on-site energy sources can be considered part of the HVAC system, such as solar power water heating and geothermal energy. Local jurisdictions may provide financial incentives to use these systems. The project team should look for these opportunities during the design charette.

15.2.9 Materials

Some rating systems consider the use of materials made locally or from recycled materials a sustainable practice. However, this is limited to non-mechanical/electrical/plumbing materials in the LEED rating system. HVAC system materials often are considered recyclable and most metal products have some recycled content.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

IAQ Management Plan: an air quality management plan for the construction period, ensuring that toxic substances do not accumulate in the building or mold form during construction. This has a lot in common with cleanroom construction management in the pharmaceutical industry.

Measurement & Verification: installing metering equipment on utilities to continuously track energy consumption patterns. This is the basis for continuous improvement of energy efficiency: you cannot manage what you do not measure.

Geothermal Energy: using the constant underground temperature (usually 10-15°C) as a heat sink or heat source for HVAC. Some areas of Taiwan may have geothermal resources that can be used.

Analogy

IAQ management during construction is like protective measures when renovating a new home: if you do not cover the air conditioning ducts and do not ventilate to clear odors during renovation, then after moving in the formaldehyde level may exceed limits and the air conditioner may be full of dust. In the construction of a pharmaceutical facility this concept matters even more, because any residual contamination can affect future GMP production.

Key Notes

The natural advantage of pharmaceutical facility construction management: the pharmaceutical industry already applies strict cleanliness controls during construction (duct end capping, environmental monitoring, cleaning validation and so on), and most of these measures already satisfy the IAQ Management requirements of sustainable design.

Energy metering is the first step in energy saving: many older facilities lack zone-level energy metering. They know only the total electricity bill of the whole building, but not how much each AHU, chiller and boiler consumes. Installing smart meters and flow meters is how you find the "energy vampires" and target improvements.

LEED restrictions on MEP materials: the LEED recycled content credit applies only to non-MEP piping materials. The metal materials of the HVAC equipment itself usually already have some recycled content, but this cannot directly earn credits.

Practice Questions

  1. Has your facility installed zone-level energy metering equipment? If you could track the energy consumption of each AHU, what energy-saving opportunities do you expect to find?
  2. Under Taiwan's climate conditions, how much supplementary benefit do solar and geothermal energy offer an HVAC system? Roughly what is the payback period?
15.2.10-15.2.14 Refrigerants, Indoor Environment & Summary

Original Text

15.2.10 Refrigerants

Refrigerants are regulated to reduce the destruction to the ozone layer and their contribution to green house gases that are identified as contributors to global warming. The use of refrigerants with low Ozone Depletion Potential (ODP) and low Global Warming Potential (GWP) is considered a sustainable design practice. The phase out of ChloroFluorocarbons (CFCs) has been regulated as a result of the Montreal Protocol of 1987 and amendment in 1992 to eliminate HCFCs as well as the Kyoto Protocol of 1997 for reduction of gasses with high GWP where applicable.

15.2.11 Indoor Environmental Quality

The concept of off gassing of Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs) from materials installed inside buildings, including HVAC system components, should be understood. VOCs have been shown to cause cancer and other diseases in humans, and specific limits have been set to reduce exposure to building occupants. Materials used inside a building must meet specific requirements, including VOCs for field applied HVAC system adhesives and caulks (including fire caulks).

Monitoring of outdoor air and use of carbon dioxide sensors in occupied space are also common elements of design in sustainable projects. Many pharmaceutical facilities use large amounts of outside air and do not permit a high CO2 condition under normal operation, as typically there is more air introduced than needed by IAQ code.

Exhausting of potentially toxic materials is a requirement in some rating programs.

Rating systems may include credits for walk-off mats and enhanced filtration in AHU systems. Most particulates in non-pharmaceutical buildings come from personnel's shoes, and grates to catch the particles often are installed at building entrances. While the added filtration used in pharmaceutical facilities reduces airborne particulate, it also requires more energy to accomplish the particulate removal.

Smoking is allowed in a green building, within specific strict constraints, as meeting a human want or need; however, most pharmaceutical facilities do not allow smoking.

15.2.12 Increased Ventilation

The building can obtain a greener rating by increasing ventilation to provide more outdoor air to a space. While this may increase energy use, the concept of added "fresh air" is seen to have a positive impact on building occupants.

15.2.13 Controllability of Systems – Thermal Comfort

One way to improve occupant comfort is to give building occupants greater control of their environment. In pharmaceutical facilities, this would have to be within the parameters of the product being handled, but facilities may look at this feature when products are not affected by changes in temperature or humidity.

15.2.14 Summary

"Many aspects of the HVAC system design are important to the sustainability of a facility. HVAC engineers are critical to the successful creation of a 'green building,' they should be engaged and understand rating systems for each project in order for the design team to be effective."

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

ODP (Ozone Depletion Potential): an indicator of how much a refrigerant damages the ozone layer. The Montreal Protocol (1987) phased out CFCs, and its amendment (1992) further phased out HCFCs. Modern refrigerants such as R-134a (HFC) have an ODP = 0, but their GWP is still relatively high.

GWP (Global Warming Potential): an indicator of a refrigerant's contribution to global warming. The Kyoto Protocol (1997) required a reduction in the use of high-GWP gases. New-generation refrigerants (such as R-1234yf) have a very low GWP.

VOCs (Volatile Organic Compounds): harmful gases that may be released by building materials and HVAC components (adhesives, sealants and so on). In sustainable design, low-VOC materials must be selected to protect the health of building occupants.

Carbon Footprint: refrigerant management is an important component of an HVAC system's carbon footprint. The greenhouse effect of one kilogram of leaked R-410A is equivalent to 2,088 kilograms of CO₂.

Analogy

Refrigerant ODP and GWP are like the health labels on food: ODP is the "ingredient harmful to your body" (damaging the ozone layer = sunburn risk), and GWP is the "ingredient harmful to the environment" (greenhouse effect = global warming). An ideal refrigerant is like an ideal food: both indicators should be low.

Key Notes

Pharmaceutical facilities naturally meet IAQ requirements: ISPE notes that pharmaceutical facilities usually bring in far more outside air than IAQ regulations require, so CO₂ concentration is not a problem under normal operation. Likewise, the high-efficiency filtration systems (HEPA/ULPA) of pharmaceutical facilities far exceed the air filtration requirements of ordinary buildings. This means pharmaceutical facilities have a natural advantage in IAQ-related sustainability credits.

Future challenges in refrigerant management: the EU F-gas Regulation and the Kigali Amendment are progressively restricting the use of high-GWP refrigerants. When selecting chillers and DX systems, consider the long-term supply risk of the refrigerant and future regulatory changes. Low-GWP refrigerants (such as R-513A and R-1234ze) may increase equipment cost, but they reduce long-term compliance risk.

The role of the HVAC engineer in sustainable design: in its summary, ISPE stresses that HVAC engineers must participate in and understand green building rating systems. This is not "extra work" but one of the core competencies of the modern HVAC engineer.

Practical Application

Summary of practical recommendations on sustainable design for CDMOs:

  • Refrigerant selection: for new equipment, prefer low-GWP refrigerants (R-513A, R-1234ze) to avoid being forced to replace them in future
  • VOC control: the adhesives, sealants and fire-stopping caulks used in HVAC construction must all comply with VOC limits
  • Make use of the natural advantages of pharmaceutical facilities: high-efficiency filtration, large outside air volumes and strict construction controls are all plus points for sustainability credits
  • Personnel comfort in non-GMP areas: office and warehouse areas can offer individual temperature control options, which both increases employee satisfaction and earns sustainability credits

Practice Questions

  1. What refrigerant does your facility currently use? What are its ODP and GWP values? Do you need to plan a future refrigerant changeover?
  2. In which areas of sustainable design do pharmaceutical facilities have a natural advantage, and which areas face the greatest challenges?
  3. ISPE says "the HVAC engineer cannot deliver the building rating alone". In your organization, how is responsibility for sustainable design allocated?

Section Summary

  • Life Cycle Cost > Capital Cost: the operating cost of an HVAC system (energy, consumables, maintenance) usually far exceeds the initial capital expenditure. A cost model should be built early in the project, and design options evaluated with financial tools such as NPV or IRR.
  • Failure impact drives redundancy investment: an HVAC failure can lead to the loss of an entire batch or the invalidation of long-term study data. Redundancy investment decisions should be based on quantified risk assessment results (probability of failure × loss amount).
  • Do not over-specify: a narrower temperature and humidity tolerance does not mean a better system. Over-specification only adds cost and maintenance complexity, and brings no extra value to product quality.
  • Each energy recovery technology has its own applications: the Run Around Coil is best suited to pharmaceutical facilities (supply and exhaust can be separated, sensible heat only, no cross-contamination risk), while the Enthalpy Wheel is rarely used in pharmaceutical facilities because of cross-contamination concerns.
  • Night setback is a low-cost, high-return energy-saving measure: going from 20+ AC/hr down to 6 AC/hr can reduce fan power to 2.7% of normal. But pressure differential relationships and critical conditions must be maintained.
  • Sustainable design is moving from optional to compulsory: green building rating systems such as LEED are being incorporated into building codes. For a CDMO, holding LEED certification may become a market differentiator in future.
  • Pharmaceutical facilities have a natural advantage on many sustainability indicators: high-efficiency filtration, large outside air volumes and strict construction controls already meet many sustainable design requirements, and making good use of them can reduce the extra cost of obtaining green building certification.
  • The HVAC engineer is a key player in sustainable design: they must be involved from the Design Charrette stage, understand the rating systems, and integrate sustainability considerations into the GMP design process.
