Chapter 12: App 10–13: Misc, References & Glossary

p247-p288

ISPE Good Practice Guide: HVAC | p246 - p265

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the three-tier classification of medical devices (Class I/II/III) and how it drives differing HVAC system design requirements
  • Master the core cleanroom equations: ideal gas law, Bernoulli equation, pressure differential-velocity relationship, particle concentration equation, and recovery time formula
  • Understand the leakage calculation and engineering advantages of cascaded HEPA filters
  • Learn alternative approaches to pressure differential control where no airlock is available
  • Understand the engineering considerations behind HEPA filter arrangement strategies and pre-filter design
  • Master the relationship between recovery period and air change rate, and its design application
  • Learn the basic principles of control valve sizing, including Cv calculation and valve authority
  • Understand typical HVAC control system description examples and I/O point schedule design
  • Master the methodology and practical planning of temperature mapping
10

Appendix 10 – Medical Devices

HVAC Design Considerations for Medical Device Areas | p246-p247

16.1 Introduction

The regulations regarding medical devices provide opportunity for risk assessment to define different requirements for the associated HVAC systems.

There are three classifications of device according to the FDA:

  • Class I – those subject to the least regulatory control, as they present minimal potential for harm to the user, hence are subject to “general controls.” Class I devices include elastic bandages, examination gloves, and hand held surgical instruments. They are subject to 21 CFR Part 820.
  • Class II – Class II devices are devices subject to special controls, i.e., those for which general controls alone are insufficient to assure safety and effectiveness, and existing methods are available to provide such assurances. Examples of such products include powered wheelchairs, infusion pumps, and surgical drapes. Again, HVAC requirements are relatively simple.
  • Class III – this is the most stringent regulatory category. Class III devices are those for which insufficient information exists to assure safety and effectiveness solely through general or special controls. Class III devices are usually those that support or sustain human life, including heart valves, silicone gel filled breast implants, and implanted cerebella stimulators.

The FDA Medical Device Quality Systems Manual makes the following statements: “A controlled environment is, to various degrees, an integral part of most production facilities. Some environmental factors to be considered are lighting, ventilation, temperature, humidity, pressure, particulates, and static electricity. Section 820.70 (c), Environmental Control, of the QS regulation, is considered by the FDA as a ‘discretionary’ requirement: that is, the degree of environmental control to be maintained should be consistent with the intended use of the device and details of how to achieve this control are left to the manufacturer to decide.”

It also makes the statement that “General air conditioning is not normally regarded as an environmental control; however, changes in temperature and lighting can have an adverse effect on employee performance and, in turn, on assuring that the device is properly assembled, inspected, and tested.”

This Guide suggests that for each operation, the manufacturer should analyze the operations to identify the controls needed for the finished device to meet the specifications and be fit for use. Many Class I and Class II devices may require only comfort HVAC or at best, CNC. Although the manufacture of some Class III devices may start in an environment similar to a machine shop (with comfort HVAC at best), at some point, they become functionally implantable, requiring CNC or classified spaces, depending on sterility of the device.

The guidance provided in the FDA “Guidance for Industry for Sterile Drug Products Produced by Aseptic Processing – Current Good Manufacturing Practice” often is used as an environmental specification in the absence of any specific guidance for Medical Devices.

Teaching Analysis

FDA Three-Class Medical Device Classification and HVAC Needs

FDA classifies medical devices into three classes by risk level, and HVAC requirements increase with risk:

  • Class I: low-risk products such as elastic bandages and examination gloves → general comfort HVAC is sufficient
  • Class II: medium-risk products such as powered wheelchairs and infusion pumps → relatively simple HVAC requirements
  • Class III: high-risk products such as heart valves and implantable devices → may require CNC (Controlled Not Classified) or classified cleanroom space

Analogy: Device Classes Are Like Food Hygiene Levels

Imagine three different food preparation situations:

  • Class I is like packaging takeaway coffee: basic hygiene is enough
  • Class II is like a restaurant kitchen: proper ventilation and smoke extraction are needed
  • Class III is like sterile meals prepared to operating-room standards (for transplant patients): the strictest clean environment is required

The more a medical device goes "into the body", the higher the HVAC environmental requirements.

Key Regulatory Concept: "Discretionary Requirement"

The environmental control provision of FDA 21 CFR 820.70(c) is regarded as a "discretionary requirement", meaning the degree of environmental control is decided by the manufacturer but must be consistent with the intended use of the device.

This means there is no fixed "device HVAC standard" to apply. The manufacturer must perform a risk assessment and define reasonable HVAC requirements according to the product's use.

CDMO Practical Application

A common challenge in a CDMO that manufactures both drugs and medical devices is that the client (the device manufacturer) cannot provide clear HVAC specifications. A common approach is then to cite the FDA aseptic processing guidance as the environmental standard, which is conservative but safe.

For Class III implantable devices (such as artificial joints), the HVAC grade must be upgraded accordingly when assembly moves from the "machining" stage to the "implantable" stage. The design should plan clear grade transition zones and airlocks.

16.2 Clean Workstations for Medical Devices

As medical devices commonly do not include potent compounds (with the exception of combination devices) horizontal flow clean workstations may be employed to protect product without endangering operators. Horizontal flow workstations are preferred as they present the lowest risk of operator contamination of components which are being assembled for implantation.

Teaching Analysis

Horizontal Flow Clean Workstation

Medical devices generally do not contain highly potent compounds (except combination devices), so a horizontal laminar flow workstation can be used:

  • Airflow direction: HEPA-filtered clean air blows horizontally from the rear toward the operator
  • Advantage: provides product protection, and when assembling implantable components the risk of the operator contaminating the product is lowest
  • Limitation: not suitable for combination devices containing toxic or highly potent substances, because the airflow carries dust toward the operator

Comparison with Pharmaceutical Manufacturing

In drug manufacturing, when a product contains a highly potent active ingredient (HPAPI), vertical laminar flow (vertical UFH) or a biological safety cabinet (BSC) is usually used to protect both product and personnel. Because medical devices contain no pharmacologically active ingredient, they can use the more efficient horizontal laminar flow. This is an important difference between device and drug HVAC design.

Appendix 11 – Miscellaneous Information
11

17.1 Equations Used in HVAC and their Derivation

Common HVAC Equations and Derivations | p248-p253

17.1.1 Room DP (Differential Pressure)

Air, like any gas, expands as it is heated and contracts (becomes more dense) as it is cooled. For every 5°F (3°C) that air is heated, it expands (becomes less dense) by approximately 1%.

The ideal gas law states that the pressure (P) and the volume (V) of a gas are proportional to its temperature (T). If a gas (in HVAC, the gas is air) is heated, it wants to expand to a larger volume, but if it is constrained in a fixed volume container, its pressure will increase and the air becomes more dense.

PV = N Ru T

Where Ru is the universal gas constant and N the mass of the gas in moles. Since Ru is constant, and N is usually fixed for a particular situation, the equation reduces to:

PV is proportional to T

Bernoulli’s Equation for fluid dynamics also plays a role in HVAC.

P/ρ + V²/2 + gh = constant

Where g is the Earth’s gravitational constant, h is elevation, and ρ (rho) is the density of air. In HVAC, air density is affected by altitude above sea level, but for practical HVAC applications (assuming the manufacturing building is less than 10 stories high), air density and elevation are essentially constant. Thus, Bernoulli’s Equation applied to HVAC is:

P/ρ + V²/2 = constant

Where the subscripts 1 and 2 imply two different points along an airflow path:

(P2 – P1) is proportional to (V1)² – (V2)²

From this, it can be deduced that pressure is proportional to the square of the airflow velocity, i.e., to double the velocity of airflow between two points along a fixed path, the pressure difference between them must be quadrupled. In HVAC, V2 often is zero (it is the air inside a space at zero velocity). If zero velocity air is to be accelerated into an opening to move it to another location or under a door to pressurize a room, according to Bernoulli:

P2 – P1 is proportional to (V1)²

This can be used in calculating the velocity of air flowing through the cracks around a door at a given DP between two rooms. Further manipulation yields the simplified method:

VP ≈ P2 – P1

Where VP is the velocity pressure of the airflow within the door crack. This equation also can be used to calculate the velocity inside the crack (from ASHRAE):

V = 4005 × √VP

Where:

  • V is in feet/minute
  • VP is in inches water gauge (1 inch wg = 254 Pascals)

4005 is a constant derived for air at roughly standard temperature (68°F) and at sea level.

This method ignores “duct” entry loss and the pressure recovery that offsets it, such that the resultant calculated air velocity will be more than is required to create a pressure differential between two rooms. In this case, VP can be replaced with DP:

V = 4005 × √DP

For example, the VP of air flowing at 890 feet per minute is 0.05 inches wg or 12.5 Pa. The above equation implies that the air flowing through the cracks between two rooms at 0.05 inch DP has a velocity of 890 feet per minute.

Using the equation Q = V × A, where Q is cubic volume per time (CFM), V is velocity (ft/min), and A is area (sq ft):

An open 20 square foot door with air flowing through it at 890 ft/min (to maintain 0.05 inch DP) requires airflow of 17,800 CFM. This may be more than the capacity of the entire HVAC system and could provide a robust justification for airlocks.

A closed “pharmaceutical grade” door typically has a crack area of 0.3 square feet or less, needing less than 300 CFM to maintain 0.05 inch wg across the closed door. A specific leakage rate should not be assumed without knowing about the type of door to be used.

Teaching Analysis

Core Derivation: Relationship between Pressure Differential and Air Velocity

Ideal gas law: PV = NRuT
  (pressure × volume = number of moles × gas constant × temperature)

Bernoulli equation (HVAC simplified form):
  P/ρ + V²/2 = constant

Pressure differential-velocity relationship:
  ΔP ∝ V²  (pressure differential is proportional to the square of velocity)

Door-gap velocity formula (ASHRAE):
  V = 4005 × √DP
  V = velocity (ft/min)
  DP = pressure differential (inch wg)
  4005 = constant for standard conditions (68°F, sea level)

Airflow formula:
  Q = V × A
  Q = airflow (CFM)
  A = cross-sectional area (ft²)

Key Physical Concepts

  • Quadratic relationship between pressure differential and velocity: doubling the velocity requires four times the pressure differential. This is why maintaining a pressure differential across a large opening (such as an open door) is extremely difficult.
  • The 4005 constant: this constant applies to standard sea-level conditions. At high altitude (e.g., Denver, where air density is about 15% lower) the constant must be corrected.

Analogy: Pressure Differential across a Door Gap Is Like a Dam Spillway

Imagine a dam (the cleanroom). The height difference of the water (pressure differential) drives flow through the spillway (the door gap):

  • Door closed: the spillway is tiny (0.3 ft²), and only a small flow (300 CFM) is needed to hold the level difference
  • Door open: the spillway is huge (20 ft²), and an enormous flow (17,800 CFM) is needed to hold the same level difference, which usually exceeds the capacity of the whole system

This is exactly the physical reason cleanrooms need airlocks!

Practical Point: Door Type Matters Greatly

  • Tight sterile-room door (with gasket): leakage is only 50 CFM at a 10 Pa pressure differential
  • Warehouse sliding door (no seal): leakage can exceed 1,000 CFM
  • When designing the air balance, you must know which type of door will be used. Small details of door sealing have a major effect on the air balance

17.1.2 Fans

A useful equation for fan power is:

HP is proportional to η × P × Q

Where HP is horsepower, η is fan efficiency at the operating point, P is fan pressure, and Q is fan airflow in cubic volume per time (such as CFM).

From the pressure equations, if airflow in an existing duct system needs to be doubled, the fan’s delivery pressure will need to be quadrupled, as well as having its airflow doubled; therefore, needing eight times the horsepower. It is considered better to slightly oversize an HVAC system’s fan and ductwork and not need all the horsepower installed, rather than run out of horsepower when the system cannot supply sufficient air to meet required room particulate levels.

Teaching Analysis

Fan Power Formula and the Cube Law

HP = η × P × Q

Effect of doubling airflow:
  Q → 2Q      (airflow doubles)
  P → 4P      (pressure rises to 4 times, because ΔP ∝ V²)
  HP → 2 × 4 = 8 times the horsepower

Conclusion: doubling the airflow requires 8 times the horsepower!

Engineering Design Principle: Better Oversized Than Undersized

The guide recommends that fans and ductwork be moderately oversized: it is better to install unused horsepower than to have insufficient system airflow, because adding airflow afterwards is very costly: it means replacing fans, modifying ductwork, or even adding local FFU units.

This is a typical application of "design margin".

17.1.3 Room Air Balance

A basic air balance equation is:

Air Volume in = Air Volume out

Supply + Infiltration = Return + Exhaust + Exfiltration

For a fixed volume (i.e., not a balloon), any air that enters the room has to leave the room. In a cleanroom, exfiltration is difficult to measure (it is the air flowing under the door and out the cracks in the wall), but it can be calculated. An air balance check should be performed on each fixed volume, including air handlers.

Note that air handled only inside a room, such as with a ceiling mounted FFU or local class 100 hood, does not actually leave the room or enter it; therefore, it does not affect the room’s air balance relative to the building. However, the FFU unit does add its air changes as well as filtered air supply volume to the room HVAC supply, and it will contribute to faster room recovery time and help reduce room airborne particle levels.

Teaching Analysis

Air Mass Balance

For any fixed volume of space:

  • Supply: air delivered through the AHU and ductwork
  • Infiltration: air entering through gaps from a higher-pressure area
  • Return: air returned to the AHU through return grilles
  • Exhaust: air discharged from the building
  • Exfiltration: air leaving through door and wall gaps into a lower-pressure area

FFUs Do Not Affect the Room Air Balance

A ceiling FFU (Fan Filter Unit) only recirculates air within the room; it neither brings in nor discharges air, so it does not affect the air balance between the room and the building. However, an FFU does increase the effective air change rate in the room, which helps lower particle levels and speed up recovery.

17.1.4 Airborne Particle Levels

Another simplified equation deals with air particles per unit volume (C):

Cavg = Cs + PGR/Q

Where:

  • Cavg is average particles per cubic foot in the pressurized room
  • Cs is the particle concentration in the air supply (often negligible)
  • PGR is the steady state internal particle generation rate in particles per minute
  • Q is the supply airflow in cubic feet/minute, including contributions from in-room fan-HEPA units

With little air mixing (turbulence) in the room, localized values of C may be orders of magnitude more or less than Cavg. When a room is at rest and PGR approaches zero (assuming no particles leaking into the room), the equation above indicates that room counts will eventually approach the particle counts in the supply air.

Note that this equation ignores air changes and room volume. The value of Cavg will be the same regardless of room volume as long as the airflow (Q) and particle generation (PGR) are constant. Hence, the particle counts in a big room running a specific process will be the same as the particle counts in a small room running that identical process, as long as the Q and particle counts of the supply airflow are the same.

Teaching Analysis

Steady-State Particle Concentration Equation

Cavg = Cs + PGR / Q

Cavg = average room particle concentration (particles/ft³)
Cs   = particle concentration of supply air (usually negligible)
PGR  = particle generation rate (particles/min)
Q    = supply airflow (CFM)

Key insight:
  - Cavg depends only on Q and PGR
  - It is independent of room size!
  - A large room and a small room running the same process
    have the same particle concentration
    as long as Q and PGR are the same

Analogy: Particle Concentration Is Like the Cloudiness of an Aquarium

Imagine an aquarium: the fish keep stirring up sand (PGR = particle generation), and the filter keeps cleaning the water (Q = supply airflow):

  • The higher the filter flow (Q increases), the clearer the water
  • The more fish or the more active they are (PGR increases), the cloudier the water
  • Regardless of aquarium size, the cloudiness is the same as long as fish activity and filter flow are the same

Local Values Can Differ Greatly from the Average

If air mixing in the room is poor (insufficient turbulence), the local particle concentration can be higher or lower than the average by several orders of magnitude. This is why the placement of supply and return grilles is so important: only good air distribution ensures uniformity throughout the room.

17.1.5 Recovery

Room volume is an element of the measurement of air changes in a room. The formula for air changes is:

AC/hr = 60 × Q / Volume

Where AC/hr is room air changes per hour, Q is CFM supply in cubic feet per minute, and Volume is the volume of the room in cubic feet.

From the two equations above it appears that AC/hr is merely an indicator of air change rates in the room and not directly associated with air quality (it is CFM that most determines steady state air quality). However, air changes per hour play two critical roles:

  1. Air changes need to be sufficiently high to assure sufficient turbulence in a room to achieve thorough mixing and dilution, such that particle counts are relatively the same throughout the room (except under local unidirectional hoods). This may require more than 10 (and usually more than 20) air changes per hour.
  2. Air changes per hour affect how quickly a room can recover from its in-use state to its at-rest state. European GMPs require this recovery to be 15 to 20 minutes.

The ISPE Baseline® Guide on Sterile Manufacturing Facilities uses the formula:

C(at rest) = (Cop – Cs) × e(-Nt) + Cs

Where Cop is in-operation particle count, N is number of air changes, t is time, and Cs is supply air particle counts (usually close to zero).

From the room recovery graph, a 100-fold recovery (from say C = 10,000/volume to C = 100/volume, typical of an EU Grade B room) would occur in less than 15 minutes with 20 air changes per hour. So, for cleaner classified rooms (EU grades B and C), a minimum starting point would be an HVAC supply CFM that creates 20 AC/hr although more Q may be necessary if internal PGR is high.

In addition to air changes, the thoroughness of airborne particle counts throughout a room depends on the configuration of air supply and return openings. A single supply outlet near a single return inlet would lead to cleaner air in the path between the two with poor mixing in other parts of the room. Such a room would show a slower recovery than a room with multiple well-distributed air supply outlets and low level returns.

Teaching Analysis

Air Change Rate and Recovery Time Formulas

Air changes:
  AC/hr = 60 × Q / Volume

Recovery time (exponential decay model):
  C(at rest) = (Cop - Cs) × e^(-Nt) + Cs

  Cop = particle count during operation
  Cs  = supply air particle count (≈0)
  N   = air change rate (per hour)
  t   = time (hours)

Example: EU Grade B 100-fold recovery
  From 10,000 → 100 particles
  20 AC/hr → about 14 minutes
  30 AC/hr → about 9 minutes

Two Key Roles of the Air Change Rate

  1. Ensuring adequate mixing: at least 10 per hour (usually 20 or more is needed) to ensure uniform particle concentration throughout the room
  2. Determining recovery speed: EU GMP requires a recovery time within 15-20 minutes, which directly determines the minimum air change rate

Important distinction: steady-state particle concentration is determined by CFM (supply airflow), while recovery speed is determined by AC/hr (air change rate). The two are mathematically related but conceptually different.

Supply and Return Layout Affects Recovery Time

Even at the same air change rate, the layout of supply and return grilles significantly affects recovery speed. A single supply with a single return creates "short-circuiting": the path between them is very clean, but the rest of the room is poorly mixed, with elevated particle levels and slow recovery.

Best practice: multiple distributed supply grilles plus low-level returns.

17.1.6 Cascaded HEPA Filters

A HEPA filter passes a percentage of upstream particles of the MPPS (Most Penetrating Particle Size — traditionally, particles at 0.3 microns). The MPPS of a modern HEPA may be closer to 0.15 to 0.25 micron. For a given particle size, the overall leakage of a series of HEPA filters in a supply air path is the product of the leakages for each of the filters:

Ltot = L1 × L2

For a pair of standard 99.97% HEPA filters (assuming 0.03% leakage at MPPS):

Ltot = 0.03% × 0.03% = 0.0009% leakage at MPPS

Therefore, placing two 99.97% HEPA filters in series with no particle sources between them creates a virtual 99.9991% HEPA filter at the MPPS.

In addition to the advantages in particle removal, there is an engineering advantage if the primary HEPA is at the air handler and the second HEPA filter is at the room (a terminal HEPA). The terminal filter will receive very little challenge, and therefore, its pressure drop increases so slowly that its flow is not reduced significantly over months or maybe years of service. Air balance of the system is easier, requiring less in-duct hardware, such as CV devices, and room pressure deviations because of decay of supply airflow are less likely.

Note: (according to EN1822) HEPA filters may be rated at MPPS. A HEPA rated 99.97% at 0.3 micron has less leakage for larger particles; it also should have less leakage for smaller particles. As bacteria and spores usually are much larger than 0.3 micron, and viruses are smaller than 0.3 micron, a 99.97% filter with MPPS at 0.3 micron is considered a suitable filter for pharmaceutical applications. Although HEPA filters capture 99.97% or better of particles at 0.3 micron, their true MPPS may be somewhat smaller with a capture rate lower than 99.97%. A HEPA filter rated at 99.97% at 0.3 micron may actually be as low as 99.9% at 0.1 to 0.2 micron MPPS. If viruses are a concern, the HEPA may be scanned to 99.99% or better using a smaller aerosol; ULPA filters may be advisable.

Teaching Analysis

Cascaded HEPA Leakage Calculation

Total leakage of cascaded HEPA filters:
  Ltot = L1 × L2

Example (two 99.97% HEPA filters):
  L1 = 0.03%, L2 = 0.03%
  Ltot = 0.0003 × 0.0003 = 0.0000009
       = 0.00009%
  Equivalent efficiency = 99.99991%

MPPS (most penetrating particle size):
  Traditional definition: 0.3 μm
  Modern HEPA: 0.15 - 0.25 μm
  ULPA: 0.10 - 0.15 μm

Dual Advantages of Cascaded HEPA

  1. Particle removal capability: two 99.97% HEPA filters in series are equivalent to one virtual super-filter of 99.9991%
  2. Engineering stability：
    • The primary HEPA in the AHU takes most of the particle challenge
    • The terminal HEPA is almost unloaded, and its pressure drop rises very slowly
    • Airflow decay is minimal → the air balance is more stable, with months or even years free of maintenance
    • Reduces the need for constant volume (CV) devices, lowering system complexity

The Truth about HEPA Efficiency: MPPS Is Not 0.3 μm

The 99.97% efficiency is measured at 0.3 μm, but the true MPPS may lie between 0.1 and 0.2 μm, where the actual efficiency may be as low as 99.9%. If protection against viruses (typically smaller than 0.3 μm) is needed, consider:

  • Scanning with a smaller aerosol (such as thermally generated PAO) to 99.99% or higher
  • Switching to ULPA filters

17.1.7 Summary of Useful Cleanroom Equations

Teaching Analysis

Quick Reference: Nine Cleanroom Equations

These equations form the mathematical basis of cleanroom HVAC design. The three most commonly used day to day are:

  1. Q = V × A (airflow = velocity × area): used to calculate airflow through door openings and for ductwork design
  2. AC/hr = 60 × Q / Volume (air change rate): used for cleanroom grade design
  3. Cavg = Cs + PGR/Q (particle concentration): used to assess the impact of a process on the environment

Practice Questions

  1. A cleanroom measuring 3 m × 4 m × 3 m has a supply airflow of 2,000 CFM. Calculate the air change rate (AC/hr). (Hint: convert the volume to ft³ first.)
  2. The pressure differential between two cleanrooms is 0.05 inch wg and the door gap area is 0.2 ft². Use the simplified formula to calculate the leakage airflow (CFM).
  3. Why does the particle concentration equation say that room size does not affect the steady-state particle level? Intuitively this seems wrong; explain the physical reason.
17.2

17.2 Pressure Control When Airlocks are not Possible

Pressure Differential Control without Airlocks | p253-p254

Original Text

New facilities, particularly those with classified rooms, should have cascaded airlocks between air classes, but it may not be possible to retrofit airlocks into older facilities. The FDA Sterile Drug Products GMP suggests a measurable DP between rooms of different classes and air velocity through open doors sufficient to keep airborne contaminants out.

Sufficient air velocity often leads to airflow volumes that are too great to pass around the cracks of a closed door and may prevent the door from closing against the very high pressure the airflow would create. For separations without airlocks, an alternative design (see Figure 17.1) can permit high airflows through open doors, while keeping DP below 15 Pa when the door is closed.

Figure 17.1: DP without an Airlock (diagram referenced in original text)

Teaching Analysis

The Dilemma of Pressure Control without Airlocks

A dilemma often met when retrofitting older facilities:

  • FDA requires a measurable pressure differential between different cleanliness grades
  • When the door is open, sufficient air velocity is needed to prevent contamination from entering
  • But the large airflow produces an excessive pressure differential when the door is closed (over 15 Pa), so the door cannot close or the gasket is overloaded

CDMO Retrofit Practice

When retrofitting an older CDMO facility, being unable to add airlocks is a common challenge. Alternatives include:

  • Install a variable air volume system: automatically increase airflow when the door opens to maintain protective velocity, and reduce airflow when the door closes to hold the pressure differential below 15 Pa
  • Use door position sensors linked to BMS control logic
  • Ensure the alternative is risk assessed and approved by the quality unit
17.3

17.3 HEPA Filter Arrangements

HEPA Filter Arrangement Strategies | p254-p256

17.3.1 Air Filtration Arrangements

It is common practice for aseptic manufacturing facilities to recirculate air back to the air handler unit. Generally, this is good practice as it limits the particle load on the filters, reduces the cost of conditioning outdoor air, and optimizes control. However, there are other factors to account for:

  • potential for cross-contamination in multi-purpose facilities
  • accidental recirculation of product-contaminated air affecting operators or plant maintenance staff

These factors may be overcome by the use of return air filters. If the logic is that these are to capture airborne contamination; however, they need to be of the “safe change” type to protect maintenance personnel.

The environmental standards in the FDA Sterile Drug Products GMP identify a 0.5 μm particle size as the reference point. Only HEPA and ULPA filters have quantified performance ratings against a most penetrating particle size, usually sizes smaller than 0.5 μm. When looking at sub-micron particle reduction by filtration, only HEPA and ULPA filters should be considered as effective.

The location of HEPA filters within a system should be at points such that there is no opportunity for the air to become re-contaminated. The use of terminal supply (ceiling) HEPA filters is recommended for classification of Grade 7 and cleaner. They also have the additional advantage of maintaining the sealed envelope of the processing area should the supply fan fail.

Figure 17.2: A Possible Aseptic Area Filter Arrangement (diagram referenced in original text)

DOP and PAO (and Sodium Flame) penetration tests use a high concentration of particles of a known spectrum (usually in the range of 0.3 μm diameter). Efficiency results then can be related to specific size of airborne particle. Only filters tested by such methods have reliable data for this size of particle. Filters grades lower than HEPA are tested by averaging methods in which specific particle size efficiencies are not identified.

Note: European H14 air filters can pass a penetration scan test, but the purchaser must request that H13 filters do so.

Teaching Analysis

Core Considerations for Air Filtration Strategy

  • Return air reuse: a common and good practice that lowers the cost of treating outside air, but cross-contamination risk must be considered in multi-product facilities
  • Return air filters: if used to capture product dust, they must be "safe change" type (Safe Change / Bag-in Bag-out) to protect maintenance personnel from exposure
  • Terminal HEPA location principle: HEPA filters should be installed where the air cannot be contaminated again, so ceiling terminal HEPA is recommended for Grade 7 (ISO 7) and higher

Additional Safety Benefit of Terminal HEPA

A terminal ceiling HEPA maintains a "sealed enclosure" effect on the manufacturing area even when the supply fan fails: the filter itself is a physical barrier that stops unfiltered air in the ductwork from entering the cleanroom. HEPA filters installed only in the AHU cannot provide this protection.

H13 vs. H14 Filters (EN 1822)

  • H14: must pass a penetration scan test to ensure there is no local leakage across the whole filter face
  • H13: a scan test is not required by default, but it can be specified at purchase
  • Pharmaceutical plants usually require all HEPA filters to undergo an in-situ integrity test after installation, whether H13 or H14

17.3.2 Prefiltration for Terminal HEPAs

A single HEPA filter bank in normal circumstances is adequate to reduce supply particulate concentration below that of a reasonable “at rest” design classification. An important consequence of using a single HEPA bank is that the supply air 0.5 μm particle count is unlikely to be near zero. This could affect the calculations of air change volume flow rate to offset particulate gains, and in particular, recovery periods.

Another potential problem to be addressed if only terminal HEPA filters are used, is that of filter blinding that can result in reversed DPs putting environmental conditions at risk.

Figure 17.3: Example of the Effects of Terminal Filter Differential Blinding

Terminal filter blinding can result in design DPs being reversed. There are a number of possible solutions:

  • Install a main bank of HEPA filters.
  • Install a main bank of high efficiency non-HEPA filters (minimum MERV 13/F7 or better) in the AHU.
  • Employ active pressure or constant air volume control.
  • Frequently replace terminal HEPA filters.
  • Install airflow or pressure drop indicators to indicate filter performance.

The option to use high efficiency pre-filters in series with the HEPA has a number of advantages:

  • The effects of differential blinding will be minimized. The performance of the terminal filters will be maintained constant for years longer, balancing the ratio between supply and extracts, and in turn, DPs.
  • Because the bank of filters handles the main particulate load and acts as a prefilter in the AHU, only these will require regular replacement. This reduces replacement maintenance costs and downtime.

It is recommended that high efficiency non-HEPA pre-filtration be installed in all new or renovated facilities employing HEPA terminal filtration.

Teaching Analysis

Cascade Effect of Filter Blinding

As the terminal HEPA filters gradually become blinded:

  1. The airflow through that filter decreases
  2. Supply air to that room decreases → pressure drops
  3. Terminal HEPA filters in other rooms blind at different rates → the airflow ratios between rooms change
  4. The design pressure differential may be reversed: a lower-grade room may end up at higher pressure than a higher-grade room!

This is a serious GMP risk.

Pre-filter Design Recommendation (Strongly Recommended)

The guide explicitly recommends that all new or renovated facilities using terminal HEPA filters install high-efficiency pre-filters (at least MERV 13 / F7) in the AHU.

Benefits include:

  • Terminal HEPA life is extended by years, with minimal change in pressure drop
  • Differential blinding is minimized → room airflow ratios stay stable → pressure differentials stay stable
  • Only the pre-filters in the AHU need regular replacement → lower maintenance cost and downtime
  • Less reliance on constant volume (CV) or active pressure control devices

Analogy: Pre-filters Are Like a Pool's Coarse Strainer

A swimming pool filtration system usually has a coarse strainer (catching leaves) and a fine filter (removing small impurities). Without the coarse strainer, the fine filter would clog quickly. Pre-filters and terminal HEPA in HVAC have exactly this relationship: the pre-filter catches most particles so the HEPA only handles the finest ones, greatly extending its service life.

17.4

17.4 Recovery Period versus Air Change Rates

Relationship between Recovery Time and Air Change Rate | p256-p257

Original Text

If a minimum recovery period is required, this factor may be the deciding criterion for the air change rate. Figure 17.4 is a simplified model for calculating the relationship between air change rate and recovery period. This model is based on two major assumptions (good mixing efficiency with clean supply air).

Figure 17.4: Recovery Period versus Air Change Rates

(Note that the curves and equation are merely basic exponential decay expressions)

Figure 17.4 shows how by assuming a simple exponential decay, the “recovery period” changes greatly with air change rate: a 100-fold recovery, from ISO 7 to ISO 5, with 20 air changes per hour, takes approximately 14 minutes; with 30 air changes per hour, it takes approximately 9 minutes.

In general, it is considered more important to achieve target recovery than to achieve target air change rate.

Teaching Analysis

Recovery Time Takes Priority over Air Change Rate

This is a key design principle of the guide:

  • The air change rate (e.g., 20 AC/hr) is only a means
  • The real goal is the "recovery time" (e.g., recovery from the operational state to the at-rest state within 15 minutes)
  • If 15 AC/hr can achieve 100-fold recovery within 15 minutes, there is no need to deliberately pursue 20 AC/hr

Practical Meaning of 100-fold Recovery

When designing, a CDMO should work backward from the target recovery time to the minimum required air change rate, rather than directly applying a fixed air change requirement.

17.5

17.5 Additional Controls Information

Supplementary Control System Information: Actuators and Control Valves | p257-p260

17.5.1 Electrical/Electronic Actuators

The actuator uses a low voltage control signal to drive an electric motor; the units can be on/off or proportional. These systems are used where the speed of actuation can be slower, typical times for a valve to go from fully open to fully closed are in the range of 1 to 2 minutes.

Installation is simple, as all signals are by cable, e.g., control signal, power supply, and feedback, such as valve position or open/closed signals. The actuators can be supplied as fail open, fail closed, or with a manual override.

17.5.2 Pneumatic Actuators

An electronic control signal (from a stand-alone controller, BMS, or Process Controller) varies the output air pressure from a pneumatic controller, which is fed to a pneumatic actuator on the controlled component.

The system requires the use of an I/P (control signal to pneumatic) converter, an instrument quality air supply, and local tubing to the actuator. In order to get the best response time, the converter should be as close as possible to the actuator.

The units use air pressure in one direction with an opposing spring to return the controlled item to the fail position. The system is proportionally controlled. These units typically have a faster response time than an electric or electronic unit. The all-pneumatic system also is ideal for hazardous areas requiring intrinsically safe installations.

Teaching Analysis

Importance of Fail Position

"Fail position" is a key concept in HVAC safety design. When power or air supply is lost, the valve must automatically return to its safe position:

  • Cooling coil valve: usually set to Fail Closed to avoid overcooling
  • Heating coil valve: in cold climates may be set to Fail Open to prevent the coil from freezing and bursting
  • The fail position of every valve should be clearly defined and documented at the design stage

17.5.3 Control Valves for Liquids

There are two types of control valve: the three port valve (mixing or diverting) and the two port valve (directly controls flow). The three-port valve was the industry standard; however, the use of two port valves with variable flow rate systems is becoming more common.

17.5.3.1 Valve Characteristic

The valve characteristic is the ratio of flow through the valve to the valve lift (opening) at a constant DP across the valve. There are three main types:

  • Fast opening – typically used for only on/off control
  • Linear – flow rate directly proportional to the amount it is open; commonly used for diverting applications
  • Equal percentage – flow rate has a logarithmic relation to the amount it is open; more commonly used in water flow and steam control applications

17.5.3.2 Flow Coefficient (Cv)

A simple flow coefficient calculation for liquids:

In English Units: Cv = gpm × (SG/dp)1/2

Where gpm = water flow (US gallons per minute), SG = specific gravity (1 for water), dp = pressure drop (psi)

In SI Units: Cv = 11.7 × CMH × (SG/dp)1/2

Where CMH = water flow (Cu.Meter/hour), dp = pressure drop (KPa)

Select a valve where the required Cv is in the 30 to 80% range of the stroke. A valve that is too small or too large would not have the ability to control the flow accurately, i.e., will not have adequate “authority.”

17.5.3.3 Valve Authority

Valve Authority is the percentage of total system pressure drop assigned to the valve. If the valve’s pressure drop is small in comparison to the pipe and heat exchanger losses, the valve will have less ability to control effectively.

Teaching Analysis

Three Elements of Control Valve Sizing

  1. Valve characteristic: choose according to the application
    • Quick opening: used only for on/off control
    • Linear: flow is proportional to opening → suitable for diverting/mixing applications
    • Equal percentage: flow has a logarithmic relationship to opening → suitable for steam and water flow control
  2. Flow coefficient Cv: the required Cv when selecting a valve should fall within 30-80% of valve travel
  3. Valve authority: the ratio of the valve pressure drop to the total system pressure drop; if the ratio is too low, control capability is insufficient

Cv Calculation Formulas

Imperial: Cv = gpm × √(SG / dp)
  gpm = flow (US gallons/minute)
  SG  = specific gravity (water = 1)
  dp  = valve pressure drop (psi)

SI: Cv = 11.7 × CMH × √(SG / dp)
  CMH = flow (cubic meters/hour)
  dp  = valve pressure drop (KPa)

Sizing rules:
  The required Cv should fall at 30-80% of travel of the valve's rated Cv
  Valve too small (< half the line size) → coarse control
  Valve too large (≥ line size) → unstable control

Analogy: Valve Authority Is Like a Water Tap

Imagine the tap in your home (the control valve) and the pressure loss of the whole piping system. If the pipe itself has large friction loss (for example, a long, narrow pipe), turning the tap from fully open to half open changes the output little, because the tap's pressure drop is only a small part of the total pressure drop.

The "authority" of an HVAC control valve is the same concept. The valve pressure drop should be at least 30-50% of the total system pressure drop to control flow effectively.

17.6

17.6 Sample Controls Description

Example HVAC Control System Description | p260-p262

Original Text

The following is a sample description of the controls operation for one HVAC system. It should be used only as a guide.

1. Control Description

1.1 Plant Operation

  • On plant startup, the fresh air damper (MD 1) and the recirculation damper (MD 2) should be fully opened.
  • On normal plant shutdown, the supply fan should be stopped and all dampers fully closed.
  • In the event that the mixed air temperature (TX 1) falls below 5°C, an alarm should be raised and the plant stopped.
  • All control valves should be closed on plant shut down.

1.2 Temperature Control

  • The supply air temperature (TX 2) should be maintained by modulation in series of the cooling coil control valve (CVM 1) and the heating coil control valve (CVM 2).
  • The supply air temperature set point (TX 2) should be adjusted (min 12°C) to ensure that the reheat control valve output is minimized.

1.3 Humidity Control

  • The return air humidity (HX 1 and HX 2) should be maintained at the required set point (60% maximum) by providing override control of the cooling coil control valve (CVM-1) to achieve dehumidification.

1.4 Fan Speed Control

  • The supply fan speed (SCM 1) should be modulated to maintain a constant supply airflow rate to the dictates of the fan mounted flow airflow measuring device (AFD 1).
  • When required to operate, the supply fan (SF 1) run status should be confirmed to start and run at a variable speed as dictated by the fan speed control loop.

1.5 Monitoring/Alarm

  • A general alarm should be raised at the central supervisor for all conditions as shown on the HVAC point schedule.

1.6 Software Set Point Adjustments

  • system operation status (on/off)
  • minimum supply air temperature set point (10 to 25°C)
  • return air temperature set point (18 to 24°C)
  • return air humidity set point (60% maximum)
  • supply fan DP set point (0 to 100 Pa)
  • supply fan high speed alarm (50 to 100%)

3. I/O Point Schedule (Table 17.1)

Key: AI = Analog Input, AO = Analog Output, DI = Digital Input, DO = Digital Output, M = Monitor, C = Control, CA = Critical Alarm, GA = General Alarm

Teaching Analysis

Structure of an HVAC Control Description Document

A complete HVAC control system description usually contains five parts:

  1. Control description: system start/stop logic, temperature control, humidity control, airflow control, monitoring and alarms
  2. Design notes: special design considerations
  3. I/O point schedule: a list of all input/output signals
  4. System schematic: piping, equipment, and sensor locations
  5. Psychrometric chart

Key Control Logic Points

  • Low-temperature protection: when the mixed air temperature (TX 1) falls below 5°C, an alarm and shutdown are required; this is a safety interlock to prevent the heating coil from freezing and bursting
  • Sequence control: the cooling coil valve (CVM 1) and heating coil valve (CVM 2) are modulated in sequence: cooling first, then heating, to avoid wasting energy by heating and cooling at the same time
  • Dehumidification strategy: when humidity exceeds the limit, the cooling coil valve accepts "override control", giving priority to dehumidification over temperature control
  • Constant airflow control: fan speed is adjusted by feedback from the airflow measuring device (AFD 1) to keep supply airflow stable

Interpreting the I/O Point Schedule

The I/O point schedule is the basic document for programming the BMS (Building Management System):

  • AI (analog input): continuous signals such as temperature and humidity → require 4-20mA or 0-10V input cards
  • AO (analog output): continuous control such as valve position and fan speed → require analog output cards
  • DI (digital input): switch status, differential pressure switches → dry contact signals
  • DO (digital output): fan start/stop → relay outputs
  • CA (critical alarm) vs. GA (general alarm): determines alarm priority and response requirements

Practice Questions

  1. Why is the low-temperature protection for mixed air temperature set at 5°C rather than 0°C? Consider sensor accuracy and response delay.
  2. Explain why humidity control uses "override control" rather than an independent control loop. Under what climate conditions is this design especially important?
  3. If the HEPA filter differential pressure switch (PDI 3) alarms but airflow is normal, what are the possible causes?
17.7

17.7 Temperature Mapping

Temperature Mapping | p262-p265

Original Text

The purpose of temperature mapping helps confirm that the area as a whole remains within its defined limits and determine the locations representing temperature extremes within the area.

The second objective defines the locations for permanently installed sensors that provide data for the quality system of record for the area, the information from which the MKT (Mean Kinetic Temperature) is calculated (if required).

There are benefits to a smaller number of sensors for this purpose, while it is necessary to use a sufficient number of sensors to ensure that the mapping study is robust.

There is very little guidance on temperature mapping; the French Standard (NF X15-140 October 2002) provides some guidance on sensor locations for mapping of environmental chambers, as summarized below.

The method is based on the size of the chamber and the area potentially occupied by product. For chambers over 700 cubic feet (20 cubic meters), the standard suggests considering:

  • door openings
  • location of the cooling system
  • position of the control sensor

Figure 17.6: Temperature Mapping for Chambers up to 2 m³ and up to 20 m³

Note: The inner box represents the working area (where product is stored); the dots represent the sensor locations.

An approach that has been used with some success is to consider the area around each HVAC outlet as a zone and apply the sensor placement logic with a sensor adjacent to the temperature control sensor as well as others monitoring the supply and return temperatures.

For an area bounded by an external wall, the area requires mapping in the seasonal extremes in order to determine the influences of heating and cooling supply temperatures from the HVAC system, and the heating or cooling effect of the external walls and roof adjacent to the racking.

Mapping Considerations

  • Product temperatures – if upon delivery these are significantly different from defined storage conditions, the product may require monitoring.
  • Loading and unloading – will the product be at a different temperature, how much is loaded/unloaded at any one time, will there be significant ingress/egress of conditioned air?
  • Is there an outside door that can be left open or is it monitored to a defined maximum time?
  • Storage locations nearest the heating/cooling system inlet/outlet
  • Internal loads – lighting, equipment, and personnel
  • Conditions during minimum (empty) and full storage capacity

Example Plan

External Heat Gains and Losses: The major heat gains and losses to the cold room are due to the influences of the external environment with the most significant being through the walls and ceiling.

Internal Heat Gains and Losses:

  • Lighting – low energy fluorescent lamps, left on during the working day
  • Product – supplied at storage temperature, will not represent additional load
  • Equipment – stacking fork truck, a relatively small intermittent load
  • People – 2 people occasionally working in the area; heat gains are small and transient

HVAC: The room is conditioned through two registers with a common return air grille located at high level in the center of the room.

Mapping Sensor Placement: The areas considered during the mapping are only the areas where product will be stored. The proposed sensor locations are based on: considering the chamber as two zones with each zone supplied by a register; placing a temperature sensor at the lowest and highest storage point at each corner on the racking nearest the perimeter; and one sensor at the center at the midpoint level.

Load Testing: The unit will be mapped during peak summer and winter seasons, considering two load scenarios: empty chamber and one half of the warehouse kept empty with the other half filled with full boxes simulating the largest stored pallet (40″ × 48″ × 46″ tall).

Note that the HVAC has constant flow rate and with the room empty, airspeed will be low. When the room is not empty, the airflow will be at a higher speed, as the same volume of air must travel through a smaller area.

Teaching Analysis

The Dual Purpose of Temperature Mapping

  1. Confirm overall compliance of the area: verify that the whole storage area stays within the defined limits
  2. Determine permanent sensor locations: find the temperature extremes, which become the installation locations of the permanent monitoring sensors in the quality record system, used to calculate MKT (Mean Kinetic Temperature)

Sensor Layout Strategy (NF X15-140, French Standard)

  • Small chambers (≤ 2 m³): a minimum number of sensors placed at the corners of the working zone
  • Medium chambers (≤ 20 m³): more sensors, covering more locations
  • Large areas (> 20 m³): treat each HVAC supply outlet as a "zone" and apply the standard layout in each zone
  • A verification sensor must be placed near the control sensor to confirm the representativeness of the control point

Necessity of Seasonal Testing

An area with external walls must undergo temperature mapping once under summer and once under winter extreme conditions, because:

  • Summer: heat transfer through external walls makes areas near the walls warmer → HVAC cooling load increases
  • Winter: heat loss through external walls makes areas near the walls colder → local low temperatures may occur
  • Results may be quite different, and the locations of the hottest and coldest points may swap

Temperature Mapping Practice for a CDMO Warehouse

For temperature mapping of a pharmaceutical warehouse, the following practical points are especially important:

  • Load testing: airflow patterns in an empty versus a full warehouse are completely different; when full, racking blocks airflow, and velocity increases but distribution may be uneven
  • Effect of receiving and dispatch: during heavy receiving and dispatch, external doors open and bring in large amounts of unconditioned outside air → the maximum door-open time must be evaluated
  • Product temperature: in winter, product brought in from outdoors may be far below the storage condition → additional temperature recovery monitoring is needed

Analogy: Temperature Mapping Is Like a Refrigerator Check-up

A household refrigerator also has a "temperature distribution" problem: it is warmer near the door, colder at the back wall, and different on upper and lower shelves. Temperature mapping is like giving the refrigerator a thorough check-up: find the hottest and coldest points, make sure every storage location is within the safe range, and then place a thermometer at the extreme location for long-term monitoring.

Practice Questions

  1. Your CDMO needs to map a 15°C-25°C finished goods warehouse, and one side of the warehouse is an external wall. List at least 5 factors to consider in your temperature mapping plan.
  2. Why does the guide recommend testing in an empty and a half-full warehouse rather than an empty and a fully loaded one? (Hint: consider the airflow paths.)
  3. How does MKT differ from a simple arithmetic mean temperature? In what situations is calculating MKT more meaningful?

Section Summary

  • Medical device HVAC: the FDA three-class system (Class I/II/III) determines the level of HVAC requirements. Environmental control is a "discretionary requirement" that the manufacturer defines through risk assessment. Class III implantable devices may require classified cleanroom space, often referencing FDA aseptic processing GMP as the environmental standard
  • Nine cleanroom equations: from the ideal gas law to cascaded HEPA calculations, these equations form the mathematical basis of HVAC design. The most useful are Q=VA (airflow), AC/hr=60Q/V (air change rate), and Cavg=Cs+PGR/Q (particle concentration)
  • Quadratic relationship between pressure differential and velocity: doubling the velocity requires four times the pressure differential and eight times the horsepower. This explains why the pressure differential is hard to maintain with the door open (17,800 CFM needed) and is the physical basis for airlocks
  • Recovery time first: design should work backward from the target recovery time to the air change rate rather than apply a fixed value. 20 AC/hr achieves 100-fold recovery within 14 minutes (EU Grade B requirement)
  • Dual advantages of cascaded HEPA: two 99.97% HEPA filters in series can reach 99.9991% efficiency, and the primary AHU HEPA takes most of the load so the terminal HEPA pressure drop stays stable for years, simplifying the air balance
  • Pre-filters strongly recommended: all facilities using terminal HEPA should install high-efficiency pre-filters (MERV 13/F7) to prevent differential blinding from reversing pressure differentials
  • Control valve sizing: consider valve characteristic (quick opening/linear/equal percentage), Cv flow coefficient (30-80% travel range), and valve authority together
  • Temperature mapping: dual purpose (confirm area compliance + determine permanent sensor locations); areas with external walls need one mapping under summer and one under winter extremes, and load tests are done in an empty and a half-full warehouse
ISPE Good Practice Guide: HVAC | p269 - p288

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the full set of reference standards behind HVAC system design and qualification, including ICH, WHO, ISO, EU GMP, FDA and national engineering standards
  • Master the abbreviations and acronyms commonly used in the HVAC field, building a shared vocabulary for professional communication
  • Understand the formal definitions of key GMP terms such as Acceptance Criteria, Critical Parameter and Direct Impact System
  • Build the ability to cross-reference regulations and standards, so you can quickly locate the original source of a specific technical requirement

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: How the References Are Organized

The 31 references in this appendix fall into the following main categories:

  • Regulations and guidance (Regulatory): ICH (Q7-Q10), EU GMP Annex 1, PIC/S, US FDA 21 CFR. These are the legal basis for compliance
  • International standards (Standards): the ISO 14644 series (cleanroom classification), ISO 14698 (biocontamination control), ASTM E2500 (equipment verification)
  • Engineering practice (Engineering Practice): ASHRAE (heating, refrigerating and air-conditioning engineers), SMACNA (ductwork construction), NEBB (environmental balancing), IEST (cleanroom testing)
  • ISPE's own documents: Baseline Guides Vol. 1-6, GAMP calibration management
  • Regional standards: EN (European filter standards), CIBSE (UK building services), NFPA (US fire protection)

Analogy

Think of this reference list as the catalogue of an HVAC engineer's toolbox. Just as a carpenter needs different saws, chisels and sandpaper for different steps, an HVAC designer has to find the relevant technical requirements in different sources:

  • ICH/FDA/EU GMP = building codes (must be complied with)
  • ISO 14644 = weights and measures (how to measure and how to classify)
  • ASHRAE/SMACNA = construction manuals (how to do the work)
  • ISPE Baseline = the pharma-specific "best-practice cookbook"

Key Notes

ICH Q9 Quality Risk Management is a core concept cited repeatedly throughout this Guide. Decisions on HVAC design, qualification and maintenance should be risk-based rather than applying fixed rules unchanged.

The ISO 14644 series is the international "common language" of cleanroom design. Part 1 (classification) and Part 3 (test methods) are the two parts HVAC engineers consult most often.

ASTM E2500 provides a systematic "design, specification, verification" approach for pharmaceutical equipment, and is highly complementary to the ISPE Baseline Vol. 5 C&Q Guide.

Practical Significance of ASHRAE and SMACNA

ASHRAE (American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers) offers more than theory; it provides executable commissioning procedures and energy-efficiency standards. In particular:

  • Guideline 0-2005: a standardized approach to the commissioning process, consistent with the spirit of GMP commissioning
  • Standard 90.1: an energy-efficiency standard, increasingly important as "sustainable pharma" gains momentum

SMACNA provides hands-on technical specifications for ductwork construction, leak testing and similar work, and is particularly useful for maintenance teams and construction quality management.

Why the EN 1822 Filter Standard Matters

The EN 1822 series (Parts 1-5) is the European standard for classifying and testing HEPA/ULPA filters. In a GMP environment, HEPA filter integrity testing (leak testing) is a key qualification item for ensuring cleanroom air quality. The "Scan Method" in Part 4 is the most widely used leak detection method in industry.

Practical Application

Scenario: You are designing the HVAC system for a new aseptic filling facility. The client asks, "What standards is your design based on?"

Suggested answer structure:

  • Regulatory requirements: EU GMP Annex 1 (cleanroom grade definitions) + FDA Aseptic Guidance (aseptic process requirements)
  • Classification standards: ISO 14644-1 (particle classification) + ISO 14644-3 (test methods)
  • Engineering practice: ASHRAE Handbooks (system design) + SMACNA (ductwork construction) + IEST RP-CC006.3 (cleanroom testing)
  • Pharma-specific: ISPE Baseline Vol. 3 (Sterile Product Manufacturing Facilities) + this HVAC Guide

Practice Questions

  1. Why is ICH Q9 (Quality Risk Management) so important for HVAC system design? How does risk management influence HVAC zoning decisions?
  2. How do ISO 14644-1 and EU GMP Annex 1 differ in cleanroom classification? Why do you need to refer to both?
  3. If you need to perform an integrity test on a HEPA filter, which Part of EN 1822 should you refer to? Why is the Scan Method the preferred choice?
