19.1 Abbreviations

Original Text

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Categories of Organization Abbreviations

These abbreviations can be grouped by function to help you find them quickly:

  • Pharmaceutical regulatory bodies: FDA (US Food and Drug Administration), EMEA (European Medicines Agency), ICH (International Council for Harmonisation), PIC/S (Pharmaceutical Inspection Co-operation Scheme), WHO (World Health Organization)
  • Engineering standards organizations: ASHRAE (American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers), SMACNA (Sheet Metal and Air Conditioning Contractors' National Association), NEBB (National Environmental Balancing Bureau), IEST (Institute of Environmental Sciences and Technology)
  • International/national standards: ISO (International Organization for Standardization), ANSI (American National Standards Institute), ASTM (American Society for Testing and Materials), NEMA (National Electrical Manufacturers Association)
  • Safety and environment: OSHA (Occupational Safety and Health Administration), EPA (Environmental Protection Agency), NFPA (National Fire Protection Association), COSHH (Control of Substances Hazardous to Health, UK)
  • Pharma-specific: ISPE (International Society for Pharmaceutical Engineering), USGBC/WGBC (Green Building Councils)

Key Notes

In a pharmaceutical HVAC project, the organization abbreviations you will meet most often are:

  • ISPE – publisher of this Guide, the authoritative source for pharmaceutical engineering
  • ASHRAE – the technical foundation of all HVAC engineering design
  • ISO – the international standards for cleanroom classification
  • FDA/EU GMP – the two pillars of regulatory compliance

Remember: pharmaceutical HVAC sits at the intersection of "GMP regulations" and "engineering standards", and you need to know both sides well.

19.2 Acronyms

Original Text

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Categories of Technical Acronyms

These acronyms cover every aspect of HVAC design, GMP quality and engineering management. They are grouped by topic below, with a plain-language explanation of each:

Core HVAC systems:

  • AHU (air handling unit) – the core equipment of an HVAC system
  • HEPA (high-efficiency particulate air filter) – efficiency ≥99.97% at 0.3 µm particles
  • ULPA (ultra-low penetration air filter) – efficiency ≥99.999% at 0.12 µm particles
  • FFU (fan filter unit) – a self-contained unit integrating a fan and a HEPA filter
  • UDAF (unidirectional airflow) – the concept formerly called laminar flow
  • VAV (variable air volume) – an energy-saving airflow control method
  • CV/CVD (constant volume / constant volume damper)

Control and monitoring:

  • BMS (building management system) – the core platform for monitoring environmental conditions
  • BAS (building automation system) – a concept close to BMS
  • DCS (distributed control system)
  • DDC (direct digital control)
  • PLC (programmable logic controller)
  • SCADA (supervisory control and data acquisition)
  • EMS (environmental monitoring system)
  • PI/PID (proportional-integral / proportional-integral-derivative control) – the basic algorithms for temperature and humidity control

GMP quality-related:

  • GMP/CGMP (good manufacturing practice / current good manufacturing practice)
  • GEP (good engineering practice)
  • CQA (critical quality attribute)
  • CPP (critical process parameter)
  • QRM (quality risk management)
  • QA (quality assurance)
  • SOP (standard operating procedure)
  • CIP (clean in place)
  • RABS (restricted access barrier system)
  • VPHP (vaporized hydrogen peroxide) – the main decontamination method for isolators

Testing and verification:

  • FAT (factory acceptance test) – performed at the manufacturer's site before the equipment ships
  • SAT (site acceptance test) – performed after the equipment is installed on site
  • TAB (testing, adjusting and balancing) – the core activity of HVAC commissioning
  • DOP/PAO (dioctyl phthalate / polyalphaolefin) – aerosols used for HEPA filter leak testing
  • FMEA (failure mode and effects analysis) – a commonly used QRM tool
  • RCFA (root cause failure analysis)

Measurements and parameters:

  • DP (differential pressure) – the core parameter for cleanroom zone segregation
  • RH (relative humidity)
  • MKT (mean kinetic temperature) – used in drug stability assessment
  • CFU (colony-forming unit) – the basic unit of microbiological monitoring
  • MERV (minimum efficiency reporting value) – filter efficiency rating
  • MPPS (most penetrating particle size) – the particle size a filter captures least effectively
  • PGR (particle generation rate) – a key input to cleanroom air change rate calculations

Analogy

Imagine you are an engineer who has just joined a pharmaceutical HVAC team, and at your first meeting you hear: "The AHU's VAV needs PID control through the BMS, the DP readings feed back from the EMS, and the TAB report has to be finished before SAT."

It is like traveling to Japan for the first time and finding road signs you cannot read. This acronym list is your "translation dictionary": get familiar with the high-frequency terms first, and you will soon follow what your colleagues are saying.

Key Notes: Top 15 Most Frequent Acronyms

In day-to-day HVAC project communication, these are the acronyms you will meet most often:

  1. AHU – air handling unit
  2. HEPA – high-efficiency filter
  3. DP – differential pressure
  4. BMS – building management system
  5. TAB – testing, adjusting and balancing
  6. FAT/SAT – factory/site acceptance test
  7. GMP/CGMP – good manufacturing practice
  8. VAV – variable air volume
  9. RH – relative humidity
  10. SOP – standard operating procedure
  11. VFD – variable frequency drive
  12. FFU – fan filter unit
  13. EMS – environmental monitoring system
  14. UDAF – unidirectional airflow
  15. P&ID / AF&ID – piping and instrumentation diagram / airflow and instrumentation diagram
19.3 Definitions

Original Text

Acceptance Criteria

The limits of conditions of critical parameters that may affect the product quality. These conditions may include temperature, humidity, and room air quality. For example, if humidity or particulates are not critical parameters affecting product quality they are not included in acceptance criteria.

Action Limit

Criteria established based on possible impact to product quality, outside the operating range (acceptance criteria). A documented response is usually required.

Air Change Rate

The number of times the total air volume of a defined space is replaced in a given unit of time. This is computed by dividing the total volume of the subject space (in cubic volume) into the total volume of air exhausted from (or supplied to) the space per unit of time.

Airflow and Instrument Diagram (AF&ID)

Based on the AFD, it shows HVAC instrumentation and controls, with critical GMP components highlighted.

Air Flow Diagram (AFD)

Schematically shows rooms and zones served by an air handler, with air balance requirements, and often room pressures.

Alert Limit

Criteria established with the intent of notification and possible corrective action prior to exceeding action limits; alert when a parameter is drifting toward extremes of the operating range.

Arrestance

A measure of the ability of an air filter to remove synthetic dust from the air when tested as described in ASHRAE Standard 52.2-2008, Method of Testing General Ventilation Air Cleaning Devices for Removal Efficiency by Particle Size. Arrestance test results typically relate to larger size particles.

As-Built Drawings

Construction drawings that represent the physical condition of the plant or system at turnover from the designer or installer at satisfactory operation. These documents supplement and complement the system manuals and protocols.

Building Management System (BMS)

A computerized system that controls, monitors, and optimizes environmental conditions, through functions and facilities such as heating, air-conditioning, lighting, and security.

Change Control

A formal system by which qualified representatives of appropriate disciplines review proposed or actual changes which might affect validated status. The intent is to determine the need for action which would ensure that the system is maintained in a validated state.

Closed

Not exposed to the room, capable of holding some pressure or purge. PDA TR-28 provides a rigid definition of closed.

Closed Process

A process condition when the product, materials, critical components or container/closure surfaces are contained and separated from the immediate process environment within closed/sealed process equipment. A process step (or system) in which the product and product contact surfaces are not exposed to the immediate room environment.

Commissioning

Commissioning is a quality oriented process for verifying and documenting that the performance of facilities, systems and assemblies meets defined objectives and criteria.

Critical Component

A component within a system where the operation, contact, data, control, alarm, or failure may have a direct impact on product quality or the ability to know product quality.

Critical Location

The location where product is exposed; the location where a cleaned product contact surface is exposed.

Critical Parameter

A processing parameter (temperature, pressure, pH, etc.) which directly influences the drug substance characterization or impurity profile in or after a critical step.

Critical Process Parameter

A process parameter whose variability impacts a quality attribute and therefore needs to be controlled to ensure the process produces the desired quality. A critical process parameter remains critical even if it is controlled.

Critical Quality Attribute

A physical, chemical, biological or microbiological property or characteristic that needs to be controlled (directly or indirectly) to ensure product quality.

Design For Impact

The practice of making design decisions related to the impact of the system in operation, at the beginning of design development.

Design Point

Provided in the basis of design as the nominal set point around which the parameter is expected to be controlled, +/- a given tolerance value (the Design Tolerance) to provide the Design Target.

Design Qualification (DQ)

Documented verification that the proposed design of the facilities, equipment, or systems is suitable for the intended purpose.

Design Target

A value for a critical parameter that is more conservative than its acceptance criterion, used by designers to assure that the system is capable of meeting the acceptance criterion. Design Targets should not be used for system qualification; they are "wishful" values that may not be achieved in reality.

Design Tolerance

The expected (design) upper and lower points of the normal operating range.

Direct Impact System

A system that is expected to have a direct impact on product quality. These systems are designed and commissioned in line with Good Engineering Practice and also are subject to Qualification Practices that incorporate the enhanced review, control and testing against specifications or other requirements necessary for GMP compliance.

DOP (Dioctyl Phthalate)

Material used in the past to generate aerosols comprising particles in the 0.1 to 0.7 micron range (typically with an average size of 0.3 micron) used to test HEPA and ULPA filters. This chemical is believed to have carcinogenic properties and has been generally replaced by a mineral oil, e.g. Emery 3004/Durasyn 164, or Shell Ondina EL.

The smoke generated from this has very similar characteristics and the term DOP testing remains, although it is now understood to mean 'Dispersed Oil Particulate.'

Dust Spot Efficiency

The measure of a the ability of a filter to remove synthetic dust when tested as described in ASHRAE Standard 52.2-2008, Method of Testing General Ventilation Air Cleaning Devices for Removal Efficiency by Particle Size.

Enhanced Design Review (EDR)

A documented review of the engineering design, at an appropriate stage in a project, for conformance to operational and regulatory expectations.

Exfiltration

Leakage of air out of a room through cracks in doors and pass-throughs through material transfer openings, etc. due to a difference in room pressures.

Exhaust Air

Air removed mechanically from the space and discarded.

Functional Design Specification

Description of acceptance criteria, in terms of ranges and logic of system operation, etc. In HVAC, a description of HOW the HVAC will meet the acceptance criteria (room air class, DP, airflow, recovery time, level of air filtration, etc.).

Good Engineering Practice (GEP)

Established engineering methods and standards that are applied throughout the project life cycle to deliver appropriate, cost-effective solutions.

Grade

Applied to air cleanliness, "grade" implies airborne particle count limits in operation, with associated bioburden limits. The number of the grade is the upper limit in operation as defined by ISO 14644-1 (i.e., Grade 5 has 0.5 micron upper particle limit of 3500/cubic meters). In the European GMP, Grades A through D also involve particle limits at rest.

High Efficiency Particulate Air (HEPA) Filter

High efficiency particulate air filter, a filter with DOP efficiency in excess of 99.97% on 0.3 μm particles.

Indirect Impact System

A system that is not expected to have a direct impact on product quality, but typically will support a Direct Impact system. These systems are designed and commissioned following Good Engineering Practice only.

Infiltration

The entry of air from an adjoining room or from outdoors through wall and ceiling openings due to a difference in air pressure between the two areas.

Laminar Flow – see Unidirectional Flow

Latent Heat

Latent heat refers to the amount of energy released or absorbed by a chemical substance during a change of state, meaning a phase transition such as the melting of ice (latent heat of fusion) or the boiling of water (latent heat of vaporization). In an HVAC application typically used to condense water from humid air.

"Nearly Massless" Particles

Particles smaller than 0.5 μm, which typically constitute less than 1% of the total mass of particles typically found in outside air, but represents a large percentage of the total number of particles in a typical sample of air. (Due to the exponential increase in the mass of a particle caused by an increase in the diameter, very small particles typically represent a small fraction of the total mass of particles in an airstream.)

Normal Operating Range

The actual observed values of the critical parameter during operations, collected over time. This range may be larger than the design tolerance, but should be well within Action Limits.

Operating Range

The validated acceptance criteria within which a control parameter must remain, wherein acceptable product is being manufactured.

PAO (Polyalphaolefin)

A synthetic oil used in lieu of DOP for HEPA filter testing.

Particle Count

Airborne particle count of both viable (living) organisms and non-viable (inert) particles. [Measured in PCF (particles per cubic foot) (multiply by ~35.3 to obtain particles per cubic meter)].

Particles Generation Rate (PGR)

Particles generated within a space by a process and occupants per unit time.

Plenum

An enclosed space used for HVAC airflow, typically at low velocity. A plenum may be constructed of duct materials (e.g., sheet metal) or may utilize interstitial spaces in building construction such as below floors, above ceilings, or in vertical chase-ways. A plenum accomplishes air distribution via static pressure difference between the plenum and surroundings, rather than using velocity and associated diversion/distribution devices, as in ductwork.

Process Validation

Establishing documented evidence that provides a high degree of assurance that a specific process will consistently produce a product meeting its predetermined specifications and quality attributes.

Psychrometry

Determination of the properties of gas-vapor mixtures. The air-water vapor system is the most commonly encountered.

Requirement Specifications

A detailed document used to specify the requirements of the client for individual aspects of the facility, item of equipment, utility, and systems in terms of function, throughput, operability, and applicable local standards.

Return Air

Air removed mechanically from the space and returned to the air handling system serving that space for recirculation.

Supply Air

Conditioned air supplied mechanically to the space (room), measured here in cubic feet per minute (CFM) (Divide by 0.6 to get cubic meters per hour CMH).

Ultra Low Penetration Air (ULPA) Filters

Extended media dry filters in a rigid frame that have a minimum particle-collection efficiency of 99.999% for particles greater than or equal to 0.12 μm in size.

Unidirectional Airflow

Controlled airflow through the entire cross-section of a clean zone with a steady velocity and approximately parallel streamlines.

Ventilation Rate

The number of times in an hour that the air volume of a room is replaced; see Air Change Rate.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Key Definitions Explained

The definitions are explained in full below:

  • Acceptance Criteria: the limits on critical parameters that may affect product quality. Note: only "critical" parameters need to be included in acceptance criteria.
  • Action Limit: a criterion beyond the operating range that requires a documented response.
  • Air Change Rate: the number of times the total air volume of a space is replaced per unit of time.
  • AF&ID (Airflow and Instrumentation Diagram): a drawing showing HVAC instrumentation and controls, with GMP-critical components identified.
  • AFD (Airflow Diagram): a schematic showing the rooms served by an air handling unit, the airflow balance and the differential pressures.
  • Alert Limit: an early-warning criterion issued before the action limit is reached.
  • Arrestance: a measure of a filter's ability to remove synthetic dust.
  • As-Built Drawings: drawings that reflect the actual condition after construction is complete.
  • BMS (Building Management System): a computer system that controls, monitors and optimizes environmental conditions.
  • Change Control: a formal system for reviewing changes that may affect the qualified state.
  • Closed: not exposed to the room environment, and able to withstand a certain pressure or flushing.
  • Closed Process: a process state in which the product and its contact surfaces are isolated from the room environment.
  • Commissioning: a quality-focused process of verifying and documenting that facility systems perform to the stated objectives.

Key Quality Terms

  • Critical Component: a component whose operation, contact, data, control, alarm or failure may directly affect product quality.
  • Critical Location: a location where the product is exposed, or where a cleaned product-contact surface is exposed.
  • Critical Parameter: a process parameter that directly affects the characteristics or impurities of the drug product.
  • Critical Process Parameter / CPP: a parameter whose variability affects a quality attribute; it remains "critical" even when it is under control.
  • Critical Quality Attribute / CQA: a physical, chemical, biological or microbiological property that must be controlled to ensure product quality.

These five "Critical" definitions are the basis of HVAC system impact assessment. Whether an HVAC system is a Direct Impact System depends on whether it controls any Critical Parameter or CQA.

Key Notes: Direct vs. Indirect Impact System

Direct Impact System: a system expected to have a direct impact on product quality. In addition to following GEP, it must be qualified, including enhanced review, control and testing.

Indirect Impact System: a system that does not have a direct impact on product quality but typically supports a Direct Impact System. It only needs to follow GEP.

This classification determines the depth of qualification and the documentation required for each component of the HVAC system. For example, an AHU serving an aseptic filling area is Direct Impact, while an AHU serving an office area is Indirect Impact.

Design-Related Terms

  • Design For Impact: considering the impact of system operation at the very start of design development.
  • Design Point: the nominal set point in the basis of design, plus or minus the tolerance.
  • Design Qualification / DQ: documented verification that the proposed design is suitable for the intended purpose.
  • Design Target: a value more conservative than the acceptance criteria, used by designers to ensure the system has sufficient capability. Note: design targets should not be used for qualification!
  • Design Tolerance: the expected upper and lower limits of normal operation.

Analogy: Action Limit vs. Alert Limit

Imagine you are driving on a highway:

  • Operating Range = 90-110 km/h (the normal driving range)
  • Alert Limit = 115 km/h (the dashboard starts flashing to warn you)
  • Action Limit = 120 km/h (go over this and you get a ticket, so it needs to be documented)
  • Design Point = 100 km/h (the best cruising speed the designer intended)

In HVAC, the Alert Limit is an "early warning" that gives you a chance to correct a drift before a real problem occurs.

HVAC-Specific Terms

  • Exfiltration: air "leaking out" of a room through door gaps and the like because of a pressure difference.
  • Infiltration: outside air "leaking into" a room because of a pressure difference. In a cleanroom, uncontrolled air infiltration must be prevented.
  • Exhaust Air: air that is mechanically removed and not reused.
  • Return Air: air that is mechanically removed but returned to the air-conditioning system for recirculation.
  • Supply Air: conditioned air mechanically delivered into a room. CFM ÷ 0.6 = CMH.
  • Plenum: an enclosed space that distributes air by static pressure difference (not air velocity); it can be under the floor, above the ceiling or in a vertical duct.
  • Latent Heat: the energy released or absorbed when a substance changes phase. In HVAC it is used to condense moisture out of humid air.
  • Psychrometry: the study of the properties of gas-vapor mixtures. The psychrometric chart is a basic tool of HVAC design.

Key Notes: DOP Has Been Replaced by PAO

DOP (dioctyl phthalate) was formerly the standard aerosol material for HEPA filter integrity testing, but because it was considered carcinogenic it has been replaced by PAO (polyalphaolefin). Industry still habitually calls it the "DOP test", now understood as an abbreviation for "Dispersed Oil Particulate".

This is a good example of why understanding the history of a term matters: if you hear someone on site say "doing a DOP test", the material actually used is almost certainly PAO.

Filter and Particle Terms

  • HEPA Filter (high-efficiency particulate air filter): efficiency >99.97% at 0.3 µm particles. This is the basic equipment of sterile areas.
  • ULPA Filter (ultra-low penetration air filter): efficiency ≥99.999% at ≥0.12 µm particles. Used in special applications requiring higher cleanliness.
  • Dust Spot Efficiency: evaluates a filter's ability to remove synthetic dust.
  • Arrestance: similar to Dust Spot Efficiency, but generally used for larger particles.
  • MPPS (most penetrating particle size): the particle size that a filter captures least effectively, typically about 0.1-0.3 µm.
  • "Nearly Massless" Particles: particles <0.5 µm, which make up <1% of the total mass of outdoor air but most of the total particle count.
  • Particle Count: includes viable and non-viable particles. PCF × 35.3 = particles per cubic meter.
  • PGR (particle generation rate): the quantity of particles generated per unit time by the process and personnel in a space; a key input for calculating the required air change rate.

Key Notes: The Dual Standard for Grade

The definition of Grade points to a key difference: ISO 14644-1 defines particle limits only for the "in operation" state, whereas EU GMP Grades A-D require particle limits in both the "at rest" and "in operation" states.

This means that when designing HVAC under the EU regulatory framework, you must make sure the system meets the limits in both states, which has a direct impact on system design.

Qualification and Documentation Terms

  • Enhanced Design Review / EDR: a documented review of the engineering design at an appropriate stage of the project, to confirm it meets operational and regulatory expectations.
  • Functional Design Specification / FDS: a document describing how the HVAC system achieves the acceptance criteria (room classification, differential pressure, airflow, recovery time, filtration level and so on).
  • GEP (Good Engineering Practice): established engineering methods and standards applied throughout the project life cycle to deliver appropriate, cost-effective solutions.
  • Process Validation: establishing documented evidence that a specific process consistently produces a product meeting its predetermined specifications.
  • Requirement Specifications: documents detailing the customer's requirements for facilities, equipment and utility systems.
  • Change Control: a formal system for reviewing changes that may affect the qualified state. Any modification to an HVAC system must go through this procedure.

Analogy: Closed Process

Imagine a sealed astronaut helmet (Closed Process) vs. an open hard hat (Open Process). The air inside the astronaut helmet is completely isolated from the outside, so no matter how harsh the environment outside, the inside is unaffected. A pharmaceutical Closed Process follows the same idea: the product and product-contact surfaces are fully enclosed by sealed equipment and do not touch the room environment.

This directly affects HVAC design: if the process is Closed, the room cleanliness requirement can be lower; if it is Open, the room must meet a higher cleanliness grade.

Formula Reference: Air Change Rate Calculation

Air Change Rate (ACR) = Supply Air Volume (CFM) x 60
                        ─────────────────────────────
                           Room Volume (cubic feet)

Air change rate = Supply air volume (CFM) x 60 / Room volume (cubic feet)

Unit conversion:
  CFM / 0.6 = CMH (cubic meters per hour)
  PCF x 35.3 = particles per cubic meter

Practical Application

Scenario: At an HVAC system impact assessment meeting, the Quality unit asks you: "Why is the supply air system Direct Impact while the exhaust air system is Indirect Impact?"

Suggested answer: Under this Guide's definition, a Direct Impact System is one that is "expected to have a direct impact on product quality". The Supply Air System delivers HEPA-filtered clean air directly to the manufacturing area and controls the Critical Parameters (temperature, humidity, particle level and so on). The Exhaust Air System removes air without recirculating it; it supports the supply air system in maintaining positive differential pressure but does not directly contact or affect product quality, so it is classed as Indirect Impact.

Practice Questions

  1. Explain the hierarchy among Design Target, Design Tolerance, Acceptance Criteria and Action Limit. Using temperature control as an example, what might the values at each level be in an HVAC system?
  2. Why does the CPP definition specifically stress "remains critical even when under control"? What does this imply for change control of HVAC systems?
  3. How do Exfiltration and Infiltration affect differential pressure management in a cleanroom? If infiltration occurs in a Grade B room, what could the consequences be?
  4. Compare the efficiency specifications of HEPA and ULPA filters. In what situations would you need ULPA rather than HEPA?
  5. How do Closed Process and Open Process differ in their HVAC design requirements? Give a common example from a CDMO.

Section Summary

  • Reference framework: HVAC system design involves 31 standards spanning regulations (ICH/FDA/EU GMP), international standards (ISO 14644), engineering practice (ASHRAE/SMACNA) and pharma-specific guidance (ISPE Baseline), so project teams need cross-disciplinary knowledge of standards
  • Organizations and abbreviations: 40+ organization abbreviations and 100+ technical acronyms form the "common language" of professional HVAC communication. The most frequent include AHU, HEPA, DP, BMS, TAB and FAT/SAT
  • The Critical term family: Critical Component, Critical Location, Critical Parameter, CPP and CQA are the basis of system impact assessment and determine which HVAC components must be qualified
  • Direct vs. Indirect Impact: this classification is the core of the HVAC qualification strategy. Direct Impact systems need GEP + Qualification, while Indirect Impact systems need only GEP
  • Hierarchy of design parameters: Design Target < Design Tolerance < Operating Range < Alert Limit < Action Limit < Acceptance Criteria. This hierarchy applies to all critical HVAC parameters
  • DOP is now the PAO test: because of concerns that DOP is carcinogenic, PAO (polyalphaolefin) is now used as the aerosol material for HEPA filter integrity testing, but the name "DOP test" is still in use
  • The dual requirement for Grade: EU GMP Grades A-D require particle limits at rest and in operation, which is stricter than ISO 14644-1 and has a direct impact on HVAC system design
